choices: Documenting the mechanism of injury in detail before taking any steps to protect the crew from traffic
Determining the patient's chief complaint before addressing any scene hazards or traffic concerns
Establishing traffic control and scene lighting/visibility to prevent secondary collisions
Beginning spinal motion restriction procedures immediately, ahead of any scene safety or traffic considerations
questions.explanation: Struck-by incidents on highways are one of the leading causes of line-of-duty death for EMS providers, so before any patient contact the crew must reduce the risk of a secondary collision by positioning apparatus to block/protect the work area, deploying cones or flares as appropriate, and wearing high-visibility reflective gear, especially at night when driver reaction time and visibility are reduced. This is a scene-safety and hazard-control priority that logically precedes chief-complaint interview, spinal precautions, or documentation, all of which are meaningless if a responder is struck while performing them. Establishing a protected work zone converts an uncontrolled, high-risk environment into one where hands-on patient care can safely begin.

questions.question: During size-up of a multi-vehicle collision, you identify four patients with varying severity of injury but only one ambulance on scene. According to scene size-up principles, what should happen next?
choices: Immediately begin treating the most severely injured patient found first
Request additional resources and consider initiating a mass/multiple-casualty incident triage process
Wait for one patient to be fully assessed before determining if more resources are needed
Transport all four patients in the single available ambulance simultaneously
questions.explanation: Determining the number of patients and matching that number against available resources is a core element of scene size-up, and when patients outnumber immediately available personnel and transport units, the correct response is to request additional resources early (more ambulances, ALS, mutual aid) and shift into a multiple-casualty incident mindset using a rapid triage system such as START, which sorts patients by survivability and treatment priority rather than order of discovery. Fixating on the first or most severely injured patient found risks pouring limited resources into someone who may not be salvageable while a more viable patient deteriorates unassessed nearby. Waiting until one full assessment is complete before calling for help unnecessarily delays the resource request, which should happen as soon as the patient-to-resource mismatch is recognized during size-up.

questions.question: You are called to a home for a 'sick person' and find the patient's spouse acting evasive and providing inconsistent explanations for visible bruising in various stages of healing. What should this prompt regarding scene size-up and ongoing awareness?
choices: Nothing; injuries in various stages of healing are a normal incidental finding unrelated to the spouse's evasive, inconsistent explanations
Immediate confrontation of the spouse about the inconsistencies in his story, demanding an explanation for the bruising
Refusing to treat the patient and withholding care until police arrive on scene to investigate
Heightened situational awareness for possible domestic violence, including safety for yourself and considering the reporting and handoff process
questions.explanation: Scene safety is not a one-time check performed only on arrival — it is a continuous process throughout the call, and findings like bruising in multiple healing stages combined with an evasive, inconsistent history are recognized red flags for ongoing abuse. This should raise the EMT's situational awareness both for personal safety (a potentially volatile abuser is present) and for the patient's welfare, prompting careful, non-judgmental documentation of objective findings and appropriate reporting/handoff to receiving staff or law enforcement per local protocol and mandatory-reporting requirements. Directly confronting the spouse is inappropriate and can escalate danger or compromise any subsequent investigation, and ignoring the finding or refusing care are both failures of the EMT's duty to the patient — care should still be provided while safety awareness is heightened.

questions.question: While sizing up a scene involving a downed power line near a car crash, the patient is calling out for help from inside the vehicle. What is the correct action?
choices: Approach and extricate the patient immediately since they are calling for help, treating the urgency of the cries as outweighing the electrical hazard
Touch the vehicle first with a bare hand to check whether it is energized before deciding on your next course of action
Treat the vehicle and surrounding ground as energized, keep a safe distance, and request the utility company/fire department before approaching
Move the power line off the vehicle yourself using a wooden tool if one is available, assuming wood is a safe insulator
questions.explanation: Electricity can travel through metal, wet ground, and even seemingly non-conductive materials in unpredictable ways, so any vehicle or terrain near a downed power line must be treated as energized until the utility company physically confirms the line has been de-energized — this is a fundamental hazard-recognition principle in scene size-up. A responder who approaches, touches the vehicle to 'test' it, or tries to move the line — even with a wooden tool, since wood can conduct electricity if wet or not rated for the voltage involved — risks becoming electrocuted and turning one patient into two or more. The correct action is to maintain a wide safe perimeter, keep the patient calm by voice if possible, and request the utility company and appropriately equipped fire/rescue personnel, even though this means the trapped patient's cries for help must be endured until the scene is truly safe.

questions.question: During transfer of care at the emergency department, you give a verbal report but the receiving nurse is called away mid-sentence before hearing your medication administration details. What is the most appropriate action?
choices: Leave the department without giving a complete verbal report since you are busy and need to return to service
Assume the medication information was heard before the nurse left and move directly on to completing your written report
Skip repeating that part of the report since the medication details will eventually appear in your written documentation
Complete the verbal handoff with a member of the care team, and document the time, care given and medications
questions.explanation: Transfer of care is not complete until a member of the receiving team has actually received the critical information, especially details as safety-critical as medications administered, doses, times, and patient response, since a gap here can lead to duplicate dosing or missed contraindications. Because the written PCR is frequently completed after the patient has already been moved to a room and treatment has begun, the verbal report cannot be skipped or assumed to have been heard — the EMT must find another available member of the care team (another nurse, tech, or physician) to finish relaying the essential information face-to-face. Leaving without completing a proper handoff, or silently deferring everything to paperwork that may not be reviewed for some time, breaks the continuity of care that the verbal report is specifically designed to protect.

questions.question: While writing your patient care report, you realize you omitted a set of vital signs taken 20 minutes into transport. The report has already been submitted. What is the correct way to add this information?
choices: Complete a dated addendum or late entry marked as a correction
Destroy the original submitted report and create a brand new one from scratch with the vitals included
Leave the omission alone and take no further action, since the report has already been submitted and finalized
Alter the original entry directly to insert the omitted vitals as if they had been recorded at that exact time
questions.explanation: The PCR is a legal medical-legal document, and its integrity depends on the record accurately reflecting when information was actually recorded, not just when the events occurred; inserting the missed vitals into the original entry as though they were documented in real time would misrepresent the timeline and could be construed as falsification of a medical record, with serious legal and professional consequences. The correct method is to add a clearly labeled late entry or addendum that carries the current date and time it is being written, explicitly states that it is a correction/addition, and references the original report, preserving an honest and traceable record. Simply leaving the gap unaddressed risks the appearance of incomplete care, and destroying and rewriting the original report is never appropriate since it erases the original record entirely.

questions.question: A patient refuses transport after a syncopal episode. Which documentation approach best protects the patient and the EMT from a legal and clinical standpoint?
choices: No additional documentation is required once the patient has signed a printed refusal form, since the signature alone satisfies the legal standard for informed refusal
Detailed documentation of the patient's mental status/capacity to refuse, risks explained, alternative care advised, and the patient's or a witness's signature
Documentation limited only to the vital signs obtained on scene, without any narrative detail describing capacity assessed or risks actually discussed
A brief note stating only 'patient refused transport' with no assessment of mental status, decision-making capacity, or risks discussed with the patient
questions.explanation: For a refusal of care to be legally valid, the patient must have decision-making capacity — oriented, not impaired by intoxication, hypoxia, head injury, or altered mental status from the underlying event (which matters greatly after syncope, a condition with potentially serious cardiac or neurologic causes) — and must give informed refusal, meaning the risks of refusing, the benefits of transport, and reasonable alternatives (calling back, follow-up with a physician) were clearly explained. Thorough documentation of the capacity assessment, the specific risks discussed, and a witness or patient signature creates a defensible record showing the EMT met the standard of care and the patient made an informed, autonomous choice. A brief note, vitals alone, or a signed form without narrative detail fails to demonstrate that capacity was assessed and informed consent to refuse was actually obtained, leaving both the patient and EMT exposed if a bad outcome follows.

questions.question: You are documenting a call in which the patient stated, 'I took about 20 of my blood pressure pills on purpose.' How should this be recorded in the PCR?
choices: As a direct quote, with objective findings and no added interpretation
As the EMT's own conclusion that the patient attempted suicide, without quoting the patient
Paraphrased in a way that removes the patient's own words
It should be omitted since it may not be true
questions.explanation: Statements bearing directly on mechanism, intent, or self-harm are among the most important pieces of information in a PCR, both clinically (guiding treatment for potential overdose and receiving-facility decisions) and legally (supporting mandatory holds or psychiatric evaluation), so they should be recorded verbatim as a direct quote attributed to the patient rather than paraphrased or summarized. The EMT documents the patient's own words plus objective findings (vital signs, physical exam, medication bottles found) but should avoid inserting an unsupported diagnostic label like 'suicide attempt' as though it were the EMT's own clinical conclusion, since that exceeds scope and could be seen as speculation rather than fact. Omitting the statement entirely because it 'may not be true' is dangerous and inappropriate — the statement itself is a fact that was made, regardless of whether it is later verified.

questions.question: During a busy multi-patient call, you provide care to a patient but another crew member completes transport of that patient in a different ambulance. What is the correct documentation practice?
choices: Only the transporting crew needs to document anything, since they are the ones who delivered the patient to the hospital
The first crew member on scene should document for all providers involved, since that report serves as the single official record for the incident
Each crew member who assessed or treated the patient should make sure that care is documented
No documentation is required for any provider's care, since multi-patient incidents are considered exempt from standard PCR requirements
questions.explanation: The legal and clinical standard is that every assessment finding and every intervention performed must be captured in the patient's record, regardless of how many providers or units were involved before a patient reached the transporting ambulance; when care is split across crews, those crews must communicate and clearly establish who documents what, either through supplemental reports or close collaboration on one accurate, comprehensive PCR. Assuming only the transporting crew needs to document risks losing the initial assessment findings and any early interventions (like oxygen or bleeding control) performed by the first crew, which could affect ongoing hospital treatment decisions and creates gaps that look like undocumented, unaccountable care in a legal review. Multiple-casualty incidents do not exempt providers from the documentation standard — they simply require more deliberate coordination to meet it.

questions.question: Which of the following PCR entries best reflects objective, appropriate documentation, avoiding the introduction of bias?
choices: 'Patient reports 9/10 abdominal pain; appeared uncomfortable, guarding the right lower quadrant on palpation.'
'Patient is clearly drug-seeking and is exaggerating his pain level in order to obtain narcotics from the hospital.'
'Patient was rude to the crew and was obviously faking his symptoms for attention.'
'Patient is a frequent flyer who calls often, so there is probably nothing seriously wrong with him.'
questions.explanation: Good PCR narrative documents what was reported and observed — the patient's own words about pain severity, and objective exam findings such as guarding, facial expression, or vital signs — without the EMT inserting personal judgments about the patient's credibility, motives, or character. Phrases like 'drug-seeking,' 'frequent flyer,' or 'obviously faking' are subjective, biased conclusions that are not clinical facts; they can mislead subsequent providers into under-treating a genuinely sick patient, and they create serious legal exposure if a bad outcome occurs and the record shows the EMT dismissed the patient's complaint based on prejudice rather than assessment. The correct approach separates subjective patient-reported information ('reports 9/10 pain') from objective EMT findings ('guarding the right lower quadrant'), which is the standard structure taught for SOAP/CHART-style documentation.

questions.question: A patient with a language barrier was assessed using a family member as an interpreter. How should this be reflected in documentation?
choices: Refuse to document any history obtained through a third party, discarding all information gathered through the family member as unusable
Document the history as though it came directly and unambiguously from the patient herself, with no mention anywhere in the report that translation occurred
Note that an interpreter (identifying the family member's relationship) was used for history-taking, since this affects the reliability and context of the information obtained
No mention of the interpreter is needed anywhere, since the history was still obtained, and the source of that information doesn't affect its reliability
questions.explanation: History obtained through a third-party interpreter, especially a family member who may unintentionally filter, summarize, or editorialize the patient's answers, carries a different level of reliability than history obtained directly from the patient, so the PCR should transparently note that an interpreter was used and identify their relationship to the patient (spouse, adult child, bystander, etc.). This context allows receiving providers to appropriately weigh the history and, if needed, arrange for a certified medical interpreter for more precise communication. Presenting interpreted information as if it came directly and unambiguously from the patient misrepresents the source of the data, while refusing to document any third-party-obtained history at all would discard clinically useful information the EMT is entitled and often obligated to gather when no other option is available.

questions.question: You are ventilating an unresponsive, apneic patient with a BVM and a properly sized OPA in place, but you notice significant resistance and the chest is not rising despite a good mask seal. What should you do first?
choices: Increase the ventilation rate to compensate for poor volume, reassessing the patient every few minutes afterward
Insert a second OPA on top of the first for better patency
Immediately switch to mouth-to-mask ventilation
Reposition the head/jaw and reassess the airway before continuing
questions.explanation: Even with an OPA in place and an adequate mask seal, resistance to ventilation and absent chest rise most commonly indicate that the head/jaw position has shifted out of a patent alignment (loss of head-tilt/chin-lift or jaw-thrust), since airway positioning is the single most common fixable cause of ineffective BVM ventilation. The correct first troubleshooting step, following the standard BVM difficulty algorithm, is to reposition the airway and reassess for obstruction before trying anything else, since simply forcing more air in at a higher rate without correcting the underlying obstruction risks gastric insufflation and still fails to oxygenate the patient. Switching ventilation methods or adding a second airway adjunct without first correcting positioning skips the most basic and most likely fix and can waste critical time in an apneic patient.

questions.question: While suctioning a patient's airway who has copious vomitus, you find that a rigid catheter cannot keep up with the volume of secretions. What is the most appropriate next action?
choices: Log-roll the patient or turn the head so gravity helps, suction intermittently, and use a soft catheter for deeper secretions
Insert an OPA immediately despite the vomitus still present, since the adjunct itself helps keep the airway open while suctioning continues
Stop suctioning and abandon the attempt since a rigid catheter alone isn't keeping up with the volume of vomitus, leaving the airway uncleared and unmanaged
Continue suctioning continuously well beyond the normal time limit, ignoring interruptions to oxygenation, until the airway is fully clear
questions.explanation: Suction devices, even rigid tonsil-tip catheters, have a finite clearance rate and cannot keep pace with truly copious vomiting, and prolonged continuous suctioning is dangerous because it interrupts oxygenation and can itself cause hypoxia, so suctioning must be applied intermittently. Using gravity as an adjunct — log-rolling the patient onto their side (maintaining spinal alignment if precautions are indicated) or simply turning the head — lets fluid drain out of the oropharynx passively while intermittent suction clears what remains, and a flexible French/soft catheter can be useful for reaching further into the airway than a rigid tip allows. Suctioning nonstop past safe time limits worsens hypoxia, abandoning suctioning entirely leaves the airway obstructed and aspiration risk high, and placing an OPA into a mouth still full of vomitus does nothing to clear the obstruction and can push material further into the airway.

questions.question: A trauma patient with suspected spinal injury is unresponsive with noisy, gurgling respirations. Which airway maneuver is most appropriate while maintaining spinal precautions?
choices: Jaw-thrust maneuver without head extension
Head-tilt chin-lift with cervical extension
Hyperextension of the neck to maximize airway opening
Sniffing position with flexed neck and extended head
questions.explanation: The jaw-thrust maneuver opens the airway by displacing the mandible forward, lifting the tongue off the posterior pharyngeal wall, without requiring any extension or flexion of the cervical spine, which makes it the appropriate choice whenever spinal injury is suspected. The head-tilt chin-lift, sniffing position, and neck hyperextension all involve moving the cervical spine, any of which could worsen an unstable spinal injury and cause neurologic damage in a patient who cannot protect their own airway or report worsening symptoms. In practice, the jaw-thrust must be performed in conjunction with manual in-line spinal stabilization, and if it fails to adequately open the airway, providers may need to accept some compromise to save the airway, but it remains the first-line technique specifically because it minimizes cervical spine motion.

questions.question: You attempt to insert an OPA in a patient who begins to gag as soon as it contacts the back of the tongue. What does this response indicate, and what should you do?
choices: The OPA should be advanced further and pushed past the gag reflex until the patient stops reacting
This is expected and normal; insertion should continue despite the gagging until the OPA is fully seated
The patient is tolerating the airway well despite the gag; proceed with full insertion and continue as planned
An intact gag reflex; remove the OPA and consider an NPA
questions.explanation: An oropharyngeal airway is only indicated for patients who are deeply unresponsive with no gag reflex, because an intact gag reflex means the patient's protective airway reflexes are still functioning and stimulating the posterior pharynx with a rigid device will provoke vomiting, creating a serious aspiration risk in a patient who cannot fully protect their own airway. As soon as gagging occurs, the OPA must be removed immediately rather than advanced further or left in place, and if airway support is still needed, a nasopharyngeal airway is generally better tolerated by patients with some intact reflexes, provided there is no contraindication such as suspected basilar skull fracture or significant facial trauma. Continuing insertion or 'pushing past' the gag reflex directly risks inducing emesis and aspiration.

questions.question: A responsive patient has a facial injury with significant midface trauma, including possible fractures around the nose and orbits, along with clear fluid draining from the nose. Which airway adjunct should be avoided, and why?
choices: Suction catheter, because inserting it could worsen bleeding from the midface and orbital injuries
OPA, because the patient is responsive and an intact gag reflex is the only true contraindication to worry about
NPA, due to the risk of intracranial placement through a possible basilar skull/cribriform plate fracture
Nonrebreather mask, because the seal against the face could dislodge clots forming around the nose
questions.explanation: Clear fluid draining from the nose after significant midface/orbital trauma is a concerning sign of cerebrospinal fluid leakage from a basilar skull fracture involving the cribriform plate, and in this setting a nasopharyngeal airway carries a small but serious risk of being inadvertently passed through the fracture and into the cranial vault rather than the nasopharynx. Because of this risk, current teaching treats significant midface trauma or suspected basilar skull fracture as a relative contraindication to NPA placement, and providers should choose an alternative airway strategy if adjunct support is needed. An OPA is not contraindicated purely by responsiveness (rather, by an intact gag reflex), and suctioning or nonrebreather use are not the primary concerns raised by this specific injury pattern.

questions.question: You are ventilating a patient with a BVM and hear a high-pitched inspiratory sound (stridor) that developed suddenly after a bee sting. What does this finding most likely represent, and what does it mean for airway management?
choices: A benign finding requiring no change in care, since a sudden new inspiratory sound appearing after an insect sting is not considered clinically significant
Lower airway bronchospasm from the sting that will resolve fully on its own over time without any treatment needed, since it's assumed unrelated to anaphylaxis
Evidence that your own ventilation technique, rather than the patient's actual airway anatomy, is the true source of the high-pitched sound heard during ventilation
Upper airway swelling from anaphylaxis — a rapidly deteriorating, potentially difficult airway needing urgent transport and epinephrine
questions.explanation: Stridor is a high-pitched sound generated by turbulent airflow through a narrowed upper airway, and its sudden onset after an insect sting strongly suggests laryngeal/pharyngeal edema from anaphylaxis, a life-threatening allergic reaction that can progress to complete airway obstruction within minutes. This finding demands urgent recognition and treatment per protocol, including epinephrine if indicated and available, along with aggressive airway monitoring and rapid transport, because the airway can close entirely with little warning. It is neither a benign finding nor evidence of bronchospasm (which produces expiratory wheezing from the lower airways, not inspiratory stridor from the upper airway), and it is a genuine anatomic airway problem, not simply a technique issue with the BVM.

questions.question: A patient with a laryngectomy (surgically created stoma) in respiratory distress needs assisted ventilation. How should this be managed?
choices: Ventilate directly through the stoma using an appropriately sized mask sealed over the neck opening
Ventilate via a standard face mask over the nose and mouth only
Perform a head-tilt chin-lift and ventilate normally over the mouth, ignoring the stoma
Do not attempt ventilation since a stoma patient cannot be ventilated in the field
questions.explanation: A total laryngectomy surgically separates the trachea from the pharynx, so the patient breathes exclusively through the neck stoma, and airflow directed at the nose or mouth in these patients will not reach the lungs at all because there is no anatomic connection remaining. Assisted ventilation therefore must be delivered directly through the stoma, using an appropriately sized pediatric-style or specialized stoma mask sealed against the neck to achieve an effective seal and deliver tidal volume. Attempting standard face-mask ventilation over the nose/mouth, or performing airway-opening maneuvers aimed at the upper airway, will fail entirely in a total laryngectomy patient, and assuming these patients cannot be ventilated in the field is incorrect — they absolutely can be, just through the correct anatomic route.

questions.question: You are managing the airway of an unresponsive patient with a full set of dentures that appear well-fitted and intact. What is the correct action?
choices: Remove dentures before any airway management as a routine precaution, since any object in the mouth is considered a choking hazard during ventilation
Break the dentures apart to allow OPA placement, since an intact denture plate blocks proper seating of the airway adjunct
Remove dentures only after transport begins, rather than assessing whether they are well-fitting and helpful for ventilation
Leave well-fitting, intact dentures in place, as they can help maintain a mask seal for BVM ventilation, and remove them only if they become loose or dislodged
questions.explanation: Dentures maintain the normal contour and structure of the lower face, and when they are well-fitting and intact they actually improve the ability to achieve a tight, effective mask seal during BVM ventilation by preventing the cheeks from collapsing inward, so current guidance is to leave them in place rather than remove them by default. Removal is indicated only if the dentures become loose, broken, or dislodged, since a loose denture is then a foreign-body aspiration/obstruction risk that must be cleared. Blanket removal 'always' or waiting until transport (rather than reassessing continuously) ignores the ventilation benefit, and deliberately breaking dentures to fit an OPA is unnecessary and inappropriate — OPA sizing and technique should accommodate intact dentures without destroying them.

questions.question: During suctioning of an infant's airway, what modification to technique is most important compared to suctioning an adult?
choices: Suctioning continuously without ever pausing to allow reoxygenation, since infants' higher metabolic rate lets them recover from brief hypoxia much more quickly than adults typically do
Applying maximum available suction pressure to compensate for the infant's smaller airway diameter, since a narrower airway requires stronger suction to clear effectively
Using a rigid catheter with high, continuous suction pressure applied for as long as needed until all visible secretions have been fully cleared
Shorter suction (about 5 seconds) at lower pressure, to avoid bradycardia or trauma
questions.explanation: Infants have proportionally smaller airways, minimal oxygen reserve, and a highly reactive vagus nerve, so aggressive or prolonged suctioning can rapidly cause hypoxia as well as vagally-mediated bradycardia, and the delicate airway mucosa is also more easily traumatized by excessive negative pressure. The correct modification is to shorten suction duration compared to what is used in adults (about 5 seconds for an infant, against 10 for a child and 15 for an adult) and to use a lower suction pressure appropriate for pediatric patients, pausing to allow reoxygenation between passes. Infants do not tolerate hypoxia better than adults — quite the opposite, since their higher metabolic rate and smaller reserves make them desaturate faster — so maximal continuous suction is exactly the wrong approach.

questions.question: A conscious patient with a partially obstructed airway is coughing weakly, has a high-pitched inspiratory sound, and is becoming cyanotic. How should this be classified and managed?
choices: Mild/adequate air exchange; encourage the patient to keep coughing forcefully on her own and take no further action or airway intervention at this point
This indicates a lower airway problem such as bronchospasm from an unknown allergic trigger, best treated with supplemental oxygen alone and close monitoring
No intervention is needed right now since the patient is technically still coughing weakly and still able to make some faint audible sound
Severe obstruction with inadequate air exchange; treat it as complete, with back blows alternating with thrusts
questions.explanation: The line between mild and severe obstruction is drawn by how much air is actually moving, not by whether the patient can still cough or make a sound: a strong, forceful cough with good air exchange is mild and should be encouraged, but a weak cough, high-pitched stridor and cyanosis together mean air exchange has become inadequate, however much the patient appears to be 'doing something.' That is a functionally complete obstruction and needs immediate manual clearance. Under the 2025 AHA guidelines that means cycles of 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts in a conscious adult or child, and 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts in an infant — not passive observation, and not oxygen alone, since oxygen cannot reach lungs behind a mechanical blockage. Waiting because the patient is 'still coughing' invites progression to complete obstruction and loss of consciousness.

questions.question: A patient with severe COPD on home oxygen at 2 L/min via nasal cannula presents with worsening dyspnea and an SpO2 of 82%. According to current EMS guidance, how should oxygen be titrated?
choices: Withhold all supplemental oxygen for this patient and simply wait for a paramedic or ALS unit to arrive before addressing his worsening hypoxia
Titrate oxygen upward as needed to relieve hypoxia and improve the patient's condition, closely monitoring mental status and respiratory effort, rather than withholding oxygen from a hypoxic patient
Cap oxygen at his home 2 L/min setting even as his condition worsens, since a higher flow rate could suppress his hypoxic respiratory drive to breathe
Place a nonrebreather at 15 L/min immediately and leave the setting unchanged for the rest of the call, since maximal oxygen is the correct fixed setting once distress reaches this severity
questions.explanation: The historical concern about suppressing a COPD patient's 'hypoxic drive' with supplemental oxygen has been de-emphasized in modern EMS education, because the far greater and more immediate danger is leaving a patient severely hypoxic — an SpO2 of 82% represents significant, potentially organ-damaging hypoxemia that must be corrected. Current guidance is to titrate oxygen upward as needed to relieve hypoxia, using the delivery device and flow rate appropriate to the severity of distress, while closely monitoring the patient's mental status and respiratory effort for any change that would prompt reassessment or ventilatory support. Rigidly capping oxygen at the patient's home flow rate, or withholding it entirely while waiting for ALS, needlessly prolongs dangerous hypoxia; conversely, blindly applying maximal oxygen and never reassessing ignores the ongoing need to titrate based on patient response.

questions.question: While ventilating a patient with a BVM, you notice the chest rises excessively with each breath and the patient's abdomen is becoming visibly distended. What is the most likely cause and correction?
choices: Gastric insufflation from ventilating too fast/forcefully; slow the rate and reduce the volume/force of each breath, ensuring just visible chest rise
Inadequate tidal volume currently being delivered; increase the ventilation force and squeeze the bag noticeably harder with each subsequent breath given to him
The mask seal is currently too tight against the patient's face and should be deliberately loosened in order to reduce the pressure being delivered with each breath
This is a normal, fully expected finding during routine BVM ventilation that requires absolutely no change in technique, rate, or force being applied
questions.explanation: When ventilations are delivered too quickly or with excessive force, airway pressure can exceed the lower esophageal sphincter's resistance, pushing air into the stomach instead of (or in addition to) the lungs — this is gastric insufflation, and visible abdominal distension during BVM ventilation is its hallmark sign. The correction is to slow the ventilation rate, reduce the force/volume of each squeeze, and deliver each breath over about one second, aiming only for just-visible chest rise rather than maximal chest excursion, since overventilation increases both gastric insufflation risk and the risk of vomiting/aspiration. This is not a normal finding to be ignored, increasing force would worsen the problem rather than fix inadequate volume, and mask seal tightness is unrelated to this particular presentation.

questions.question: A patient's pulse oximeter reads 97% but he is cyanotic around the lips, has a depressed respiratory rate, and pinpoint pupils after a suspected opioid overdose. How should you interpret the SpO2 reading in this context?
choices: The reading confirms adequate oxygenation and no intervention is needed
Cyanosis and pulse oximetry cannot occur together, so one measurement must be equipment error requiring device replacement only
The SpO2 may be lagging; act on the clinical signs and support ventilation
Pinpoint pupils confirm the oximeter reading is accurate and no further action is needed
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry measures the percentage of hemoglobin saturated with oxygen, but it can lag behind acute changes in ventilation, read falsely reassuring values in poor peripheral perfusion or motion artifact states, and does not measure ventilation (CO2 clearance) at all — a patient can have a 'normal' SpO2 while breathing far too slowly and shallowly to clear carbon dioxide adequately. In an opioid overdose with visible cyanosis, a depressed respiratory rate, and pinpoint pupils, these direct clinical signs of inadequate ventilation are far more reliable and urgent than a single numeric SpO2 value, and the EMT should provide ventilatory support (BVM assistance, oxygen, and naloxone per protocol if indicated) regardless of what the oximeter displays. Assuming the reading is fully accurate and withholding intervention, or concluding the device must simply be broken and needs only replacement, both ignore the priority of treating the patient based on clinical presentation.

questions.question: Which combination of findings would most strongly indicate the need to switch from passive oxygen therapy to active ventilatory assistance?
choices: Respiratory rate 6/min, shallow tidal volume, altered mental status, and cyanosis
Respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 94% on room air, patient speaking comfortably in full sentences
Respiratory rate 20/min, clear and equal lung sounds bilaterally, with normal warm, pink skin color
Respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air, with only mild situational anxiety present
questions.explanation: The decision to move from passive oxygen delivery to active positive-pressure ventilation is based on adequacy of breathing as a whole — rate, tidal volume, mental status, and oxygenation together — rather than any single vital sign in isolation. A respiratory rate of 6/min combined with shallow tidal volume, altered mental status, and cyanosis represents inadequate minute ventilation and significant hypoxia that passive oxygen (nasal cannula or mask alone) cannot correct, because the patient simply is not moving enough air to bring supplemental oxygen deep into the alveoli; this combination requires immediate BVM-assisted ventilation. The other options describe patients with normal or only mildly abnormal rates, adequate mentation, and reassuring oxygenation/color, none of which meet the threshold for abandoning passive oxygen therapy.

questions.question: You are ventilating a patient with a BVM at a facemask seal that appears adequate, but the reservoir bag fails to refill fully between breaths. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: This is a normal finding during BVM ventilation and no troubleshooting or flow adjustment is needed
The mask is too large for the patient's face, causing the reservoir bag to underfill between breaths
The patient's lungs are too compliant, allowing air to move too easily out of the reservoir bag
The oxygen flow rate to the reservoir is too low or the tubing/valve is obstructed
questions.explanation: The reservoir bag on a BVM is refilled by a continuous flow of oxygen from the tank/regulator, and if it fails to fully re-expand between ventilations, the most likely cause is an inadequate oxygen flow rate feeding the reservoir (it should typically be set around 15 L/min or per manufacturer/device specification) or a mechanical obstruction such as a kinked line, closed valve, or malfunctioning one-way valve preventing oxygen from reaching the bag. This must be corrected promptly because an underfilled reservoir means the patient is being ventilated with a much lower FiO2 than intended, undermining the entire purpose of using the reservoir. Lung compliance and mask fit affect delivery of the breath to the patient, not whether the reservoir refills between breaths, so those are not the explanation for this specific problem.

questions.question: A patient who survived a drowning is breathing spontaneously but has diffuse crackles throughout both lung fields and an SpO2 of 89% on room air. What is the most likely underlying process, and the priority intervention?
choices: Bronchospasm from an underlying asthma exacerbation triggered by the cold water; administer a bronchodilator per protocol and reassess breath sounds
Impaired gas exchange from pulmonary edema after the drowning; give high-concentration oxygen and be ready to ventilate
Pneumothorax caused by the immersion event; prepare to perform needle decompression on scene per your local EMT protocol
A normal post-immersion finding requiring no oxygen, since crackles are simply expected after any water exposure and will clear on their own
questions.explanation: Even a small amount of aspirated water disrupts pulmonary surfactant and can damage the alveolar-capillary membrane, leading to fluid leakage into the alveoli (a form of noncardiogenic pulmonary edema) that produces diffuse crackles and impaired gas exchange, often worsening over the hours following a submersion event even in patients who initially appear stable. The priority intervention is high-concentration supplemental oxygen to address the hypoxia, along with close reassessment for deterioration, since these patients can progress to respiratory failure and may ultimately require assisted or full ventilatory support. This presentation is not a normal or benign post-immersion finding that can be left untreated, it is not the expiratory-wheeze pattern of bronchospasm calling for a bronchodilator, and diffuse bilateral crackles are inconsistent with a pneumothorax, which typically produces unilateral diminished/absent sounds and is outside EMT scope to treat with needle decompression regardless.

questions.question: While assisting a patient's ventilations with a BVM connected to supplemental oxygen at 15 L/min without a reservoir bag attached, approximately what FiO2 is being delivered compared to a BVM with a reservoir at the same flow rate?
choices: The same FiO2, close to 100%, is delivered whether or not the reservoir bag is attached
A higher FiO2 without a reservoir, since removing it creates less resistance to oxygen flow into the mask being worn
A lower FiO2 (roughly 40-60%) without the reservoir, compared to near 100% with a properly filled reservoir
0% FiO2 without a reservoir bag attached, since no oxygen reaches the patient without one
questions.explanation: Without a reservoir bag, the BVM entrains room air (roughly 21% oxygen) each time it re-expands after a squeeze, diluting the delivered oxygen concentration to only a moderate level, commonly cited in the range of roughly 40-60% even at a full 15 L/min flow, because the incoming oxygen alone cannot fully fill the bag before the next breath is given. Attaching a reservoir bag and allowing it to properly fill essentially eliminates that room-air dilution, allowing delivery of oxygen concentrations approaching 100%, which is why reservoir attachment is a standard and important step in BVM setup for any patient requiring high FiO2. Oxygen is still actively flowing and being delivered without the reservoir (ruling out 0%), and there is no physiologic mechanism by which removing the reservoir would increase FiO2.

questions.question: A patient with suspected pneumonia has a respiratory rate of 24/min, mild use of accessory muscles, and an SpO2 of 93% on room air, and is able to speak in full sentences. What is the most appropriate initial oxygen delivery method?
choices: No oxygen, since speaking in full sentences is a reliable sign that oxygenation is adequate
Nonrebreather mask at maximal flow from the start, left in place for the remainder of the call, since this SpO2 level warrants the highest available concentration without further titration
Nasal cannula or simple face mask titrated to improve SpO2, breathing being adequate for now
Immediate BVM positive-pressure ventilation, since the elevated respiratory rate indicates inadequate breathing
questions.explanation: This patient's ability to speak in full sentences, along with a respiratory rate and effort that are elevated but not severely compromised, indicates adequate (if mildly impaired) breathing rather than respiratory failure, so the appropriate intervention is titrated passive oxygen therapy — a nasal cannula or simple face mask adjusted upward as needed per local protocol to correct the mild-to-moderate hypoxia reflected by the 93% SpO2 — rather than jumping straight to positive-pressure ventilation, which is reserved for inadequate breathing. An SpO2 of 93% still represents measurable hypoxia that should be treated, so withholding all oxygen is inappropriate, but it also does not by itself justify a fixed maximal-flow nonrebreather applied without ongoing reassessment, since oxygen therapy should always be titrated to the patient's response and re-evaluated as the condition evolves.

questions.question: You are ventilating a patient through a tracheostomy tube using a BVM, but air seems to be escaping around the tube and from the patient's mouth and nose with each ventilation. What should you do?
choices: Seal the patient's mouth and nose (e.g., with a gloved hand or mask) while ventilating through the tracheostomy to reduce the leak and improve delivered volume
Ignore it, since some degree of air leak escaping around a tracheostomy tube during ventilation is expected, normal, and requires no corrective action

Increase the ventilation rate substantially to compensate for the lost volume, without ever identifying or actually addressing the true source of the leak, or checking the tube's cuff pressure or position
Remove the tracheostomy tube completely and instead ventilate over the patient's mouth and nose using a standard bag-valve mask and normal face seal
questions.explanation: Unlike a total laryngectomy, a tracheostomy patient's upper airway (mouth, nose, pharynx) often still connects to the trachea above the tube, so positive-pressure air delivered through the trach can escape upward through the mouth and nose instead of being pushed down into the lungs, resulting in reduced effective tidal volume. Sealing the mouth and nose, for example with a gloved hand or a small mask held snugly, directs the delivered volume into the lungs by preventing this upward escape route, correcting the underlying problem rather than compensating for it. Simply ignoring a significant leak or increasing the ventilation rate without addressing the leak both fail to fix the actual volume-delivery problem, and removing the tracheostomy tube is inappropriate and dangerous — it is the patient's primary or supplemental airway and should not be pulled out to attempt ventilation through an upper airway that may be partially or fully bypassed by the trach.

questions.question: A patient with a known history of asthma presents with severe respiratory distress, a silent chest on auscultation, and a slowing respiratory rate. How should this presentation be interpreted?
choices: An indication to withhold any further bronchodilator treatment entirely, since the disappearance of audible wheezing means the bronchospasm has already resolved
A pre-respiratory-arrest sign; the silence indicates minimal air movement (not resolution), and the patient requires aggressive ventilatory support
A sign that the patient's asthma attack has fully resolved, meaning no further treatment, monitoring, or transport urgency is needed here
Improving asthma since the wheezing sound has stopped entirely, suggesting the underlying bronchospasm is beginning to fully resolve on its own without treatment
questions.explanation: Wheezing is generated by air being forced through severely narrowed bronchioles, so paradoxically, as an asthma attack worsens to the point that almost no air is moving at all, the wheeze can disappear entirely — this 'silent chest' does not mean the attack is resolving, it means airflow has become so critically reduced that there is no longer enough turbulent movement to generate sound. Combined with a slowing respiratory rate (a sign of impending fatigue and respiratory failure rather than improvement) and continued severe distress, this is an ominous, pre-arrest presentation requiring aggressive ventilatory support, prompt treatment per protocol, and rapid transport, since the patient is at high risk of complete respiratory arrest. Interpreting silence as improvement, or withholding bronchodilator therapy, would be dangerous misreadings of a genuinely worsening, life-threatening picture.

questions.question: A patient with a spontaneous pneumothorax reports sudden, sharp, one-sided chest pain and shortness of breath after a coughing fit, with no trauma history. On exam, breath sounds are diminished on the affected side. What underlying process caused this?
choices: A blood clot that has traveled and lodged in the pulmonary artery, blocking blood flow to that lung
Fluid slowly accumulating within the pericardial sac surrounding the heart itself
An underlying infection causing consolidation and fluid filling of the lung tissue itself
Rupture of a small air-filled bleb on the lung surface allowing air to leak into the pleural space
questions.explanation: A primary spontaneous pneumothorax classically occurs when a small, weak, air-filled sac (a bleb or bulla) on the surface of the lung ruptures, often in tall thin young adults or during a Valsalva-like event such as a forceful coughing fit, allowing air to leak out of the lung and into the pleural space where it does not belong. This accumulation of air between the lung and chest wall causes partial lung collapse, producing the sudden sharp one-sided pain, dyspnea, and diminished breath sounds on the affected side described, with no external trauma required. A blood clot in the pulmonary artery describes a pulmonary embolism (a different disease process affecting perfusion, not producing this exam pattern), pericardial fluid describes cardiac tamponade, and infection/consolidation describes pneumonia — none of which explain a sudden traumatic-appearing unilateral lung collapse after a cough.

questions.question: You sealed a stab wound to the chest with an occlusive dressing five minutes ago. The patient now has worsening respiratory distress, jugular venous distension, tracheal deviation away from the injured side, and absent breath sounds on that side. What does this suggest, and what is the EMT priority?
choices: A simple, stable pneumothorax; leave the dressing alone and transport routinely
Cardiac tamponade from fluid building around the heart from the wound; the EMT should perform an emergency pericardiocentesis right there on scene immediately
A tension pneumothorax; check the occlusive dressing is not making it worse, burp it if needed, and transport fast
A simple isolated rib fracture from the stabbing; splint the entire chest wall firmly with bulky dressings to stabilize the fractured ribs in place fully
questions.explanation: Jugular venous distension, tracheal deviation away from the injured side, and absent breath sounds after penetrating chest trauma are the classic triad of a tension pneumothorax, in which air trapped under increasing pressure in the pleural space collapses the lung and progressively shifts the mediastinum, compressing the great vessels and heart and severely reducing cardiac output — a rapidly fatal condition if not addressed. EMT scope does not include needle decompression, so the key field priorities are ensuring any occlusive/chest-seal dressing over the wound is not itself contributing to a building tension (for example using or checking a vented/flutter-valve dressing, and 'burping' a fully occlusive seal if tension appears to be worsening), supporting ventilation and oxygenation, and providing rapid transport to a facility capable of definitive decompression. This is not simply a stable simple pneumothorax that can be transported routinely, it is not cardiac tamponade (which is caused by fluid around the heart, not air in the pleural space, and pericardiocentesis is well outside EMT scope regardless), and firmly splinting the chest wall is inappropriate and would worsen ventilation.

questions.question: A patient with congestive heart failure presents sitting bolt upright, unable to lie flat, with pink, frothy sputum and bilateral crackles. What is this presentation most consistent with, and what position should the patient be kept in?
choices: A spontaneous pneumothorax; place the patient lying down on the affected side to splint it
Pulmonary edema; keep the patient in a high-Fowler's (upright) position to ease breathing
An asthma exacerbation; place the patient in the recovery position on his side to protect the airway
Simple anxiety attack; lay the patient supine flat on the stretcher to help calm them down
questions.explanation: In decompensated congestive heart failure, the failing left ventricle cannot keep up with venous return, causing blood to back up into the pulmonary circulation and fluid to leak into the alveoli, producing the classic triad of orthopnea (inability to tolerate lying flat), bilateral crackles, and pink, frothy sputum from blood-tinged edema fluid mixing with air in the airways — this is acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema. These patients should be kept in a high-Fowler's (fully upright, often with legs dependent) position, which both eases the mechanical work of breathing by reducing pressure on the diaphragm and helps reduce venous return ('preload') to an already volume-overloaded heart, improving the pulmonary congestion. Laying the patient supine would worsen both breathing mechanics and venous return, and this presentation is neither simple anxiety, asthma, nor a pneumothorax — the bilateral, fluid-related findings and profile don't fit any of those alternative processes.

questions.question: A pediatric patient with a barking cough, inspiratory stridor, and a low-grade fever is diagnosed by history as likely croup. Which action is most appropriate if the child is currently in only mild distress?
choices: Keep the child calm and in a position of comfort (often on a caregiver's lap), avoid agitating exams, and provide blow-by oxygen if needed and tolerated
Immediately attempt to directly visualize the airway using a tongue depressor placed in the mouth to look closely for the exact source of obstruction present here
Aggressive suctioning of the upper airway in an attempt to physically remove the secretions causing the subglottic swelling and obstruction
Restrain the child firmly and securely on the stretcher in order to perform a thorough, complete oral cavity and airway examination right away
questions.explanation: Croup causes swelling and narrowing of the subglottic airway, and because a pediatric airway is already small, any additional agitation-induced crying, struggling, or forceful exam maneuvers can increase airway resistance and precipitate rapid, severe worsening of the obstruction — this is the same reasoning applied to epiglottitis, another 'do-not-agitate' pediatric airway emergency. The correct approach for a child in only mild distress is to minimize agitation entirely: keep the child calm, ideally in a position of comfort on a caregiver's lap, avoid invasive or forceful examinations, and offer blow-by oxygen gently if the child tolerates it, reserving more aggressive interventions for signs of severe or worsening distress. Aggressive suctioning, tongue-depressor visualization, or physical restraint for an oral exam are all likely to provoke crying and agitation that can dangerously worsen the airway swelling, and none of them address the actual cause of the obstruction in croup.

questions.question: A patient with a suspected pulmonary embolism presents with sudden-onset pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, and tachycardia after a long plane flight, with clear lung sounds on auscultation. Why might lung sounds be clear despite significant respiratory distress?
choices: Because a PE primarily affects upper airway structures like the trachea and larynx, which routine lung auscultation does not assess
Because clear lung sounds in this clinical setting point toward a psychiatric or anxiety-related cause rather than a true pulmonary or vascular problem
Because a PE is understood to cause fluid buildup within the alveoli that produces audible crackles on auscultation, so clear lung sounds effectively rule out any PE
A PE blocks perfusion rather than filling or narrowing the airways, so lung sounds can stay clear
questions.explanation: A pulmonary embolism is fundamentally a vascular event — a clot (often originating from a deep vein, and prolonged immobility such as a long flight is a well-known risk factor) lodges in the pulmonary arterial circulation and blocks blood flow to a portion of lung tissue, creating a ventilation-perfusion mismatch — rather than a process that fills the alveoli with fluid, triggers bronchospasm, or causes airway consolidation the way pneumonia, CHF, or asthma do. Because the airways and alveolar spaces themselves are often structurally unaffected, auscultation can be entirely clear even though the patient is significantly hypoxic and in respiratory distress, which is exactly why PE is a classic 'clear lung sounds but sick patient' presentation that should not be dismissed just because the lungs sound normal. This mismatch between exam findings and severity is a key teaching point, and clear lungs certainly do not rule out PE, nor do they imply a psychiatric cause or an upper-airway-only process.

questions.question: A patient with known anaphylaxis has been given epinephrine via auto-injector per protocol but continues to have stridor and worsening respiratory distress after several minutes. What should the EMT do?
choices: Reassess and, per local protocol/medical direction, consider whether a repeat dose of epinephrine is indicated while continuing to support the airway and transport rapidly
Administer a second full dose of epinephrine via auto-injector immediately, without any regard for the protocol-specified minimum timing interval between doses
Withhold all further treatment at this point and simply wait for the ambulance to arrive at the hospital without doing anything else
Assume the epinephrine already given has failed permanently and conclude that no additional dose could possibly help this patient going forward
questions.explanation: Anaphylaxis can be severe and refractory, meaning a single dose of epinephrine does not always fully reverse the reaction, particularly if the allergen exposure is ongoing or the reaction is especially severe, and many EMS protocols specifically anticipate this by allowing a repeat dose after a defined time interval if symptoms persist or worsen. The correct action is to continuously reassess the patient, follow local protocol or contact medical direction regarding a repeat dose, and continue supporting the airway (positioning, oxygen, readiness for ventilatory assistance) while transporting rapidly, rather than assuming the first dose was a permanent failure with nothing more to offer. However, repeat doses should still follow the protocol's specified timing interval rather than being given indiscriminately, since epinephrine carries its own risks (tachyarrhythmias, hypertension) that must be balanced against the benefit.

questions.question: A patient thought to be hyperventilating from acute anxiety presents with perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm, and a respiratory rate of 40/min but normal SpO2 and no other medical history. What is the most important next step before assuming a purely anxiety-based cause?
choices: Physically restrain the patient's hands and arms in an attempt to stop the visible muscle spasm and tingling sensation from continuing further
Withhold oxygen since the SpO2 reading is currently normal and the apparent anxiety is enough on its own to explain the tachypnea
Rule out other serious causes of tachypnea (such as DKA, PE, sepsis, or salicylate overdose) before attributing it to anxiety
Immediately have the patient breathe into a paper bag in order to rebreathe exhaled carbon dioxide and stop the perioral tingling and spasm right away
questions.explanation: Rapid, deep breathing that blows off excess carbon dioxide produces the classic symptoms described — perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm from resulting hypocapnia and a shift in ionized calcium — but this exact physiologic picture can be produced by tachypnea from many serious underlying conditions that compensate for or mimic anxiety, including diabetic ketoacidosis (Kussmaul respirations), pulmonary embolism, sepsis, and salicylate overdose, all of which require very different management than reassurance alone. Because 'anxiety-driven hyperventilation' is ultimately a diagnosis of exclusion in the field, a thorough history (medical conditions, medications, recent illness, possible ingestion) and assessment should be performed to look for these dangerous mimics before assuming the cause is purely psychological. Paper-bag rebreathing is discouraged in current practice because it can worsen hypoxia if the underlying cause is not truly benign hyperventilation. Deciding about oxygen from the normal SpO2 alone skips the same step, since several of these mimics present with a normal reading, and restraining the patient addresses neither the symptom nor any potential underlying cause.

questions.question: A patient with chest pain has taken three of his own nitroglycerin tablets before EMS arrival with no relief, and his blood pressure is now 92/58 with a heart rate of 110. What is the priority action?
choices: Administer aspirin only at this time and disregard the low blood pressure reading, treating it as unrelated to the chest pain
Withhold further nitroglycerin because of the low pressure and notify medical direction
Place the patient in a high-Fowler's upright position, expecting this to raise his falling blood pressure
Assist with a fourth dose of nitroglycerin immediately, despite the falling blood pressure reading
questions.explanation: Nitroglycerin works by causing venous and arterial vasodilation to reduce cardiac workload and relieve angina, but that same vasodilating effect can cause or worsen hypotension, and administering it to a patient whose systolic pressure has already fallen below the standard protocol threshold (commonly around 90-100 mmHg) risks precipitating dangerous hypoperfusion, especially concerning in a possible acute coronary syndrome where coronary perfusion pressure is already compromised. With a blood pressure of 92/58 and a compensatory tachycardia of 110, further nitroglycerin should be withheld (he has also already taken three doses, the usual maximum), and the EMT should treat and transport based on this now-hypotensive, potentially cardiogenic-shock-trending presentation, notifying medical direction promptly for further guidance. Ignoring the blood pressure to give aspirin alone or attempting to passively raise pressure with positioning does not substitute for recognizing that the patient's hemodynamic status has changed and now requires a different treatment approach.

questions.question: A patient presents with sudden crushing chest pain, diaphoresis, and nausea. His 12-lead (if your service carries one) or presentation is concerning for inferior wall MI, and he also reports the pain worsened right after his last dose of a medication for erectile dysfunction. Why is this history critical before considering nitroglycerin?
choices: It means aspirin should also be withheld from this patient, since antiplatelet medications carry the same dangerous interaction with PDE-5 inhibitors as nitrates do
PDE-5 inhibitors (e.g., sildenafil) taken recently can cause severe, refractory hypotension when combined with nitrates, making nitroglycerin contraindicated
It is not relevant to nitroglycerin administration in this case, since erectile dysfunction medications act locally and do not enter the systemic circulation
It means the patient's crushing chest pain is not actually cardiac in origin, and the erectile dysfunction medication caused all of his symptoms instead
questions.explanation: PDE-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil, tadalafil, and vardenafil, commonly prescribed for erectile dysfunction, work through a nitric-oxide-mediated vasodilatory pathway that overlaps significantly with the mechanism of nitrates; combining the two causes a synergistic, profound, and often treatment-resistant drop in blood pressure that can be life-threatening. Because of this dangerous interaction, obtaining a focused medication history that specifically screens for recent PDE-5 inhibitor use is a mandatory step before administering or assisting with nitroglycerin, and a positive history makes nitroglycerin contraindicated regardless of how classic the chest pain presentation looks for cardiac ischemia. This medication history does not mean the chest pain is non-cardiac (inferior MI is still a real concern requiring appropriate management), and it has no bearing on whether aspirin, which works through a completely different mechanism, should be given.

questions.question: During CPR on an adult, the patient's ribs crack audibly during the first several compressions. What should the rescuer do?
choices: Switch to rescue breathing without compressions to avoid further rib fractures
Stop CPR since the patient has clearly been injured by the compressions being performed
Reduce compression depth below the recommended targets to avoid causing the patient any further rib injury
Continue compressions; rib fractures are a generally accepted risk of CPR
questions.explanation: Achieving adequate compression depth (approximately 2-2.4 inches in an adult, per current AHA guidance) is necessary to generate sufficient blood flow to the brain and heart during cardiac arrest, and because the sternum and rib cage must be compressed significantly to reach that depth, rib and even sternal fractures are a well-recognized, generally unavoidable complication of properly performed CPR, not a sign that something has gone wrong. Rescuers should continue compressions at the recommended rate and depth despite the sensation or sound of fractures, because reducing depth to avoid causing injury would compromise perfusion and directly reduce the patient's chance of survival, and a fractured rib is a far more survivable and treatable injury than a failed resuscitation. Stopping CPR or switching to breaths-only in response to rib fractures would abandon effective chest compressions based on a complication that is expected and acceptable in the context of a life-threatening cardiac arrest.

questions.question: An AED analyzes a patient in cardiac arrest and advises 'no shock indicated.' The patient remains pulseless and apneic. What is the correct next action?
choices: Assume the patient has achieved return of spontaneous circulation and stop resuscitation
Repeat the analysis immediately without resuming CPR
Immediately resume high-quality CPR, beginning with compressions
Remove the AED pads since a shock is not needed
questions.explanation: A 'no shock advised' message simply means the AED's algorithm did not detect a shockable rhythm (ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia) in the analyzed segment — it does not mean the patient has a perfusing rhythm or has achieved ROSC, since the underlying rhythm could still be a non-shockable arrest rhythm such as asystole or pulseless electrical activity, both of which remain cardiac arrest and require continued resuscitation. Because the patient remains pulseless and apneic, the correct action is to immediately resume high-quality CPR, beginning with chest compressions, minimizing any further interruption, and continuing per the standard AED cycle of CPR followed by re-analysis at the appropriate interval. Assuming ROSC without confirming a pulse, repeatedly re-analyzing without providing any compressions in between, or removing the pads prematurely would all needlessly withhold circulation-generating CPR from a patient still in cardiac arrest.

questions.question: A patient in cardiac arrest has a do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order that a family member presents, but the document appears outdated and is not signed by a physician as required by your state's form. What should you do?
choices: Refuse to treat, on the family's request alone
Begin resuscitation while you check the document's validity and contact medical direction
Honor the DNR on the strength of the document and the family's verbal request together
Ask the family to sign the form themselves right now to make the outdated, unsigned document legally valid
questions.explanation: A DNR order withholds resuscitation only if it meets the specific legal validity requirements of the state's approved form, typically including proper physician signature, patient/proxy signature, and being current/unrevoked; a document that appears outdated or lacks the required physician signature does not meet those criteria and cannot be presumed valid on its face. When validity is in doubt, the default and legally safer course is to begin resuscitation efforts, since starting CPR/ALS care can always be withdrawn later if a valid DNR is subsequently confirmed, whereas withholding care based on an invalid document that turns out not to reflect the patient's true wishes cannot be undone. The EMT should continue resuscitation while evaluating the document's validity and contacting medical direction or following local protocol for guidance, rather than honoring an unverified document, refusing care based solely on family request, or allowing family members to retroactively 'validate' a form that requires a physician's signature.

questions.question: A patient in stable condition reports palpitations and you note an irregularly irregular pulse on palpation, with no other significant symptoms. What is the most likely underlying rhythm being suggested, and what is the appropriate EMT action?
choices: Ventricular fibrillation, requiring immediate defibrillation, since any irregular pulse finding in a stable patient indicates a shockable arrest rhythm
An irregularly irregular pulse such as atrial fibrillation; monitor, get vitals, and transport — the rhythm itself is beyond EMT scope
A normal sinus rhythm requiring no further action, since palpitations with an irregular pulse are simply anxiety and not clinically significant
Complete heart block requiring transcutaneous pacing by the EMT, since the irregular pulse indicates a dangerously slow AV conduction defect
questions.explanation: An 'irregularly irregular' pulse — one with no discernible repeating pattern in either timing or strength — is the classic bedside finding associated with atrial fibrillation, in which chaotic atrial electrical activity produces unpredictable ventricular contractions. EMTs do not have ECG interpretation or 12-lead diagnosis within their scope of practice, so the appropriate action is to recognize this palpable finding as clinically significant, obtain a full set of vital signs, monitor the patient closely for any deterioration, and transport for definitive evaluation and rhythm diagnosis by ALS or hospital staff. Ventricular fibrillation would present as a pulseless patient in cardiac arrest, not a stable patient with palpable palpitations, complete heart block classically produces a slow, regular (not irregular) bradycardic pulse and transcutaneous pacing is an ALS/hospital intervention, not an EMT skill, and assuming a normal sinus rhythm ignores the clearly abnormal, clinically significant irregularity that was found on palpation.

questions.question: A patient with a history of heart failure presents with bilateral lower extremity edema, jugular venous distension, and hepatomegaly reported by history, but clear lung sounds. What does this pattern most likely suggest?
choices: Acute pulmonary edema from left-sided failure, with the peripheral findings a downstream effect of it
A pulmonary embolism causing all of these findings, since sudden clot obstruction of the pulmonary vasculature explains chronic peripheral and hepatic congestion
Normal aging changes requiring no clinical significance, since edema, JVD, and hepatomegaly are common incidental findings in older adults
Right-sided heart failure/fluid backup into the systemic venous system, as opposed to primarily pulmonary (left-sided) congestion
questions.explanation: The right ventricle receives blood returning from the systemic veins and pumps it to the lungs, so when it fails, blood backs up into the systemic venous system, producing jugular venous distension, hepatic congestion (hepatomegaly), and dependent (peripheral) edema. The left ventricle handles pulmonary venous return, so when it fails, fluid backs up into the lungs instead, producing crackles, dyspnea, and frothy sputum — findings this patient does not have, since the lungs are clear. Isolated right-sided failure can occur on its own (for example from chronic lung disease or as a downstream effect of long-standing left heart failure) and does not require pulmonary symptoms to be present. The pulmonary embolism option is wrong because a PE typically causes acute dyspnea and hypoxia rather than this chronic congestive picture, and the normal-aging option dismisses objective findings that clearly represent decompensated heart failure, not benign aging.

questions.question: You are treating a patient in cardiac arrest with a working mechanical/automated CPR device available on your unit. When is it most appropriate to use this device instead of manual compressions?
choices: Only after the patient has already achieved ROSC, to help maintain circulation once a pulse has returned
Only for pediatric patients, since mechanical devices are sized and designed exclusively for smaller chest dimensions
Prolonged resuscitation, or movement and transport, where it keeps compression quality up and frees rescuers
Never, since manual CPR is always superior and outcome data show it consistently outperforms mechanical devices in every scenario
questions.explanation: High-quality CPR requires consistent rate, depth, and full chest recoil with minimal interruptions, but manual compressions inevitably degrade over time from rescuer fatigue and become dangerous or impossible during patient movement, stair descents, or ambulance transport. A mechanical CPR device delivers uniform compressions regardless of fatigue or motion and frees rescuers to manage the airway, establish IV/IO access, or prepare medications simultaneously — improving overall resuscitation efficiency. These devices are not restricted to pediatric use (in fact most are sized for adults) and outcome data have not shown them clearly superior to well-performed manual CPR in every scenario, so 'never use' and 'pediatric only' are both incorrect; likewise, applying it only after ROSC defeats its purpose, since ROSC means compressions are no longer needed at all.

questions.question: A patient points to the center of his chest and describes a heavy pressure that spreads to his left arm. When asked directly whether he has chest pain, he says no. He clearly appears uncomfortable, diaphoretic, and short of breath. What does this teach about assessing suspected cardiac patients?
choices: A patient who describes pressure or tightness rather than pain is unlikely to be having cardiac ischemia
Diaphoresis in this context is unrelated to a cardiac cause and should be attributed instead to anxiety or ambient temperature
This patient cannot be having a cardiac event since he denies pain, and his diaphoresis and dyspnea are better explained as anxiety about his symptoms
Ischemia is often described as pressure or tightness, so don't rely on the word 'pain'
questions.explanation: Myocardial ischemia is transmitted through visceral afferent nerves, which produce a diffuse, poorly localized sensation that patients commonly describe as pressure, tightness, squeezing, heaviness, or 'an elephant sitting on my chest' rather than sharp 'pain.' If the EMT anchors the assessment to the single word 'pain,' a patient like this — who denies pain but is diaphoretic, dyspneic, and visibly uncomfortable with classic radiation to the left arm — could be dangerously under-triaged. Effective assessment uses open-ended questions (OPQRST) and weighs the entire clinical picture — associated diaphoresis, dyspnea, and radiation are all independently significant cardiac red flags, not incidental findings to be dismissed. Ruling out ACS based on semantics alone risks missing a true emergency.

questions.question: During resuscitation of a hypothermic cardiac arrest patient found in cold water, standard protocols suggest which modification compared to a normothermic arrest?
choices: Withhold CPR, since compressions on a cold heart cause fatal arrhythmias
Continue resuscitation longer than usual while rewarming
Defibrillate and give drugs more often than normal, since a cold heart needs more frequent stimulation
Terminate on scene, since hypothermic arrest is not survivable
questions.explanation: Deep hypothermia slows metabolism and oxygen demand enough to protect the brain through a downtime that would be unsurvivable at normal temperature, which is what 'not dead until warm and dead' means: resuscitation continues, and transport to a facility capable of active rewarming is the priority. What has changed is the handling of defibrillation. The older teaching was to shock once and then withhold further shocks and drugs until the core reached about 30°C (86°F). Current guidance is that it is reasonable to follow the standard defibrillation algorithm alongside rewarming rather than rationing shocks by temperature. Handle the patient gently, remove wet clothing and prevent further heat loss. Withholding CPR and terminating on scene both abandon a patient who may be salvageable; shocking more often than the algorithm calls for has no basis.

questions.question: A patient who received an implanted pacemaker two years ago is now in cardiac arrest with no pulse and no respirations. How does the presence of the pacemaker change your AED use?
choices: Withhold the AED, treating the implanted device as a contraindication to external defibrillation
The pacemaker will automatically resuscitate the patient, so an AED is not needed once the device detects the cardiac arrest
The pacemaker must be surgically removed before AED use to avoid damaging both the device and the myocardium
Use the AED, but place the pad at least an inch from the pacemaker generator rather than over it
questions.explanation: A pacemaker paces the heart's electrical rhythm but cannot defibrillate a shockable arrhythmia like ventricular fibrillation, and even a patient with an implanted defibrillator still gets the AED when in arrest, so AED use remains fully indicated and should never be withheld or delayed. The only modification is pad placement: placing a pad directly over the palpable generator (usually visible as a firm lump under the skin, typically upper chest) can attenuate the delivered energy and potentially damage the device, so the pad is offset roughly an inch away while still achieving good skin contact and current pathway across the heart.
