questions.question: A 4-year-old with a high fever is brought to you seizing for the first time, with no prior seizure history. The seizure resolves spontaneously after about 90 seconds. What is this presentation most consistent with, and how should it be managed?
choices: A sign of meningitis in all cases, requiring immediate antibiotic administration by the EMT to treat the presumed underlying infection
A breath-holding spell requiring no further action or transport, since these episodes are typically brief, self-limited, and unrelated to fever
Epilepsy requiring the EMT to make long-term anticonvulsant therapy decisions in the field, since a seizure with fever is treated as proof of an underlying seizure disorder
A likely febrile seizure; supportive care and transport for evaluation, even though the seizure has already stopped
questions.explanation: A brief, generalized seizure occurring in a young child (typically between about 6 months and 5 years) in the setting of a rapidly rising fever, with no prior seizure history, is the classic presentation of a simple febrile seizure, which is generally self-limited (as demonstrated here by spontaneous resolution within about 90 seconds, well within the typical short duration) and usually carries a favorable prognosis. Even though the seizure has already stopped, appropriate management still includes supportive care — protecting the airway, positioning the patient safely (typically recovery position if postictal), managing the fever per local protocol, and transporting for physician evaluation to rule out more serious underlying causes and to reassure/educate the family, since a first-time seizure always warrants medical evaluation. This presentation should not be labeled epilepsy requiring field decisions about long-term anticonvulsants (entirely outside EMT scope and premature after a single event), dismissed as a breath-holding spell needing no transport (a different presentation, not fever-related), or assumed to always mean meningitis warranting EMT-given antibiotics, since antibiotics are far outside EMT scope and febrile seizures are usually due to the fever itself rather than direct CNS infection.

questions.question: An infant is found unresponsive, not breathing, with no pulse. On exam, you note lividity (pooling of blood) and rigor in the extremities, and the caregiver reports the infant was last checked several hours ago. What does this finding indicate, and how should it change resuscitation efforts?
choices: These findings mean the infant should be transported emergently with lights and sirens running so that full resuscitation can continue en route and at the receiving hospital
These are early, potentially reversible findings consistent with a very recent arrest, so full resuscitation should still be attempted regardless of how long the infant was last checked
Rigor mortis indicates true death; lividity alone is a reversible finding that still requires full resuscitation efforts
Lividity and rigor are obvious signs of death; under most protocols resuscitation is not begun, though family support still matters
questions.explanation: Dependent lividity (blood settling and pooling under gravity's influence in the lowest body areas after circulation has stopped) and rigor mortis (stiffening of muscle tissue from postmortem biochemical changes) are both well-established, objective, irreversible signs of death that develop only after a period of time following cessation of circulation — they are fundamentally different from findings seen in a recently arrested, potentially salvageable patient, which is why calling them early, reversible findings of a very recent arrest is incorrect. Per most EMS protocols, when these clear signs of obvious death are present, resuscitation efforts are not initiated regardless of the patient's age, since CPR and other interventions cannot reverse tissue changes that have already occurred; this applies to infants just as it does to adults, and the claim that lividity alone is reversible and still demands full resuscitation misunderstands that either sign, when clearly present, is sufficient. This is an emotionally profound scenario, particularly involving an infant, so alongside following protocol-based determination the EMT must also provide compassionate, clear communication and support to the grieving caregiver, and emergent lights-and-sirens transport for resuscitation would be inappropriate once obvious death has been confirmed.

questions.question: A 2-year-old chokes on a piece of food and is now unable to cry, cough, or make any sound, with visible cyanosis developing. What is the correct sequence of maneuvers for this age group?
choices: Blind finger sweeps first, to locate and remove the object before anything else is tried
Cycles of 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts, until the object clears or the child becomes unresponsive
Alternating back blows and chest thrusts, the sequence used for an infant under one year
No physical intervention, forceful maneuvers risking injury to a child this young
questions.explanation: A two-year-old is a child, not an infant. Under the 2025 AHA guidelines a choking child gets cycles of 5 back blows between the shoulder blades followed by 5 abdominal thrusts, repeated until the object comes out or the child goes unresponsive — at which point you begin CPR, looking in the mouth before each rescue breath. The back blows are the new part: children used to get abdominal thrusts alone. What still separates a child from an infant is the second half of the cycle, which under one year is 5 chest thrusts rather than abdominal thrusts, because an infant's liver is large and relatively unprotected. Blind finger sweeps are not done at any age, since they can push the object deeper, and doing nothing is not an option in a child who cannot cry, cough or make a sound.

questions.question: A school-age child with a history of asthma presents with severe respiratory distress, is unable to speak, has a silent chest, and is becoming drowsy. Compared to a milder asthma exacerbation, what does drowsiness in this context indicate?
choices: An unrelated finding, likely just simple tiredness from crying and struggling earlier during this episode, with no real bearing on the child's current respiratory status
A normal, expected response to the albuterol treatment already given, since bronchodilators like albuterol commonly cause temporary drowsiness as breathing eases
Improvement, since the child appears calmer and noticeably less agitated than before, suggesting the underlying airway distress and bronchospasm are beginning to resolve on their own
A dangerous sign of hypoxia and impending respiratory failure — a drowsy child in severe distress is tiring, not improving
questions.explanation: In a severe asthma attack, a silent chest and inability to speak already indicate airflow is so limited that wheezing can no longer be generated — a far more ominous finding than loud wheezing. When this child also becomes drowsy, it reflects cerebral hypoxia and exhaustion of the respiratory muscles, meaning the child is decompensating toward respiratory arrest rather than settling down. Providers who mistake this quieting for improvement can miss the window for aggressive airway support (high-flow oxygen, assisted ventilation, and rapid transport with ALS backup). The other options are dangerously wrong because they interpret a pre-arrest sign as reassurance, delaying the intervention this child urgently needs.

questions.question: A 6-month-old infant presents with a fever, is unusually irritable with a high-pitched cry, and has a bulging fontanelle. What serious condition should be strongly suspected, and what physical exam finding should be handled especially gently?
choices: Possible meningitis; the bulging fontanelle means raised intracranial pressure. Note it, do not press, transport fast
A dental teething issue causing the fever and irritability, requiring no further workup since teething commonly causes fever and irritability in infants this age
A simple viral cold; the fontanelle finding is treated as a normal variant requiring no further concern or workup
Dehydration; a bulging fontanelle is often seen with significant fluid loss in infants
questions.explanation: The anterior fontanelle is an unfused area of the infant skull that normally sits flat or slightly depressed; when it bulges, it signals rising intracranial pressure, which in the setting of fever and a high-pitched 'cerebral' cry is classic for bacterial meningitis or another intracranial infection/inflammatory process. Because the underlying tissue is fragile and pressure is already elevated, the fontanelle should be observed visually rather than palpated firmly, and the infant should be handled gently while being rapidly transported for antibiotics and further workup. A sunken fontanelle, not a bulging one, points toward dehydration, which is a different (though sometimes coexisting) problem, so blaming the bulge on fluid loss conflates the two findings, and dismissing this presentation as a simple cold or teething ignores red-flag signs of a life-threatening CNS infection.

questions.question: A toddler presents with several bruises in different stages of healing on the back and buttocks (areas not typically injured by normal childhood activity), along with a caregiver's story that doesn't match the pattern of injury. What should the EMT do?
choices: Refuse to transport the child until the caregiver provides a fully satisfactory explanation for the observed pattern and history of the bruising found
Treat this as possible non-accidental trauma: document objectively, treat the child's injuries, and report as your state's law requires
Ignore the finding, toddlers commonly bruising from normal play and falls even in less typical locations like the back and buttocks
Confront the caregiver on scene and accuse them of causing the bruising, to address the suspected abuse there and then
questions.explanation: Normal toddler bruising from falls and play typically occurs over bony prominences like shins, knees, and foreheads; bruises clustered on protected, padded areas such as the back and buttocks, especially in multiple stages of healing, are a well-recognized red flag for inflicted injury. Combined with a history that is inconsistent with the injury pattern, EMS providers — who are mandatory reporters in essentially all US jurisdictions — must objectively document exactly what they see and hear (without speculative diagnoses), provide any needed medical care, and report their concern through the proper channel (law enforcement, child protective services, or per local protocol). Confronting the caregiver on scene can escalate danger to the child and crew and may compromise a later investigation, while refusing transport pending an explanation abandons the child's medical needs and is neither the EMT's role nor legally appropriate.

questions.question: You are ventilating an infant with a BVM and notice the chest is rising excessively with each breath, more than the gentle rise expected. What risk does this create, and how should technique be adjusted?
choices: The mask should be removed and mouth-to-mouth ventilation used instead, since this method makes it easier to control the volume of air delivered
The current technique should remain unchanged, since infants require proportionally larger tidal volumes per breath relative to body size than adults do
Barotrauma and gastric distension leading to aspiration; ventilate gently, using only enough volume for a visible chest rise
A larger, more visible chest rise indicates more effective ventilation and better oxygen delivery in infants than a subtle rise would, so no adjustment is needed
questions.explanation: An infant's tidal lung volume is a small fraction of an adult's, and infant airway structures and alveoli are far more delicate, so delivering adult-scale volumes or pressure over-distends the lungs (risking barotrauma such as pneumothorax) and forces air past a relatively lax esophageal sphincter into the stomach. Gastric distension in turn splints the diaphragm, reduces effective ventilation, and significantly raises the risk of vomiting and aspiration. The correct technique is to ventilate slowly and gently, squeezing just enough to produce a subtle, visible chest rise rather than a dramatic one, which is why 'more chest rise is better' and 'infants need larger volumes' are both incorrect and potentially harmful assumptions; switching to mouth-to-mouth does nothing to fix an over-ventilation problem and abandons a more controllable, protected ventilation method.

questions.question: A 7-year-old with a fever and sore throat is sitting in the 'sniffing position,' drooling, refusing to lie down, and has a muffled voice. The caregiver reports rapid onset over just a few hours, and the child has not received the Hib vaccine. What condition should be strongly suspected, and how should the exam proceed?
choices: Strep throat, which commonly causes drooling and voice changes in children this age; have the child gargle salt water and take oral fluids before transport begins
Croup, which typically requires prompt intubation by EMS to secure the airway before transport
Possible epiglottitis: do not agitate the child, do not examine the throat, and transport promptly in the position of comfort
A simple cold; a thorough oral exam using a tongue depressor should be performed on the child to confirm this diagnosis before proceeding with transport to the hospital
questions.explanation: The classic epiglottitis picture — rapid onset over hours, high fever, drooling (from painful/impaired swallowing), a muffled 'hot potato' voice, and self-positioning in the tripod/sniffing posture to maximize airway patency — is exactly what this child shows, and the lack of Hib vaccination further raises risk since Haemophilus influenzae type b is a classic causative organism. The swollen epiglottis can obstruct completely with very little provocation, so any agitation, crying, forced supine positioning, or instrumentation of the airway (like a tongue depressor exam) can trigger sudden, complete airway closure; the correct approach is to keep the child calm, let them remain in their self-chosen position of comfort, provide blow-by oxygen if tolerated, and transport promptly to a facility that can secure a definitive airway. Attempting an oral exam, treating this as simple pharyngitis, or assuming croup (which has a more gradual, barky-cough presentation and is not managed with EMT-performed intubation) all risk precipitating the very obstruction the EMT must avoid causing.

questions.question: At a multi-agency incident, you notice that both fire and EMS command are giving conflicting instructions to responders on scene. What structural element of the Incident Command System is likely missing or not being followed?
choices: The National Incident Management System, which applies mainly to federally declared disasters rather than routine multi-agency responses
Unified command, which allows multiple agencies to coordinate through a single, integrated command structure with agreed-upon objectives
A rehabilitation (rehab) sector staffed by EMS
The use of radios, which should be replaced with in-person communication, since verbal relay between crews resolves most conflicting orders
questions.explanation: ICS is built to prevent exactly this kind of conflict: when multiple agencies with jurisdiction over an incident each try to command independently, responders receive contradictory orders and safety/efficiency suffer. Unified command solves this by having agency leaders jointly set incident objectives and priorities and issue coordinated, single-source direction, while each agency retains its own authority over its personnel. Radio use and rehab sectors address different operational needs and would not fix a command-structure conflict, and NIMS is a national framework meant to apply broadly to incidents of any scale (including day-to-day multi-agency responses), not just federally declared disasters, so that option misstates its scope.

questions.question: During a mass-casualty incident, you are assigned as a triage officer under ICS. To whom should you report your triage counts and updates?
choices: Directly to incident command, bypassing any intermediate supervisors, since command needs every detail firsthand to make decisions
Directly to the hospital emergency department charge nurse, bypassing the on-scene ICS structure to save time
To local media to keep the public informed of the ongoing triage counts and casualty updates
To your immediate supervisor within the ICS structure
questions.explanation: ICS is organized around a defined chain of command and manageable span of control, meaning each person reports to one designated supervisor rather than to whichever authority seems most convenient in the moment. As a triage officer, your reports normally flow to your immediate ICS supervisor (such as a medical group or branch supervisor), who consolidates information from all assigned units before it moves up the chain to incident command; this keeps command from being overwhelmed with direct reports from every position and preserves an accurate, organized information flow. Reporting straight to the hospital, straight to incident command, or to the media all bypass this structure, which can create duplicated, conflicting, or premature information reaching people who are not positioned to act on it appropriately.

questions.question: You are providing a radio report to the receiving hospital for a critical trauma patient. Which format best ensures the report is clear, organized, and complete?
choices: A stream-of-consciousness narrative covering whatever assessment details come to mind first for the crew, without any particular order, structure, or format applied
A structured format (such as unit ID/ETA, patient age/sex, chief complaint, pertinent history, vital signs, treatment given, and response to treatment) delivered concisely
A report focused exclusively on describing the mechanism of injury in detail, while deliberately omitting any vital signs or treatment information from the transmission to save airtime
The patient's name and a requested room number on arrival, without any clinical details about condition, vitals, or treatment
questions.explanation: A standardized radio report format exists precisely because it guarantees that the most clinically important information is transmitted in a predictable order, letting the receiving team mentally prepare (mobilizing trauma team, blood products, imaging) before the patient arrives. Key elements — identifying data, chief complaint, relevant history, vital signs, treatment given, and the patient's response to that treatment — allow the hospital to triage the severity and needs of the incoming patient efficiently over a brief radio transmission. An unstructured narrative risks omitting critical details or burying them under less important information, while giving only a name/room request or omitting vital signs entirely deprives the hospital of the objective data it needs to prepare an appropriate resuscitation response.

questions.question: During a large-scale incident, cellular and radio communications become overloaded and unreliable. What backup communication strategy is most appropriate for maintaining coordination between units?
choices: Abandon any attempt at coordinated communication and operate independently until normal channels happen to be restored on their own at some point
Wait indefinitely on scene for normal communications to be fully restored before taking any further action, decision, or resource request whatsoever
Rely solely on personal cell phones to text incident command directly, since cell networks typically remain reliable even during large-scale incidents
Use predetermined backups such as runners, rally points or alternate channels
questions.explanation: Effective incident management assumes that primary communication systems can fail or become saturated during large-scale events, which is why the incident action plan should include a dedicated communications plan specifying backup frequencies, designated rally/reporting points, and low-tech options like runners for face-to-face relay of critical information. Falling back on these pre-established, agreed-upon methods keeps operations coordinated and safe even when radios or cell networks are jammed. Operating independently abandons the coordination that keeps responders and patients safe, waiting indefinitely delays necessary care and resource allocation, and relying solely on personal cell phones is unreliable at scale (networks are often the first system to fail) and is not part of a structured, redundant communications plan.

questions.question: You are the first EMS unit to arrive at a large, complex incident with multiple patients and hazards. Before treating any patient, what should be your first action regarding incident command?
choices: Begin transporting patients individually as each one is found, with no overall size-up performed and no organized triage system applied to the scene
Wait for a chief officer to physically arrive before taking any action, since only a chief officer has the authority to establish initial command
Immediately begin treating the most visibly injured patient found first, without broadcasting any size-up report or organizing the overall scene beforehand
Report to or establish incident command and give an initial size-up to incoming units — your first actions frame the whole response
questions.explanation: The first unit on scene at a complex, multi-patient incident has a critical organizational responsibility: establishing command (even briefly, until a more qualified officer arrives to assume it) and broadcasting an initial size-up that identifies scene hazards, approximate patient count, and needed resources. This report becomes the foundation every subsequently arriving unit uses to allocate personnel, request additional resources, and approach the scene safely, so skipping it in favor of immediately treating one patient can leave the rest of the incident unmanaged and unsafe. Waiting passively for a chief officer wastes valuable early minutes when rapid triage and resource requests matter most, and transporting patients individually without an overall size-up risks missing patients, misallocating resources, and losing situational awareness of scene hazards.

questions.question: At a hazardous materials incident, you are assigned to work in the rehab area (set up in the cold zone). What is the primary purpose of this ICS functional area?
choices: To store equipment that is unrelated to patient care, kept separate from any responder rest, hydration, or medical monitoring function nearby
To serve as the primary incident command post from which all responding agencies coordinate operations at the ongoing hazardous materials incident
To provide definitive decontamination of contaminated patients before they are allowed to move any deeper into the warm zone toward the treatment sector itself for further care
To monitor and support responder health and safety (rest, hydration, vital sign checks) during extended operations, reducing risk of responder injury or illness
questions.explanation: Rehab exists because extended operations — especially in protective equipment, extreme temperatures, or high physical/psychological stress environments like a hazmat incident — place responders themselves at real risk of dehydration, heat or cold injury, cardiac strain, and exhaustion. The rehab sector systematically rotates crews through rest, hydration, and vital sign/medical monitoring so that fatigued or physiologically stressed personnel are identified and rested before they become patients themselves. It is distinct from decontamination (which removes contamination from patients/responders) and from the incident command post (which coordinates overall strategy), so confusing rehab with either of those functions misunderstands its dedicated responder-welfare purpose.

questions.question: You are handing off a patient to a flight crew for air medical transport at a rural scene. What is a key safety consideration specific to helicopter operations that ground EMS must follow?
choices: There are no special safety considerations different from ground ambulance operations when working around a landed helicopter
Approaching the aircraft while it is still landing, to save time before the rotors fully settle
Approach only from the front or sides, in the pilot's view, never near the tail rotor, and only when signaled
Approaching the helicopter from the rear, near the tail rotor, since this offers the fastest, most direct approach to the aircraft
questions.explanation: Helicopter landing zone safety is built around one dominant hazard: the tail rotor, which spins at extremely high speed, is often nearly invisible, and is fatal on contact, so ground personnel must never approach from the rear of the aircraft. Approaching from the front or sides, staying within the pilot's direct line of sight, and waiting for explicit clearance from the flight crew (rather than assuming it is safe once the aircraft looks stationary) are core landing-zone safety rules taught specifically because rotor-wing aircraft carry hazards ground ambulances do not. Approaching during landing is dangerous due to rotor wash, shifting aircraft position, and reduced visibility, which is why crews wait for the aircraft to fully settle and the flight crew to signal before anyone approaches.

questions.question: During interfacility transport, you receive a detailed handoff report from the sending facility nurse but notice a discrepancy between the reported medication dose and what is documented on the paperwork. What should you do?
choices: Ignore both the verbal report and the paperwork, and administer a different dose based on your own independent protocol
Guess which one is correct and use your own judgment silently, without raising the discrepancy with sending staff
Clarify the discrepancy directly with the sending facility staff before departing, to ensure an accurate understanding of the patient's actual treatment
Proceed with the documented dose without clarifying the discrepancy, since the written paperwork is generally the more reliable source
questions.explanation: Accurate handoff information is the foundation of safe ongoing patient care during transport — if the EMT does not know exactly what medication and dose the patient has actually received, they cannot safely monitor for expected effects, recognize adverse reactions, or communicate accurately to the receiving facility. Any discrepancy between verbal report and written documentation should be resolved on scene, before departure, by directly asking the sending staff to clarify which is correct, since this is the only way to close the information gap with certainty. Silently proceeding with unverified information, guessing, or unilaterally substituting a different dose based on personal judgment all risk perpetuating or compounding a medication error rather than catching and correcting it.

questions.question: You are dispatched to a scene already being managed by a fire department using ICS, and you are the ranking EMS officer arriving. What should your first action be regarding the command structure already in place?
choices: Ignore the existing ICS structure and direct EMS operations independently of the fire department's command
Immediately establish a separate, independent EMS command structure alongside the fire department's existing command
Report to the established incident commander rather than creating a separate command
Take command from the fire department immediately, since medical care is the primary need and EMS should direct the overall response
questions.explanation: One of the core purposes of ICS is to ensure that all responding resources integrate into a single command structure rather than each agency running its own parallel operation, which is exactly the conflict-generating scenario ICS is designed to prevent. As the ranking EMS officer arriving after command is already established, the correct action is to report to the existing incident commander, offer EMS branch/group leadership as appropriate, and — for a genuinely multi-agency incident — help form a unified command with shared objectives, rather than declaring a competing EMS command. Simply seizing command because medical care is now involved, or ignoring the ICS structure to operate independently, undermines the coordinated, single-point-of-command principle that keeps large incidents organized and safe.

questions.question: A mutual aid ambulance from a neighboring jurisdiction arrives to assist at a large incident but uses different terminology and slightly different triage tag colors than your local system. What ICS principle is designed to help address this kind of interoperability challenge?
choices: The mutual aid unit's own agency leadership should make decisions for that crew, operating independently of local incident command for the whole incident
Common terminology and standard procedures, with a quick briefing on local variations
Mutual aid units should be sent back home upon arrival if their terminology or equipment differs from the local system, since integrating them safely under those conditions is difficult
Mutual aid units should not be integrated into ongoing operations when their terminology or equipment differs from the local system
questions.explanation: ICS was developed nationally in large part to solve exactly this problem: agencies from different jurisdictions historically used inconsistent terminology, position titles, and procedures, which caused dangerous confusion when they had to work together on large or multi-jurisdictional incidents. Common terminology and standardized organizational structure are foundational ICS principles meant to make any trained responder from any agency able to plug into an incident's command structure; where local variations still exist (like slightly different triage tag color schemes), incident command's responsibility is to quickly brief incoming mutual aid units on those specifics rather than let the mismatch cause errors. Sending mutual aid units home over a terminology difference wastes needed resources, and letting an incoming unit operate under its own independent leadership defeats the entire purpose of a unified, coordinated incident response.

questions.question: A competent adult patient with a life-threatening condition refuses transport after being informed of the risks, including possible death. The EMT believes this decision is unwise. What is the legally and ethically correct action?
choices: Call the patient's family to override the patient's own decision, treating family consent as superior to the competent patient's own wishes
Transport the patient against their will, since a life-threatening condition overrides the patient's right to refuse
Respect the refusal if the patient has capacity, understands the risks, and it is documented
Sedate the patient to allow transport despite the refusal, since sedating her resolves the conflict between ensuring safety and respecting her wishes
questions.explanation: The legal doctrine of patient autonomy holds that a competent adult has the right to make decisions about their own body and medical care, including refusing treatment or transport that others — even trained medical providers — believe is medically unwise, as long as the patient demonstrates decision-making capacity (understands their condition, the risks of refusing, and the alternatives) and the refusal is informed and voluntary. The EMT's role in this scenario is to ensure the patient truly understands the risks, offer alternatives, and thoroughly document the informed refusal (ideally with a witness and patient signature), not to override that decision. Transporting against the patient's will, letting family override a competent adult's own wishes, or sedating the patient to force compliance would all constitute battery/false imprisonment and are serious legal and ethical violations, since none of those parties has the authority to override a competent adult's informed refusal.

questions.question: You are treating a 16-year-old patient with a significant injury, and the patient's parents cannot be reached. Under the doctrine EMS typically relies on in this situation, how should you proceed?
choices: Require the minor to sign their own legal consent form before treatment, since a 16-year-old is generally considered old enough to independently authorize their own care
Withhold all treatment until a parent or guardian can be contacted, since treatment generally requires direct parental consent before it can begin
Provide necessary emergency treatment under implied consent, since a reasonable parent would want necessary care for their injured/ill child, and continue attempting to reach a parent
Call law enforcement to make all medical decisions for the minor, since officers are considered to hold authority over treatment choices in this situation
questions.explanation: Implied consent is the legal principle that assumes a reasonable person — in the case of a minor, a reasonable parent or guardian — would want emergency treatment provided to prevent death or serious harm, even when they cannot be reached to give actual consent in the moment. This allows EMS to proceed with necessary emergency care for an injured minor without delay while simultaneously making ongoing efforts to reach a parent or guardian for further information and formal consent as soon as possible. Withholding all treatment pending parental contact could allow a treatable emergency to worsen unnecessarily, minors generally lack the legal capacity to provide their own binding medical consent outside specific emancipated-minor or mature-minor exceptions, and law enforcement does not have authority to make medical treatment decisions for a minor in this context.

questions.question: An EMT documents a patient assessment finding that was not actually performed, in order to make the patient care report appear more complete. What is this practice called, and why is it a serious concern?
choices: Standard, generally acceptable practice within busy EMS systems, since a plausible-looking finding fills documentation gaps without causing real harm
Acceptable as long as the patient's ultimate outcome happened to be good, since a favorable outcome justifies the inaccurate documentation entry after the fact
A minor administrative shortcut carrying no real consequence, since the PCR is often treated as a paperwork formality rather than a genuine clinical or legal document
Falsification of records — an ethical violation and potentially illegal, since it creates inaccurate medical and legal records
questions.explanation: The patient care report (PCR) is both a clinical handoff document and a legal record; entering a finding or intervention that was never actually performed is falsification, which undermines the accuracy every downstream provider relies on to make treatment decisions and can directly harm patient care if it masks a missed assessment or omitted treatment. Beyond the clinical danger, falsified documentation is a serious breach of professional ethics and, in many jurisdictions, a violation of law or licensing regulations that can result in decertification, termination, and civil or criminal liability for both the individual EMT and the agency. A good patient outcome does not retroactively make falsification acceptable, since the harm lies in the corrupted record itself and the precedent it sets, not merely in whether this particular patient happened to do well.

questions.question: A bystander who is a physician arrives on scene and begins directing care that conflicts with your protocols, without any documented relationship with your EMS system or medical direction. How should the EMT handle this situation?
choices: Ignore the bystander physician and refuse any interaction with them, since an unaffiliated bystander physician has no real authority or useful role in this situation
Explain that you work under your service's medical direction, and keep following it unless the physician takes over care, rides in, and accepts documented responsibility
Immediately abandon your own established protocols in order to fully comply with the bystander's instructions, since a physician's direction on scene supersedes the EMT's own protocols
Always defer to any physician present on scene, since any active medical license outranks established EMS protocol
questions.explanation: EMS providers operate under a specific medical director's standing orders and protocols, and that legal relationship — not the mere presence of any physician on scene — is what governs the care given. A bystander physician with no established relationship to the EMS system or the patient's care generally cannot simply override the EMT's protocols; most systems require that physician to clearly identify themselves, take explicit responsibility for directing care, and typically accompany the patient to the hospital before deviating from standard protocol, which creates accountability and a documented chain of medical oversight. Automatically deferring to any physician disregards this accountability structure, while ignoring the bystander outright is neither professional nor practical, since their offered expertise may still be useful within the proper framework.

questions.question: An unconscious patient is found with a medical alert bracelet indicating a specific allergy and chronic condition. Is the EMT legally permitted to act on this information without the patient's ability to verbally consent?
choices: Only law enforcement can authorize use of a medical alert bracelet's information, since interpreting it falls outside EMS authority
The information should be ignored since it cannot be verified in the field, and information that cannot be verified should not be used to guide treatment decisions
No, all care must stop until verbal consent is obtained, since implied consent does not apply to an unresponsive adult patient who cannot verbally agree
Yes, this falls under implied consent for emergency care, and the medical alert information should be used to inform treatment decisions
questions.explanation: Implied consent applies whenever a patient is unresponsive or otherwise unable to grant or withhold consent for emergency care, based on the reasonable legal assumption that a person facing a life-threatening emergency would want necessary treatment. A medical alert bracelet is a recognized, practical source of clinical information in exactly this situation, and using it to avoid a known allergen or to anticipate complications from a documented chronic condition is a standard part of good assessment and treatment under implied consent. Halting all care pending verbal consent, disregarding the bracelet as unverifiable, or waiting for law enforcement authorization would all unnecessarily delay appropriate treatment for an unconscious patient who cannot otherwise communicate this critical safety information.

questions.question: You witness a fellow EMT perform a skill incorrectly in a way that could have harmed the patient, though the patient appears to be unaffected in the immediate term. What is the most appropriate ethical action?
choices: Say nothing to the coworker or anyone else in order to avoid conflict, since the patient appearing currently unaffected removes any need to report the error
Alter your own documentation of the call in order to quietly cover for the coworker's error, since this protects the coworker without further harming the patient
Raise it through your service's channels, with the coworker or a supervisor, and make sure the patient gets any follow-up care needed
Publicly confront the coworker in front of the patient and family right at the scene, since immediate correction ensures accountability
questions.explanation: EMS professionals have an ethical duty to prioritize patient safety and honest reporting over interpersonal comfort or workplace loyalty, and a skills error that could have harmed the patient — even if no harm is currently apparent — needs to be surfaced so the patient's ongoing care is properly informed and so systemic issues can be corrected before they harm a future patient. The appropriate response is to address it through legitimate channels: a direct, professional conversation with the coworker when appropriate, and/or reporting through a supervisor or quality improvement process, while making sure the patient receives any follow-up care and that documentation accurately reflects what occurred. Staying silent risks repeat harm and normalizes unsafe practice, publicly confronting a colleague in front of the patient damages trust and professionalism, and altering documentation to cover for the error compounds the original mistake with falsification, which is itself a serious ethical and legal violation.

questions.question: A patient with capacity refuses a specific intervention (such as a splint on an injured wrist) but consents to transport and other care. How should the EMT proceed?
choices: Apply the refused splint anyway, since agreeing to transport implies consent to every other proposed intervention
Consider the patient's entire consent invalid because of this one partial refusal, treating any single declined intervention as voiding all of the other agreed-upon care
Respect a refusal of specific interventions alongside consent to others, document it, and give the care the patient agreed to
Refuse to transport the patient unless the patient consents to every single proposed intervention, treating informed consent as a strict all-or-nothing package deal
questions.explanation: Informed consent is not an all-or-nothing agreement — a competent patient can consent to some aspects of care while declining others, and each intervention generally requires its own specific consent. When a patient with capacity agrees to transport and general care but declines a specific intervention like a splint, the EMT should respect that boundary, clearly document the specific refusal (including that the patient was informed of relevant risks/benefits), and proceed with everything the patient did agree to rather than treating the encounter as an all-or-nothing transaction. Refusing to transport at all, performing the declined intervention anyway (which would constitute battery), or treating the partial refusal as invalidating the patient's other consents all fail to respect the patient's legitimate, selective decision-making authority.

questions.question: During transport, a patient's condition changes such that continuing to a further, specialized facility (per protocol) versus a closer general hospital becomes a judgment call, and the patient's family is pressuring you to go to the closer facility against your protocol-based destination decision. What should guide your decision?
choices: Always defer to the family's stated wishes over your protocol-based destination criteria, since family preference should outweigh established transport protocols when they disagree
Refuse to communicate with the family about the decision, since explaining the protocol-based reasoning to them would only add to their distress
Go with whichever facility the family requests when both options seem reasonable, since their preference and protocol carry similar weight in this kind of judgment call
Follow your protocol's destination criteria, consult medical direction if needed, and explain the reasoning to the family
questions.explanation: Destination protocols for time-critical conditions (stroke centers, trauma centers, STEMI-receiving facilities) exist because outcomes data show that routing appropriate patients to specialized centers, even when slightly farther, meaningfully improves survival and functional outcomes — this is the entire rationale behind regionalized systems of care. When family pressure conflicts with protocol-based criteria, the EMT should still follow the established criteria (contacting medical direction for guidance if there is genuine clinical ambiguity) while taking the time to explain the reasoning to the family compassionately, since a well-informed family is more likely to understand and support the decision even if they initially disagree. Simply deferring to family preference, deciding arbitrarily, or refusing to communicate at all either abandons evidence-based care or unnecessarily damages the family's trust and understanding during a stressful moment.

questions.question: You respond to a call and recognize the patient as a coworker's family member with a sensitive medical/psychiatric condition. What ethical obligation applies regarding patient confidentiality in this situation?
choices: The same confidentiality obligations apply whatever the personal relationship, so do not discuss the patient with the coworker
Confidentiality does not apply to personal acquaintances like this coworker, since a known personal relationship removes the usual legal protections
Confidentiality can be verbally waived by the EMT alone without the patient's own consent, since the treating provider has sole discretion over disclosure decisions

It is acceptable to discuss the case details freely with the coworker since they are considered 'part of the EMS family,' and being part of the same EMS organization is generally accepted as sufficient authorization to share those details
questions.explanation: Confidentiality protections under HIPAA and general EMS professional ethics attach to the patient and the information itself, not to the particular relationship between the provider and the person asking about it, so recognizing the patient as a coworker's relative creates no special exception to share details. The EMT must limit disclosure to those with a legitimate need to know for treatment, payment, or operations purposes, and generally should not discuss the patient's condition with the coworker (even out of a sense of shared 'EMS family' concern) without the patient's proper authorization or another legally recognized exception. Believing personal acquaintance removes confidentiality, treating coworker status as a special exception, or assuming the EMT alone can unilaterally waive confidentiality on the patient's behalf are all misunderstandings of how these protections actually work.

questions.question: At a crash involving a hybrid car, the dashboard shows the vehicle is still powered on and the patient is trapped in the driver's seat. Which hazard should guide your approach?
choices: An energized car body, so no one may touch the vehicle until the utility company arrives
An imminent battery explosion, so the patient must be pulled out before any assessment
Orange high-voltage cables, and a silent car that can still move
Fuel leaks only, since hybrids carry no electrical hazard once the airbags have deployed
questions.explanation: A hybrid or electric car can be powered on yet silent, so it may move if the drive engages; it is chocked, put in park and turned off with the key or fob moved well away, as the manufacturer's emergency response guide describes. The high-voltage system runs through cables that are usually bright orange, and responders do not cut, crush or touch them. The car body is not normally energized the way a vehicle under a downed power line is, so once the car is stabilized and powered down the patient can be reached and assessed. A damaged battery can catch fire, which is a reason for fire department support and monitoring, not for skipping the assessment.

questions.question: While extricating a patient from a vehicle with a partially deployed side-curtain airbag that has not fully discharged, what safety precaution should the crew take?
choices: Manually trigger the airbag to deploy first in order to eliminate the risk before continuing, since intentionally triggering it under controlled conditions is safer than leaving it live

Treat the undeployed airbag as a hazard capable of still deploying, and take precautions (such as disconnecting the battery and keeping personnel clear of the airbag's deployment path) before extrication
Remove the entire airbag module using hand tools before beginning extrication, since physically detaching the module fully eliminates the underlying hazard
Ignore the airbag's status and proceed with extrication as normal, since a partially deployed airbag has already released all of its stored energy
questions.explanation: A side-curtain airbag that has only partially deployed or shows signs of a fault can still retain enough stored energy or an intact triggering circuit to fire fully during extrication, and a late deployment near a responder's head or hands can cause serious injury. Standard vehicle hazard precautions call for treating any undeployed or partially deployed airbag as an active hazard: following protocol to disable the vehicle's electrical system (such as disconnecting the battery once the vehicle is stabilized) and keeping all personnel and tools out of the airbag's projected deployment path throughout extrication. Attempting to manually trigger the airbag or physically remove the module with hand tools is far more dangerous than simply avoiding the hazard zone, and ignoring the airbag status entirely disregards a documented and preventable extrication hazard.

questions.question: You arrive at a scene where a patient is in obvious distress inside a structure that has active fire showing from a window, with no fire department on scene yet. What is the correct EMT action?
choices: Enter the structure to rescue the patient at once, delaying rescue posing a greater risk than the active fire
Stage at a safe distance and wait for fire department resources
Enter with a wet cloth over your face, since speed matters more than full protective gear
Attempt to fight the fire yourself with an ambulance-mounted extinguisher before rescuing the patient, since a quick knockdown can clear a safe path inside
questions.explanation: Interior structural fires involve extreme heat, toxic smoke, rapidly changing fire behavior, and structural collapse risk that require specialized turnout gear, self-contained breathing apparatus, and specific training that EMTs do not have — entering under these conditions would very likely turn one emergency into two, with the EMT becoming a second victim requiring rescue. The correct action is to stage at a safe distance, request or await fire department resources who are equipped and trained for this exact scenario, and then provide medical care once fire crews have removed the patient to a safe area outside the hazard zone. Entering without protective equipment, attempting to extinguish an active structure fire with an ambulance-mounted extinguisher, or otherwise improvising a rescue all place the EMT in a situation they are not equipped to survive, let alone perform a rescue within.

questions.question: During a violent weather event, you are dispatched to a reported injury in an area under an active tornado warning. What should guide your response and on-scene operations?
choices: Coordinate the timing of the response with dispatch, put crew safety first and shelter if a tornado is imminent, then treat once it is safe
Ignore all weather-related guidance since patient care takes precedence, and crew safety concerns can be addressed afterward
Refuse to respond to the call during an active tornado warning, since the entire warning area should be treated as equally unsafe throughout
Respond at once and begin patient care regardless of the severe weather, the patient's needs outweighing the storm danger
questions.explanation: Scene safety extends to environmental hazards, and an active tornado warning represents a real, potentially lethal threat to the crew, so responding blindly into that risk can result in the crew themselves becoming casualties, which helps no one and can further strain already-stretched emergency resources. The appropriate approach is to coordinate response timing with dispatch or incident command (who may have better real-time information on storm tracking), take appropriate shelter if a tornado is imminent or bearing down on the response route or scene, and then proceed with patient care once conditions are reasonably safe to operate in. Blanket refusal to ever respond during a warning is overly rigid and ignores that many warnings cover broad areas without an imminent, localized threat, while ignoring weather guidance altogether abandons basic scene-safety judgment in favor of an unsafe 'patient care above all' mindset that ultimately serves no one well.

questions.question: You respond to a residence with several aggressive, unrestrained dogs visible in the yard as you approach, and the patient is located inside the home. What is the correct approach?
choices: Attempt to befriend or feed the dogs before entering, since offering food or acting calm will prevent an attack
Request that the dogs be secured and enter only once they are
Enter quickly, hoping the dogs will not notice, since moving quickly minimizes the chance of provoking them
Use physical force against the dogs to clear a path inside, since this is the fastest way to reach the patient
questions.explanation: Aggressive, unrestrained animals are a well-recognized scene hazard, and dog bites/attacks can cause serious injury that removes a crew member from service and delays care for the actual patient, so this hazard must be addressed before crew members expose themselves to it. The correct approach is to request that a resident, animal control, or law enforcement secure the animals (in a separate room, a kennel, or physically restrained) before EMS enters, ensuring crew safety is established first without unnecessarily delaying overall patient care. Rushing in and hoping to avoid notice, attempting to befriend or distract unfamiliar aggressive animals, or using physical force against them are all unpredictable and unsafe strategies that increase the likelihood of a serious bite injury to the crew.

questions.question: At a scene involving a suspected clandestine drug lab (evidenced by unusual chemical smells and improvised lab equipment visible through a window), what is the correct EMS action upon recognizing these signs?
choices: Open windows and doors to ventilate the structure yourself before entering, so the fumes dissipate enough for safe patient access
Enter the structure to retrieve the patient quickly, drug lab chemical hazards being typically minor
Withdraw to a safe distance, treat it as a hazmat scene, and request hazmat and law enforcement before doing anything else
Attempt to collect samples of the chemicals for identification so responding hazmat crews know what they are dealing with
questions.explanation: Clandestine drug labs (such as methamphetamine labs) commonly involve volatile, toxic, corrosive, and sometimes explosive chemicals, along with booby traps and armed occupants in some cases, making them one of the more dangerous hazardous scenes an EMT can encounter — the danger is often far greater than it appears from the chemical smell or visible equipment alone. Recognizing the warning signs (unusual chemical odors, improvised glassware/equipment, ventilation modifications) should prompt immediate withdrawal to a safe distance and treating the scene as a hazmat incident, requesting specially trained and equipped hazmat and law enforcement resources rather than attempting entry. Trying to ventilate the structure, collect chemical samples, or enter to retrieve the patient all expose untrained, unprotected EMS personnel to potentially lethal toxic exposure, fire, or explosion risk.

questions.question: You are operating at a highway incident and need to move your ambulance to a safer position. What is a key operational principle regarding ambulance placement at roadway scenes?
choices: Park the ambulance directly at the scene facing oncoming traffic, since this positioning allows the fastest possible departure once the patient is loaded aboard
Angle the ambulance to block the work area from traffic, keep a clear path out, and set out cones, flares and lighting
Ambulance placement has little real bearing on scene safety at roadway incidents, since drivers are responsible for avoiding the scene regardless of parking
Park as far from the scene as space allows, distance alone being what keeps responders safe from oncoming traffic
questions.explanation: Struck-by incidents involving responders and equipment at roadway scenes are a significant and preventable cause of line-of-duty injury and death, which is why deliberate apparatus placement is a core part of highway scene safety rather than an afterthought. Positioning the ambulance (often up-traffic and angled, per local protocol and available space) to create a physical buffer/block between oncoming traffic and the working crew, combined with reflective cones, flares, and appropriate emergency lighting, reduces the risk that a distracted or impaired driver strikes responders or patients. Parking to face oncoming traffic, ignoring placement altogether, or parking so far away that patient access and equipment transport become impractical all fail to balance the competing needs of traffic protection and efficient patient care that thoughtful positioning is meant to achieve.

questions.question: While responding emergency traffic (lights and sirens) to a call, you approach a red light with heavy cross traffic. What is the correct practice regarding intersections during an emergency response?
choices: Proceed through the intersection at normal speed without slowing, since lights and sirens grant the right of way over cross traffic
Increase speed through intersections to minimize the time spent in the danger zone where cross traffic could strike the vehicle
Come to a complete stop, confirm every lane has yielded, and then proceed only when it is clearly safe
Turn off sirens at intersections to avoid startling other drivers, since a quieter approach reduces the chance of a panicked or unpredictable reaction
questions.explanation: Lights and sirens ask other drivers for the right of way; they do not grant it, and they do not suspend the duty to drive with due regard. At a red light that means a complete stop, eye contact with the stopped traffic where possible, and clearing each lane in turn before moving — cross traffic has a green light and no reason to expect you. Intersection collisions are the single most common and most lethal category of ambulance crash, and they happen at speed, to crews who assumed the siren had been heard. Speeding up to shorten the exposure increases both the chance of a collision and its severity, and turning the siren off removes the only warning the cross traffic has.

questions.question: You arrive at a scene involving downed trees and utility lines after a storm, with a patient trapped nearby. Which action best reflects appropriate scene size-up and safety practice?
choices: Have the trapped patient attempt to move themselves away from the wire on their own before you make any contact with them or assess the surrounding scene
Use a wooden tree branch or similar improvised tool to move the downed wire aside, on the belief that wood does not conduct electricity even when wet
Assume that any wire not currently and visibly sparking or arcing is safe enough to move aside or step over on the direct way toward the trapped patient nearby
Treat every downed wire as energized until the utility company says otherwise; hold a safe perimeter and wait for the utility crew
questions.explanation: A downed power line can be fully energized and lethal even without visible sparking, arcing, or any other obvious sign of activity, which is why the only safe assumption is that every downed wire is live until the utility company or a qualified authority explicitly confirms it has been de-energized. The correct scene management is to establish and maintain a safe perimeter well clear of the wire and any conductive surfaces (including wet ground) it may be in contact with, and to wait for the utility company or trained personnel before approaching the patient if lines are near them. Assuming safety from lack of sparking, attempting to move the wire personally with an improvised tool like a wooden branch (which does not reliably insulate against high voltage, especially if wet), or instructing the patient to move themselves through a potentially electrified area all risk a second casualty or the patient's electrocution.

questions.question: A patient involved in a fall from standing height is found alert, but you notice unequal chest rise with each breath and use of accessory muscles, though the patient denies any breathing difficulty. What should guide your primary assessment interpretation?
choices: Rely solely on the patient's own verbal denial of breathing difficulty and move on directly to the next assessment step without any further scrutiny of the exam finding
Delay assessing the patient's breathing any further, since the fact that he remains alert and speaking suggests his ventilation is currently adequate
Assume the unequal chest rise observed is simply a normal anatomical variant unique to this particular patient and therefore not worth any further investigation right now
Trust the objective findings — unequal chest rise, accessory muscle use — over his denial, since patients underreport
questions.explanation: The primary assessment is built around objective, observable signs of adequate perfusion and ventilation precisely because patient self-report can be unreliable — pain, adrenaline, altered perception, or even denial/minimization can cause a patient to underreport symptoms that are objectively present. Unequal chest rise and accessory muscle use are hard physical findings suggestive of a significant chest injury (such as a pneumothorax, hemothorax, or flail segment) that can worsen rapidly even in a patient who is currently alert and speaking in full sentences, so these findings should drive the EMT's clinical concern and management (high-flow oxygen, close reassessment, rapid transport) regardless of what the patient reports. Dismissing the finding as a normal variant or delaying further evaluation because the patient is talking both ignore objective red flags that fall directly within the scope of the primary assessment's breathing evaluation.

questions.question: You are assisting ventilations on an obese patient and struggle to maintain an adequate BVM mask seal using a one-handed technique. What is the most effective correction?
choices: Switch to a two-rescuer BVM technique, with one provider maintaining the mask seal with both hands while the second squeezes the bag
Switch to a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min while you reposition the patient
Use a smaller mask than indicated for the patient's face, since a smaller mask is easier to seal completely against the face
Increase the oxygen flow rate to the bag to compensate for the poor mask seal and leaking air
questions.explanation: A one-handed mask seal (the 'C-E' grip with one hand) is inherently harder to maintain on patients with anatomical challenges like obesity, facial hair, or edentulous features, because a larger or irregular facial contour makes it difficult for one hand alone to both maintain jaw thrust/head position and press the mask evenly against the face. Switching to a two-rescuer technique — one provider using both hands to achieve and maintain an optimal seal while dedicating full attention to airway positioning, and a second provider dedicated solely to squeezing the bag — reliably produces a better seal and more effective tidal volume delivery, and is the standard correction taught for exactly this problem. Abandoning BVM ventilation in favor of a nonrebreather mask does not provide positive pressure ventilation for a patient who needs assisted breathing, using an undersized mask worsens rather than improves the seal, and increasing oxygen flow does nothing to fix a mechanical seal/leak problem.

questions.question: A patient with a suspected pneumothorax after blunt trauma has an SpO2 of 91% on a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min, with increasing work of breathing. What should this trend suggest about the adequacy of the current oxygen delivery method?
choices: The current oxygen delivery method is fully adequate as-is, and no change in monitoring, escalation, or intervention is needed despite the low SpO2 and the rising work of breathing observed
The trend suggests the underlying problem (developing pneumothorax) may be progressing beyond what passive oxygen alone can correct
The nonrebreather mask currently in use should be replaced with a nasal cannula, since a lower-flow device may be better tolerated given his ongoing distress
The SpO2 reading itself should be disregarded as inaccurate in this patient, since pulse oximetry is often unreliable in trauma patients like this one
questions.explanation: A nonrebreather mask delivers a high concentration of supplemental oxygen to a spontaneously breathing patient, but it cannot compensate for a mechanical ventilation problem — if a pneumothorax is progressively collapsing lung tissue or, worse, developing tension physiology, the patient's SpO2 remaining low (91%) and their work of breathing increasing despite maximal passive oxygen delivery is a warning sign that the underlying pathology is outpacing what oxygen alone can fix. This trend should prompt the EMT to closely monitor for further deterioration and be prepared to assist ventilations with a BVM (and, depending on scope/protocol, needle decompression by more advanced providers) if the patient's breathing becomes inadequate, rather than assuming the current therapy will remain sufficient. Disregarding the SpO2 reading or switching to a lower-concentration nasal cannula for 'comfort' would both be inappropriate responses to a worsening, potentially life-threatening trend that calls for escalation, not de-escalation, of respiratory support.

questions.question: A patient with COPD and long-standing barrel chest deformity presents with acute worsening dyspnea, and you are unable to clearly assess for a pneumothorax by chest rise alone due to the chronic deformity. What should guide your assessment in this case?
choices: Skip any further respiratory assessment, since the barrel chest deformity makes any meaningful evaluation of this patient's breathing impossible
Assume that no pneumothorax is possible in patients with COPD, since their lungs are already so chronically diseased that a further acute lung injury like pneumothorax essentially cannot occur
Chest rise alone should always remain the sole determinant used to assess for a pneumothorax, regardless of the patient's known baseline chest wall anatomy or overall shape

Rely on a combination of findings — auscultation for symmetry of breath sounds, SpO2, mental status, and the patient's reported baseline — rather than chest rise alone, given the altered baseline anatomy
questions.explanation: The classic barrel-chest deformity of chronic COPD (from years of air trapping and hyperinflation) permanently alters chest wall shape and baseline movement, which makes subtle asymmetries in chest rise much harder to detect visually compared to a patient with normal chest anatomy. In this situation, the EMT should broaden the assessment to a combination of findings — auscultating for symmetry (or asymmetry) of breath sounds between the two lung fields, trending SpO2, evaluating mental status for signs of hypoxia, and comparing current presentation against the patient's known baseline — rather than relying on a single sign that is unreliable in this population. COPD patients are actually at increased risk for spontaneous pneumothorax due to bullae and weakened lung tissue, so assuming it cannot occur is incorrect, and simply abandoning assessment because one sign is hard to interpret ignores the other reliable tools still available to the EMT.

questions.question: A patient in cardiac arrest is being ventilated with a BVM while compressions continue without an advanced airway in place. What is the correct approach to timing ventilations relative to compressions in adult two-rescuer CPR without an advanced airway?
choices: Deliver one breath for every 5 compressions on a continuous, uninterrupted cycle throughout the resuscitation
Ventilate once every 2 minutes, at each rhythm check
Ventilate continuously with the BVM without any pause in chest compressions, delivering breaths whenever convenient
Pause compressions briefly to give 2 breaths after every 30 compressions
questions.explanation: Current adult CPR guidelines call for a 30:2 compression-to-ventilation ratio for both one- and two-rescuer CPR when no advanced airway (such as a supraglottic airway or endotracheal tube) is in place, meaning compressions pause briefly after every 30 compressions to deliver 2 ventilations with a BVM before compressions resume. This ratio balances the critical need for high-quality, minimally interrupted chest compressions (which generate the blood flow that keeps vital organs perfused) against the also-important need for adequate ventilation and oxygenation, and it changes only once an advanced airway is placed, at which point ventilations become asynchronous (roughly one breath every 6 seconds) with continuous, uninterrupted compressions. Ventilating continuously without pausing compressions, using a 1:5 ratio, or ventilating only once every 2 minutes are all inconsistent with the evidence-based 30:2 ratio and would compromise either oxygenation or the quality/continuity of compressions.

questions.question: A patient with new-onset facial droop and slurred speech has a blood glucose of 38 mg/dL. After treating the hypoglycemia, the facial droop and slurred speech fully resolve within minutes. What does this course suggest?
choices: Hypoglycemia and focal stroke-like neurological symptoms are unrelated physiologic processes, so this rapid resolution was just a coincidence of timing
The neurological symptoms were likely a stroke mimic caused by hypoglycemia
The patient should not be transported since the neurological symptoms have already fully resolved on their own right after the glucose was administered
The patient had a true ischemic stroke that happened to resolve spontaneously on its own within minutes, and since it resolved, this presentation requires no further workup
questions.explanation: Severe hypoglycemia can starve the brain of its primary fuel source and produce focal neurological deficits — including facial droop, slurred speech, and even hemiparesis — that closely mimic an acute ischemic stroke, which is exactly why checking blood glucose is a routine, essential step embedded early in every stroke assessment protocol. The fact that this patient's neurological symptoms resolved rapidly and completely after glucose was corrected strongly supports hypoglycemia as the actual cause rather than a stroke, since a true ischemic stroke would not typically reverse this quickly with glucose alone. This resolution is not coincidental given the well-documented mechanism connecting brain glucose deprivation to focal deficits, and the patient should still be transported for evaluation, since the underlying cause of the hypoglycemia itself (medication error, missed meal, etc.) needs to be identified and the patient monitored for recurrence.

questions.question: A patient has significant bleeding from a scalp laceration, which the patient reports has been bleeding heavily since the injury. How should the EMT approach direct pressure on a scalp wound, especially if there's a possible underlying skull fracture?
choices: Apply direct pressure carefully, around rather than onto the area if a fracture or depressed segment is suspected, to avoid driving fragments inward
Apply a tourniquet snugly and circumferentially around the entire head to control the scalp bleeding, in a manner similar to how one would be applied to a limb injury
Apply firm, direct pressure straight onto the wound itself regardless of any suspected underlying skull fracture or depressed bone segment located beneath the laceration
Leave scalp bleeding alone, scalp bleeding rarely being life-threatening
questions.explanation: Scalp wounds bleed heavily and disproportionately to their size because the scalp is extremely vascular, so bleeding control still matters and can meaningfully contribute to hypovolemia if left unaddressed, especially in children or with prolonged bleeding. However, if there is any suspicion of an underlying skull fracture — particularly a depressed fracture where bone fragments may already be displaced inward — firm, direct pressure applied straight onto the fracture site risks pushing bone fragments further into brain tissue, so technique must be modified to a lighter touch or pressure applied around the periphery of the injury rather than directly on a suspected depressed segment. A tourniquet is never appropriate for the head/scalp since there is no way to create circumferential compression of a limb-like structure, and abandoning bleeding control altogether ignores a real, manageable risk simply because the wound is not immediately life-threatening in every case.

questions.question: A patient with suspected traumatic brain injury has vomited once and is at risk for aspiration, but also has a suspected spinal injury requiring motion restriction. How should the EMT manage the airway in this situation?
choices: Withhold spinal motion restriction because of the vomiting risk present, since airway management cannot be safely combined with spinal precautions
Keep the patient strictly supine and rely on suction alone, since spinal precautions come before turning him
Be ready to log-roll him, keeping alignment, to clear the airway if he vomits again — the airway takes priority
Insert an oropharyngeal airway despite the gag reflex, so vomit cannot block the airway
questions.explanation: In EMS's hierarchy of priorities, airway always comes first — an obstructed or aspirated airway kills faster than almost any other single problem, including an unstabilized spinal injury, so airway protection takes precedence even in a patient who also requires spinal motion restriction. The correct technique when vomiting occurs or is anticipated is to log-roll the patient as a coordinated unit (maintaining inline spinal alignment throughout the maneuver) onto their side long enough to clear the airway, then return them to a supine position with continued spinal precautions, rather than either abandoning spinal precautions entirely or rigidly keeping the patient supine and allowing aspiration. Inserting an oropharyngeal airway in a patient who still has an intact gag reflex would provoke further vomiting or gagging and is contraindicated; an OPA is reserved for patients without a gag reflex.

questions.question: You are treating a combative patient with a significant head injury who is refusing spinal motion restriction and other necessary care, and his combativeness appears to be caused by the injury itself rather than by a separate, informed refusal. How should the EMT approach this situation?
choices: Abandon all further care on the strength of the patient's verbal refusal at this moment, treating the outburst as a legally binding refusal
Treat the head injury as impairing his capacity to refuse, so no informed refusal is possible, and proceed under implied consent with law enforcement if needed
Wait indefinitely on scene for the patient to spontaneously calm down before providing any care, regardless of how his underlying head injury may already be worsening in the meantime
Restrain the patient physically using any means available without ever considering safety, proportionality, or whether a genuinely less restrictive option might be available and appropriate
questions.explanation: For a refusal to be legally valid, the patient must have decision-making capacity — the ability to understand their condition, the risks of refusing care, and the consequences of that decision — and a traumatic brain injury causing combativeness and altered mental status is a classic example of an injury that itself strips the patient of that capacity, meaning the 'refusal' is not a legally protected informed choice. In this circumstance, implied consent applies (as it would for any patient unable to make a valid decision due to their medical condition), allowing the EMT to proceed with necessary care using the safest, least restrictive approach possible, and calling for additional resources such as law enforcement if needed to manage safety during treatment and restraint if required. Abandoning care entirely, waiting indefinitely while a head-injured patient potentially deteriorates, or restraining the patient with excessive or disproportionate force are all inappropriate responses that either neglect a patient who cannot truly refuse or create unnecessary additional harm.

questions.question: A woman at approximately 12 weeks gestation presents with vaginal bleeding, cramping, and passage of tissue. What is the most likely process occurring, and what is the priority for EMS?
choices: An indication for an immediate cesarean delivery to be performed by the EMT right there at the scene, given the described severity of the bleeding and tissue passage
A normal, benign finding of pregnancy at this gestational age requiring no evaluation, monitoring, or transport whatsoever from the responding EMS crew on scene
Preterm labor requiring the EMT to administer a tocolytic medication on scene in an attempt to stop the ongoing uterine contractions before beginning transport
A likely miscarriage; supportive care, watch for shock, emotional support, and transport with any passed tissue
questions.explanation: Vaginal bleeding accompanied by cramping and the passage of tissue in the first half of pregnancy (before roughly 20 weeks) is the classic presentation of a spontaneous abortion (miscarriage), and this combination of findings together is what distinguishes it from simple spotting or a benign finding requiring no concern. EMS priorities center on treating this as a genuine medical and emotional emergency: monitoring vital signs closely for developing hypovolemic shock from blood loss, providing calm and compassionate emotional support given the significant psychological impact of pregnancy loss, and transporting the patient along with any passed tissue (which can aid in medical evaluation) to a facility for definitive assessment. EMTs have no scope-of-practice role administering tocolytic medications or performing any form of delivery/surgical intervention, so those options describe interventions entirely outside EMT training and authority.

questions.question: A 3-year-old presents with sudden onset of stridor and drooling while playing with small toys, with no fever and a sudden onset over minutes rather than hours. How does this presentation help differentiate the likely cause from epiglottitis or croup?
choices: It cannot be differentiated from an infectious cause in any meaningful way, so treatment approach and transport priority would stay the same either way
Sudden onset without fever, while playing with small objects, points to a foreign body rather than croup or epiglottitis, which build over hours
