questions.explanation: A brief pause after keying prevents the first words from being cut off while the system establishes the transmission. Speaking immediately clips the message, holding the microphone against the lips distorts the audio, and rushing makes the message unintelligible.

questions.question: Which of the following details is most useful to the receiving facility when a patient was extricated from a vehicle?
choices: The mechanism, intrusion, and time required for extrication
The make and model of the vehicle involved
The tools that were used by the rescue crew
The name of the towing company that responded
questions.explanation: Mechanism, compartment intrusion, and entrapment time all inform the hospital's expectation of hidden injuries and crush effects. Tool selection, towing details, and vehicle model do not change the clinical evaluation.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct action when smoke is visible coming from an occupied structure?
choices: Enter to search for patients while wearing a surgical mask
Stage at a safe distance and wait for fire suppression
Enter the rooms where smoke is not yet visible
Have bystanders bring the patients out to the ambulance
questions.explanation: Structure fires require self-contained breathing apparatus and fire training, neither of which EMS crews carry, so staging is the only safe option. Masked entry, partial entry, and directing bystanders inside all send unprotected people into a toxic and unpredictable environment.

questions.question: Select the (2) circumstances in which a patient's information may be disclosed without his specific permission.
choices: To satisfy a mandatory reporting law for suspected abuse
To a family member who arrives after transport
To the clinicians assuming his care at the hospital
To a coworker who is curious about the outcome
To a reporter who asks for a statement at the scene
questions.explanation: Disclosure to the clinicians continuing care and disclosure required by a mandatory reporting law are both permitted. Coworker curiosity and a reporter's request never justify disclosure. A family member who arrives after transport is not automatically entitled to the information: HIPAA lets you share what is relevant with family involved in the patient's care when he agrees or does not object, or by professional judgment if he cannot, which is a judgment call rather than a standing permission.

questions.question: Select the (2) actions expected of the first arriving unit before additional resources arrive at a large incident.
choices: Transport the nearest patient to clear the scene
Begin definitive treatment of the first critical patient
Establish command and identify a staging location
Provide a scene size-up report over the radio
Assign a bystander to stay with each patient
questions.explanation: A size-up report tells incoming units what they are facing, and establishing command with a staging location organizes their arrival. Committing to treatment of one patient or transporting early removes the only crew available to organize the response. Assigning a bystander to each patient is not a first-unit task.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the purpose of body substance isolation practices?
choices: To make patients feel more confident in the crew
To satisfy a hospital requirement for facility entry
To keep uniforms clean during patient contact
To prevent transmission of infection during contact
questions.explanation: These practices create a barrier against pathogens moving in either direction between provider and patient. Uniform cleanliness, patient perception, and facility access requirements are incidental rather than the purpose.

questions.question: Which of the following should be documented when a patient is transferred to another EMS unit?
choices: The names and roles of everyone present at the time of the transfer
The receiving provider's level and the time of transfer
The reason the original crew was unable to continue
The distance the original crew traveled to the scene
questions.explanation: Recording who assumed care, at what level, and when demonstrates that the transfer was to an equal or higher level of care. Crew availability reasons, travel distance, and a list of bystanders do not establish the validity of the transfer.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the greatest risk to EMS providers during highway operations?
choices: Lacerations from broken glass around the vehicle
Exposure to fuel vapors from a damaged vehicle
Back injury from lifting patients on uneven ground
Being struck by a passing vehicle while working
questions.explanation: Being struck by traffic accounts for the most severe and fatal injuries at roadway incidents, which is why blocking and visibility measures exist. Vapor exposure, lifting injuries, and lacerations are real hazards but rarely produce comparable outcomes.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate response when a patient asks whether he is going to die?
choices: Avoid answering and change the subject
Promise the patient that everything will certainly be fine
Tell the patient it is not appropriate to discuss it
Answer honestly without false reassurance while remaining supportive
questions.explanation: Honest, compassionate acknowledgment respects the patient while providing reassurance that he will not be abandoned. False promises destroy trust if things deteriorate, deflection isolates the patient, and refusing the conversation is dismissive.

questions.question: Which of the following is the appropriate action when two agencies give conflicting instructions at an incident?
choices: Follow the direction of the established incident commander
Ask the patient which approach he prefers
Choose the instruction that seems most practical
Follow whichever instruction was received first
questions.explanation: A single incident commander exists precisely to resolve conflicting direction, so the command structure governs. Timing of receipt, individual judgment about practicality, and patient preference cannot substitute for a unified command decision.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes appropriate documentation of a patient's mental health complaint?
choices: Objective description of behavior and the patient's own words
A diagnostic label based on the provider's impression
A judgment about whether the complaint is genuine
A summary of the provider's advice to the patient
questions.explanation: Describing observed behavior and quoting the patient gives the receiving team accurate information without imposing an untrained diagnosis. Labels, credibility judgments, and advice summaries all inject opinion into what should be a factual record.

questions.question: Which of the following is the appropriate action when a patient must be carried down an icy exterior staircase?
choices: Have one provider carry the patient while another spots
Move quickly to limit the time spent on the ice
Use a wheeled stretcher to roll down the steps
Request additional personnel and clear or treat the surface first
questions.explanation: Extra hands and a treated surface control the hazard before anyone carries a load down a slippery incline. Rushing, single-provider carries, and rolling a wheeled stretcher down steps all increase the chance of dropping the patient and injuring the crew.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes why a patient tracking system is used at a large incident?
choices: It records where each patient was transported for later accounting
It assigns each patient to a triage category
It determines which patients receive treatment first
It identifies which crew performed the best triage
questions.explanation: Tracking prevents patients from being lost in the system and allows families and investigators to locate them afterward. Treatment priority and triage category are set by triage, and crew evaluation is not the purpose of tracking.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the appropriate action when a patient's advance directive conflicts with the family's wishes?
choices: Follow the valid directive and involve medical direction if needed
Delay all decisions until arrival at the hospital
Ask the family to produce their own written statement
Follow the family's wishes instead, the family being physically present at the scene
questions.explanation: A valid directive reflects the patient's own decision and takes precedence over family preference, with medical direction available for difficult situations. Deferring to family, requesting competing documents, and delaying decisions all subordinate the patient's expressed wishes.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes when a verbal report should be given at the hospital?
choices: Only after the written report has been finished
Only when the patient's condition changed during transport
Before transferring the patient and completing the written record
Only if the receiving staff specifically request one
questions.explanation: The verbal report communicates the essential picture immediately, well before the written record is complete or available. Waiting for documentation, requiring a request, and limiting reports to changed conditions all leave the receiving team without needed information.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the correct response when an ambulance is involved in a collision while transporting a patient?
choices: Continue to the hospital without stopping or reporting
Notify dispatch, assess everyone aboard, and request assistance
Have the patient transferred to a passing vehicle
Wait for the patient to report any new complaints
questions.explanation: Reporting immediately brings additional resources while the crew assesses the patient and themselves for new injuries. Continuing without reporting, using a passing vehicle, and waiting for complaints all fail the patient and violate operational requirements.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the purpose of a debriefing after a difficult call?
choices: To determine which provider made the most errors
To satisfy a specific documentation requirement mandated by the service
To support providers and identify lessons for future calls
To decide who will be assigned to similar calls later
questions.explanation: Debriefings give crews an opportunity to process a difficult event and capture operational lessons. Assigning blame, meeting paperwork requirements, and making future assignments are not the function of the process.

questions.question: Which of the following is the appropriate action when a patient offers a cash gift to the crew?
choices: Accept the gift and quietly donate it to the service anonymously each time
Accept the gift and divide it among the crew members
Decline politely and explain that gifts cannot be accepted
Accept the gift to avoid offending the patient
questions.explanation: Declining politely avoids any perception that care depends on payment, which is why most services prohibit accepting gifts. Accepting and dividing, redirecting the money, or accepting to avoid awkwardness all create the appearance of a conflict.

questions.question: Arrange the components of a standard verbal handoff report in the order they are typically given.
choices: Assessment findings and vital signs
Pertinent history, allergies, and medications
Age, sex, and chief complaint
Treatments given and the patient's response
questions.explanation: The report opens with who the patient is and why he called, moves to relevant history that shapes interpretation, then presents examination findings and vital signs, and closes with what was done and how the patient responded.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the correct use of a power stretcher?
choices: Use a single provider whenever the device is powered
Disable the safety features to speed the loading process
Follow the weight limits and use the required number of providers
Exceed the weight limit briefly when necessary for speed
questions.explanation: Powered devices reduce but do not eliminate lifting demands, and their weight ratings and staffing requirements exist because failures occur under overload. Single-provider operation, exceeding the rating, and disabling safety features all invite catastrophic drops.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the concept of proximate cause in a negligence claim?
choices: The provider was the closest person to the patient
The provider was the first to arrive on the scene
The provider's action or omission directly led to the harm
The harm occurred near the location of the incident
questions.explanation: Proximate cause requires a direct causal link between the breach of duty and the resulting harm, which is often the hardest element to establish. Physical proximity, geographic location, and arrival order are unrelated to the legal meaning of the term.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate handling of a request for information from a family member by phone?
choices: Confirm only whether the patient was transported
Provide a summary of the patient's condition immediately
Give the information if the caller states the patient's name
Decline to confirm details and refer them to the hospital
questions.explanation: Identity cannot be verified over the phone, so information is not released and the caller is directed to the facility. Providing a summary, confirming transport, and relying on a stated name all risk disclosing protected information to an unverified person.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate documentation when a patient is found deceased and resuscitation is not attempted?
choices: The crew's agreement that the effort would have been futile
The specific findings that indicated resuscitation was not indicated
A note that the family requested no resuscitation be attempted
A statement that the patient appeared to be beyond help
questions.explanation: Documenting the objective signs, such as rigor mortis or dependent lividity, establishes the basis for the decision. General impressions, crew consensus, and family statements do not provide the objective justification a record requires.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes appropriate use of a stair chair with a bariatric patient?
choices: Have the patient walk while providers support each arm
Use two separate stair chairs side by side for added total carrying capacity
Verify the device's rating and use additional trained personnel
Use the device regardless of the manufacturer's weight limit
questions.explanation: Matching the device rating to the patient and adding trained hands prevents equipment failure and provider injury. Exceeding the rating risks structural failure, walking an unstable patient on stairs is dangerous, and two chairs cannot be combined into one device.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate response when a family member records video of patient care?
choices: Continue care and address privacy concerns without confrontation
Stop treatment until the recording is turned off
Seize the device to protect the patient's privacy
Demand that the family member delete the recording
questions.explanation: Patient care continues while privacy concerns are raised calmly, since interrupting treatment harms the patient. Stopping care, seizing property, and demanding deletion all escalate the situation and create additional legal exposure.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the correct approach when hospital destinations must be chosen during a multiple-casualty incident?
choices: Match patient acuity to facility capability across several hospitals
Send all patients to the closest emergency department
Allow each crew to choose independently without coordination
Send all critical patients to the same trauma center
questions.explanation: Distributing patients according to acuity and each facility's capability prevents any single hospital from being overwhelmed. Sending everyone to the nearest facility, concentrating all critical patients in one place, and uncoordinated choices all defeat that purpose.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes what should be recorded about the treatments provided?
choices: The names of everyone present on the scene
What was done, when, and how the patient responded
Only the treatments that produced improvement
A general summary without specific times
questions.explanation: Intervention, timing, and response together let the receiving team understand what has been tried and what worked. Recording only successes distorts the picture, omitting times removes the sequence, and a list of everyone on scene says nothing about the treatment.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why an ambulance should be parked with the exhaust away from the working area?
choices: Exhaust creates a fire hazard on dry pavement
Exhaust carbon monoxide can affect crew and patient
Exhaust noise interferes with the crew's radio transmissions
Exhaust heat can damage nearby medical equipment
questions.explanation: Exhaust contains carbon monoxide, which accumulates in still air and can affect anyone working nearby. Radio interference, equipment heat damage, and pavement fire risk are not the reasons for this positioning practice.

questions.question: Which of the following would most clearly establish that a duty to act existed?
choices: A provider observed an emergency while driving off duty and chose not to stop
The crew was dispatched and arrived at the patient's side
A provider discussed a symptom with a friend socially
A provider received a phone call about a distant incident
questions.explanation: Being dispatched and making patient contact while on duty creates an unambiguous duty to act. Observing an emergency off duty, informal social conversation, and receiving a call about a remote incident do not establish that obligation in most jurisdictions.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate radio report for a critical trauma patient?
choices: Report delayed until the patient is fully packaged
Report given if the trauma team requests one
Detailed report covering the complete history and all findings
Brief report emphasizing mechanism, findings, and estimated arrival
questions.explanation: A short report with mechanism, key findings, and arrival time lets the trauma team assemble before the patient arrives. Exhaustive detail, delaying until packaging is complete, and waiting for a request all reduce the preparation time available.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best reason to document the position in which a patient was transported?
choices: It may be clinically relevant to the patient's condition
It justifies the time spent at the scene
It records which crew member packaged the patient
It demonstrates that the crew followed the stretcher manual exactly
questions.explanation: Transport position affects breathing, perfusion, and spinal considerations, so it is clinically meaningful information. Equipment compliance, packaging assignments, and scene time justification are not why the detail matters.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the appropriate response when a provider feels unsafe at a scene that has already been entered?
choices: Complete the assessment quickly and then withdraw
Withdraw to a safe location and request law enforcement
Ask the patient directly whether the situation is actually dangerous first
Continue working while remaining alert for changes
questions.explanation: A provider's recognition that a scene has become unsafe is acted on immediately by withdrawing and requesting help. Finishing an assessment first, continuing while alert, and seeking reassurance from the patient all keep the crew in a deteriorating environment.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the relationship between certification and licensure?
choices: Certification and licensure are interchangeable terms
Licensure verifies training and certification permits practice
Certification verifies competency and licensure grants legal authority
Certification is issued by the employer and licensure by the crew chief
questions.explanation: Certification attests that a standard of training and testing has been met, while licensure is the state's grant of legal permission to practice. The terms are not interchangeable, the definitions are not reversed, and neither is issued by an employer or crew chief.

questions.question: Which of the following should be reported immediately to command at an incident?
choices: The number of supplies used from the ambulance
A patient's request to be taken to a particular hospital
Discovery of a hazard that affects responder safety
A crew member's question about the next shift
questions.explanation: A newly discovered hazard affects every responder on scene and must reach command without delay. Supply usage, a patient's hospital preference, and shift questions are not immediate operational concerns.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the correct approach when responding to a scene where a patient may have been exposed to a radiological source?
choices: Assume the exposure is harmless if the patient feels well
Limit time near the source, maximize distance, and use shielding
Treat the patient at the source to avoid moving contamination
Approach as quickly as possible to minimize the patient's total radiation exposure
questions.explanation: Time, distance, and shielding are the fundamental principles of radiation protection and apply to responders as well as patients. Rapid approach, treating at the source, and assuming safety from the patient's appearance all increase responder dose unnecessarily.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate response when a patient's story changes between the scene and the hospital?
choices: Record only the version given at the scene
Ask the patient to confirm which version is actually accurate later
Record only the version given at the hospital
Document both versions with the times they were given
questions.explanation: Documenting both accounts with their timing preserves information that may be clinically or legally significant. Selecting one version discards data, and pressing the patient to choose assumes he is able or willing to resolve the difference.

questions.question: Which of the following is primarily an ethical rather than a legal obligation?
choices: Documenting a refusal of care accurately in the record
Providing the same standard of care regardless of a patient's background
Reporting suspected abuse of a child to the proper authority
Obtaining consent before treating a competent adult
questions.explanation: Treating every patient equally regardless of background is primarily an ethical commitment, though discrimination can also carry legal consequences. Mandatory reporting, consent, and accurate documentation are all defined and enforceable legal duties.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate use of a helicopter landing zone?
choices: A cleared level area free of wires and loose debris
An area near trees to shelter the aircraft from wind
The nearest paved road regardless of the surroundings
A sloped field that allows water to drain away
questions.explanation: Rotor wash turns loose debris into projectiles and overhead wires are a primary cause of aircraft accidents, so a clear level area is required. Roads with adjacent hazards, tree-sheltered areas, and sloped ground all create risks during landing.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the safest practice when lifting a patient with a partner of different height?
choices: Lift at different times to reduce the peak load
Have the taller provider take most of the weight
Coordinate the lift with clear commands and adjust hand positions
Have the shorter provider lift from the head end
questions.explanation: Clear communication and adjusted grips keep the load level and shared, which protects both providers. Unequal loading, staggered timing, and fixed position assignments based on height all produce uneven forces and unstable lifts.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes why the time of each intervention should be documented?
choices: It determines the reimbursement rate for the transport
It records which provider performed each intervention
It allows the response to treatment to be evaluated over time
It demonstrates how efficiently the crew worked
questions.explanation: Timing lets anyone reviewing the record connect each intervention to the change that followed it, which is how effectiveness is judged. Crew efficiency, reimbursement, and provider attribution are secondary to that clinical purpose.

questions.question: Which structure provides oxygen and nutrients to the fetus?
choices: The perineum
The cervix
The amniotic sac
The placenta
questions.explanation: The placenta is the interface where oxygen and nutrients pass from maternal to fetal circulation and waste passes back. The amniotic sac contains protective fluid, the cervix is the opening of the uterus, and the perineum is external tissue.

questions.question: Which finding indicates that delivery is imminent?
choices: Contractions occurring every ten minutes
The mother's report that her water broke an hour ago
A history of two previous full-term deliveries
Crowning of the infant's head at the vaginal opening
questions.explanation: Visible crowning means the presenting part is at the opening and delivery will occur within moments, so preparation happens on scene. Contractions ten minutes apart, ruptured membranes an hour ago, and a delivery history all suggest labor without indicating it is imminent.

questions.question: What is the correct action once the infant's head delivers?
choices: Pull gently on the head to speed the delivery
Insert a finger into the mouth to clear the airway
Support the head and check for a cord around the neck
Ask the mother to stop pushing until transport arrives
questions.explanation: Supporting the head and checking for a nuchal cord prevents strangulation as the body delivers. Traction on the head can injure the infant, delivery cannot be stopped once the head has emerged, and blind finger sweeps risk injury.

questions.question: A cord is found wrapped tightly around the infant's neck and cannot be slipped over the head. What is the appropriate action?
choices: Wait for the remainder of the delivery before addressing it
Pull the infant through the loop as quickly as possible
Push the infant's head back to relieve the tension
Clamp the cord in two places and cut between the clamps
questions.explanation: A tight nuchal cord that cannot be reduced is clamped and cut so the body can deliver without strangulation. Pulling the infant through, waiting, and pushing the head back all allow continued compression of the cord and the infant's neck.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate care for a newborn who is crying vigorously?
choices: Perform chest compressions right away until a pulse can be clearly confirmed
Dry, warm, and place the infant skin to skin with the mother
Suction the mouth and nose deeply with a rigid catheter
Begin positive pressure ventilation with a pediatric bag
questions.explanation: A vigorous crying newborn needs warmth, drying, and contact with the mother, since heat loss is the primary threat. Ventilation, deep suctioning, and compressions are all interventions for a newborn who is not breathing or has a low heart rate.

questions.question: Which finding in a pregnant patient at 34 weeks is most concerning?
choices: Painless bright red vaginal bleeding
Mild swelling of both ankles at the end of the day
Occasional irregular contractions that stop with rest
Increased frequency of urination during the day
questions.explanation: Painless bright red bleeding in the third trimester suggests placenta previa, which can hemorrhage rapidly. Ankle swelling, irregular contractions that resolve with rest, and urinary frequency are all common in late pregnancy.

questions.question: A pregnant patient at 36 weeks has a headache, visual changes, and a blood pressure of 168 over 106. What is the greatest concern?
choices: A migraine unrelated to the pregnancy itself
An infection causing the elevated blood pressure reading
Dehydration from inadequate fluid intake during pregnancy
Progression to seizures from a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy
questions.explanation: Hypertension with headache and visual disturbance late in pregnancy indicates preeclampsia, which can progress to seizures that threaten both mother and fetus. Dehydration, infection, and migraine do not explain this combination of findings in the third trimester.

questions.question: Why should a pregnant patient in the third trimester be transported tilted to the left?
choices: The position reduces the mother's nausea during transport
The uterus can compress the vena cava when she lies flat
The position prevents the amniotic sac from rupturing
The left side improves the fetal position for delivery
questions.explanation: A supine position allows the gravid uterus to compress the inferior vena cava, reducing venous return and blood pressure. The tilt is not about fetal positioning, nausea control, or membrane integrity.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes appropriate management of the placenta after delivery?
choices: Let it deliver on its own and bring it along
Discard it once delivery is complete
Delay transport until it has fully delivered
Pull firmly on the cord to speed its delivery
questions.explanation: The placenta delivers spontaneously and is transported for examination, since missing fragments indicate a risk of ongoing bleeding. Cord traction can cause inversion or hemorrhage, discarding it loses clinical information, and transport is not delayed waiting for it.

questions.question: During delivery, a single arm presents at the vaginal opening. What is the appropriate action?
choices: Transport immediately in a knee-chest or hips-elevated position
Push the presenting arm back in and rotate the infant inside using firm manual pressure
Wait on scene for the rest of the infant to deliver on its own
Apply gentle traction to the arm to complete the delivery
questions.explanation: A limb presentation cannot deliver vaginally in the field and requires surgical delivery, so rapid transport with positioning to reduce cord compression is the priority. Manipulating the limb, applying traction, and waiting on scene all risk fetal death and maternal injury.

questions.question: Which is a normal heart rate range for an infant under one year of age?
choices: 100 to 160 beats per minute
180 to 220 beats per minute
40 to 70 beats per minute, similar to a resting adult
60 to 100 beats per minute
questions.explanation: Infants maintain a higher baseline rate because their stroke volume is small and output depends heavily on rate. The adult range is too slow for an infant, rates in the forties indicate severe bradycardia, and sustained rates above 180 suggest a dysrhythmia or severe distress.

questions.question: Which finding in a child indicates the most severe respiratory compromise?
choices: A respiratory rate at the upper end of normal for age
Nasal flaring during periods of crying
Mild intercostal retractions at rest
Bradycardia developing during respiratory distress
questions.explanation: A slowing heart rate in a child who is working hard to breathe signals hypoxia severe enough to depress cardiac function, which precedes arrest. Flaring, a rate at the upper limit of normal, and mild retractions all indicate increased effort without that degree of compromise.

questions.question: Why is hypotension a late sign of shock in children?
choices: Blood pressure cuffs read falsely high in small children
Children lose blood more slowly than adults do
Children have larger blood volumes relative to their size
Children compensate strongly with vasoconstriction and tachycardia
questions.explanation: Efficient compensatory mechanisms maintain pressure until a large volume deficit exists, after which decompensation is abrupt. Children have smaller absolute blood volumes, cuff readings are not systematically high with correct sizing, and blood loss is not inherently slower.

questions.question: What is the correct compression depth for a child during CPR?
choices: About one third of the depth of the chest
The same depth used for an adult patient regardless of body size
About one inch regardless of chest size
As deep as a palpable pulse requires
questions.explanation: Pediatric compression depth is proportional, about one third of the anterior-posterior chest diameter, which accounts for widely varying body sizes. A fixed inch is too shallow for most children, adult depth is excessive for small chests, and pulse palpation during compressions is unreliable.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the correct approach to assessing a frightened toddler?
choices: Complete the entire assessment while the child is lying supine alone
Assess from least to most distressing while the parent holds him
Begin with the most painful area to complete it quickly
Separate the child from the parent to reduce distraction
questions.explanation: Keeping the child with a caregiver and moving from least to most distressing preserves cooperation for the parts of the exam that matter most. Separation, starting with painful areas, and isolating the child supine all escalate distress and make the assessment less reliable.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of cardiac arrest in children?
choices: A primary abnormal heart rhythm
Respiratory failure leading to hypoxia
A congenital valve abnormality
A sudden blockage of a major coronary artery vessel
questions.explanation: Pediatric arrest usually results from progressive respiratory failure and hypoxia rather than a primary cardiac event, which is why airway management is emphasized. Primary dysrhythmias, coronary occlusion, and valve abnormalities are far less common causes in children.

questions.question: Which finding in a febrile child most suggests a serious bacterial infection rather than a routine viral illness?
choices: Irritability that improves when the child is held
Lethargy that persists after the fever is reduced
A runny nose with a mild cough for two days
A temperature of 102 that responds to medication
questions.explanation: Persistent lethargy after fever reduction is a red flag suggesting the child is genuinely ill rather than simply febrile. A responsive fever, upper respiratory symptoms, and irritability that settles with comfort all fit common viral illness.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a febrile seizure?
choices: A seizure occurring in children over the age of ten
A seizure caused directly by a bacterial brain infection
A prolonged focal seizure occurring after the fever resolves
A brief generalized seizure in a young child with a rapid fever rise
questions.explanation: Febrile seizures are brief generalized events in young children, typically associated with a rapidly rising temperature. Prolonged focal events, seizures from direct brain infection, and seizures in older children all fall outside this description and warrant investigation for other causes.

questions.question: Which airway difference makes children more vulnerable to obstruction than adults?
choices: Their tracheas are proportionally wider and shorter
Their epiglottis is smaller and more rigid
Their tongues are proportionally larger in the oral cavity
Their nasal passages are proportionally larger
questions.explanation: A proportionally large tongue occupies more of the small oropharynx and obstructs easily when muscle tone is lost. Pediatric tracheas are narrower rather than wider, the epiglottis is larger and floppier, and the nasal passages are smaller and more easily blocked.

questions.question: Which factor makes an elderly patient more susceptible to a head bleed after a minor fall?
choices: Thicker, denser skull bones that trap blood tightly inside the skull
Increased brain volume within a fixed skull
A higher blood pressure at the time of impact
Brain shrinkage that stretches the bridging veins
questions.explanation: As the brain atrophies with age, the bridging veins stretch across a wider space and tear with relatively minor force. Skull thickness is not what makes these bleeds more likely, blood pressure is not the mechanism, and brain volume decreases rather than expands.

questions.question: Which presentation of a heart attack is more common in elderly patients?
choices: Weakness or confusion without any chest pain
Sharp pain reproduced by pressing the chest wall
Severe crushing chest pain radiating to the arm
Pain that comes on with vigorous exercise and settles with rest
questions.explanation: Older adults frequently present with weakness, confusion, or shortness of breath instead of chest pain, which delays recognition. Classic radiating pain occurs but is less reliable, reproducible pain suggests the chest wall, and exertional-only pain describes stable angina.

questions.question: Which medication class most commonly masks the tachycardia expected in an elderly patient with blood loss?
choices: Beta blockers
Diuretics
Antibiotics
Antihistamines
questions.explanation: Beta blockers blunt the heart's response to sympathetic stimulation, so a bleeding patient may maintain a deceptively normal rate. Diuretics affect volume, antibiotics treat infection, and antihistamines do not prevent the compensatory heart rate rise.

questions.question: Which finding most suggests possible elder abuse or neglect?
choices: A caregiver who asks questions during the assessment
Injuries that do not match the explanation given
A single bruise on the shin of an active patient
A home that is cluttered but has adequate food
questions.explanation: An explanation that does not fit the pattern or severity of injury is the classic warning sign and requires reporting. A single shin bruise, a cluttered but adequately supplied home, and an engaged caregiver are not by themselves indicators of abuse.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate approach to a patient with hearing loss?
choices: Write all questions rather than attempting speech
Face the patient, speak clearly, and avoid shouting
Communicate through a family member present
Speak loudly into the ear from directly behind the patient instead
questions.explanation: Facing the patient allows lip reading and facial cues, and clear speech at a normal volume is more intelligible than shouting, which distorts sound. Speaking from behind removes visual cues, routing everything through family bypasses the patient, and writing everything is unnecessary when speech works.

questions.question: Select the (2) findings that indicate a child is in decompensated shock.
choices: A heart rate at the upper end of normal for age
A blood pressure below the expected range for age
A markedly decreased level of consciousness
Capillary refill of two seconds at the fingertips
Cool hands and feet with a strong central pulse
questions.explanation: Hypotension and a significantly depressed mental status both indicate that compensation has failed in a child. A heart rate at the top of the normal range and a capillary refill of two seconds are both consistent with adequate perfusion. Cool hands and feet with a strong central pulse show compensated, not decompensated, shock.

questions.question: Select the (2) findings that would lead you to prepare for delivery on scene rather than transport.
choices: The mother reports an overwhelming urge to push
The membranes ruptured earlier in the morning
The presenting part is visible at the vaginal opening
Contractions have been occurring for two hours
This is her third baby and labor has started
questions.explanation: A visible presenting part and an uncontrollable urge to push both indicate the second stage of labor with delivery imminent. Two hours of contractions and membranes that ruptured earlier indicate labor is underway without establishing that delivery is about to occur. A third baby suggests labor may move faster, but labor starting is not a sign that delivery is imminent.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct action if the umbilical cord presents before the infant?
choices: Have the mother push harder to complete the delivery
Attempt to push the cord back into the uterus
Clamp and cut the cord to allow the delivery to proceed
Relieve pressure on the cord and transport immediately
questions.explanation: A prolapsed cord is compressed by the presenting part, cutting off fetal oxygen, so a gloved hand relieves the pressure during rapid transport for surgical delivery. Replacing the cord, cutting it, and encouraging pushing all worsen fetal compromise.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most important immediate concern for a newborn after delivery?
choices: Preventing heat loss through drying and warming
Measuring an accurate birth weight
Determining the exact time of delivery
Obtaining a complete set of vital signs
questions.explanation: Newborns lose heat rapidly through a large surface area and wet skin, and hypothermia worsens every other physiological problem. Weight, a full vital sign set, and delivery time are all recorded but none carries the same immediate consequence.

questions.question: A mother is bleeding heavily after delivery of the placenta. Which action is most appropriate?
choices: Delay transport until the bleeding has fully stopped
Massage the uterine fundus and monitor for shock
Pack the vagina with sterile gauze to stop the bleeding
Have the mother sit upright to reduce the blood flow
questions.explanation: Fundal massage stimulates uterine contraction, which clamps the vessels at the placental site and is the primary field treatment for postpartum hemorrhage. Vaginal packing is not performed, upright positioning does not reduce bleeding, and delaying transport wastes time.

questions.question: You are the only rescuer performing CPR on a 4-month-old, and your hands are too small to encircle the infant's chest. Which compression technique should you use?
choices: One hand under the back with the other pressing the upper third of the sternum
The heel of one hand on the lower half of the sternum
Two hands stacked, heel on heel, the way an adult chest is compressed
Two fingers placed over the lower half of the sternum
questions.explanation: The 2025 AHA guidelines eliminated the two-finger technique for infant chest compressions: it did not reliably reach the required depth of about one third of the chest's front-to-back diameter. Two techniques replace it — the two thumb-encircling hands technique, and the heel of one hand — and when the rescuer cannot physically get their hands around the infant's chest, the heel of one hand is what is recommended. Stacking two hands as for an adult delivers far more force than an infant chest can tolerate, and pressing the upper third of the sternum is the wrong landmark at any age.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why children become dehydrated more quickly than adults?
choices: They absorb oral fluids more slowly than adults do
They have larger fluid reserves that empty rapidly
They lose fluid through vomiting rather than through the skin
They have a higher fluid turnover relative to body size
questions.explanation: A higher metabolic rate and greater surface area relative to mass mean children cycle through fluid faster, so losses deplete reserves quickly. They have smaller rather than larger reserves, lose fluid through skin and breathing as well, and absorb oral fluids normally.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate approach to a patient with dementia who becomes agitated during assessment?
choices: Complete the assessment quickly without explanation
Explain the full plan in complete detail before beginning each single step
Restrain the patient to complete the assessment safely
Use a calm voice, simple phrases, and a familiar caregiver
questions.explanation: Simple language, a calm tone, and the presence of a familiar person reduce fear in a patient who cannot process complex information. Detailed explanations overwhelm, restraint escalates agitation, and rushing without explanation increases confusion and resistance.

questions.question: Which factor most increases an elderly patient's risk of medication-related problems?
choices: A written medication list kept on the refrigerator
A single medication taken consistently for many years without changes
An over-the-counter vitamin supplement taken daily
Multiple medications prescribed by different providers
questions.explanation: Multiple prescribers and multiple drugs increase the chance of interactions and duplications that no one is tracking. Long-term use of a single stable medication, a daily vitamin, and maintaining a medication list all reduce rather than increase the risk.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes why an elderly patient may not report significant pain?
choices: Pain nerves are completely absent in older patients
Elderly patients rarely experience painful conditions
Pain medication use eliminates all sensation permanently
Pain perception can be blunted and symptoms are often minimized
questions.explanation: Reduced pain perception combined with a tendency to attribute symptoms to aging leads many older patients to underreport. Pain nerves remain present, painful conditions are more rather than less common with age, and medications do not abolish sensation entirely.

questions.question: Which of the following is the appropriate ventilation rate for a child in respiratory arrest with a pulse?
choices: 6 to 8 breaths per minute
10 breaths per minute
20 to 30 breaths per minute
40 to 50 breaths per minute
questions.explanation: Children require more frequent ventilation than adults because of their higher metabolic rate and oxygen consumption. Ten per minute is the adult rate, six to eight is inadequate for a child, and forty to fifty would cause harmful hyperventilation.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the correct position for a mother about to deliver?
choices: Sitting fully upright on a firm chair
Lying back with knees flexed and thighs apart
Lying flat on her abdomen with both legs fully extended
Standing with support from a family member
questions.explanation: A semi-reclined position with flexed knees provides access to the birth canal and allows control of the delivery. Standing risks dropping the infant, a firm chair blocks access, and a prone position makes delivery impossible.

questions.question: Arrange the steps of caring for a newborn immediately after delivery, from first to last.
choices: Warm, dry and stimulate the infant, positioning the airway and clearing secretions if needed
Assess breathing and heart rate
Keep the infant warm and reassess continuously during transport
Begin positive pressure ventilation if apneic, gasping, or heart rate is below 100
questions.explanation: The initial steps come first and are done together in the opening seconds: warm and dry the infant, replace wet linens, stimulate, and position the airway, clearing secretions only if they block it. Breathing and heart rate are then assessed, and that assessment decides the next step: an infant who is apneic, gasping or has a heart rate below 100 gets positive pressure ventilation. Warming is not a final step; it starts at birth and continues, with repeated reassessment, throughout transport.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate way to communicate with a patient who is blind?
choices: Raise your voice to ensure the patient understands
Speak to the accompanying family member instead
Guide the patient physically without speaking first
Announce your presence and describe what you are about to do
questions.explanation: Announcing yourself and narrating each step gives the patient the information sight would normally provide. Touching without warning is startling, directing conversation to family bypasses the patient, and volume has nothing to do with vision.

questions.question: Which of the following should raise suspicion of child abuse during an assessment?
choices: A parent who appears anxious about the child's condition
A scraped knee in a child who was learning to ride a bike
A bruise on the forehead of a toddler who is walking
A delay in seeking care that is not explained
questions.explanation: An unexplained delay between injury and seeking care is a recognized warning sign that warrants careful documentation and reporting. Scraped knees, parental anxiety, and forehead bruises in walking toddlers are all common and expected findings.

questions.question: Which of the following is the appropriate response if a newborn's heart rate is below 100 after drying and stimulation?
choices: Continue drying and rechecking every five minutes
Begin chest compressions without ventilation
Begin positive pressure ventilation with room air or oxygen
Transport at once without further intervention
questions.explanation: A newborn heart rate below 100 usually reflects inadequate ventilation, and positive pressure breaths correct it in most cases. Compressions are added only below 60, continued drying alone allows deterioration, and transport without intervention neglects the treatable cause.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why elderly patients are at higher risk of hypothermia?
choices: Greater physical activity generating unstable temperatures
Reduced ability to sense and regulate body temperature
Increased body fat that conducts heat away
Higher metabolic rates that consume heat rapidly
questions.explanation: Aging reduces both temperature perception and the ability to generate and conserve heat, so cold conditions produce hypothermia sooner. Metabolic rate falls with age, body fat insulates rather than conducts heat away, and activity levels generally decline.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate approach to obtaining a history about a young child?
choices: Gather information from the caregiver while observing the child
Obtain history after the child has been transported
Ask the child questions without the caregiver present
Rely on what the child is able to describe
questions.explanation: Caregivers provide the reliable history while direct observation of the child yields assessment information that questioning cannot. Relying solely on a young child's account, deferring history entirely, and excluding the caregiver all discard the best available information.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the danger of a breech presentation in the field?
choices: The mother is certain to require a surgical delivery
The head may become trapped after the body delivers
The infant cannot receive oxygen until the head delivers
The placenta detaches before the infant delivers
questions.explanation: In a breech delivery the largest part comes last, and entrapment of the head with the cord compressed is the principal danger. The infant receives oxygen through the cord until it is compressed, surgical delivery is common but not certain, and placental detachment is not inevitable.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct compression-to-ventilation ratio for two-rescuer child CPR?
choices: 30 compressions to 2 breaths
10 compressions to 2 breaths
5 compressions to 1 breath
15 compressions to 2 breaths
questions.explanation: Two rescuers use a fifteen-to-two ratio in children, reflecting the greater importance of ventilation in pediatric arrest. Thirty to two is the single-rescuer ratio, and the other ratios are not used in current practice.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate handling of a patient's mobility aid during transport?
choices: Bring it with the patient so it is available at the hospital
Secure it in the driver's compartment during transport away from the patient
Leave it at the residence to reduce clutter in the ambulance
Have a family member deliver it to the hospital later
questions.explanation: A cane, walker, or wheelchair is essential to the patient's independence, and leaving it behind can strand him at discharge. Leaving it at home, relying on family to deliver it, and storing it in the driver's area all separate the patient from a necessary device.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the correct approach to a choking infant who is conscious and cannot cry?
choices: Alternate five back slaps with five chest thrusts
Hold the infant upright and pat the back gently
Perform a blind finger sweep of the mouth
Perform abdominal thrusts until the object is expelled
questions.explanation: Five back blows alternating with five chest thrusts, the chest thrusts delivered with the heel of one hand on the lower sternum, generate the pressure needed to expel the object without risking the abdominal injury that thrusts cause in infants. The 2025 AHA guidelines replaced the older two-finger technique with the heel of one hand because it reaches greater depth. Abdominal thrusts are not used in infants, blind sweeps push objects deeper, and gentle patting generates nowhere near enough force.

questions.question: Which of the following would most suggest a pregnant patient is experiencing placental abruption rather than previa?
choices: Abdominal pain with a firm tender uterus
Bleeding that began after intercourse with no pain
A history of a previous cesarean delivery
Painless bleeding with a soft relaxed uterus
questions.explanation: Abruption involves premature separation of the placenta, producing pain and a rigid tender uterus, often with concealed bleeding. Painless bleeding with a soft uterus is characteristic of previa, and neither postcoital bleeding nor a cesarean history distinguishes the two.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes an appropriate approach to a patient who uses a communication device?
choices: Allow adequate time for the patient to compose responses
Assume the patient cannot understand complex information
Direct all questions to the caregiver to save time
Ask questions requiring yes or no answers exclusively
questions.explanation: Allowing time for the device to be used respects the patient's ability to communicate directly. Restricting all questions to yes or no, bypassing the patient, and assuming impaired comprehension all underestimate a patient whose communication method differs from speech.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the first stage of labor?
choices: From the onset of contractions until the cervix is completely dilated
From full dilation until the infant is delivered
From delivery of the infant until the placenta delivers
From the rupture of membranes until crowning occurs
questions.explanation: The first stage covers the period of cervical dilation, which is usually the longest phase. The second stage runs from full dilation to delivery of the infant, the third stage covers placental delivery, and membrane rupture can occur at various points.

questions.question: Which question is most important when assessing a woman in labor?
choices: Whether she has eaten anything earlier in the day
The hospital where her physician usually practices
Her gestational age and number of prior deliveries
How far she traveled before calling for help today
questions.explanation: Gestational age predicts the likely condition of the infant, and previous deliveries generally proceed faster, both of which determine whether to deliver on scene. Physician affiliation, recent meals, and travel distance do not change that decision.

questions.question: Which of the following would most increase concern in a woman who reports decreased fetal movement at 38 weeks?
choices: A report that the movements were strong yesterday
Mild swelling of both feet noticed in the evening hours
Vaginal bleeding accompanying the decreased movement
A history of two uncomplicated prior pregnancies
questions.explanation: Bleeding together with reduced fetal movement raises concern for placental separation compromising fetal circulation. Strong movement the previous day, an uncomplicated obstetric history, and mild dependent edema do not add urgency in the same way.

questions.question: Which of the following describes appropriate management of the umbilical cord after a normal delivery?
choices: Clamp in two places and cut between the clamps
Leave the cord completely uncut and attached during the entire transport
Tie the cord with any available string and cut it
Cut the cord without clamping it first
questions.explanation: Two clamps prevent bleeding from both the infant and placental ends before the cord is divided. Cutting without clamping causes hemorrhage, improvised ties are unreliable and unsterile, and while delayed clamping has a role, leaving the cord intact for a full transport complicates care.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why a pregnant trauma patient may show few signs of shock despite significant blood loss?
choices: The fetus absorbs the blood lost by the mother
Pregnancy completely prevents any blood from ever leaving the circulation
Pregnancy raises blood pressure above normal levels
Increased blood volume during pregnancy delays the signs
questions.explanation: Blood volume increases substantially during pregnancy, so a mother can lose a large amount before her vital signs change, even while fetal perfusion is already compromised. Pregnancy does not prevent blood loss, the fetus does not absorb lost blood, and blood pressure typically falls slightly rather than rising.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appearance component of the pediatric assessment triangle?
choices: Respiratory rate, retractions and audible airway sounds
Tone, interactiveness, consolability, gaze, and speech or cry
Skin color, temperature, and capillary refill time
Blood pressure, pulse rate, and pulse quality
questions.explanation: Appearance assesses how the child's brain is functioning through muscle tone, engagement, ability to be consoled, eye contact, and the quality of speech or cry. Skin findings belong to the circulation component, effort findings to work of breathing, and vital signs are measured separately.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management of a child with suspected epiglottitis?
choices: Keep the child calm in a position of comfort and transport
Encourage the child to drink fluids for comfort
Lay the child flat and insert an oral airway
Examine the throat with a tongue depressor
questions.explanation: Agitation and airway manipulation can precipitate complete obstruction, so the child is kept calm and undisturbed. Examining the throat, lying the child flat with an oral device, and offering fluids all risk triggering obstruction in a swollen airway.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why blood pressure is not the primary assessment of perfusion in young children?
choices: It has no relationship to circulating blood volume at any age
It is elevated in frightened children
It remains normal until compensation fails abruptly
It cannot be measured accurately in any child
questions.explanation: Children maintain normal pressure through vigorous compensation until they decompensate suddenly, so mental status, skin, and heart rate detect trouble earlier. Pressure can be measured with the correct cuff, fear does not universally raise it, and it does relate to volume once compensation fails.

questions.question: Which finding in a child with a fever and a rash is most concerning?
choices: A rash that appeared as the fever resolved
A rash confined to the area of a new detergent
A red raised rash that blanches with pressure
Purple spots that do not fade when pressed
questions.explanation: Non-blanching purple lesions suggest bleeding into the skin and can indicate a severe bacterial infection requiring immediate care. A blanching rash, a contact-limited rash, and a rash appearing as fever resolves all suggest far less dangerous causes.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the correct approach to a school-age child during assessment?
choices: Explain each step simply and allow the child to ask questions
Perform the assessment without explanation to save time
Speak to the parent about what will happen
Use medical terminology to convey professionalism
questions.explanation: School-age children understand simple explanations and cooperate better when included, which improves the quality of the assessment. Skipping explanation, addressing only the parent, and using unfamiliar terminology all increase anxiety and resistance.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a common presentation of pneumonia in an elderly patient?
choices: High fever with shaking chills and chest pain
Sudden wheezing that resolves with an inhaler
Confusion and weakness without fever or a productive cough
Sharp pain reproduced by pressing on the ribs
questions.explanation: Blunted immune and cough responses mean older adults often present with mental status change and weakness rather than classic infectious signs. High fever with chills, inhaler-responsive wheezing, and reproducible chest wall pain all point elsewhere.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate approach to obtaining a history from an elderly patient?
choices: Allow extra time and verify details with available records
Assume the patient cannot provide accurate information
Obtain the entire history exclusively from a nearby family member instead
Limit questions to save time during transport
questions.explanation: Older patients often need more time and may have complex histories, so patience combined with medication lists and records produces the most accurate picture. Bypassing the patient, rushing, and presuming inaccuracy all discard information the patient can provide.

questions.question: An elderly patient fell and now has hip pain with the leg shortened and rotated outward. What does this most suggest?
choices: A dislocation of the knee joint
A muscular strain of the thigh
A compression fracture of the spine
A fracture of the proximal femur
questions.explanation: Shortening with external rotation is the classic presentation of a proximal femur fracture, which is common after low-energy falls in older adults. A knee dislocation produces deformity at the knee, a strain does not shorten the limb, and a spinal compression fracture produces back pain.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate transport consideration for a patient with severe kyphosis?
choices: Strap the patient flat to correct the spinal alignment
Pad and support the existing curvature of the spine
Transport the patient seated upright without any support
Place the patient prone to accommodate the curve
questions.explanation: A fixed spinal curve cannot be straightened without causing pain and injury, so padding maintains the patient's natural position. Forcing the spine flat, providing no support, and prone positioning all risk fractures and respiratory compromise.

questions.question: Select the (2) findings that indicate a child's work of breathing is significantly increased.
choices: Grunting heard at the end of each exhalation
Retractions visible between the ribs at rest
A respiratory rate of 24 in a six-year-old
Clear breath sounds heard in all lung fields
A respiratory rate of 30 in a sleeping 1-year-old
questions.explanation: Grunting represents exhaling against a partly closed glottis to keep alveoli open, and retractions show accessory muscles pulling against airway resistance. A rate of 24 is normal for a six-year-old, and clear breath sounds indicate adequate air movement. A rate of 30 in a sleeping 1-year-old is within the normal range for age.

questions.question: Select the (2) findings that indicate a newborn requires immediate intervention beyond drying and warming.
choices: A heart rate of 80 after initial stimulation
Vigorous crying with flexed extremities
Persistent apnea with no respiratory effort
Pink color of the trunk with blue hands
A heart rate of 140 after drying and stimulation
questions.explanation: A heart rate below 100 and absent respiratory effort both call for positive pressure ventilation. Vigorous crying with good tone indicates a healthy newborn, and blue hands with a pink trunk is a common transitional finding in the first minutes of life. A heart rate of 140 after drying and stimulation is normal.

questions.question: Which of the following would be the most appropriate action for a woman with a suspected ectopic pregnancy?
choices: Delay transport until the pain improves
Encourage oral fluids and observe the patient on scene closely
Treat for shock and transport without delay
Apply heat to the abdomen for pain relief
questions.explanation: A ruptured ectopic pregnancy bleeds rapidly into the abdomen and requires surgical treatment, so shock management and immediate transport are the priorities. Oral fluids, heat application, and waiting for pain relief all delay the only treatment that helps.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the concern when a pregnant patient in the third trimester is involved in a collision?
choices: The fetus is protected and rarely affected by trauma
The placenta may separate even without external injury
Bleeding will be visible if the fetus is injured
Abdominal injury is less likely because of the uterus
questions.explanation: Deceleration forces can shear the placenta from the uterine wall without any visible external injury, threatening both mother and fetus. The fetus is not immune to trauma, abdominal injury risk is not reduced, and abruption bleeding is often concealed.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the correct technique for opening the airway of an infant?
choices: Flex the chin firmly toward the chest
Turn the head fully to one side
Position the head in a neutral sniffing position
Hyperextend the neck fully backward to straighten the entire airway
questions.explanation: An infant's large occiput already flexes the neck when supine, so a neutral position with slight extension aligns the airway best. Hyperextension and flexion both kink the soft trachea, and turning the head does not open the airway.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate use of an automated external defibrillator in a child under eight years old?
choices: Use pediatric pads or an attenuator when available
Do not use the device in children under eight under any circumstances
Use adult pads at full energy without modification
Place both pads on the child's back
questions.explanation: Pediatric pads or an energy attenuator deliver an appropriate dose for a small child, and adult pads are used only if pediatric equipment is unavailable. Withholding defibrillation entirely removes the only treatment for a shockable rhythm, and back-only placement does not create a path through the heart.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the concern with a child who has ingested a button battery?
choices: It can cause tissue burns within hours of lodging
It passes harmlessly through the digestive tract
It only causes problems if it is chewed first
It presents a risk only in children under one year
questions.explanation: A lodged button battery generates current that burns through tissue within a few hours, making it a true emergency. These batteries do not reliably pass harmlessly, chewing is not required for injury, and the risk applies to children of any age.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate approach when a patient has a tracheostomy and communicates by writing?
choices: Provide writing materials and allow time for responses
Assume the patient's mental status is impaired
Ask questions the patient can nod to
Direct all questions to a caregiver instead
questions.explanation: Supplying writing materials lets the patient answer fully in his own words. Restricting to yes or no questions loses detail, bypassing the patient disregards him, and assuming impaired mentation from a speech barrier is a serious error.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes why an elderly patient may develop shock with less blood loss than a younger adult?
choices: Elderly patients generally have larger circulating blood volumes overall
Older patients feel pain more intensely during injury
Blood clots more slowly in older patients
Reduced cardiac reserve limits the compensatory response
questions.explanation: A stiffened heart and blunted responsiveness limit the increase in rate and contractility available to compensate for volume loss. Clotting speed is not the central issue, blood volume does not increase with age, and pain perception is often reduced rather than heightened.

questions.question: Which of the following is the appropriate action when a child's caregiver refuses transport for a child who appears seriously ill?
choices: Accept the refusal and document it without further action
Transport the child against the caregiver's stated wishes
Involve medical direction and consider law enforcement
Ask the child to make the decision about transport
questions.explanation: A refusal that places a child at serious risk requires escalation through medical direction and, where necessary, law enforcement acting in the child's interest. Simply accepting the refusal abandons the child, unilateral transport creates legal problems, and a child cannot make this decision.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate action when a mother delivers and the infant is limp and not breathing?
choices: Suction deeply with a rigid catheter for one minute
Perform chest compressions before any ventilation
Wait 60 seconds to see whether breathing begins
Dry, stimulate, and begin positive pressure ventilation promptly
questions.explanation: Drying and stimulation are attempted briefly, and ventilation follows immediately when the infant does not respond, because hypoxia is the usual cause. Compressions before ventilation, prolonged deep suctioning, and a full minute of waiting all delay the intervention that corrects the problem.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the significance of a bulging fontanelle in an infant?
choices: It indicates the infant is well hydrated
It may indicate increased pressure inside the skull
It is a normal finding during quiet sleep
It suggests the infant is quite hungry and needs feeding very soon
questions.explanation: A fontanelle that bulges when the infant is calm and upright suggests raised intracranial pressure from infection, bleeding, or swelling. It is not a normal sleeping finding, and neither hydration status nor hunger causes it to bulge.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate action when an elderly patient's medication list includes a blood thinner and he has fallen?
choices: Transport for evaluation regardless of whether an injury is apparent
Advise the patient to stop taking the medication until they are evaluated
Release the patient if he can walk without difficulty
Observe at the residence for one hour before deciding
questions.explanation: Anticoagulation makes delayed intracranial bleeding a real possibility even after apparently minor falls, so evaluation is warranted. Releasing the patient, observing on scene, and advising him to stop a prescribed medication all carry significant risk.

questions.question: Arrange the steps of assessing a conscious child in respiratory distress, from first to last.
choices: Auscultate the lung fields and obtain vital signs
Apply oxygen in a manner the child will tolerate
Form an impression using appearance, breathing, and circulation
Allow the child to remain with the caregiver in a position of comfort
questions.explanation: A hands-off impression is formed first, the child is kept calm with the caregiver because agitation worsens distress, oxygen is offered in a tolerable way, and hands-on assessment with vital signs follows once the child is settled.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate action if a mother in labor reports a history of a prior cesarean delivery?
choices: Delay transport until contractions become more regular
Prepare for a routine field delivery without additional concern
Encourage the mother to push to speed the delivery
Recognize the increased risk of uterine rupture and transport
questions.explanation: A uterine scar carries a risk of rupture during labor, which is a life-threatening emergency for both mother and fetus, so prompt transport is appropriate. Treating the delivery as routine, encouraging pushing, and waiting on scene all ignore that risk.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why a child's head is more likely to be injured in a fall than an adult's?
choices: The neck muscles are stronger and resist movement
The brain is smaller and moves less within the skull
The head is proportionally larger and leads the fall
The skull is thicker and transfers more force inward
questions.explanation: A child's head represents a larger fraction of total body mass and typically strikes first in a fall. The skull is thinner rather than thicker, neck musculature is weaker rather than stronger, and the brain moves more rather than less within the skull.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate way to assess an elderly patient's baseline function?
choices: Ask what the patient was able to do before this illness began
Rely on the current physical examination findings alone
Assume the patient was fully independent before the call
Compare the patient to others of a similar age
questions.explanation: Knowing what the patient could do before the illness reveals how much has changed, which is what indicates acuity. Assuming full independence, relying on the current exam alone, and comparing to others of the same age all miss the individual's own baseline.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management of a child with a suspected febrile seizure who is now postictal?
choices: Give oral medication to reduce the fever
Immerse the entire child in cold water to lower the body temperature quickly
Withhold transport since febrile seizures are harmless
Protect the airway, monitor breathing, and avoid overcooling
questions.explanation: Airway protection and monitoring during the postictal period matter most, and aggressive cooling causes shivering that raises temperature. Cold immersion is harmful, oral medication is unsafe in a postictal child, and even a benign-appearing seizure requires evaluation for its cause.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes appropriate care for the mother immediately after a normal delivery?
choices: Apply firm pressure to the abdomen continuously
Discourage contact between the mother and the infant, even if the mother requests otherwise
Monitor for bleeding and keep both mother and infant warm
Have the mother stand to help deliver the placenta
questions.explanation: Postpartum hemorrhage is the main immediate risk, and warmth matters for both mother and newborn. Standing risks syncope, separating mother and infant impedes bonding and warmth, and continuous firm abdominal pressure is not the same as intermittent fundal massage.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the most common cause of injury among elderly patients?
choices: Falls occurring at ground level
Motor vehicle collisions at high speed
Injuries during recreational sports
Assaults by strangers in public
questions.explanation: Ground-level falls account for the majority of injuries and injury deaths in older adults, since reduced bone density turns a low-energy fall into a significant fracture. Vehicle collisions, assaults, and sports injuries occur but contribute far less to the overall burden.

questions.question: Which of the following would most suggest that a newly delivered mother is developing hypovolemic shock?
choices: Mild cramping as the uterus begins to contract
A small amount of bloody discharge after delivery
A rising pulse with cool skin and increasing anxiety
Fatigue and a strong desire to sleep soon after an otherwise normal delivery
questions.explanation: A climbing pulse with cool skin and anxiety indicates compensation for blood loss and precedes a fall in pressure. Cramping, a small amount of discharge, and post-delivery fatigue are all expected findings after a normal birth.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate size of a blood pressure cuff for a child?
choices: The smallest cuff carried should be used
Any available adult-sized cuff is generally acceptable for all children
The bladder should cover about two thirds of the upper arm
Cuff size does not affect the accuracy of the reading
questions.explanation: A cuff bladder covering roughly two thirds of the upper arm produces an accurate reading in a child. Adult cuffs read falsely low on small arms, the smallest cuff reads falsely high on larger children, and size clearly affects accuracy.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes an appropriate consideration when a patient has a hearing aid?
choices: Remove it before transport to prevent loss
Ensure it is in place and turned on before speaking
Speak loudly enough to be heard without the device even at a distance
Communicate in writing rather than using the device
questions.explanation: A functioning hearing aid is the simplest way to restore communication with the patient. Removing it isolates the patient, shouting over the absence of the device distorts speech, and defaulting to writing is unnecessary when the device works.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most concerning sign in an infant with a fever?
choices: Fussiness that settles when the infant is held
Difficulty waking the infant for a feeding
A temperature that falls after medication
An increased number of wet diapers today
questions.explanation: An infant who cannot be roused to feed has a significantly depressed level of consciousness, which suggests serious illness. Consolable fussiness, a fever responding to medication, and good urine output all suggest the infant is tolerating the illness.

questions.question: Which of the following describes a normal finding in the minutes after delivery of the placenta?
choices: A soft boggy uterus that cannot be located
Continuous bright red bleeding that soaks pads
A rapidly falling blood pressure with pallor
A firm uterus felt at the level of the navel
questions.explanation: A firm uterus at the level of the umbilicus indicates effective contraction clamping the placental vessels. A boggy uterus, continuous heavy bleeding, and falling pressure with pallor all indicate hemorrhage requiring intervention.
