questions.explanation: Walking does not exclude a spinal injury, so the decision rests on assessment criteria such as midline tenderness, neurological findings, and reliability. Assuming no injury, applying precautions reflexively, and having the patient continue walking all bypass the assessment that should drive the decision.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes appropriate management of an avulsed flap of skin?
choices: Apply a tourniquet above the avulsed area
Remove the flap and dress the wound
Return the flap to its normal position and dress the area
Fold the flap back and leave the wound exposed
questions.explanation: Replacing the flap in its anatomical position preserves the tissue's blood supply and improves the chance it survives. Removing the flap discards viable tissue, folding it back exposes the wound bed, and a tourniquet is reserved for uncontrolled bleeding.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why a patient ejected from a vehicle is considered high risk?
choices: Ejected patients land on soft surfaces
Ejection prevents injuries from the vehicle interior
Ejection indicates forces great enough to cause multisystem injury
Ejected patients are protected by being thrown clear
questions.explanation: The energy required to eject an occupant is enough to produce injuries throughout the body, and impact with the ground adds more. Landing surfaces vary, avoiding interior contact does not offset the greater forces, and being thrown clear is associated with far worse outcomes.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate action for a patient with severe bleeding from a groin wound?
choices: Pack the wound with a hemostatic dressing and apply pressure
Elevate both legs and apply a loose dressing
Apply pressure to a distal point below the wound
Apply a tourniquet as high as possible on the thigh
questions.explanation: Junctional wounds at the groin cannot be controlled with a tourniquet, so wound packing with direct pressure is the appropriate technique. A thigh tourniquet cannot reach above the injury, elevation with a loose dressing does not control arterial bleeding, and distal pressure does not affect flow into the wound.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the assessment priority for a patient burned in an enclosed space?
choices: Accurate measurement of the total burn surface area percentage involved
Determination of how the fire started
Airway assessment for signs of inhalation injury
Estimation of the property damage involved
questions.explanation: Burns in enclosed spaces carry a high risk of airway swelling from heat and irritants, which can obstruct rapidly. Surface area estimation matters for fluid planning, and fire cause and property damage are not clinical priorities.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the concern with a penetrating wound below the fifth rib?
choices: It cannot involve the diaphragm at any point
It may involve both chest and abdominal structures
It always produces obvious external bleeding
It is always strictly limited to injuries of the chest wall only
questions.explanation: The diaphragm rises well above the costal margin during exhalation, so wounds below the nipple line can enter both cavities. Such wounds are not limited to the chest wall, they frequently involve the diaphragm, and penetrating injuries often bleed internally rather than externally.

questions.question: Arrange the steps for managing a trauma patient with a suspected spinal injury who must be moved from a vehicle, from first to last.
choices: Assess motor function, sensation, and circulation in all extremities
Apply manual in-line stabilization of the head
Secure the patient to the device and reassess circulation
Move the patient as a unit onto the transfer device
questions.explanation: Manual stabilization is established before anything else moves the patient, a neurological baseline is documented before movement changes it, the patient is moved as a unit onto the device, and securing with reassessment completes the sequence.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate transport decision for a patient with uncontrolled internal bleeding?
choices: Delay transport until the bleeding is controlled
Transport at a routine, unhurried pace to avoid any further injury
Rapid transport to a facility with surgical capability
Transport to the nearest facility of any type
questions.explanation: Internal bleeding is stopped only in the operating room, so the destination and the speed of transport both matter. The nearest facility may lack surgical capability, the bleeding cannot be controlled in the field, and a routine pace wastes time the patient does not have.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate management of a patient with a suspected sprain?
choices: Apply heat to reduce the swelling quickly
Immobilize, apply cold, and assess distal circulation
Manipulate the joint to restore range of motion
Have the patient bear weight to test the severity
questions.explanation: Immobilization with cold application limits swelling and pain while circulation checks confirm the limb remains perfused. Weight bearing worsens the injury, heat increases swelling early, and manipulation risks further damage to injured ligaments.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes why hyperventilating a head-injured patient is generally avoided?
choices: It raises carbon dioxide levels and worsens swelling
It increases the risk of a skull fracture worsening
It has no physiological effect on the injured brain
It constricts cerebral vessels and reduces blood flow to the brain
questions.explanation: Driving carbon dioxide down constricts cerebral vessels, which reduces blood flow to tissue that is already injured. Hyperventilation lowers rather than raises carbon dioxide, has no effect on fracture patterns, and clearly does affect cerebral perfusion.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes an appropriate consideration for a trauma patient who is pregnant?
choices: Pregnancy makes the mother less likely to be seriously injured
Treating the mother effectively is the best care for the fetus
The fetus should be assessed before the mother is treated
Fetal monitoring should take priority during transport
questions.explanation: Fetal survival depends on maternal perfusion and oxygenation, so stabilizing the mother is the most effective fetal intervention available. Assessing the fetus first, assuming reduced maternal risk, and prioritizing fetal monitoring all divert attention from the intervention that helps both.

questions.question: Which of the following findings would most suggest that a patient's bleeding is venous rather than arterial?
choices: Slow oozing from a superficial abrasion
Dark red blood flowing steadily from the wound
Bright red blood spurting forcefully with each rapid heartbeat
No visible bleeding with abdominal distention
questions.explanation: Venous blood has given up its oxygen, making it darker, and it flows under lower steady pressure. Spurting bright red blood is arterial, oozing is capillary, and distention without visible blood indicates internal bleeding.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management of a burn patient with a large surface area involved?
choices: Cover with a dry sterile sheet and prevent heat loss
Cover with wet sheets to cool the entire body
Leave the burns uncovered to allow air to circulate freely
Apply topical ointments to the burned areas
questions.explanation: Large burns destroy the skin's ability to retain heat, so dry coverage protects the wounds while preventing hypothermia. Wet sheets cause rapid heat loss, ointments interfere with hospital assessment, and leaving burns uncovered increases contamination and heat loss.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate action for a patient with a head injury who becomes combative?
choices: Assume the patient is intoxicated and restrain him
Consider hypoxia or rising intracranial pressure as the cause
Leave the patient alone until he calms down
Discontinue the assessment and transport quietly
questions.explanation: Combativeness after head injury frequently reflects hypoxia or increasing intracranial pressure rather than a behavioral problem, and both are treatable. Assuming intoxication, withdrawing, and abandoning the assessment all miss a physiological cause that is worsening.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why blood pressure is a poor early indicator of hemorrhage?
choices: Blood pressure rises rather than falls with blood loss
Blood pressure is unrelated to circulating volume
Compensation maintains pressure until a large volume is lost
Blood pressure cannot be measured accurately in trauma
questions.explanation: Vasoconstriction and tachycardia hold pressure near normal until roughly a third of blood volume is gone, so pressure falls late. Measurement remains feasible, pressure does not rise with ongoing loss, and it is ultimately very much related to volume.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate approach to a patient injured in a diving incident in shallow water?
choices: Have the patient swim to the edge under their own power before you assess
Support the head and neck in line and keep that stabilization throughout the extraction from the water
Pull the patient from the water by the arms to clear the airway as fast as possible
Complete a full in-water assessment before any attempt to move the patient
questions.explanation: Shallow water diving injuries frequently involve the cervical spine, so in-line stabilization is maintained throughout the extraction. Having the patient swim, pulling by the arms, and delaying extraction for a full in-water assessment all risk worsening a cord injury or drowning.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes why an open fracture requires urgent attention?
choices: The exposed bone heals faster than in a closed fracture
The exposed bone carries a high risk of deep infection
Open fractures always bleed more than closed fractures
Open fractures never require surgical repair
questions.explanation: Direct communication between the outside environment and bone makes deep infection a major risk, which is why these injuries need prompt surgical care. Blood loss varies, surgery is usually required, and healing is slower rather than faster.

questions.question: Which of the following would most suggest a significant injury after blunt chest trauma?
choices: Pain with movement of the shoulder on the same side as impact
Tenderness over one rib with normal breath sounds
A bruise on the chest wall with equal expansion
Unequal chest expansion with decreased breath sounds
questions.explanation: Unequal expansion with diminished sounds suggests air or blood in the pleural space preventing the lung from expanding. Isolated rib tenderness, a bruise with equal expansion, and shoulder-related pain all suggest less serious chest wall injury.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the correct approach to a patient with multiple bleeding wounds?
choices: Control the most severe bleeding first
Dress the smallest wounds first to save supplies
Dress the wounds in the order they are found
Delay bleeding control until the full survey is complete
questions.explanation: The wound losing the most blood is addressed first because that is the one threatening life. Working in the order found, starting with minor wounds, and deferring control until a full survey is finished all allow the worst bleeding to continue.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate handling of a patient with a suspected spinal injury and a deformed extremity?
choices: Have the patient hold the limb in position himself
Address the spine and life threats before splinting the limb
Splint the extremity before addressing any other concern, even as the deformity remains visible
Ignore the extremity injury during transport
questions.explanation: Spinal protection and life threats take priority, and extremity splinting follows once those are managed. Splinting first delays higher priorities, ignoring the injury allows further damage, and asking the patient to hold his own limb is neither reliable nor safe.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why a patient with a spinal cord injury may become hypothermic?
choices: The injury prevents the patient from feeling any pain
Loss of vascular tone below the injury prevents heat conservation
Spinal injuries increase the body's metabolic rate
Spinal injuries cause the skin to become thicker
questions.explanation: Sympathetic control is lost below the injury, so vessels cannot constrict to conserve heat and the patient takes on the environmental temperature. Metabolic rate does not rise, pain perception is unrelated to heat loss, and skin thickness does not change.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes appropriate care for a patient with an object impaled in the cheek that is obstructing the airway?
choices: Cut the object and leave the remainder in place
Remove the object carefully and control bleeding from both sides
Stabilize the object in place and transport at once
Push the object through to the outside of the cheek
questions.explanation: An object impaled in the cheek that obstructs the airway is one of the two exceptions to the rule against removing impaled objects (the other is an object that interferes with CPR), because the airway takes priority and bleeding can be controlled from both the inside and the outside of the cheek. Stabilizing it in place leaves the airway obstructed, pushing it through worsens the injury, and cutting it does not relieve the obstruction.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response when a patient in shock asks for water?
choices: Offer small sips of water as long as the patient remains alert and oriented
Allow the patient to drink freely to help restore lost fluid volume
Explain that nothing can be given by mouth, and keep the patient NPO
Give ice chips, to moisten the mouth without filling the stomach
questions.explanation: Oral intake risks aspiration and can complicate surgery that a shock patient is likely to need, so nothing is given by mouth. Sips, unrestricted intake, and ice chips all introduce material into a stomach that may need to be empty.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes appropriate care for a patient with burns to the hands?
choices: Separate the fingers with dressings and remove jewelry
Apply a tight compression wrap to reduce swelling
Wrap the hand as a single unit with the fingers together
Leave rings in place to avoid causing further injury
questions.explanation: Separating the digits prevents them from fusing during healing, and jewelry is removed before swelling makes it a tourniquet. Wrapping fingers together, leaving rings on, and applying compression all cause preventable complications.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes an appropriate consideration for a patient injured during cold weather?
choices: Delay treatment until the patient reaches the ambulance
Keep the patient in wet clothing for warmth
Apply direct heat to the extremities
Remove wet clothing and prevent further heat loss
questions.explanation: Wet clothing accelerates heat loss dramatically, and hypothermia impairs clotting in a trauma patient. Leaving wet clothing on, applying direct heat to the extremities, and delaying all care allow the patient's temperature to continue falling.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate response when a trauma patient's abdomen becomes progressively more distended?
choices: Apply firm pressure to the abdomen to limit the bleeding
Have the patient lie prone to reduce the distention
Wait for a change in vital signs before acting
Treat for shock and expedite transport to surgical care
questions.explanation: Progressive distention indicates ongoing internal bleeding that only surgery can stop, so shock management and rapid transport are the priorities. Abdominal pressure does not control internal bleeding, prone positioning is unhelpful, and waiting for vital signs to change wastes the compensated period.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the purpose of checking pulse, motor, and sensory function distal to an injury?
choices: It establishes the mechanism that caused the injury
It measures the patient's overall pain tolerance
It detects nerve or vascular compromise from the injury or splint
It determines whether the bone is actually fractured
questions.explanation: These checks reveal whether the nerves and vessels beyond the injury are intact, before and after any intervention. They do not diagnose fractures, measure pain tolerance, or establish the mechanism of injury.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the significance of subcutaneous emphysema in a chest trauma patient?
choices: Fluid has accumulated in the subcutaneous layer
The patient has developed an allergic swelling of the chest wall
The patient has a superficial bruise beneath the skin
Air has escaped from the airway or lung into the tissues
questions.explanation: The crackling sensation under the skin indicates air leaking from an injured airway or lung, which signals a significant injury. Bruising, fluid accumulation, and allergic swelling all produce different findings on palpation.

questions.question: Which of the following patients with a head injury is at greatest risk for rapid deterioration?
choices: One with a small scalp laceration and no other symptoms
One who takes an anticoagulant and struck his head
One who reports a headache that is improving steadily
One who remembers the entire event clearly
questions.explanation: Anticoagulation allows intracranial bleeding to continue unchecked, so deterioration can occur hours after an apparently minor impact. A small laceration, an improving headache, and intact memory all suggest a low-risk injury.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of shock in a patient with a femur fracture and no external bleeding?
choices: Blood loss into the soft tissues of the thigh
An allergic reaction to the splinting material
A neurological response to the fracture
Dehydration from the pain of the injury
questions.explanation: A femur fracture can bleed a liter or more into the thigh without any external evidence, which is enough to cause shock. Splint allergy, pain-induced dehydration, and a neurological response do not produce the volume loss that explains shock in this setting.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate action for a patient with a suspected spinal injury who is vomiting?
choices: Remove the spinal precautions and turn the patient
Rotate the patient and board as a unit and suction
Have the patient turn his head to the side himself
Sit the patient upright to allow the vomit to drain
questions.explanation: Turning the patient and the immobilization device together lets the vomit drain while spinal alignment is maintained. Sitting upright is impossible when immobilized, removing precautions risks cord injury, and turning only the head moves the cervical spine.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a full thickness burn?
choices: Superficial peeling that develops several days later
Destruction of all skin layers with little or no pain at the site
Redness and pain without any blistering present
Blistering with severe pain and moist tissue
questions.explanation: Full thickness burns destroy the nerve endings along with all skin layers, which is why the burned area itself may be painless. Redness without blisters is superficial, blistering with severe pain is partial thickness, and delayed peeling follows superficial injury.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes an appropriate action when applying a commercial tourniquet?
choices: Place it directly over a joint for supposedly better overall compression
Tighten until the bleeding slows noticeably
Cover it with a dressing so it is not disturbed
Tighten until bleeding stops and note the time applied
questions.explanation: A tourniquet must be tight enough to stop arterial flow, and the application time is recorded for the hospital. Partial tightening allows continued arterial bleeding into the limb, joint placement prevents effective compression, and covering it hides a device the trauma team must see.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the assessment finding of guarding?
choices: Tensing of the abdominal muscles when the area is touched
Rhythmic movement of the abdomen with breathing
Visible pulsation of the abdominal wall at rest
Complete relaxation of the abdomen during palpation
questions.explanation: Guarding is muscular tensing in response to palpation and suggests underlying irritation of the peritoneum. Relaxation is a normal finding, abdominal movement with breathing is normal, and a visible pulsation suggests an aneurysm.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why a young trauma patient may maintain normal vital signs despite serious injury?
choices: Strong compensatory mechanisms mask the volume loss
Young patients bleed more slowly than older patients
Young patients rarely sustain serious internal injuries
Vital signs are unreliable in patients under thirty
questions.explanation: Healthy young patients compensate vigorously, holding pressure and mentation normal until they decompensate abruptly. Young people do sustain serious injuries, vital signs remain meaningful, and bleeding rate is determined by the injury rather than by age.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate action for a patient with a gunshot wound to the abdomen?
choices: Cover the wounds, treat for shock, and transport rapidly
Probe the wound to determine the bullet's path
Apply a tourniquet above the abdominal wound
Delay transport to complete a detailed examination
questions.explanation: Penetrating abdominal injury requires surgical control of bleeding, so wounds are covered, shock is treated, and the patient moves quickly. Probing worsens the injury, detailed on-scene examination wastes time, and a tourniquet cannot be applied to the torso.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate approach to a patient with a suspected fracture who refuses splinting?
choices: Document the refusal and provide no further care
Refuse to transport until the splint is accepted
Explain the benefits and risks and respect the decision
Apply the splint anyway for the patient's own good, reassessing the patient every few minutes afterward
questions.explanation: A capacitated patient may refuse an intervention, and the provider's role is to ensure the decision is informed while continuing other care. Splinting against refusal is battery, conditioning transport on compliance is coercive, and withdrawing care abandons the patient.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the concern with a patient who has a bruise across the lower chest from a steering wheel?
choices: The bruise indicates the injury was limited to the skin, typically resolving on its own without treatment
Underlying injury to the liver, spleen, or lungs is possible
Bruising confirms that no internal injury occurred
The pattern indicates rib fractures alone
questions.explanation: A visible impact pattern marks where significant energy was transferred, and the organs beneath may be injured even when the patient feels well. External bruising says nothing about the depth of injury and never excludes damage beneath it.

questions.question: Select the (2) actions appropriate for a patient with severe external bleeding and signs of shock.
choices: Keep the patient warm and transport without delay
Control the bleeding with direct pressure or a tourniquet
Delay transport until the vital signs improve
Give the patient fluids by mouth to replace the loss
Apply cold packs over the whole body to slow the bleeding
questions.explanation: Stopping the bleeding addresses the cause and warmth preserves clotting function while rapid transport reaches definitive care. Oral fluids risk aspiration and cannot replace intravascular volume, and waiting for vital signs to improve wastes the compensated period. Cold packs over the whole body cause hypothermia, which worsens bleeding.

questions.question: Select the (2) findings that suggest a patient's head injury is worsening during transport.
choices: A blood pressure that rises as the pulse slows
A blood pressure that remains stable with a steady pulse
A pupil that becomes larger and less reactive
A headache that the patient reports as improving
A respiratory rate that stays regular at 16
questions.explanation: A dilating unreactive pupil suggests pressure on the oculomotor nerve, and rising pressure with a slowing pulse reflects the reflex response to rising intracranial pressure. An improving headache and stable vital signs both suggest the patient is not deteriorating.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes appropriate management of a patient with a suspected fracture of the forearm and no circulation distal to the injury?
choices: Apply a tourniquet above the injury at once
Apply gentle traction to realign and recheck the pulse
Splint in the position found without any manipulation of the limb
Transport without splinting to save time
questions.explanation: Absent distal circulation justifies one attempt at gentle realignment, since restoring flow prevents tissue death. Splinting as found leaves the limb without perfusion, a tourniquet stops what little flow exists, and transporting unsplinted allows further injury.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate response to a patient with a possible spinal injury who is wearing a motorcycle helmet?
choices: Remove the helmet with two providers maintaining alignment
Leave it on unless it blocks the airway or fits loosely
Have the patient remove his own helmet carefully
Cut the helmet apart with available tools
questions.explanation: A well-fitted helmet holds the head in a stable relationship with the neck, and taking it off means moving the head at the exact moment you least want to. So it stays on unless it is actively in the way: it blocks access to the airway or prevents ventilation, it fits loosely enough that the head moves inside it, or it stops you immobilizing the patient properly. When removal is genuinely necessary it takes two providers, one holding in-line stabilization throughout — but the decision to remove comes first, and it is not automatic. Asking the patient to do it themselves gives up all control of the neck, and cutting a helmet apart on scene is neither necessary nor safe.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate initial action for a patient with an amputated finger and active bleeding?
choices: Reattach the finger before dressing the wound
Apply direct pressure to the stump and care for the part
Place the finger back on the stump and bandage it
Apply a tourniquet to the arm above the elbow
questions.explanation: Direct pressure controls bleeding from a digit, and the amputated part is preserved separately for possible reattachment. A proximal tourniquet is excessive for a finger, and attempting to reattach or replace the part in the field damages the tissue.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate care for a patient with a suspected pelvic injury who is hypotensive?
choices: Log roll the patient repeatedly to assess the back
Apply traction splints to both lower extremities
Delay transport until the blood pressure improves
Apply a binder, minimize movement, and transport rapidly
questions.explanation: A binder reduces pelvic volume to help control bleeding, and minimal movement preserves any clot that has formed. Repeated rolling, bilateral traction, and waiting for pressure to improve all worsen bleeding or waste time.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate action for a patient who has been struck by lightning?
choices: Assess for cardiac arrest and begin resuscitation if needed
Assume the patient will recover without intervention
Avoid touching the patient because of residual charge
Treat the visible burns at the strike point
questions.explanation: Lightning most often kills through cardiac and respiratory arrest, and patients frequently recover with prompt resuscitation. Patients carry no residual charge, surface burns are often minor compared with the internal effects, and spontaneous recovery cannot be assumed.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the reverse triage principle sometimes used after a lightning strike with multiple victims?
choices: Patients are treated in the order they are discovered regardless of severity
Patients in cardiac arrest are treated first rather than last
Patients with minor injuries are treated before critical ones
Patients who can walk are treated before all others
questions.explanation: Lightning arrest patients often respond to prompt resuscitation and rarely have other lethal injuries, so they receive priority in contrast to usual triage. Treating minor injuries first, using discovery order, and prioritizing ambulatory patients all misapply triage principles here.

questions.question: Which of the following would most suggest that a patient's shock is not from blood loss?
choices: Cool clammy skin with a rapid weak pulse
Pale skin with delayed capillary refill
Anxiety with a narrowing pulse pressure
Warm dry skin with a slow pulse after a back injury
questions.explanation: Warm dry skin with bradycardia after a spinal injury indicates neurogenic shock from lost sympathetic tone rather than hypovolemia. Cool clammy skin, delayed refill, and a narrowing pulse pressure are all consistent with blood loss.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes appropriate management of a patient with a head injury who is unresponsive?
choices: Elevate the head of the stretcher to 90 degrees
Maintain the airway, support ventilation, and monitor mentation
Restrict oxygen to avoid increasing cerebral blood flow
Hyperventilate the patient to bring down the intracranial pressure
questions.explanation: Preventing hypoxia and hypotension while monitoring for changes protects the injured brain more than any other field intervention. Routine hyperventilation reduces cerebral blood flow, extreme head elevation compromises perfusion, and restricting oxygen worsens the injury.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate care for a patient with a large partial thickness burn to the back?
choices: Cover with a dry sterile dressing and monitor temperature
Apply cool wet dressings to the entire burned area
Apply an antibiotic ointment before covering the area
Break the blisters before applying a dressing
questions.explanation: Large burns lose heat rapidly, so dry sterile coverage with temperature monitoring balances wound protection against hypothermia. Extensive wet dressings cause heat loss, breaking blisters opens the wound, and ointments interfere with hospital evaluation.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate approach to a trauma patient with a language barrier?
choices: Delay assessment until an interpreter arrives on scene, leaving real injuries unassessed for too long
Rely on gestures alone for the entire assessment
Use an interpreter service while proceeding with assessment
Assume the patient cannot provide any useful history
questions.explanation: Assessment proceeds while interpretation is arranged, since time-critical injuries cannot wait for perfect communication. Delaying assessment, relying only on gestures, and assuming no useful history all reduce the quality and timeliness of care.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the correct action when a patient has a deep laceration with an embedded piece of glass?
choices: Apply pressure directly over the embedded glass
Stabilize the glass in place and control bleeding around it
Push the glass deeper to prevent it from moving
Remove the glass and then apply a pressure dressing
questions.explanation: Leaving the object in place avoids converting a tamponaded wound into an actively bleeding one, and pressure is applied around rather than over it. Removal risks hemorrhage, pushing it deeper causes further damage, and direct pressure drives it further in.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why a burn patient's fluid needs are estimated from the burn surface area?
choices: Surface area determines how quickly the burn will heal
Burn area determines the amount of pain medication needed
Fluid shifts out of the circulation in proportion to the area burned
Larger burns involve greater external blood loss
questions.explanation: Damaged capillaries leak plasma into the tissues across the burned area, so the larger the area the greater the intravascular loss. Burns do not primarily cause external blood loss, and area does not determine analgesic dosing or healing speed in this calculation.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes why a patient with a chest injury may prefer to sit upright?
choices: The position prevents any bleeding into the chest
The position eliminates the need for supplemental oxygen
The position reduces the risk of further rib fractures
The position allows better chest expansion and comfort
questions.explanation: Sitting upright lets the diaphragm work more efficiently and reduces the pain of chest wall movement. Position does not prevent fractures, does not stop bleeding into the pleural space, and does not remove the need for oxygen.

questions.question: Arrange the steps for the initial management of a critically injured trauma patient, from first to last.
choices: Package the patient and begin rapid transport
Assess and manage the airway with spinal precautions
Assess breathing and provide ventilation as needed
Control life-threatening external bleeding
questions.explanation: Massive external hemorrhage comes first. The old A-B-C order was written before it was clear how fast an arterial extremity bleed kills: a patient can exsanguinate in the time it takes to work through a careful airway assessment, so current trauma practice puts catastrophic bleeding ahead of the airway — the X in X-ABC, the M in MARCH. Control the bleeding, then airway with spinal precautions, then breathing, then package and transport. This is a reordering of priorities, not a replacement: the airway still kills the patient who has no bleeding to control, and when bleeding is present but not life-threatening the airway still comes first.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate action for a patient with bleeding controlled by a tourniquet who now reports severe limb pain?
choices: Remove the tourniquet completely once the bleeding has stopped
Loosen the tourniquet slightly to reduce the pain
Reposition the tourniquet farther down the limb
Leave the tourniquet in place and provide reassurance
questions.explanation: Pain is expected with a correctly applied tourniquet and is not a reason to loosen or remove a device that is preventing fatal bleeding. Loosening, removing, and repositioning distally all risk renewed hemorrhage.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes an appropriate action when caring for a patient with an open fracture?
choices: Irrigate the wound thoroughly with sterile water
Leave the bone exposed and splint the limb tightly
Push the exposed bone back beneath the skin
Cover the wound with a sterile dressing before splinting
questions.explanation: Sterile coverage protects the exposed bone from further contamination before immobilization. Pushing bone back introduces contamination internally, field irrigation of an open fracture is not performed, and leaving it exposed increases infection risk.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate action if a patient with a suspected spinal injury reports tingling in the hands?
choices: Disregard the symptom since it will likely pass
Have the patient move the hands to see if it resolves
Massage the hands to restore normal sensation
Document the finding and maintain spinal precautions
questions.explanation: Tingling suggests cord or nerve root involvement, which is documented as a baseline and managed with continued precautions. Encouraging movement, massaging, and dismissing the symptom all risk worsening an injury and losing important information.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why a trauma patient may develop shock several hours after an apparently minor injury?
choices: The body produces less blood after any injury
Pain alone produces the findings of shock over time
Slow internal bleeding gradually depletes the circulating volume
Minor injuries cause delayed allergic reactions
questions.explanation: Slow bleeding from an organ such as the spleen can continue for hours before compensation fails and shock becomes apparent. Delayed allergy, reduced blood production, and pain alone do not account for the volume loss that produces shock.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate approach to a trauma patient who is combative and refusing care?
choices: Consider hypoxia or head injury as a cause of the behavior
Assume the patient is intoxicated and withdraw from the scene
Restrain the patient without further assessment
Accept the refusal and clear the scene without documentation
questions.explanation: Combativeness in a trauma patient often reflects hypoxia, hypoglycemia, or brain injury rather than a genuine refusal, and those causes are treatable. Assuming intoxication, restraining reflexively, and accepting a refusal without documentation all fail a patient who may lack capacity.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate response when a patient's clothing is stuck to a burn?
choices: Soak the area until the clothing releases from the skin
Cut around the adherent material and leave it in place
Leave all clothing in place without any removal
Pull the clothing free to expose the entire burn
questions.explanation: Cutting around adherent material avoids tearing away skin that is still attached to it, while removing the rest of the clothing stops ongoing burning. Pulling it free strips viable tissue, prolonged soaking causes heat loss, and leaving all clothing may allow continued injury.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate action for a patient with a suspected skull fracture and clear drainage from the nose?
choices: Allow the drainage to flow and apply a loose sterile dressing
Pack the nostrils to stop the drainage completely
Have the patient blow the nose to clear the passages
Apply firm pressure to the nose to control it
questions.explanation: Blocking cerebrospinal fluid drainage can raise intracranial pressure and increase the risk of infection, so the fluid is allowed to flow into a loose dressing. Packing, firm pressure, and nose blowing all obstruct or force flow in the wrong direction.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes an appropriate reason to reassess a trauma patient frequently during transport?
choices: Reassessment is required before the report can be closed
Compensated shock can decompensate without warning
Frequent checks reduce the patient's anxiety level
Vital signs have to be recorded a specific number of times
questions.explanation: A patient who is compensating can deteriorate rapidly, and only repeated assessment detects the change in time to act. Closing the report, anxiety reduction and a set number of recorded vital signs are not the clinical reason for repeated assessment.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes an appropriate action when a trauma patient's mechanism suggests serious injury but the exam is normal?
choices: Have the patient wait and call back if symptoms appear
Release the patient at the scene after documentation
Perform a second examination and then release
Transport for evaluation based on the mechanism alone
questions.explanation: Significant mechanisms can produce injuries that remain silent during the compensated period, so evaluation is based on more than the current exam. Releasing the patient, repeating an exam that will be equally normal, and waiting for symptoms all risk missing a developing injury.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate care for a patient with a suspected fracture of the clavicle?
choices: Apply a sling and swathe to support the arm
Apply a traction splint to the affected arm
Have the patient hold the arm overhead to reduce swelling
Splint the arm straight against the body
questions.explanation: A sling and swathe supports the weight of the arm and limits shoulder movement, which is what stabilizes a clavicle injury. Traction splints are for femur fractures, splinting straight increases discomfort, and raising the arm worsens the injury.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes why a patient with a diaphragm injury may develop respiratory distress?
choices: The diaphragm contracts more forcefully after injury
The diaphragm produces fluid that fills the chest
The injury directly punctures both lungs
Abdominal contents can move into the chest cavity
questions.explanation: A torn diaphragm allows abdominal organs to herniate into the chest, compressing the lung and impairing ventilation. The injured diaphragm loses rather than gains function, the lungs are not necessarily punctured, and the diaphragm does not produce fluid.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate use of a pressure dressing?
choices: Applied firmly enough to control bleeding while preserving distal pulses
Applied after a tourniquet has been removed
Applied loosely so that blood can drain from the wound
Applied tightly enough to eliminate the distal pulse
questions.explanation: A pressure dressing controls bleeding while allowing circulation to continue beyond the wound, which is confirmed by checking the distal pulse. Eliminating the pulse makes it a tourniquet, loose application does not control bleeding, and its use does not depend on tourniquet removal.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes an appropriate consideration when a trauma patient has been drinking alcohol?
choices: Intoxicated patients rarely sustain serious injuries
Alcohol can mask pain and complicate the assessment
Alcohol improves the patient's ability to describe symptoms
Intoxication explains all abnormal findings present
questions.explanation: Alcohol blunts pain perception and alters mentation, which hides injuries and makes assessment unreliable. Attributing findings to intoxication, assuming low injury risk, and expecting better symptom reporting all lead to missed injuries.

questions.question: A hypotensive multi-system trauma patient with a suspected spinal injury also has a painful, deformed thigh. How should the leg be managed?
choices: Apply a traction splint and individual splints to every injury before moving the patient
Secure the leg with the rest of the body on a long board, scoop or vacuum mattress and transport rapidly
Leave the leg unsecured so it can be examined at the hospital
Have the patient hold the leg still with their hands during transport
questions.explanation: In an unstable, high-priority trauma patient, time on scene matters more than splinting each injury, so the leg is secured to the device and the rest of the body during spinal motion restriction, which supports it as a unit, and the patient is transported rapidly. Stopping to apply a traction splint and individual splints delays definitive care for shock, leaving the leg unsecured lets the broken bone ends move and cause more damage, and a patient cannot reliably hold a fractured femur still.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the significance of unequal pupils in a trauma patient?
choices: It may indicate pressure on the nerve from an intracranial bleed
It indicates the patient has consumed alcohol recently
It indicates direct trauma to one of the eyes
It is a normal variation present in most patients
questions.explanation: Compression of the oculomotor nerve by rising intracranial pressure produces a dilated pupil on the affected side, which is an ominous finding. Direct eye trauma can also cause it, a small minority have naturally unequal pupils, and alcohol does not produce unilateral dilation.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management of a patient with signs of shock and no identified source of bleeding?
choices: Assume the findings are caused by anxiety
Treat for shock and transport while reassessing frequently
Withhold treatment until the source is identified
Limit care to oxygen administration
questions.explanation: Shock is treated based on the physiological findings, and a hidden internal source is assumed until proven otherwise. Waiting to identify the source, attributing findings to anxiety, and limiting care to oxygen all delay treatment of a life-threatening condition.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why a restrained driver may still sustain serious internal injury?
choices: Organs continue moving after the body is stopped by the belt
Seat belts increase the total energy of the collision
Restraints cause injuries to the chest wall
Restrained occupants absorb more energy than unrestrained ones
questions.explanation: The restraint stops the body while internal organs continue forward, which can tear vessels and attachments even when external injury is minimal. Belts reduce total energy transferred to the occupant, restraint injuries are not limited to the chest wall, and restrained occupants fare far better overall.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes an appropriate action when a patient has a suspected fracture and significant swelling?
choices: Apply a tight bandage to prevent further swelling
Leave all jewelry in place to avoid moving the limb
Cut the jewelry after arrival at the hospital
Remove jewelry from the affected limb before swelling worsens
questions.explanation: Jewelry that becomes trapped by swelling acts as a tourniquet, so it is removed early while it still slides off. Leaving it in place, deferring removal to the hospital, and applying tight bandaging all risk compromising circulation.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes appropriate care for a patient who has an eye that has been displaced from its socket?
choices: Apply a dry pressure dressing over the eye
Attempt to replace the eye into the socket gently
Have the patient close the eyelid over the eye
Cover with a moist sterile dressing and protect from pressure
questions.explanation: Moist sterile covering with a protective shield prevents drying and further injury while the eye is left in position. Replacing it, applying pressure, and forcing the lid closed all risk permanent damage to the globe.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate action when a trauma patient's pulse becomes weaker and faster during transport?
choices: Recheck the primary assessment and look for ongoing bleeding
Continue transport without changing the assessment plan already in place
Slow the vehicle to reduce the patient's anxiety
Wait until arrival to report the change
questions.explanation: A weakening faster pulse indicates deteriorating perfusion, which prompts a repeat of the primary assessment to find the cause. Continuing unchanged, slowing transport, and deferring the report all delay recognition of a patient who is decompensating.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate splinting principle for a suspected joint injury?
choices: Allow slight movement of the joint to maintain circulation
Immobilize the bones above and below the injured joint
Immobilize the joint itself without the adjacent bones
Immobilize the entire limb from shoulder to fingertips
questions.explanation: Immobilizing the bones on either side prevents movement at the injured joint. Splinting the joint alone allows the adjacent bones to move it, immobilizing the whole limb is unnecessary, and permitting movement defeats the purpose of the splint.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes an appropriate consideration when transporting a trauma patient a long distance?
choices: Reduce monitoring to conserve crew energy for arrival
Assume the patient will remain stable during the trip
Complete all documentation before departing the scene
Plan for reassessment intervals and anticipate deterioration
questions.explanation: Longer transports increase the opportunity for deterioration, so planned reassessment intervals and preparation for changes are essential. Reducing monitoring, assuming stability, and delaying departure for paperwork all increase risk to the patient.

questions.question: Which of the following is the body's largest organ and first barrier against infection?
choices: The stomach
The lungs
The skin
The liver
questions.explanation: The skin covers the entire body and forms the primary barrier against pathogens, which is why any break in it creates an infection risk. The liver, lungs, and stomach all serve essential functions but none acts as the body's outer protective barrier.

questions.question: Which term describes a break in the continuity of a bone?
choices: Strain
Fracture
Dislocation
Sprain
questions.explanation: A fracture is any break in a bone, whether complete or partial. A sprain involves stretched or torn ligaments, a strain involves muscle or tendon, and a dislocation is displacement of bones at a joint.

questions.question: Which term describes an injury in which a ligament is stretched or torn?
choices: Sprain
Contusion
Fracture
Strain
questions.explanation: Ligaments connect bone to bone, and injury to them is called a sprain. A strain involves muscle or tendon, a fracture is a broken bone, and a contusion is a bruise of soft tissue.

questions.question: Which term describes a closed soft tissue injury causing discoloration under intact skin?
choices: Laceration
Abrasion
Contusion
Avulsion
questions.explanation: A contusion is a bruise, where vessels bleed into tissue beneath skin that remains intact. An abrasion scrapes the surface, a laceration cuts through it, and an avulsion tears a flap of tissue away.

questions.question: Which term describes a wound in which the skin is scraped away by friction?
choices: Abrasion
Avulsion
Amputation
Puncture
questions.explanation: An abrasion removes the outer skin layers through friction against a surface. An avulsion tears a flap loose, a puncture is a narrow deep wound, and an amputation is complete removal of a body part.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of injury?
choices: The exact time elapsed since the injury first occurred
The forces that caused the patient's injuries
The specific injuries the patient sustained
The treatment plan chosen for the patient
questions.explanation: Mechanism of injury describes how the energy was applied to the body, which predicts what may be injured. The injuries themselves, the treatment plan, and elapsed time are all separate elements of the assessment.

questions.question: Which of the following is a sign of a possible skull fracture?
choices: A mild headache that resolves completely within just a few minutes
Bruising around both eyes without direct eye trauma
A small bump on the scalp that is tender
Dizziness that clears when the patient sits down
questions.explanation: Bruising around the eyes without a direct blow suggests blood tracking from a basilar skull fracture. A brief headache, a tender scalp bump, and transient dizziness are all common after minor head impacts.

questions.question: Which of the following is the first priority when caring for any burn patient?
choices: Estimating the burn surface area
Applying a burn-specific dressing
Determining the cause of the fire
Stopping the burning process
questions.explanation: Tissue continues to be damaged until the source of heat or chemical is removed, so stopping the process limits the injury. Area estimation, cause determination, and dressing application all follow.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of shock in a trauma patient?
choices: A psychological reaction to witnessing the traumatic event itself
Blood loss reducing the circulating volume
Infection developing at the injury site
An allergic reaction to a medication
questions.explanation: Hemorrhage, whether internal or external, is by far the most common cause of shock after injury. Allergic reactions, infection, and psychological responses cause shock or shock-like presentations far less often in trauma.

questions.question: Which of the following describes penetrating trauma?
choices: The body is exposed to extreme temperature
Force is applied without breaking the skin
Repeated physical stress is applied over a long period of time
An object passes through the skin into the body
questions.explanation: Penetrating trauma involves an object breaching the skin and entering the body, as with stab and gunshot wounds. Force without skin breakage is blunt trauma, temperature exposure causes thermal injury, and repeated stress causes overuse injury.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why a patient with a chest injury can develop shock without external bleeding?
choices: The chest cavity can hold a large volume of lost blood
Chest injuries always reduce the heart's electrical activity
Chest injuries prevent the heart from filling with air
Blood in the chest is reabsorbed and replaced immediately
questions.explanation: Each side of the chest can hold liters of blood, so a hemothorax produces major volume loss that is entirely concealed. Electrical activity is not universally affected, blood is not rapidly reabsorbed, and the heart does not fill with air.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why the brain is particularly vulnerable to swelling after injury?
choices: The rigid skull leaves no room for expansion
Brain tissue swells more than any other tissue
The brain has no blood supply of its own
Swelling in the brain resolves more slowly than elsewhere
questions.explanation: Because the skull cannot expand, any increase in volume raises pressure and compresses the tissue and its blood supply. Brain tissue does not swell uniquely, it is richly perfused, and the central problem is the fixed container rather than the resolution rate.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why a patient with extensive burns is at risk of hypothermia?
choices: Damaged skin can no longer regulate heat and fluid loss
Burn patients have significantly reduced metabolic rates overall
Burned tissue actively draws heat from the core
Cooling is required for all burns regardless of size
questions.explanation: The skin's barrier function is destroyed, so heat and fluid escape freely from the burned surface. Burned tissue does not draw heat from the core, metabolic rate typically rises after major burns, and extensive cooling is avoided precisely because of this risk.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes why a patient struck by a vehicle should be assessed for multiple injury patterns?
choices: Impact, hood strike, and ground contact each cause injuries
Ground contact rarely causes any additional injury beyond the initial impact
Only the point of first contact produces significant injury
Pedestrian injuries are always limited to the lower legs
questions.explanation: A pedestrian is typically struck by the bumper, thrown onto the hood, and then onto the ground, producing three distinct sets of injuries. Injuries are not confined to the legs or to the initial contact point, and ground impact frequently causes head and spinal injury.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why capillary refill is less reliable in a cold environment?
choices: Cold speeds capillary refill and hides poor perfusion
Cold causes vasoconstriction that delays refill independently
Cold has no measurable effect on capillary refill
Cold makes the nail beds impossible to blanch
questions.explanation: Cold-induced vasoconstriction delays refill even in a well-perfused patient, producing a false indication of shock. Cold does not speed refill, it clearly affects the measurement, and nail beds can still be blanched.

questions.question: Which of the following would most suggest that a chest injury patient is developing a hemothorax rather than a pneumothorax?
choices: Decreased breath sounds with distended neck veins
Subcutaneous air felt across the upper chest
Decreased breath sounds with dull percussion and shock signs
Sharp pain that increases with deep inspiration
questions.explanation: Blood in the pleural space produces dull percussion along with signs of volume loss, unlike air, which produces hyperresonance. Distended neck veins suggest tension physiology, positional sharp pain is nonspecific, and subcutaneous air suggests an air leak.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains the risk associated with a burn involving the perineum?
choices: High infection risk from contamination in that area
The area has no blood supply to support healing once it has been burned
Burns there extend into the abdominal cavity
The area contains no nerve endings to signal injury
questions.explanation: Burns in this region are readily contaminated by urine and stool, which makes infection a major concern and is why they are referred to burn centers. Nerve endings are present, the burns do not extend into the abdomen, and the area is well perfused.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why children sustain internal injuries with less external evidence than adults?
choices: Force disperses away from the body in children
Flexible bones transmit force inward without fracturing
Children have thicker skin that hides external injury from view
Children have smaller organs that resist injury
questions.explanation: A child's pliable ribs and bones bend rather than break, transmitting energy to the organs beneath while leaving little external sign. Children's skin is thinner, their organs are proportionally larger and less protected, and force is not dispersed away from the body.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why a patient with severe bleeding should not be given oral fluids?
choices: Oral fluids dilute the remaining blood dangerously
Drinking causes an immediate and dangerous drop in blood pressure
Surgery may be required and aspiration risk is increased
Fluids by mouth increase the rate of external bleeding
questions.explanation: A bleeding patient is likely to need anesthesia and surgery, both of which are complicated by stomach contents, and shock itself raises the aspiration risk. Oral fluids do not meaningfully dilute blood, increase bleeding, or drop blood pressure directly.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the concern when a trauma patient has both a head injury and hypotension?
choices: Hypotension indicates the head injury is minor
The two conditions are unrelated and treated separately
The combination substantially worsens brain injury outcomes
Hypotension protects the brain from further swelling
questions.explanation: Hypoxia and hypotension are the two insults that most worsen outcomes after brain injury, because the injured brain cannot maintain its own perfusion. Low pressure does not protect the brain, the conditions interact directly, and hypotension does not indicate a minor injury.

questions.question: A trauma patient has a heart rate of 132, a blood pressure of 88 over 74, cool skin, and confusion. Which stage of shock does this represent?
choices: Decompensated shock with failing compensation
A normal physiological stress response
Irreversible shock beyond any treatment
Compensated shock with compensatory mechanisms still intact
questions.explanation: Hypotension with a narrow pulse pressure and confusion indicates that compensatory mechanisms can no longer maintain perfusion. Compensated shock preserves pressure and mentation, irreversible shock is defined retrospectively, and this is well beyond a normal stress response.

questions.question: A patient with a stab wound to the left chest has distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds, and hypotension with clear bilateral breath sounds. Which condition is most likely?
choices: Massive hemothorax filling the entire left side of the chest cavity
Isolated rib fracture with splinting
Cardiac tamponade compressing the ventricles
Tension pneumothorax on the left side
questions.explanation: Distended neck veins, muffled tones, and hypotension with clear lungs indicate blood in the pericardial sac restricting cardiac filling. Both tension pneumothorax and massive hemothorax would alter breath sounds on the affected side, and a rib fracture does not cause hypotension with distended veins.

questions.question: A patient trapped under a collapsed wall for three hours is about to be freed. Which preparation is most important?
choices: Expect the patient to improve as soon as they are released
Plan to splint all extremities before any movement occurs
Prepare to apply tourniquets to all compressed limbs
Anticipate rhythm disturbances and prepare for rapid deterioration
questions.explanation: Release of prolonged compression floods the circulation with potassium and metabolic byproducts, which can cause lethal dysrhythmias within minutes. Splinting is secondary, prophylactic tourniquets are not standard practice, and deterioration rather than improvement is the expected pattern.

questions.question: A patient in a vehicle collision has a rigid abdomen, a pulse of 128, and a blood pressure of 92 over 76 with 15 minutes to the nearest trauma center. What is the best course of action?
choices: Transport immediately with assessment continued en route
Transport to a closer facility without surgical capability
Wait for air transport regardless of the added delay
Remain on scene to complete a full secondary assessment
questions.explanation: Internal bleeding requires surgical control, and fifteen minutes to a trauma center is a short interval to spend on transport rather than on scene. Completing an assessment on scene, choosing a facility without surgery, and waiting for a helicopter all add delay without benefit.

questions.question: A patient with a head injury has a pulse of 52, a blood pressure of 192 over 100, and irregular respirations. What does this indicate about the patient's status?
choices: A response to pain that will resolve with reassurance
A cardiac cause unrelated to the head injury
Critically elevated intracranial pressure requiring rapid transport
Adequate compensation that requires routine monitoring
questions.explanation: Hypertension with bradycardia and an irregular respiratory pattern indicates dangerously high pressure within the skull and impending herniation. This is not adequate compensation, is not explained by a primary cardiac problem, and is not a pain response.

questions.question: A patient with a thigh wound has bleeding controlled by a tourniquet applied 90 minutes ago. What is the most important consideration during a prolonged transport?
choices: Document the time and communicate it clearly to the trauma team
Reapply the tourniquet in a new position every hour
Loosen the tourniquet every 20 minutes to help restore circulation during transport
Remove the tourniquet once bleeding has stopped completely
questions.explanation: Ischemia time determines the hospital's management decisions, so the application time is documented and communicated clearly. Periodic loosening, removal, and repositioning all risk renewed catastrophic bleeding from an injury that required a tourniquet.

questions.question: Select the (2) findings that indicate a trauma patient is compensating for blood loss.
choices: Cool pale skin with a normal blood pressure
A blood pressure of 72 systolic with confusion
A heart rate that has risen to 118
Warm dry skin with a heart rate of 68
Warm, flushed skin with a low blood pressure
questions.explanation: Tachycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction with a maintained blood pressure are the hallmarks of compensated shock. Hypotension with confusion indicates compensation has failed, and warm dry skin with a normal rate indicates no significant volume loss. Warm, flushed skin with a low blood pressure suggests distributive shock, such as neurogenic or septic, rather than compensation for blood loss.

questions.question: Select the (2) burns that should be transported to a burn center under standard criteria.
choices: A small superficial burn on the upper arm
A partial thickness burn involving the face
A full thickness burn encircling the forearm
A sunburn across both shoulders
A partial thickness burn covering 5% of the back in a healthy adult
questions.explanation: Facial burns carry airway implications and circumferential full thickness burns threaten circulation, so both require specialized care. A small superficial burn and a sunburn can be managed without a burn center. A partial-thickness burn of 5% of the back in a healthy adult is below the burn center threshold of 10% total body surface area.

questions.question: Select the (2) findings that indicate a chest injury is immediately life threatening.
choices: Tenderness over a single rib on palpation
Absent breath sounds with tracheal deviation
Paradoxical movement of a chest wall segment
A superficial abrasion across the sternum
Pain on deep breathing with normal vital signs
questions.explanation: A flail segment impairs ventilation and usually accompanies underlying lung injury, and absent sounds with tracheal deviation indicate a tension pneumothorax. Isolated rib tenderness and a superficial abrasion are painful but not immediately life threatening. Pain on deep breathing with normal vital signs is concerning but not immediately life threatening.

questions.question: Select the (2) mechanisms that should raise a high index of suspicion for spinal injury.
choices: A diving incident in shallow water
A twisted ankle while walking on grass
A fall from a roof onto a hard surface
A rear-end collision at 5 mph with no complaints
A trip from standing onto an outstretched hand
questions.explanation: A significant fall and a shallow water dive both apply axial loading forces to the spine. A twisted ankle and a trip from standing onto an outstretched hand do not load the spine, and a 5 mph rear-end collision with no complaints is a low-energy mechanism.

questions.question: Select the (2) actions that are appropriate in the initial management of an open abdominal wound with evisceration.
choices: Replace the organs into the abdominal cavity gently
Apply a dry pressure dressing directly over the organs
Cover the exposed organs with a moist sterile dressing
Position the patient supine with the knees flexed
Sit the patient upright to relieve pressure on the wound
questions.explanation: Moist coverage prevents drying, and flexing the knees reduces tension on the abdominal wall. Replacing organs introduces contamination and injury, and a dry pressure dressing damages the exposed tissue. Sitting the patient upright increases tension on the abdominal wall.

questions.question: Arrange the steps for splinting a suspected forearm fracture with intact circulation, from first to last.
choices: Assess pulse, motor function, and sensation distal to the injury
Reassess pulse, motor function, and sensation after application
Expose the injury site by removing or cutting away clothing
Secure the splint without compromising circulation
questions.explanation: The injury is exposed first so the whole site can be seen, a neurovascular baseline is established before the device is applied, the splint is secured without compromising flow, and the reassessment confirms circulation remains intact. Any open wound found on exposure is covered with a sterile dressing before the splint goes on.

questions.question: Arrange the steps for managing an open chest wound, from first to last.
choices: Monitor for signs of a developing tension pneumothorax
Assess breath sounds and respiratory effort
Expose the chest and identify all wounds present
Apply an occlusive dressing over the wound
questions.explanation: The chest is exposed so every wound is found, and an open wound is sealed with an occlusive dressing as soon as it is found, because every breath can draw more air into the pleural space while it stays open. Breath sounds and respiratory effort are then assessed to set the baseline after the seal, and ongoing monitoring detects a tension pneumothorax if one develops.

questions.question: Arrange the stages of shock in the order they occur as a patient deteriorates.
choices: Blood pressure falls and mental status declines
Organ damage becomes irreversible despite treatment
Initial blood loss occurs without any visible change
Heart rate rises while blood pressure is maintained
questions.explanation: Early loss produces no measurable change, compensation then raises the heart rate while preserving pressure, decompensation follows with falling pressure and declining mentation, and irreversible organ injury develops last.

questions.question: Arrange the steps for approaching a patient pinned under a vehicle, from first to last.
choices: Assess the scene for hazards and request rescue resources
Stabilize the vehicle to prevent any movement
Perform a primary assessment and manage life threats
Remove the patient once the vehicle is secured
questions.explanation: Hazard assessment with early resource requests comes first, the vehicle is stabilized so it cannot shift onto patient or rescuers, life threats are addressed as access allows, and removal follows once the scene is secured.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate care for a patient whose finger is caught in a ring with significant swelling?
choices: Cut the finger free of the ring using shears
Attempt removal with lubricant and transport if unsuccessful
Apply ice for 20 minutes before attempting removal
Leave the ring in place without any intervention
questions.explanation: A gentle attempt with lubrication may succeed, and the hospital has ring cutters when it does not. Cutting the finger is obviously inappropriate, leaving it without any attempt allows swelling to worsen the constriction, and prolonged icing delays care without resolving the problem.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate care for a patient with a nosebleed after facial trauma with a suspected skull fracture?
choices: Apply ice directly over the bridge of the nose
Allow the blood to drain and avoid packing the nostrils
Have the patient tilt the head back to slow the flow
Pack both nostrils tightly with rolled gauze to fully control the bleeding
questions.explanation: With a possible skull fracture, packing can force material toward the fracture and blocking drainage can raise intracranial pressure. Tilting the head back causes blood to be swallowed, and ice does not address the concern with this mechanism.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the significance of a patient who becomes suddenly quiet after being agitated following trauma?
choices: It indicates the patient has calmed down appropriately
It confirms the patient was not seriously injured
It may indicate worsening perfusion or brain injury
It suggests the pain has resolved on its own
questions.explanation: A trauma patient who becomes quiet and withdrawn after being agitated is often deteriorating rather than settling, as cerebral perfusion falls. Interpreting the change as calm, resolved pain, or evidence against injury misses a patient who is declining.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate action for a patient with a laceration and an embedded foreign body that is small and superficial?
choices: Leave the object in place and bandage around it
Remove the object and irrigate the wound thoroughly
Apply a tourniquet above the wound as a precaution
Push the object beneath the skin for protection
questions.explanation: Embedded objects are left in place for removal under controlled conditions, since removal can cause bleeding or leave fragments. Field removal, pushing the object deeper, and applying a tourniquet for a minor wound all cause unnecessary harm.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes an appropriate action when multiple trauma patients are present and resources are limited?
choices: Transport the patients who are closest to the ambulance
Treat the patients who are calling for help first
Triage to identify those who benefit most from immediate care
Treat each patient completely before moving to the next
questions.explanation: Triage directs limited resources toward the patients most likely to survive with prompt intervention. Complete treatment one at a time, proximity-based selection, and responding to whoever calls for help all misallocate limited resources, since the quiet patient may be the sickest.

questions.question: Which of the following would most concern you about a patient who fell from a ladder and complains only of back pain?
choices: A muscular strain that will resolve on its own
Possible spinal fracture with delayed neurological symptoms
Discomfort caused by the position he was found in
Pain that developed from lying on a hard surface
questions.explanation: A fall from height with back pain suggests a vertebral fracture, and neurological symptoms can appear later if the spine moves. Attributing the pain to a strain, to positioning, or to the surface he was lying on all risk allowing that movement to occur.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate care for a patient with a suspected fracture who is in severe pain during movement?
choices: Minimize movement, immobilize, and support the limb during transfers
Have the patient move himself to control his own pain
Delay immobilization until the pain subsides on its own
Move the patient quickly to reduce the total time in pain
questions.explanation: Limiting movement and supporting the limb during every transfer is what reduces pain and prevents further injury. Moving quickly increases the movement at the fracture, self-movement is unreliable, and waiting for pain to subside leaves the fracture unstable.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate management of a patient with a wound that continues bleeding despite a pressure dressing?
choices: Apply a cold pack over the dressing to constrict vessels
Apply direct manual pressure and consider a tourniquet
Elevate the limb and wait for the bleeding to slow
Remove the dressing and inspect the wound repeatedly
questions.explanation: Firm manual pressure, followed by a tourniquet for extremity wounds, escalates the control appropriately. Repeated inspection disrupts clot formation, elevation alone does not control arterial bleeding, and cold does not stop significant hemorrhage.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes an appropriate action when a trauma patient's family asks about his condition at the scene?
choices: Provide brief factual information while continuing care
Tell the family the patient will certainly be fine
Provide a detailed prognosis for the patient's recovery
Decline to speak with the family under any circumstances
questions.explanation: Brief factual updates support the family without interrupting care or overstating what is known. Prognostic predictions exceed the provider's scope, refusing to speak is needlessly harsh, and false reassurance can be devastating if the patient deteriorates.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate action when a trauma patient has both an obvious open fracture and signs of shock?
choices: Complete the splinting of the fracture before any other care is given
Address the shock first while covering the fracture wound
Delay all treatment until arrival at the hospital
Treat the fracture as the visible injury
questions.explanation: Shock threatens life immediately, so perfusion is addressed while the open wound is covered, with definitive splinting during packaging or transport. Prioritizing the splint, treating only the visible injury, and deferring all care leave the perfusion deficit untreated.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate action for a patient with a burn who is wearing a synthetic shirt that has melted onto the skin?
choices: Peel the melted material off the skin carefully
Scrub the area vigorously to remove all of the melted plastic residue
Leave the shirt intact without cutting
Cool the area and cut around the adherent material
questions.explanation: Cooling stops the burning process, and cutting around the adherent material avoids stripping away skin that remains attached to it. Peeling and scrubbing both remove viable tissue, and leaving the garment entirely intact may allow continued heat transfer.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes an appropriate reason to consider internal bleeding in a patient with no visible injury?
choices: A history of a similar event several years earlier
A preference for transport to a specific hospital
A patient's report that he feels generally unwell
Signs of shock with a mechanism capable of causing injury
questions.explanation: Perfusion findings combined with a mechanism capable of producing injury are what raise suspicion for concealed bleeding. A general complaint, a remote history, and hospital preference provide no evidence of ongoing internal blood loss.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes an appropriate consideration when a patient has been trapped for an extended period in a cold environment?
choices: Both hypothermia and crush effects may complicate care
Cold exposure protects against all injury complications
The traumatic injuries are what require attention
Hypothermia is unlikely if the patient is conscious
questions.explanation: Prolonged entrapment in cold conditions combines hypothermia, which impairs clotting, with the metabolic consequences of prolonged compression. Focusing only on trauma, assuming cold is protective, and using consciousness to exclude hypothermia all miss significant complications.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate action when a patient with a chest injury has increasing difficulty breathing after an occlusive dressing was applied?
choices: Increase the oxygen flow and continue without changes
Apply additional dressings to reinforce the seal
Remove the dressing permanently and leave the wound open
Lift a corner of the dressing to release trapped air
