questions.explanation: Worsening distress after sealing a chest wound suggests air is accumulating under pressure, and briefly lifting the dressing allows it to escape. Reinforcing the seal traps more air, permanently removing it allows air to enter again, and additional oxygen does not relieve the pressure.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the appropriate care for a patient with a suspected hip fracture?
choices: Straighten the leg fully before securing the patient
Have the patient walk to the stretcher with assistance
Apply a traction splint to the affected leg
Immobilize with padding and move the patient as a unit
questions.explanation: Padding to support the limb in the position found with movement as a unit limits pain and further injury. Traction splints are for midshaft femur fractures, walking risks displacement, and forced straightening causes additional damage.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes why a trauma patient's mental status is monitored closely?
choices: Mental status is the only finding that must be documented
Changes in mentation should always be expected in every trauma patient
Mental status is the best guide to how much pain the patient has
Changes often signal falling perfusion before other findings
questions.explanation: The brain is highly sensitive to reduced oxygen delivery, so confusion, agitation, or drowsiness often appear before pressure falls. Mental status is not a reliable guide to pain, is one of many documented findings, and a change is never dismissed as expected.

questions.question: What is the standard adult dose delivered by an epinephrine auto-injector?
choices: 0.3 mg
1.0 mg
3.0 mg
questions.explanation: An adult auto-injector delivers 0.3 mg of epinephrine intramuscularly. The 0.15 mg junior device is the pediatric strength, and 1.0 mg is the cardiac-arrest IV/IO dose given by ALS — not a dose an EMT gives by auto-injector.

questions.question: A 22 kg child is in anaphylaxis after eating a peanut-containing snack. Which auto-injector strength is indicated?
choices: 0.3 mg, on the basis that any patient in anaphylaxis gets the adult dose
0.15 mg (the junior device)
0.05 mg, halved again for a child this small
No auto-injector — children are managed with oxygen and transport alone
questions.explanation: The 0.15 mg junior auto-injector is intended for children roughly 15-30 kg, so a 22 kg child falls squarely in that range. Auto-injectors come in fixed strengths and cannot be partially administered, and withholding epinephrine in anaphylaxis is never the safer choice.

questions.question: An adult in anaphylaxis has received one 0.3 mg auto-injector. Ten minutes later the stridor and hypotension are unchanged and transport is still 15 minutes out. What is the appropriate action?
choices: Wait for the first dose to take full effect; a second dose is outside EMT scope
Contact medical direction about a second dose, since the symptoms persist
Switch to a 0.15 mg junior device to avoid overdosing
Withhold further epinephrine and give oral antihistamines instead
questions.explanation: Anaphylaxis that does not improve after an initial dose commonly needs a repeat, typically 5-15 minutes later, and many systems allow a second auto-injector on standing order or after contacting medical direction. Antihistamines are far too slow for airway compromise and shock, and a smaller pediatric dose would make the undertreatment worse.

questions.question: Where and how is an epinephrine auto-injector administered?
choices: Into the outer thigh muscle, through clothing if needed
Subcutaneously into the abdomen, on bare skin only
Intravenously into the forearm
Intramuscularly into the buttock, on bare skin only
questions.explanation: The device is designed to be pressed firmly against the anterolateral thigh (the vastus lateralis), where the large muscle gives fast, reliable absorption, and it will fire through ordinary clothing — which matters when seconds count. Auto-injectors are not an intravenous route, and the thigh is preferred over the buttock.

questions.question: Why is epinephrine effective in anaphylaxis?
choices: It blocks histamine at the receptor, reversing the reaction at its source
It constricts blood vessels, relaxes bronchial smooth muscle, and increases cardiac output
It neutralizes the allergen still circulating in the bloodstream
It sedates the patient so the airway swelling is better tolerated
questions.explanation: Epinephrine acts on alpha receptors to constrict vessels (raising blood pressure and reducing airway edema) and on beta receptors to dilate bronchioles and increase heart rate and contractility — so it works on all three of the things killing the patient at once. It does not block histamine (that is what antihistamines do, far more slowly) and does nothing to the allergen itself.

questions.question: An adult with suspected cardiac chest pain and no contraindications is given aspirin. Which dose and route are correct?
choices: 81 mg, swallowed whole
162–325 mg, chewed
650 mg, swallowed whole
1000 mg, dissolved in water
questions.explanation: Field guidance for suspected acute coronary syndrome is 162–325 mg (often given as 324 mg, four 81 mg chewable tablets, or one 325 mg tablet) of non-enteric-coated aspirin, chewed rather than swallowed. Chewing breaks the tablet up so it dissolves and is absorbed much faster than a tablet swallowed whole, which is the whole point when the goal is to inhibit platelet aggregation as quickly as possible.

questions.question: A 58-year-old with crushing chest pain tells you he took a tablet for erectile dysfunction last night. What does this change?
choices: Nitroglycerin is contraindicated; aspirin is not
Both aspirin and nitroglycerin are contraindicated
Nothing changes; the dose was over 12 hours ago
Aspirin is contraindicated; nitroglycerin is not
questions.explanation: Sildenafil-type drugs and nitrates are both vasodilators, and together they can produce profound hypotension that does not respond to the usual measures. The window is 24 to 48 hours depending on the drug, so last night is well inside it. Aspirin is unaffected and should still be given. Ask this question of every patient before nitroglycerin, not only the men: the same drugs are prescribed for pulmonary hypertension.

questions.question: Before assisting a patient with a second dose of their nitroglycerin, what must you do?
choices: Take another blood pressure
Confirm the pain has not changed in character
Recheck the oxygen saturation
Wait a full 10 minutes from the first dose
questions.explanation: A blood pressure before every dose, not only the first. Nitroglycerin drops preload, and a patient whose pressure was acceptable before dose one can be below the threshold before dose two. The usual limit is a systolic under 100, though some protocols use 90. The interval is 5 minutes, up to three doses. Oxygen saturation and the character of the pain are both worth reassessing, but neither is the thing that stops you giving the next dose.

questions.question: A patient with an inferior wall myocardial infarction becomes markedly hypotensive after one dose of nitroglycerin. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The right ventricle is involved and depends on the preload nitroglycerin removed
The nitroglycerin tablet had expired and released too large a dose
The patient is having an allergic reaction to the nitroglycerin
The blood pressure cuff was the wrong size for the patient's arm
questions.explanation: An inferior MI often involves the right ventricle, and a failing right ventricle depends heavily on venous return to fill it. Nitroglycerin works by reducing exactly that, so a normal dose can drop the pressure catastrophically. Lay the patient supine (leg elevation only if your protocol allows it), give oxygen if indicated, and call for ALS. Nitroglycerin allergy is rare and would not present as isolated hypotension.

questions.question: What is the adult dose of epinephrine from an auto-injector for anaphylaxis, and where is it given?
choices: 0.3 mg into the lateral thigh
0.15 mg into the lateral thigh
0.3 mg into the upper arm
1 mg into the buttock
questions.explanation: 0.3 mg intramuscularly into the lateral thigh for an adult, 0.15 mg for a child under about 30 kg. The lateral thigh is chosen because the muscle there is large and well perfused, so absorption is fast and reliable, and it can be reached through clothing. The buttock is not used: absorption is slower and less predictable.

questions.question: A patient in anaphylaxis has a history of coronary artery disease. How does this affect giving epinephrine?
choices: It does not; there is no absolute contraindication in true anaphylaxis
Epinephrine is contraindicated and only antihistamines should be given
The dose should be halved
Medical control must authorize it before any dose is given
questions.explanation: There is no absolute contraindication to epinephrine in a patient who is actually in anaphylaxis. Heart disease, hypertension and age are cautions worth knowing about, not reasons to withhold the only drug that treats the airway swelling, the bronchospasm and the hypotension at once. Antihistamines do none of those things and do not work quickly. Whether you need authorization first is a protocol question, and it is answered before the shift, not on scene.

questions.question: A patient given epinephrine for anaphylaxis improves completely within minutes and asks to stay home. What is the correct response?
choices: Explain that the reaction can return hours later and transport is advised
Accept the refusal — the epinephrine has clearly worked
Accept the refusal if a second dose is left with the patient
Accept the refusal provided a family member stays with them
questions.explanation: A biphasic reaction can return hours after the first has resolved, when the epinephrine has worn off and nobody is watching. That is why every patient who receives epinephrine is transported, however well they look. Leaving a spare auto-injector does not address the problem, because the patient may be alone or unconscious when the second reaction starts.

questions.question: A patient with an opioid overdose is breathing 4 times a minute. What should be done first?
choices: Begin ventilating with a bag-valve mask
Give naloxone intranasally
Apply a non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min
Perform a sternal rub to rouse the patient
questions.explanation: Opioid overdose kills by respiratory depression, and hypoxia is what does the damage. A bag-valve mask fixes that immediately; naloxone takes minutes to work and does nothing for the intervening time. Naloxone follows, it does not lead. A non-rebreather delivers oxygen but does nothing for a patient who is not moving enough air to use it, and a sternal rub treats nothing.

questions.question: Why must a patient who responds to naloxone still be transported?
choices: Naloxone can wear off before the opioid does
Naloxone causes permanent kidney damage that needs monitoring
The patient will be unable to walk for several hours
Naloxone must be reversed at the hospital with a second drug
questions.explanation: Naloxone has a shorter duration than many opioids, particularly long-acting ones, so a patient who wakes up can go back down once it wears off. That is the whole reason transport is not optional, and it is the point a patient in withdrawal is least willing to hear. Naloxone is not reversed at hospital and does not damage the kidneys.

questions.question: What should you expect after giving naloxone to a patient in a deep opioid overdose?
choices: Possible vomiting, agitation and combativeness from acute withdrawal
A gradual, calm return to normal mentation over 20 minutes
A sustained drop in heart rate and blood pressure
Immediate resolution with no further monitoring needed
questions.explanation: Naloxone strips the opioid off the receptors at once, and the patient can wake into acute withdrawal: nauseated, vomiting, frightened and sometimes combative. Plan for it. Have suction ready, position to protect the airway, and think about your own safety and your partner's before the patient wakes rather than after.

questions.question: A conscious patient with a COPD history has a saturation of 86% and is working hard to breathe. What is the correct approach to oxygen?
choices: Give oxygen, titrated to relieve the hypoxia
Withhold oxygen to avoid suppressing their drive to breathe
Give a fixed 2 L/min by cannula regardless of the response
Withhold oxygen until the saturation falls below 80%
questions.explanation: A hypoxic patient gets oxygen. The old teaching that COPD patients should be denied oxygen out of concern for a hypoxic drive has been dropped, because leaving a patient hypoxic is the greater and more immediate danger. Titrate toward the patient's own baseline, often the low 90s rather than 100%, and watch mental status and respiratory effort as you go.

questions.question: What is the usual nebulized dose of albuterol?
choices: 2.5 mg in 3 mL of saline
0.5 mg in 3 mL of saline
5 mg in 1 mL of saline
10 mg in 5 mL of saline
questions.explanation: 2.5 mg in 3 mL of saline, nebulized over roughly 5 to 15 minutes and driven by oxygen. By metered-dose inhaler a patient typically takes two puffs (more in a severe attack, per protocol), ideally through a spacer, which gets far more of the drug past the mouth and into the lung than a bare inhaler does.

questions.question: After a nebulized albuterol treatment, an asthmatic patient's wheezing has stopped, but they are more drowsy and their work of breathing has fallen. What does this suggest?
choices: Deterioration — too little air is moving to produce a wheeze
Improvement; the wheeze has resolved
A normal response to the drug that needs no further action
An allergic reaction to the albuterol
questions.explanation: A wheeze is the sound of air being forced past a narrowed airway, so it requires air to be moving. A chest that falls silent while the patient becomes drowsy and stops working to breathe has not improved; it has run out of reserve. The silent chest is a pre-arrest finding. Judge the response by mental status and work of breathing, never by the wheeze alone.

questions.question: What side effect should you expect after giving albuterol?
choices: Tachycardia and tremor
Bradycardia and drowsiness
Hypotension and flushing
Constricted pupils and salivation
questions.explanation: Albuterol is a beta-2 agonist, but the selectivity is not absolute, so beta-1 effects come with it: a faster heart rate, tremor, and a jittery, nervous feeling patients often find unpleasant. Warn them it is coming. It is an expected effect rather than a reason to stop the treatment.

questions.question: A diabetic patient is confused but can follow commands and swallow on request. Their glucose is 48 mg/dL. What is appropriate?
choices: Oral glucose gel between the cheek and gum
Nothing by mouth; request ALS for intravenous dextrose
A full glass of orange juice, drunk quickly
Oral glucose only once the glucose falls below 40 mg/dL
questions.explanation: A patient who can swallow and protect their airway can have oral glucose, given a little at a time between the cheek and the gum with the patient sitting up. A large volume of liquid taken quickly by a confused patient is an aspiration risk, which is why gel is preferred to juice here. Waiting for a lower number treats the meter rather than the patient.

questions.question: What single finding most clearly rules out giving oral glucose?
choices: The patient cannot swallow safely
The patient has type 2 rather than type 1 diabetes
The glucose reading is above 50 mg/dL
The patient has already eaten today
questions.explanation: The airway decides this one. Oral glucose needs a patient who can actively swallow and protect their own airway; without that, the gel pools in the oropharynx and is aspirated. Ask them to swallow on command and watch them do it, rather than judging from how awake they seem. Which type of diabetes they have does not change the treatment.

questions.question: A hypoglycemic patient recovers fully after oral glucose. Which finding in their history most strongly argues against accepting a refusal of transport?
choices: They take a long-acting sulfonylurea
They have had hypoglycemia once before
They have not eaten since breakfast
They live alone and drove home earlier
questions.explanation: A long-acting oral agent keeps driving insulin release for many hours, while a tube of glucose gel lasts perhaps one. That mismatch means the patient will very likely go hypoglycemic again, probably at home and possibly alone, after you have cleared. Missed meals and living alone both add risk, but the pharmacology is the specific and compelling argument.

questions.question: Which of these is the correct sequence when a patient in respiratory distress needs assisted ventilation?
choices: Open and clear the airway, then ventilate with a BVM and oxygen
Apply a non-rebreather first and reassess in five minutes
Give a nebulized bronchodilator before any ventilation is attempted
Insert an airway adjunct and apply a nasal cannula
questions.explanation: Airway before breathing, every time. A bag-valve mask cannot ventilate past an obstruction, and the adjunct or suction that clears it comes first. Once the airway is open, assisted ventilation with supplemental oxygen is what a patient who is not moving enough air needs; a mask only helps a patient who is still ventilating adequately on their own.

questions.question: An EMT may 'assist' a patient with their own medication. What does that generally require?
choices: The medication is prescribed to this patient and protocol allows it
The patient is over 18 and able to consent
A family member confirms the medication is the right one
The medication is in its original container
questions.explanation: Assisting means the drug belongs to this patient, by prescription, and your protocol permits you to help them take it. Both halves matter. An original container and a family member's word are useful checks on identity, and consent is always needed, but neither answers the question of whether you are permitted to act. Know which drugs your service allows before the call, not during it.

questions.question: Which of the following patients should receive high-flow oxygen regardless of the pulse oximeter reading?
choices: A patient rescued from a house fire with suspected carbon monoxide exposure
A patient with a saturation of 97% and mild anxiety
A patient with a sprained ankle and normal vital signs
A diabetic patient with a glucose of 60 mg/dL and normal breathing
questions.explanation: A pulse oximeter cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, so a carbon monoxide patient can read 100% while their tissues are starved. Give high-flow oxygen on the history rather than the number. In every other listed patient the reading means what it says, and none of them is hypoxic.

questions.question: Which set of findings together meets the criteria for anaphylaxis rather than a simple allergic reaction?
choices: Hives plus wheezing and hoarseness after eating shellfish
Widespread hives and intense itching, with normal vital signs
A localized rash at the site of a bee sting
Nausea alone, an hour after a meal with no known allergen
questions.explanation: Anaphylaxis needs more than one body system involved after a likely exposure, or hypotension following a known allergen. Skin plus airway, as here, qualifies. Skin findings on their own, however widespread and uncomfortable, are an allergic reaction and are treated supportively while you watch closely for progression. A single symptom with no identified exposure does not meet the definition.

questions.question: You find a man in cardiac arrest on a soft bed in his home. Moving him to the floor would take your crew about a minute. What should you do?
choices: Move him to the floor first, since compressions on a mattress do not work
Start compressions in the bed now; move him or slide a board under him only if it does not delay CPR
Wait for the backboard from the ambulance before starting compressions
Give rescue breaths only until he can be moved to a firm surface
questions.explanation: The 2025 AHA guidelines put starting compressions ahead of finding the perfect surface: CPR begins where the patient is found if high-quality compressions can be given there, because every delay before the first compression lowers the chance of survival. A firm surface is still better, so a board can be slid underneath or the patient moved to the floor when it can be done quickly without holding up compressions, and on a soft mattress the rescuer has to push harder to reach a depth of at least 2 inches. Waiting for a backboard, or giving breaths alone, delays the blood flow the patient needs most.

questions.question: You are doing compressions on a patient lying on a soft mattress. Which adjustment matters most for compression quality?
choices: Slow the rate to about 80 per minute so the mattress can rebound
Switch to a two-finger technique so you sink less into the mattress
Push harder, so the chest itself is compressed at least 2 inches
Stop after every 30 compressions to reposition the patient on the bed
questions.explanation: A soft mattress absorbs part of each compression, so the rescuer pushes harder to move the chest itself at least 2 inches (and no more than 2.4 inches) at 100 to 120 per minute. A board or the floor helps when it can be arranged without stopping CPR, but compressions are not delayed for it. Slowing the rate lowers blood flow, the two-finger technique was an infant technique and the 2025 AHA guidelines dropped it even there, and repeated pauses to reposition cut the time spent compressing.

questions.question: After an uncomplicated field delivery, the term newborn is crying, has good tone and is pink centrally. When should the umbilical cord be clamped?
choices: Immediately, within the first 10 seconds, so the baby does not lose blood to the placenta
Only after the placenta has delivered
Once the 5-minute APGAR score has been recorded
After at least 60 seconds, while the baby is dried and kept warm on the mother
questions.explanation: For a vigorous newborn who needs no resuscitation, current guidance (the 2025 AHA neonatal guidelines and the Neonatal Resuscitation Program) is to delay clamping the cord for at least 60 seconds. Blood keeps moving from the placenta into the baby during that time, which improves the baby's iron stores and, in preterm babies, lowers the risk of death. Meanwhile the baby is dried, kept warm and assessed on the mother's chest. Immediate clamping gives up that benefit and is kept for a newborn who needs resuscitation at once; waiting for the placenta or a 5-minute score has nothing to do with how the timing is decided. Follow your local protocol.

questions.question: A newborn delivered in the field is limp and not breathing despite drying and stimulation. How should cord clamping be handled?
choices: Clamp and cut the cord promptly so ventilation can start without delay
Wait at least 60 seconds before clamping, as for every newborn
Wait until the cord stops pulsating before starting ventilation
Milk the cord repeatedly for several minutes before doing anything else
questions.explanation: The 60-second delay in cord clamping is for newborns who are breathing or crying with good tone. A limp newborn who is not breathing after drying and stimulation needs positive-pressure ventilation within the first minute of life, so the cord is clamped and cut promptly and the baby moved to where the airway can be managed and ventilation started. Waiting 60 seconds, or until the cord stops pulsating, delays the ventilation that most newborns in trouble need, and several minutes of cord milking delays it further. Some hospital teams resuscitate with the cord intact or milk it; in the field, clamp and cut so ventilation is not delayed.

questions.question: You arrive at each of these calls. Sort each one by what you do first.
choices: A man who fell from a ladder in his backyard and has a painful wrist
A car crash with a power line lying across the hood of the car
A reported assault where the caller says the attacker is still in the house
A man slumped in a closed garage with the car engine still running
A woman with low blood sugar in her kitchen; her husband lets you in
questions.explanation: Scene safety comes before patient care, because an injured EMT cannot help anyone. The woman in her kitchen and the man in the backyard present no hazard you can see, so you go to them. An attacker who is still inside makes the scene unsafe until law enforcement has secured it, so you stage nearby out of sight. A downed power line can energize the car and the ground around it; treat every wire as live and wait for the utility company or fire service to make it safe. A closed garage with a running engine is filling with carbon monoxide, which you cannot see or smell; entering without breathing protection can make you a second patient, so the fire service ventilates the space or removes him first.

questions.question: Sort each mechanism by the risk of serious injury it suggests under the 2021 national field triage guideline.
choices: Another occupant of the same car died at the scene
An unrestrained passenger partly ejected through a side window
A healthy 30-year-old who tripped and fell from standing onto carpet
A low-speed rear-end crash; the belted driver is walking around the scene
An adult who fell 15 feet from a roof onto concrete
A bicyclist thrown from the bike after being struck by a car
questions.explanation: The 2021 National Guideline for the Field Triage of Injured Patients lists high-risk mechanisms that justify a trauma center even before injuries are found. Partial or complete ejection, a death in the same passenger compartment, a fall of more than 10 feet at any age, and a pedestrian or bicyclist thrown, run over or hit with significant impact are all on that list. A low-speed rear-end crash with a belted driver who is up and walking, or a fall from standing in a healthy adult, does not by itself predict serious injury. The patient still gets a full assessment, and injuries or abnormal vital signs found on exam can still send them to a trauma center.

questions.question: You are triaging adults at a bus crash using START. Sort each patient into a triage category.
choices: Not walking; breathing 18 a minute, no radial pulse
Not walking; breathing 22 a minute, radial pulse present, follows commands
Not breathing; still not breathing after you reposition the airway
Walking around the scene holding a cut forearm
Not walking; breathing 36 times a minute
Not walking; breathing 20 a minute, radial pulse present, cannot follow simple commands
questions.explanation: START sorts adults in seconds using walking, respirations, perfusion and mental status. Anyone who can walk is Minor (green). A patient who is not breathing gets one airway repositioning; if breathing does not start, the patient is tagged Deceased (black) and you move on. A respiratory rate over 30 is Immediate (red). With a rate of 30 or less, check perfusion: an absent radial pulse (or a capillary refill over 2 seconds) is Immediate. If perfusion is adequate, check mental status: a patient who cannot follow simple commands is Immediate, and one who can is Delayed (yellow). The patient breathing 22 with a radial pulse who follows commands is the only Delayed patient here.

questions.question: During scene size-up, sort each situation by whether you should call for more resources now.
choices: A teenager with a twisted ankle at a soccer field
Three injured patients from a two-car crash and one ambulance on scene
A 450-pound patient on the second floor with a narrow staircase
A conscious adult with a nosebleed that stopped with pressure
A strong smell of natural gas in the house where the patient is
questions.explanation: Size-up includes deciding early whether you have enough people and equipment, because help called late arrives late. More patients than your crew can care for means more ambulances. A gas smell is a fire and explosion hazard that needs the fire service, and you should not use anything that could spark while you wait. Moving a very heavy patient down narrow stairs safely needs a lift assist so that neither the patient nor the crew is injured. A controlled nosebleed and a twisted ankle are single patients your crew can assess and treat without help.

questions.question: At a hazardous materials leak, sort each activity into the control zone where it belongs.
choices: The incident command post and ambulance staging
EMS triage and treatment of patients who have been decontaminated
The area immediately around the leaking tanker
Rescue of victims by an entry team in chemical protective suits
The decontamination corridor
questions.explanation: Hazardous materials scenes are divided into zones so that contamination does not spread. The hot zone is the contaminated area around the release; only trained hazmat responders in the right protective equipment enter it, to rescue victims and stop the leak. The warm zone sits between the hot and cold zones and holds the decontamination corridor, where people and equipment are cleaned before leaving. The cold zone is clean and upwind; command, staging, and EMS triage and treatment of decontaminated patients belong there. An EMT without hazmat training and equipment works in the cold zone.

questions.question: Standard precautions call for gloves on every patient. For each situation, choose the protection you add.
choices: Suctioning vomit from the airway of a patient with no known airborne infection
Assessing a child with suspected measles
Assessing a patient with fever, cough and known untreated tuberculosis
Applying a cold pack to a closed ankle injury with intact skin
Controlling bleeding that is spurting from a wound
questions.explanation: Protection is chosen by how the germ spreads and what could reach you. Tuberculosis and measles are airborne: they spread on tiny particles that hang in the air, so a fit-tested N95 (or higher) respirator is needed, along with a mask on the patient if tolerated. Suctioning and spurting blood can splash or spray body fluid into your eyes, nose and mouth, so eye protection and a mask are added. A closed injury with intact skin carries little exposure risk, and gloves alone are enough.

questions.question: For each clue you notice as you walk in, decide what it mainly tells you about the call.
choices: A bent steering wheel
Empty pill bottles on the nightstand
Insulin syringes on the kitchen table
A star-shaped crack in the windshield in front of the passenger
A home oxygen concentrator running in the living room
A ladder lying on its side next to the patient
questions.explanation: Part of size-up is reading the scene for what happened. Pill bottles, a home oxygen concentrator and insulin syringes point to the nature of illness: a possible overdose, chronic lung disease and diabetes. A bent steering wheel suggests the driver’s chest struck it, a star-shaped windshield crack suggests the head struck the glass, and a fallen ladder suggests a fall. Those describe the mechanism of injury and raise your suspicion for injuries that may not be obvious yet.

questions.question: You arrive at a night-time highway crash where a fire engine is already parked to block the lane behind it. For each action, decide whether to do it.
choices: Make sure the crashed car is in park with the ignition off before working inside it
Walk up to the car while a downed wire lies across it
Leave your high beams pointed at oncoming drivers
Park the ambulance past the crash so loading happens in the protected area
Put on a high-visibility safety vest before leaving the ambulance
questions.explanation: Highway scenes kill responders, so visibility and positioning come first. A high-visibility vest makes you seen by passing drivers. White headlights pointed at oncoming traffic blind drivers approaching the scene, so turn high beams off and rely on warning lights. The fire engine blocks upstream of the crash, and the ambulance parks past it so the patient is loaded in the area the block protects. A downed wire may be live; stay clear until the power company says it is safe. Before working inside a crashed vehicle, stabilize it: in park, ignition off, and chocked if needed, so it cannot move.

questions.question: For each dispatch, decide whether you would ask for law enforcement before you arrive.
choices: A child whose seizure has stopped; the mother is calm
A caller reports a man threatening people with a knife
A suicidal patient who has a gun in the house
An 80-year-old who fell in her bathroom; her daughter is with her
An overdose at a house where the caller says people are fighting
questions.explanation: Information from dispatch is your first chance to spot a dangerous scene. A weapon, an active fight, or a suicidal patient with access to a firearm are all reasons to request law enforcement and to stage until the scene is secured. A fall in the bathroom with family present and a child whose seizure has ended carry no sign of violence, so you respond normally while staying alert, because any scene can change.

questions.question: For each finding on arrival, decide whether it points to a scene hazard.
choices: A woman in labor in a tidy apartment
A strong chemical odor next to a spilled cleaning product
Several people in one house all have a headache and nausea
An older man with chest pain who lives alone
A farm worker collapsed inside a manure pit
A large dog growling and unrestrained in the yard
questions.explanation: Some hazards are obvious and some are invisible. When several people in the same building have the same headache and nausea, suspect carbon monoxide and get everyone, including your crew, out to fresh air. A collapse inside a manure pit, silo or other confined space suggests toxic gas or low oxygen; rescuers who go in without breathing protection often become patients. A strong odor next to a chemical spill means fumes that could harm you. An unrestrained aggressive dog is a scene hazard to control before you approach. Chest pain in a man who lives alone and labor in a tidy apartment do not by themselves suggest any danger to the crew.

questions.question: Sort each step into the part of the assessment where it belongs.
choices: Check whether the pupils react to light
Palpate all four quadrants of the abdomen
Check mental status with AVPU
Look for and control major bleeding
Perform a detailed head-to-toe exam
Decide whether breathing is adequate
questions.explanation: The primary assessment finds and fixes immediate threats to life: general impression, mental status (AVPU), airway, breathing, circulation including major bleeding, and the transport decision. The secondary assessment is the systematic physical exam that follows: a head-to-toe or focused exam, palpating the abdomen, and checking pupils as part of the exam and vital signs. Doing the detailed exam before the life threats are handled wastes the minutes that matter most.

questions.question: During the primary assessment of a trauma patient, sort each finding by when you deal with it.
choices: Snoring respirations in an unresponsive patient
Bright red blood spurting from the thigh
Abrasions on both knees
A swollen, deformed forearm with a strong radial pulse
An open chest wound that sucks air with each breath
A respiratory rate of 6 with shallow breaths
questions.explanation: The primary assessment stops to fix anything that threatens airway, breathing or circulation as soon as it is found. Snoring means the tongue is partly blocking the airway, so open it with a jaw thrust or head-tilt chin-lift as the mechanism allows. Spurting arterial bleeding can kill in minutes and is controlled at once. An open chest wound is sealed with an occlusive dressing. A rate of 6 with shallow breaths is inadequate breathing, so you ventilate with a bag-valve mask. A deformed forearm with a good pulse and abrasions on the knees are real injuries but not life threats; they are splinted and dressed later.

questions.question: At the end of the primary assessment you decide on transport priority. Sort each patient.
choices: A patient who is responsive but cannot follow commands
Chest pain with a systolic blood pressure of 88
An alert adult with a finger cut; the bleeding is controlled
An alert adult with mild ankle pain and normal vital signs
Difficulty breathing that allows only two or three words at a time
Bleeding from a leg wound that will not stop despite pressure
questions.explanation: High-priority patients need quick transport with care continued on the way. The usual list includes a poor general impression, unresponsiveness or a patient who is responsive but cannot follow commands, difficulty breathing, signs of shock, chest pain with a low blood pressure, uncontrolled bleeding, complicated childbirth and severe pain anywhere. A finger cut with the bleeding controlled and mild ankle pain with normal vital signs are stable; they can have a fuller assessment on scene.

questions.question: Sort each finding by the stage of shock it most typically signals in an adult.
choices: Thirst
Confusion progressing to unresponsiveness
Anxiety and restlessness
Absent radial pulses
A fast heart rate with a normal blood pressure
A falling systolic blood pressure
questions.explanation: In compensated shock the body is still holding blood pressure up by speeding the heart and narrowing blood vessels, so the early signs are anxiety or restlessness, a fast pulse, pale cool skin and thirst while the blood pressure is still normal. Once those defenses fail the shock is decompensated: the systolic pressure falls, peripheral pulses weaken and disappear, and the brain is underperfused, so the patient becomes confused and then unresponsive. A normal blood pressure does not rule out shock; waiting for it to fall means waiting for the late stage.

questions.question: Sort each adult by whether the breathing is adequate.
choices: Rate 40, shallow, and the patient is becoming confused
Rate 6 with shallow breaths
Rate 16, good chest rise, speaks in full sentences
Rate 10 with barely visible chest rise and blue lips
Rate 22, anxious, speaks in full sentences, SpO₂ 93%
questions.explanation: Breathing is judged on rate and depth together, plus how the patient looks. A normal rate with good chest rise and full sentences is adequate. An anxious patient breathing 22 with full sentences is also moving air adequately; give oxygen to bring the saturation up, but the patient does not need a bag-valve mask. A rate of 6 or 10 with shallow breaths and cyanosis moves too little air, so assist with a bag-valve mask. A rate of 40 that is shallow is also inadequate, because each breath is mostly dead space; confusion shows the brain is already short of oxygen, so you assist ventilations.

questions.question: Sort each patient into the AVPU level that describes their mental status.
choices: Eyes open and looking at you, but unsure of the date and where he is
Eyes closed; opens them and mumbles when you speak loudly
Only moans and pulls away when you squeeze the trapezius
No response to your voice or to a painful stimulus
Eyes open, answers your questions
questions.explanation: AVPU sorts the level of responsiveness. Alert means eyes open and aware of you without any stimulus; a patient can be alert and still disoriented, which you record separately as orientation (person, place, time, event). Verbal means the patient responds only when spoken to, even if the response is a mumble. Painful means a response only to a painful stimulus such as a trapezius squeeze. Unresponsive means no response to either. The patient whose eyes are open but who is confused about the date is Alert and disoriented, not Verbal.

questions.question: Sort each observation into the part of the pediatric assessment triangle it belongs to.
choices: Pale lips and nail beds
Whether the child can be comforted by a parent
Nasal flaring and retractions
Muscle tone and how the child interacts with you
Mottled skin on the legs
Head bobbing and grunting
questions.explanation: The pediatric assessment triangle is a look-and-listen check done from across the room. Appearance covers tone, interactiveness, consolability, look or gaze, and speech or cry; it is the best quick sign of how well the brain is perfused and oxygenated. Work of breathing covers abnormal sounds and visible effort: nasal flaring, retractions, head bobbing and grunting. Circulation to skin covers pallor, mottling and cyanosis. Any abnormal side of the triangle makes the child a higher priority.

questions.question: Sort each finding by where in the airway the problem most likely is.
choices: A long, drawn-out expiration
Stridor on inspiration
Crackles at the bases of both lungs
Drooling and trouble swallowing
Wheezing on expiration
A barking cough in a toddler
questions.explanation: Upper airway problems narrow the passage above the lungs: the throat, larynx and trachea. Stridor is a harsh high-pitched sound, usually on inspiration, from that narrowing; drooling and trouble swallowing point to swelling in the throat; and a barking cough is typical of croup. Lower airway problems are in the bronchi, bronchioles and alveoli. Wheezing and a prolonged expiration come from narrowed small airways, as in asthma or COPD, and crackles come from fluid in the alveoli, as in pulmonary edema or pneumonia.

questions.question: For each unresponsive adult, decide whether to start chest compressions.
choices: Breathing normally with a strong carotid pulse
No breathing, only occasional gasps, and no definite pulse after 10 seconds
No breathing and no pulse; the arrest was witnessed a minute ago
Not breathing, but a definite carotid pulse is present
Unresponsive after a seizure, breathing 14 a minute, pulse 110
questions.explanation: Compressions start when an unresponsive patient has no normal breathing (absent or only gasping) and no definite pulse after a check of no more than 10 seconds. Gasping is not breathing; it is a sign of cardiac arrest. A patient who is breathing normally with a pulse, including a postictal patient, needs airway care and positioning, not CPR. A patient with a definite pulse who is not breathing is in respiratory arrest: give rescue breaths, one about every 6 seconds for an adult, and recheck the pulse about every 2 minutes, starting compressions if it is lost.

questions.question: Sort each description by the type of bleeding it describes.
choices: Bright red blood spurting from the wound
Slow bleeding from tiny vessels that usually stops on its own
Dark blood welling up steadily from a deep cut on the calf
Slow oozing from a scraped knee
Dark red blood flowing steadily
Blood that pulses out in time with the heartbeat
questions.explanation: Arterial blood is under high pressure and rich in oxygen, so it is bright red and spurts or pulses with each heartbeat; it is the hardest to control and the most dangerous. Venous blood is darker and under lower pressure, so it flows steadily, though a large vein can still bleed heavily. Capillary bleeding is a slow ooze from small vessels, as in an abrasion, and usually clots on its own.

questions.question: Sort each child by whether the findings show respiratory distress or respiratory failure.
choices: Alert and anxious, with retractions and nasal flaring
Sleepy and limp, breathing more slowly than before
Cyanosis that persists despite high-flow oxygen
Fast breathing with good color, crying loudly
A struggling infant whose heart rate falls from 160 to 80
Sitting up and leaning forward to breathe, fully awake
questions.explanation: A child in respiratory distress is working hard but still compensating: alert, anxious, breathing fast, using accessory muscles, and holding a position that helps. Respiratory failure is when the effort is failing: the child becomes sleepy or limp, breathing slows or weakens even though the problem has not improved, cyanosis persists despite oxygen, and the heart rate falls. A slowing heart rate in a struggling infant is an ominous sign of hypoxia. Failure needs assisted ventilation with a bag-valve mask, while distress needs oxygen, a position of comfort and close watching.

questions.question: Sort each patient by the type of shock the findings most suggest.
choices: Widespread hives and low blood pressure after a bee sting
Spinal cord injury with low blood pressure, warm dry skin and a normal heart rate
Absent breath sounds on one side, distended neck veins and falling blood pressure after chest trauma
Fever, confusion and low blood pressure in a nursing home resident
Crackles in both lungs and low blood pressure after a large heart attack
Three days of vomiting and diarrhea, dry mouth, fast weak pulse
questions.explanation: Shock types are grouped by what fails. Hypovolemic shock is lost volume: blood, or fluid from vomiting and diarrhea. Distributive shock is vessels that dilate too widely, so the blood that is there no longer fills them: anaphylaxis, sepsis, and neurogenic shock from a spinal cord injury, which often shows warm dry skin and no compensating fast heart rate. Cardiogenic shock is a pump that fails, often after a large heart attack, and fluid backs up into the lungs as crackles. Obstructive shock is something blocking blood flow to or from the heart, such as a tension pneumothorax with absent breath sounds and distended neck veins.

questions.question: For each finding, decide whether the airway is open or needs action now.
choices: Snoring respirations in an unresponsive patient
An infant crying loudly
Gurgling sounds with each breath
Vomit pooling in the mouth of an unresponsive patient
Stridor and drooling in a child who cannot swallow
The patient speaks clearly in full sentences
questions.explanation: A patient who can speak or cry loudly is moving air through an open airway. Gurgling means fluid in the airway that must be suctioned. Snoring means the tongue is partly blocking the airway, so reposition it. Vomit pooling in the mouth of an unresponsive patient must be cleared at once, by suction and by rolling the patient onto the side if needed, before it is inhaled. Stridor with drooling signals upper airway swelling that can close the airway; keep the child calm in the position of comfort and transport rapidly without putting anything in the mouth.

questions.question: Each patient is calm and at rest. For each pulse, decide whether it is normal for the age.
choices: A 6-month-old with a heart rate of 130
An adult with a heart rate of 160
An adult with a heart rate of 72
A 1-month-old with a heart rate of 70
A 4-year-old with a heart rate of 50
questions.explanation: Normal heart rates fall with age. A resting adult is normally about 60 to 100, so 72 is normal and 160 is too fast. Infants normally run about 100 to 160 at rest, so 130 is normal for a 6-month-old, while 70 in a 1-month-old is too slow; in an infant a slow heart rate usually means hypoxia and is treated as a breathing problem first. A preschool child normally runs about 80 to 140, so 50 is too slow and is an ominous sign in a child.

questions.question: For each skin finding, decide whether it points to poor perfusion.
choices: A capillary refill of 4 seconds in a 3-year-old
Pale, cool, clammy skin
A capillary refill under 2 seconds in a child
Warm, pink, dry skin
Mottled skin on an infant’s legs
questions.explanation: Skin signs are a quick window on perfusion. When perfusion falls, the body shunts blood away from the skin, which turns pale, cool and clammy, and in infants may look mottled. Capillary refill is most reliable in children under 6: normal is under 2 seconds, and a refill of 4 seconds is delayed. Warm, pink, dry skin and a brisk refill suggest the skin is being perfused normally.

questions.question: For each wound, choose the first way you control the bleeding.
choices: Life-threatening spurting bleeding from the mid-thigh
Steady bleeding from a forearm cut that slows with pressure
Heavy arm bleeding when you must move on to other patients at a crash
Heavy bleeding from the groin crease
Bleeding from a scalp laceration
A partial amputation of the lower leg with heavy bleeding
questions.explanation: For life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg, current guidance (Stop the Bleed, American College of Surgeons) is to apply a tourniquet 2 to 3 inches above the wound (not over a joint) right away rather than waiting to see if pressure works; a partial amputation and spurting mid-thigh bleeding qualify, and so does a heavy arm bleed when you cannot stay to hold pressure. Bleeding that slows with pressure is managed with direct pressure. A tourniquet cannot be placed on the groin crease or the scalp, so junctional bleeding is packed tightly with gauze and held with firm pressure, and scalp bleeding gets direct pressure. Note that the psychomotor skill sheet scores direct pressure first in its own scenario; follow the sheet at the station.

questions.question: For each description, choose the breath sound it describes.
choices: A musical sound throughout both lungs in a COPD flare-up
A harsh, high-pitched sound on inspiration heard without a stethoscope in a child with croup
Wet, bubbling sounds over one lung in pneumonia
Fine popping at the bases of the lungs in heart failure
A high-pitched whistling on expiration during an asthma attack
questions.explanation: Wheezes are musical, whistling sounds from narrowed lower airways, loudest on expiration, as in asthma and COPD. Crackles (also called rales) are popping or bubbling sounds from fluid in the small airways and alveoli, as in heart failure with pulmonary edema or pneumonia. Stridor is a harsh, high-pitched sound, usually on inspiration, from a narrowed upper airway such as in croup; it is often loud enough to hear without a stethoscope and is an airway warning sign.

questions.question: For each finding after chest trauma, choose the life threat it points to.
choices: Severe distress, absent breath sounds on one side, distended neck veins, falling blood pressure
A wound that bubbles with each breath
A sucking sound from a stab wound to the chest
Crepitus over several adjacent ribs that move opposite to the rest of the chest
The trachea shifted away from the injured side, a late finding
A segment of the chest wall moves in when the rest moves out
questions.explanation: A flail chest is two or more adjacent ribs broken in two or more places, so the loose segment moves opposite to the rest of the chest (paradoxical movement), often with crepitus. An open pneumothorax is a chest wound that lets air in and out; it may bubble or suck with each breath and is covered with an occlusive dressing. A tension pneumothorax is air trapped under pressure that collapses the lung and squeezes the heart and great vessels: severe distress, absent breath sounds on one side, distended neck veins, falling blood pressure and, late, a shifted trachea. If an occlusive dressing is in place and these signs develop, lift a corner to let the air escape.

questions.question: Each patient is calm and at rest. For each respiratory rate, decide whether it is normal for the age.
choices: A newborn breathing 45 times a minute
An adult breathing 32 times a minute
An adult breathing 8 times a minute
A 6-year-old breathing 40 times a minute
A 1-year-old breathing 12 times a minute
A 15-year-old breathing 16 times a minute
questions.explanation: Normal resting respiratory rates fall with age: about 30 to 60 for a newborn, about 24 to 40 for a toddler, about 18 to 30 for a school-age child, and about 12 to 20 for adolescents and adults. A newborn at 45 and a teenager at 16 are normal. A 6-year-old at 40 and an adult at 32 are too fast. An adult at 8 and a 1-year-old at 12 are too slow; a slow rate in a child is especially worrying, because it often means the child is tiring and heading toward respiratory failure.

questions.question: For each patient after a possible allergen exposure, decide what the findings call for.
choices: Hives with a blood pressure of 80/50
Hives with wheezing and shortness of breath
Widespread hives with vomiting and cramping after eating peanuts
Swelling only around a bee sting on the hand
Itchy hives only, with normal breathing and blood pressure
Swollen lips and tongue with a hoarse voice
questions.explanation: Anaphylaxis is a severe, whole-body reaction. It is likely when skin signs such as hives come with breathing trouble, low blood pressure or persistent gut symptoms, or when the airway itself swells (lips, tongue, hoarse voice). Epinephrine by auto-injector is the first treatment and should not be delayed. Hives alone with normal breathing and blood pressure, or swelling only at the sting site, is a milder reaction: give oxygen if needed, monitor closely, and follow medical direction, because a mild reaction can progress.

questions.question: For each conscious choking patient, decide whether the airway obstruction is mild or severe.
choices: Coughing forcefully and able to speak
Hands at the throat, turning blue, no air moving
An infant with a weak, ineffective cry and worsening breathing
Wheezing between strong coughs
Cannot speak or cry, with a silent cough
questions.explanation: A patient with a mild obstruction is still moving air: coughing forcefully, speaking, perhaps wheezing between coughs. Encourage coughing, stay with them and be ready to act. A severe obstruction is a patient who cannot speak or cry, has a silent or weak cough, cannot move air or is turning blue. For an adult or child, give back blows and abdominal thrusts in cycles (the 2025 AHA sequence is 5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts). For an infant, give 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts; abdominal thrusts are never used on an infant.

questions.question: For each finding in a diabetic patient, decide which emergency it points to.
choices: Came on over minutes
Took insulin this morning, then skipped lunch
Several days of thirst and frequent urination
A fruity odor on the breath with deep, rapid breathing
Cool, clammy skin
Warm, dry skin and signs of dehydration
questions.explanation: Hypoglycemia develops quickly, often after insulin is taken without eating or after unusual exercise, and the body’s adrenaline response makes the skin cool, pale and clammy. Diabetic ketoacidosis builds over days: high sugar pulls water out through the kidneys, causing thirst, frequent urination and dehydration with warm, dry skin, and ketones cause a fruity breath odor and deep, rapid (Kussmaul) breathing. Check the blood glucose where your protocol allows; it settles the question.

questions.question: In a patient with a head injury, decide whether each finding points to rising pressure inside the skull.
choices: An irregular breathing pattern
Awake and oriented with a mild headache that is not getting worse
One pupil dilated and slow to react
Abnormal flexion or extension posturing
A scalp laceration that is bleeding heavily
Blood pressure rising while the pulse slows
questions.explanation: As pressure rises inside the skull, the brain is squeezed. Late signs include Cushing’s triad (rising blood pressure, slowing pulse and irregular breathing), a dilated or sluggish pupil on one side from pressure on the nerve that controls it, and abnormal posturing. A falling level of consciousness is often the earliest sign. A patient who is awake and oriented with a stable mild headache does not show these signs, though you keep reassessing. A heavily bleeding scalp wound looks alarming but reflects the scalp’s rich blood supply, not pressure inside the skull.

questions.question: For each patient working in the heat, decide which heat emergency the findings point to.
choices: Headache and cool, moist skin, alert and oriented
Confused and combative
Heavy sweating, dizziness and nausea, fully alert
A seizure
A very high body temperature with an altered mental status
questions.explanation: The dividing line between heat exhaustion and heat stroke is the brain. Heat exhaustion causes heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, nausea and headache, often with cool moist skin, but the patient stays alert. Heat stroke is a failure of temperature control: a very high body temperature with an altered mental status, which may include confusion, combativeness, seizures or coma. The skin may be dry or still sweaty, so sweating does not rule it out. Heat stroke is a life threat that needs aggressive cooling and rapid transport.

questions.question: For each finding in a pregnant patient near term, decide whether it is an emergency or expected in labor.
choices: The umbilical cord visible at the vaginal opening before the baby
Blood-tinged mucus (bloody show)
A seizure in a patient with high blood pressure at 36 weeks
A gush of clear fluid as the bag of waters breaks
Contractions 2 minutes apart with an urge to push
Heavy, bright red, painless bleeding in the third trimester
questions.explanation: Bloody show, clear fluid from ruptured membranes, and contractions close together with an urge to push are all part of normal labor; the last means delivery may be imminent, so prepare to deliver. A prolapsed cord is an emergency: the baby can compress it and cut off its own blood supply, so position the mother to take pressure off it, insert a gloved hand to hold the presenting part off the cord, and transport rapidly. Heavy, painless bright red bleeding late in pregnancy suggests placenta previa. A seizure in a pregnant patient with high blood pressure suggests eclampsia. Both need rapid transport.

questions.question: A 68-year-old has sudden weakness and trouble speaking. Sort each finding.
choices: Her right arm drifts down when both are held out
Slurred speech that began 30 minutes ago
A seizure just before the weakness began
Sudden loss of balance and trouble walking
The right side of the face droops when she smiles
A blood glucose of 38 mg/dL
questions.explanation: Stroke scales such as BE-FAST look for sudden balance loss, vision changes, facial droop, arm drift and speech trouble, each of which supports a stroke. Some conditions can mimic a stroke, and low blood sugar is the most important to check: a glucose of 38 can cause one-sided weakness and slurred speech that resolve once it is treated. Weakness after a seizure (postictal weakness) can also mimic a stroke. Record the time the patient was last known well, because it decides which treatments the hospital can offer.

questions.question: Sort each question into the history tool it belongs to.
choices: Does the pain spread anywhere?
When did you last eat or drink?
Are you allergic to any medications?
Did it come on suddenly or gradually?
How bad is it on a scale of 0 to 10?
Have you had any medical problems in the past?
questions.explanation: OPQRST explores the chief complaint, especially pain: Onset (sudden or gradual), Provocation, Quality, Region and radiation (where it is and whether it spreads), Severity (a 0 to 10 rating) and Time. SAMPLE gathers the patient’s background: Signs and symptoms, Allergies, Medications, Pertinent past history, Last oral intake, and Events leading up to the call. The two work together: OPQRST describes the problem, and SAMPLE puts it in context.

questions.question: For each patient during transport, choose how often you reassess.
choices: An alert adult with a sprained ankle and normal vital signs
A chest pain patient with a systolic blood pressure of 86
An alert adult with mild abdominal pain and normal vital signs
A patient whose mental status is getting worse
An unresponsive patient after a fall from a roof
questions.explanation: Reassessment repeats the primary assessment, vital signs and focused checks, and evaluates the effect of your treatment. An unstable patient, such as one who is unresponsive, hypotensive or deteriorating, is reassessed about every 5 minutes. A stable patient is reassessed about every 15 minutes. You also reassess after every intervention and whenever the patient’s condition changes, whatever the schedule.

questions.question: For each trend in repeat vital signs, decide whether the patient is improving or getting worse.
choices: In an asthma attack, respiratory rate falls from 32 to 20 and the patient is now drowsy
Skin changes from cool and clammy to warm and dry after the patient lies flat and is kept warm
GCS falls from 14 to 11
In a trauma patient, pulse rises from 110 to 128 while blood pressure falls from 110/70 to 92/60
In an asthma attack, respiratory rate falls from 28 to 18 and the patient now speaks in full sentences
SpO₂ rises from 88% to 95% after oxygen
questions.explanation: A single set of vital signs is a snapshot; the trend tells you the direction. A rising saturation after oxygen and warm, dry skin replacing cool, clammy skin are improvements. A rising pulse with a falling blood pressure in trauma suggests worsening shock, and a falling GCS means the brain is getting worse. A slowing respiratory rate in an asthma patient is good news only if the patient looks better too: with full sentences it is improvement, but with drowsiness it signals exhaustion and impending respiratory failure, and the patient needs assisted ventilation.

questions.question: For each patient who needs help keeping the airway open, choose the airway adjunct, if any.
choices: After a seizure, breathing with snoring sounds, jaw clenched
Awake and talking
Unresponsive with no gag reflex and clear fluid draining from the nose after a head injury
Responds to pain, has a gag reflex, and the teeth are clenched
Unresponsive, snoring, no gag reflex
questions.explanation: An OPA is only for a patient with no gag reflex; in anyone who gags it can cause vomiting and aspiration. An NPA is tolerated by patients who still have a gag reflex, and it can be placed when the teeth are clenched, which makes it useful after a seizure. An NPA should be avoided when there is clear fluid from the nose or ears or severe facial trauma after a head injury, because of the risk of a skull base fracture; that patient, without a gag reflex, gets an OPA. A patient who is awake and talking is maintaining an open airway and needs no adjunct.

questions.question: Each adult has chest pain your protocol treats as possibly cardiac. Sort each patient by the aspirin decision.
choices: Black, tarry stools for two days
Takes a daily low-dose aspirin and has new chest pressure today
A known allergy to aspirin
Too drowsy to swallow safely
No allergies and able to chew and swallow
questions.explanation: Aspirin reduces platelet clumping in a coronary artery and is given chewed, usually 162 to 324 mg depending on protocol, to adults with chest pain of suspected cardiac origin. It is withheld for a known aspirin allergy, for signs of active bleeding such as black, tarry stools (bleeding in the upper gut), and for anyone who cannot swallow safely. A patient who already takes a daily low-dose aspirin still gets the full dose for new chest pain, because the daily dose is not enough to treat an acute event; follow your medical direction.

questions.question: Each adult has chest pain your protocol treats as possibly cardiac. Sort each patient by the nitroglycerin decision.
choices: Has her own prescribed nitroglycerin; pain continues 5 minutes after the first dose, systolic blood pressure 128
Has her own prescribed nitroglycerin; systolic blood pressure 138
Has her own prescribed nitroglycerin; systolic blood pressure 84
Has already taken three doses for this episode
Wants to use the nitroglycerin prescribed to her husband
Took sildenafil (an erectile dysfunction drug) last night
questions.explanation: An EMT may help a patient take her own prescribed nitroglycerin under medical direction, typically 0.4 mg under the tongue every 5 minutes up to three doses, rechecking blood pressure before each dose. Nitroglycerin widens blood vessels and can drop the blood pressure, so it is withheld when the systolic pressure is low (84 here). It is also withheld after recent use of erectile dysfunction drugs such as sildenafil, which can combine with it to cause severe hypotension, after three doses have already been taken, and when the medication is not prescribed to the patient.

questions.question: Sort each adult by the oxygen delivery you would choose.
choices: Severe distress with adequate rate and depth, SpO₂ 84%
Alert after smoke exposure in a house fire; carbon monoxide suspected
Mild shortness of breath, alert, SpO₂ 92%
Breathing 6 times a minute with shallow breaths
Not breathing, with a carotid pulse
questions.explanation: Choose the device by how well the patient is breathing and how much oxygen is needed. A nasal cannula gives low concentrations and suits mild hypoxia in a patient breathing adequately. A nonrebreather mask gives high concentrations to a patient who is breathing adequately without help but is severely hypoxic, and it is used for suspected carbon monoxide poisoning, where a pulse oximeter can read falsely normal. A patient whose breathing is inadequate or absent needs ventilation with a bag-valve mask and oxygen; a mask on its own does nothing if air is not moving.

questions.question: Sort each injury by whether a traction splint is appropriate.
choices: A suspected pelvic fracture
An isolated closed midshaft femur fracture
A hip fracture in an older woman
A midshaft femur fracture with a fractured lower leg on the same side
A knee injury with deformity
questions.explanation: A traction splint pulls the thigh muscles back to length, which reduces pain and bleeding from a midshaft femur fracture. It is appropriate for an isolated midshaft femur fracture. It is not used for injuries at or near the hip or pelvis, because the device anchors against the pelvis and the pull can worsen those injuries, nor for knee injuries. A fracture lower on the same leg rules it out, because the ankle hitch would pull through the second fracture. Those injuries are splinted another way.

questions.question: Sort each adult with shortness of breath by whether CPAP is appropriate under your protocol.
choices: Systolic blood pressure of 82
A COPD flare-up; alert, follows commands, adequate blood pressure, breathing on his own
Unresponsive
Absent breath sounds on one side after a fall; suspected pneumothorax
Actively vomiting
Alert, crackles in both lungs, severe shortness of breath, blood pressure 164/96
questions.explanation: CPAP pushes air gently into the lungs to keep the small airways and alveoli open. It suits alert patients who are breathing on their own but working hard, such as pulmonary edema from heart failure or a COPD flare-up, as long as the blood pressure is adequate. It is contraindicated when the patient cannot protect the airway or follow commands (unresponsive or vomiting), when the blood pressure is low (the added pressure in the chest reduces blood return to the heart), and when a pneumothorax is suspected, because the pressure can worsen it. A patient who is not breathing adequately needs bag-valve mask ventilation instead.

questions.question: Each patient is in anaphylaxis. Sort each patient by the epinephrine auto-injector strength.
choices: A 55 kg teenager
A 20 kg child
An 18 kg child
A 70 kg adult
questions.explanation: Epinephrine auto-injectors are chosen by weight. The adult device delivers 0.3 mg and is used for patients of about 30 kg and above, which includes most teenagers and adults. The pediatric device delivers 0.15 mg and is used for children of about 15 to 30 kg. The injection goes into the anterolateral thigh, held in place for the time on the device label, and can be given through clothing. Follow your local protocol for the exact weight cutoffs, which vary a little between manufacturers and protocols.

questions.question: For each patient with a blood glucose under 60 mg/dL, decide about oral glucose.
choices: No gag reflex
Unresponsive
Having a seizure
Alert and shaky after skipping lunch
A known diabetic, confused but able to swallow and follow commands
questions.explanation: Oral glucose (typically one 15 g tube) is placed between the cheek and gum or swallowed, so the patient must be awake enough to swallow and protect the airway. A confused patient who can still follow commands and swallow, and an alert, shaky patient, can take it. A patient who is unresponsive, has no gag reflex or is seizing cannot protect the airway, and glucose in the mouth could be inhaled. Manage the airway, give oxygen and transport; advanced providers can give glucose by vein.

questions.question: For each trauma patient, decide whether spinal motion restriction is indicated.
choices: Intoxicated after a car crash, complaining of neck pain
A gunshot wound to the thigh; alert, with no neurological deficit
Numbness and tingling in both hands after diving into shallow water
A stab wound to the side of the neck, with no neurological deficit
Fell from a ladder and has midline neck tenderness
Alert and sober after a low-speed crash, no midline tenderness, no deficit, no distracting injury
questions.explanation: Spinal motion restriction is guided by findings, not by mechanism alone. It is indicated for altered mental status or intoxication, midline spinal pain or tenderness, a focal neurological deficit such as numbness or weakness, a distracting injury, or an anatomic deformity of the spine. An alert, sober patient with none of these after a low-speed crash does not need it. Penetrating trauma without a neurological deficit is not an indication: a collar can hide injuries, hinder airway care and delay transport. Follow your local protocol.

questions.question: A patient has a small thermal burn on the hand, a few minutes old. For each action, decide whether to do it.
choices: Apply butter or an ointment
Cover the burn with a dry sterile dressing
Put ice directly on the burn
Break the blisters so the burn can drain
Remove rings and bracelets from the burned hand
Cool the burn with cool running water
questions.explanation: Cooling a small, fresh burn with cool running water stops it from deepening and eases pain; limit cooling for large burns, which can make the patient hypothermic. Ice damages tissue further. Remove rings and bracelets early, before swelling traps them. Leave blisters intact, because they protect the tissue underneath from infection. Cover the burn with a dry sterile dressing. Butter and ointments hold in heat, contaminate the wound and have to be scrubbed off at the hospital.

questions.question: Your system has all three types of center within reach. Choose the destination each patient needs.
choices: A gunshot wound to the abdomen
Partly ejected from a vehicle in a rollover
Sudden trouble speaking and loss of vision on one side, starting 20 minutes ago
Chest pain with a STEMI on the 12-lead ECG your crew transmitted
Sudden facial droop and arm weakness; last known well 40 minutes ago
questions.explanation: Destination is part of treatment, because the right hospital changes the outcome. Penetrating injuries to the torso and high-risk mechanisms such as ejection go to a trauma center. Sudden neurological deficits with a recent last-known-well time go to a stroke center, where clot-busting drugs or clot removal may be possible. A STEMI identified on a 12-lead ECG goes to a hospital that can open the artery in a cardiac catheterization lab, and an early notification lets the team be ready. Follow your regional destination protocols.

questions.question: You have just delivered a healthy, crying baby. For each action, decide whether to do it.
choices: Pull on the umbilical cord to speed delivery of the placenta
Massage the top of the uterus if bleeding is heavy after the placenta delivers
Dry the baby and keep him warm
Place the baby skin to skin on the mother’s chest
Wait at least 60 seconds before clamping the cord
questions.explanation: Newborns lose heat fast, so drying and warming come first, and skin-to-skin contact with the mother is an excellent way to keep a healthy baby warm. Current newborn guidance is to delay cord clamping for at least 60 seconds in a vigorous baby. Never pull on the cord: it can tear or invert the uterus and cause severe bleeding. The placenta usually delivers on its own within about 30 minutes. If bleeding is heavy after it delivers, firm massage of the top of the uterus (fundal massage) helps it contract and slows the bleeding.

questions.question: A patient is found outdoors on a cold night, cold to the touch and slow to respond. For each action, decide whether to do it.
choices: Rub his frostbitten fingers to warm them
Remove his wet clothing
Place heat packs at the armpits and groin
Move and handle him gently
Give him a hot drink
questions.explanation: A severely cold heart is irritable, and rough handling can trigger ventricular fibrillation, so move the patient gently and keep him horizontal. Get him out of the cold, remove wet clothing and insulate him. Heat packs at the armpits, groin and neck warm the core where large vessels run close to the skin. Do not rub frostbitten tissue, which damages it further. Do not give anything by mouth to a patient who is slow to respond, because he may not protect his airway.

questions.question: You are writing a SOAP narrative. Sort each item into the part of the report it belongs to.
choices: Blood pressure 148/92
"My chest feels tight."
A 3 cm laceration on the left forearm
Pupils equal and reactive to light
His wife says he fainted before you arrived
The patient rates his pain 7 out of 10
questions.explanation: Subjective information is what the patient or bystanders tell you: complaints, descriptions, the pain rating the patient gives, and the history a family member provides. Objective information is what you observe, measure or find on exam: vital signs, wound size and location, and pupil findings. Keeping the two apart lets the next provider see what was reported and what was found.

questions.question: At a mass-casualty incident run under the Incident Command System, sort each task to the role responsible for it.
choices: Sets the incident objectives and oversees the whole response
Watches for hazards and can stop unsafe actions
Assigns START categories to patients where they lie
Cares for patients in the collection area until they leave
Coordinates with hospitals and tracks which ambulance took whom
questions.explanation: In ICS, the incident commander sets objectives and has overall responsibility, supported by command staff such as the safety officer, who monitors hazards and can stop an unsafe operation, plus the public information and liaison officers. In the medical branch, triage sorts patients, treatment cares for them in the treatment area, and transport works with hospitals to send each patient to an appropriate destination and keeps a record of where everyone went.

questions.question: Each patient says no to care. Sort each one by whether the refusal can be accepted.
choices: An alert, oriented adult who can explain the risks of refusing
An adult who is confused after hitting his head
A 15-year-old, not emancipated, with no parent or guardian present
An intoxicated adult with slurred speech who cannot repeat back the risks
An emancipated minor who understands and can explain the risks
questions.explanation: A valid refusal needs a patient with decision-making capacity who has been told the risks of refusing and can show that they understand them. An alert, oriented adult and an emancipated minor who meet that standard can refuse. Intoxication and confusion after a head injury impair capacity, so the refusal is not valid; try to persuade, involve medical direction and law enforcement as your protocol says, and document carefully. A minor who is not emancipated generally cannot refuse; consent comes from a parent or guardian. Laws vary by state, so follow your protocols.

questions.question: Sort each disclosure of patient information by whether HIPAA permits it without the patient’s written authorization.
choices: Posting a photo of the crash scene with the patient visible on social media
Reviewing the call with your medical director for quality improvement
Making a mandated report of suspected child abuse
Giving a verbal report to the receiving nurse
Telling the patient’s employer why he left work in an ambulance
Reporting a gunshot wound to police where state law requires it
questions.explanation: HIPAA allows protected health information to be shared without authorization for treatment (the handoff to the receiving nurse), for health care operations such as quality review with your medical director, and when the law requires it, as with mandated abuse reports and state-required reports of gunshot wounds. Sharing it with anyone else, such as an employer or the public on social media, needs the patient’s authorization. Posting a patient’s image is also a serious professional breach.

questions.question: For each patient, decide which kind of consent lets you treat.
choices: An alert patient who says, "Yes, please help me"
An adult who is unresponsive after a seizure
An alert adult nods and holds out her arm for a blood pressure
An unresponsive adult after a car crash
A child with a life-threatening injury whose parents cannot be reached
questions.explanation: Expressed consent is given by a competent patient, in words or by an action such as holding out an arm, after you explain what you plan to do. Implied consent applies when a patient cannot consent, such as an unresponsive adult, and assumes that a reasonable person would want emergency care. It also covers a minor with a life-threatening condition when no parent or guardian can be reached.

questions.question: For each driving practice during an emergency response, decide whether it is safe.
choices: Passing a school bus that has its red lights flashing
Using a spotter at the rear when backing up
Coming to a full stop at a red light, then proceeding only when every lane is clear
Every crew member not giving patient care wears a seat belt
Assuming other drivers hear the siren and will yield
questions.explanation: Most ambulance crashes happen at intersections, so stop at red lights and stop signs and go through only when every lane has yielded. Lights and sirens only ask for the right of way; many drivers do not hear or see them, so never assume they will yield. Back up with a spotter, because the rear of the ambulance is a blind spot. Do not pass a school bus with its red lights flashing unless the driver or a police officer waves you through. Everyone who is not actively caring for the patient stays belted.

questions.question: Each adult is pulseless and not breathing. Decide whether to start or withhold resuscitation, unless your local protocol says otherwise.
choices: A valid, signed DNR order is presented and matches the patient
A family member says he did not want CPR, but there is no paperwork
Pulled from cold water after 10 minutes under, with no signs of obvious death
Rigor mortis and dependent lividity are present
A DNR form is shown, but it is unsigned and undated
questions.explanation: A valid DNR or POLST order (signed, current and matching the patient) means you withhold resuscitation. Obvious signs of death such as rigor mortis and dependent lividity also mean withholding it. A verbal wish from family without documentation, or a form that is not valid, is not enough, so start resuscitation and contact medical direction. A cold-water drowning without obvious signs of death gets full resuscitation, because cold can protect the brain.
