questions.question: Two lengthwise sections divide a body into left and right portions. Only one passes through the midline. What distinguishes the midline section?
choices: It is midsagittal and creates equal left and right halves
It is sagittal, so any such section must create equal halves
It is coronal because it runs lengthwise
It is transverse because it crosses the midline
questions.explanation: Midsagittal is the particular sagittal plane that creates equal left and right halves.

questions.question: Which group consists entirely of axial skeletal structures?
choices: Skull, vertebral column, and thoracic cage
Clavicle, scapula, and humerus
Femur, tibia, and fibula
Sternum, radius, and ulna
questions.explanation: The axial skeleton includes the skull, vertebral column, and thoracic cage.

questions.question: A force pulls the bones at a joint apart. Which structure primarily connects one bone to another and helps stabilize that joint?
choices: Ligament
Tendon
Articular cartilage
Skeletal muscle
questions.explanation: Ligaments connect bone to bone and stabilize joints.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly distinguishes the normal movement of two joint types?
choices: Shoulder: ball-and-socket motion; elbow: hinge flexion and extension
Shoulder: hinge flexion and extension only; elbow: ball-and-socket rotation
Hip: hinge flexion and extension only; knee: ball-and-socket motion
Elbow: ball-and-socket motion; hip: hinge motion only
questions.explanation: Shoulder and hip are ball-and-socket joints; elbow and knee are hinge joints.

questions.question: Which sequence gives the number of cervical, thoracic, and lumbar vertebrae, respectively?
questions.explanation: There are 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, and 5 lumbar vertebrae.

questions.question: In anatomic position, which pairing correctly identifies the lateral bone in the forearm and the lateral bone beside the tibia?
choices: Radius and fibula
Ulna and fibula
Radius and femur
Ulna and tibia
questions.explanation: The radius lies on the thumb side of the forearm; the fibula lies lateral to the tibia.

questions.question: Besides supporting and protecting the body, which pair describes functions of bones?
choices: Calcium storage and blood-cell production
Synovial-fluid production and voluntary contraction
Hormone secretion and voluntary contraction
Synovial-fluid production and hormone secretion
questions.explanation: The skeletal system stores calcium and helps create blood cells, in addition to providing shape, protection, and movement.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly matches muscle type with its control and location?
choices: Cardiac: involuntary, in the heart
Skeletal: involuntary, attached to bones
Smooth: voluntary, in intestinal walls
Cardiac: voluntary, in blood vessel walls
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle is involuntary and found in the heart.

questions.question: During elbow flexion, the biceps contracts while the triceps relaxes. What principle does this illustrate?
choices: They coordinate opposing pulls to move the joint in different directions
They shorten together to move the joint in both directions at once
One supplies voluntary movement while the other supplies only involuntary movement
One pulls the bone while the other pushes it back through its tendon
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscles act in opposing groups; coordinated contraction and relaxation produces movement.

questions.question: A cold patient begins shivering. Which muscle function most directly explains how shivering helps?
choices: Repeated skeletal muscle contractions generate heat
Repeated skeletal muscle contractions conserve heat mainly by preventing heat loss
Relaxation of skeletal muscle is the main source of the additional heat
Antagonistic muscles stop working so energy is retained as heat
questions.explanation: Muscle activity produces heat; shivering uses repeated contractions for that purpose.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly follows air from the trachea toward the gas-exchange surface?
choices: Carina → main bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli
Main bronchi → carina → alveoli → bronchioles
Bronchioles → main bronchi → carina → alveoli
Carina → bronchioles → alveoli → main bronchi
questions.explanation: The trachea branches at the carina into main bronchi, which divide into smaller airways ending at alveoli.

questions.question: Which structure marks the division between the upper and lower airways?
choices: Larynx
Carina
Alveoli
Diaphragm
questions.explanation: The larynx is the boundary between upper and lower airways.

questions.question: Which structure helps keep food and liquid from entering the trachea during swallowing?
choices: Epiglottis
Cricoid cartilage
Parietal pleura
Carina
questions.explanation: The epiglottis is the protective flap associated with swallowing.

questions.question: Which description correctly matches the two pleural layers?
choices: Visceral pleura covers the lung; parietal pleura lines the chest wall
Parietal pleura covers the lung; visceral pleura lines the chest wall
Visceral pleura covers both the lung and the chest wall
Parietal pleura covers both the lung and the chest wall
questions.explanation: Visceral pleura covers the lungs, while parietal pleura lines the chest cavity; fluid allows them to glide.

questions.question: During normal inhalation, the diaphragm contracts. Which sequence follows?
choices: Thoracic volume increases → internal pressure decreases → air enters
Thoracic volume decreases → internal pressure increases → air enters
Thoracic volume increases → internal pressure increases → air leaves
Thoracic volume decreases → internal pressure decreases → air leaves
questions.explanation: Diaphragm contraction expands the thorax, lowers pressure relative to outside air, and draws air in.

questions.question: A healthy adult is breathing quietly at rest. Which mechanism primarily produces the exhalation phase?
choices: The diaphragm and inspiratory muscles relax, allowing the chest to return toward its resting volume
The diaphragm contracts and moves downward, expanding the chest cavity
The intercostal muscles contract and elevate the ribs, expanding the chest cavity
The abdominal muscles actively contract, compressing the chest cavity
questions.explanation: Normal quiet exhalation is passive. The diaphragm and inspiratory muscles relax, the thoracic cavity returns toward its resting size and shape, and air leaves the lungs.

questions.question: Air moves into a patient’s lungs, but oxygen has difficulty crossing the alveolar membrane. Which distinction best describes the problem?
choices: Ventilation occurs, but gas exchange is impaired
Gas exchange occurs normally because ventilation is present
Ventilation is absent because oxygen has not crossed the membrane
Neither process can occur unless the respiratory rate increases
questions.explanation: Ventilation is air movement; respiration includes gas exchange. Air movement alone does not establish effective exchange.

questions.question: A patient changes from 12 breaths/min at 500 mL per breath to 24 breaths/min at 200 mL per breath. What happens to minute volume?
choices: It decreases from 6,000 to 4,800 mL/min
It doubles from 6,000 to 12,000 mL/min
It stays at 6,000 mL/min because faster breathing offsets any decrease in depth
It decreases from 500 to 200 mL/min
questions.explanation: Minute volume is respiratory rate times tidal volume: 12 × 500 = 6,000; 24 × 200 = 4,800 mL/min.

questions.question: Carbon dioxide rises in blood and cerebrospinal fluid. Which response follows the normal respiratory control pathway?
choices: Lower pH stimulates the medulla, which drives diaphragm activity through the phrenic nerves
Lower pH stimulates the medulla, which sends the breathing command through the vagus nerve instead of the phrenic nerves
Higher pH stimulates the medulla and drives diaphragm contraction through the phrenic nerves
Lower pH makes diaphragm contraction depend entirely on voluntary cerebral control
questions.explanation: Increasing CO₂ lowers pH; medullary respiratory control sends signals through the phrenic nerves to the diaphragm.

questions.question: Air reaches the alveoli, but an embolus blocks blood flow through part of the pulmonary circulation. Which component is most directly disrupted?
choices: Perfusion of the ventilated alveoli
Ventilation of the affected region as the primary blocked process
Air passage through the upper airway
Diaphragm contraction throughout the chest
questions.explanation: A pulmonary embolus obstructs blood flow, disrupting the perfusion side of ventilation-perfusion matching.

questions.question: Which sequence follows blood from the right ventricle until it reaches the left ventricle?
choices: Pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → left ventricle
Pulmonary veins → lungs → pulmonary artery → left atrium → left ventricle
Aorta → body → venae cavae → left atrium → left ventricle
Pulmonary artery → lungs → venae cavae → right atrium → left ventricle
questions.explanation: The right ventricle sends blood through the pulmonary artery to the lungs; pulmonary veins return it to the left atrium and then left ventricle.

questions.question: What makes the pulmonary artery an artery?
choices: It carries oxygen-rich blood to the lungs
It carries blood away from the heart
It carries blood toward the heart
It carries blood directly into the left atrium
questions.explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, regardless of oxygen content. The pulmonary artery carries relatively oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle toward the lungs.

questions.question: Why does the left ventricle produce higher pressure than the right ventricle?
choices: It pumps through the systemic circulation rather than only through the pulmonary circuit
It receives systemic venous blood directly from the venae cavae
It pumps only into the coronary arteries rather than into the aorta
It fills during systole while the right ventricle fills during diastole
questions.explanation: The left ventricle supplies the higher-pressure systemic circuit; the right supplies the lower-pressure pulmonary circuit.

questions.question: Which vessels supply blood to the heart muscle itself?
choices: Coronary arteries branching from the aorta
Pulmonary arteries branching from the right ventricle
Pulmonary veins returning to the left atrium
Venae cavae returning to the right atrium
questions.explanation: The coronary arteries arise from the aorta and supply the myocardium.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly describes normal cardiac electrical conduction?
choices: SA node → AV node → bundle of His → Purkinje fibers
AV node → SA node → Purkinje fibers → bundle of His
SA node → bundle of His → Purkinje fibers → AV node
Purkinje fibers → AV node → SA node → bundle of His
questions.explanation: The normal conduction pathway begins at the SA node, proceeds through the AV node and bundle of His, then reaches Purkinje fibers.

questions.question: Heart rate rises from 80 to 120 beats/min while stroke volume falls from 75 to 40 mL/beat. Which conclusion is supported?
choices: Cardiac output falls from 6,000 to 4,800 mL/min despite the faster rate
Cardiac output rises because heart rate alone determines it
Cardiac output remains 6,000 mL/min because compensation preserves it
Cardiac output falls from 75 to 40 mL/min
questions.explanation: Cardiac output equals heart rate × stroke volume: 80 × 75 = 6,000; 120 × 40 = 4,800 mL/min.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly relates blood pressure to the cardiac cycle?
choices: Systolic: ventricular contraction; diastolic: ventricular relaxation and filling
Systolic: ventricular filling; diastolic: ventricular contraction
Systolic: only atrial relaxation; diastolic: only atrial contraction
Systolic and diastolic: two stages of ventricular contraction
questions.explanation: Systolic pressure occurs with ventricular contraction; diastolic pressure corresponds to relaxation and filling.

questions.question: Which vessel type is the principal site where gases, nutrients, and wastes move between blood and tissues?
choices: Capillaries
Arterioles
Venae cavae
Aorta
questions.explanation: Thin-walled capillaries connect arterioles with venules and support exchange with tissues.

questions.question: A patient’s blood has fewer erythrocytes. Which blood function is most directly reduced by that change?
choices: Oxygen transport by hemoglobin
Initial clot formation by platelets
Immune defense by leukocytes
Liquid transport by plasma
questions.explanation: Erythrocytes contain hemoglobin, which carries oxygen.

questions.question: Which set correctly matches receptor effects during sympathetic activation?
choices: Alpha: vessel constriction; beta-1: increased heart rate and force; beta-2: bronchodilation
Alpha: bronchodilation; beta-1: vessel constriction; beta-2: slower heart rate
Alpha: slower heart rate; beta-1: bronchodilation; beta-2: vessel constriction
Alpha: vessel dilation; beta-1: reduced force; beta-2: bronchoconstriction
questions.explanation: Alpha stimulation constricts vessels; beta-1 increases cardiac rate and force; beta-2 dilates bronchi.

questions.question: Following blood loss, a patient develops a faster pulse and constricted peripheral vessels. What is the best interpretation?
choices: These are compensatory responses intended to support circulation; they do not prove adequate tissue perfusion
These are compensatory responses, so the tissues must be receiving enough blood
They demonstrate that the parasympathetic system is increasing cardiac activity
They show that circulating blood volume has already returned to normal
questions.explanation: Increased heart rate and vasoconstriction can compensate for blood loss, but compensation may be insufficient as loss increases.

questions.question: A patient’s tissues receive too little circulating blood to meet their needs. Which term best describes this condition?
choices: Hypoperfusion
Hypoxia
Hypercapnia
Dehydration
questions.explanation: Hypoperfusion means inadequate tissue perfusion and is also called shock.

questions.question: Which grouping correctly separates the central nervous system from the peripheral nervous system?
choices: Central: brain and spinal cord; peripheral: nerves outside them
Central: brain and all motor nerves; peripheral: spinal cord and sensory nerves
Central: spinal cord only; peripheral: brain and cranial nerves
Central: autonomic nerves only; peripheral: cerebrum and cerebellum
questions.explanation: The CNS is the brain and spinal cord; the PNS consists of nervous structures outside them.

questions.question: A person feels a touch on the hand and then deliberately moves that hand. Which directions describe the two signals?
choices: Sensory: hand to CNS; motor: CNS to muscles
Sensory: CNS to hand; motor: muscles to CNS
Both sensory and motor: hand to CNS
Both sensory and motor: CNS to hand
questions.explanation: Sensory nerves carry information toward the CNS; motor nerves carry commands from the CNS to muscles.

questions.question: Which brain region is most directly associated with coordinating movement, balance, and posture?
choices: Cerebellum
Cerebrum
Medulla
Occipital lobe
questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates movement, balance, and posture.

questions.question: An injury interferes with automatic control of breathing and cardiac activity. Which brain region contains the vital control centers most directly involved?
choices: Brainstem
Parietal lobe
Cerebellum
Occipital lobe
questions.explanation: The brainstem contains centers supporting vital respiratory and cardiovascular functions.

questions.question: Which example best illustrates autonomic rather than somatic nervous system control?
choices: Heart rate increases during an involuntary stress response
A person deliberately raises an arm
A person voluntarily flexes the knee
A person intentionally turns the head
questions.explanation: The autonomic system regulates involuntary functions such as heart rate; the somatic system controls voluntary skeletal muscle actions.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly matches a cerebral lobe with a major function?
choices: Frontal: planning and judgment; occipital: vision
Frontal: vision; occipital: planning and judgment
Parietal: hearing and language; temporal: spatial processing
Temporal: planning and judgment; frontal: hearing and language
questions.explanation: The frontal lobe supports planning and judgment; the occipital lobe processes vision.

questions.question: Which description correctly places the skin’s protective surface and its deeper vessels and glands?
choices: Epidermis forms the outer barrier; dermis contains vessels and glands
Dermis forms the outer barrier; epidermis contains the deeper vessels and glands
Subcutaneous fat forms the exposed barrier; dermis lies above the epidermis
Epidermis and dermis are both layers beneath subcutaneous fat
questions.explanation: The epidermis is superficial; the deeper dermis contains vessels, glands, and other supporting structures.

questions.question: Which combination best describes how the skin and tissue beneath it contribute to temperature control?
choices: Sweat glands support cooling; subcutaneous fat provides insulation
Sweat glands provide insulation; subcutaneous fat provides evaporative cooling
Sweat glands and subcutaneous fat both function primarily as sensory receptors
Sweat glands primarily store energy; subcutaneous fat primarily releases sweat
questions.explanation: The skin supports temperature regulation, and subcutaneous fat helps insulate the body.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the liver and gallbladder in fat digestion?
choices: Liver produces bile; gallbladder stores it
Gallbladder produces bile; liver stores it
Liver produces bile; pancreas stores it
Pancreas produces bile; gallbladder stores it
questions.explanation: The liver produces bile, and the gallbladder stores and concentrates it for digestion.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the pancreas as serving both digestive and endocrine functions?
choices: It releases digestive enzymes and produces hormones such as insulin and glucagon
It releases digestive enzymes and stores liver-produced bile
It absorbs water from stool and produces insulin and glucagon
It stores bile and produces hormones such as insulin and glucagon
questions.explanation: The pancreas provides digestive enzymes and also produces hormones including insulin and glucagon.

questions.question: Which comparison correctly distinguishes the small and large intestines?
choices: Small intestine: major nutrient absorption; large intestine: remaining absorption and stool formation
Small intestine: stool storage; large intestine: major nutrient absorption
Small intestine: bile storage; large intestine: stool formation
Small intestine: major nutrient absorption; large intestine: pancreatic-enzyme production
questions.explanation: Digestion and nutrient absorption involve the small intestine; the large intestine absorbs water and helps form stool.

questions.question: An EMT is considering which vascular organ could be injured by a blow to the left upper abdomen. Which organ best fits that location?
choices: Spleen
Liver
Appendix
Urinary bladder
questions.explanation: The spleen is a highly vascular organ in the left upper quadrant and may bleed after blunt trauma.

questions.question: Which function is performed by lymph nodes?
choices: Filtering lymph to help remove harmful materials
Filtering worn-out cells directly from circulating blood
Filtering blood wastes into newly formed urine
Producing clotting factors for release into plasma
questions.explanation: Lymphatic structures support immune defense, and lymph nodes filter lymph.

questions.question: How do endocrine hormones reach and act on their targets?
choices: They enter the bloodstream and act on specific target tissues
They pass through ducts and act only at the end of those ducts
They move along nerve fibers as electrical impulses
They enter the bloodstream and have the same effect on every organ
questions.explanation: Endocrine glands release hormones into blood to regulate functions in specific target tissues.

questions.question: How do endocrine feedback loops normally help prevent illness from hormone excess or deficiency?
choices: Feedback maintains appropriately balanced hormonal signals
Feedback keeps all gland secretions increasing together
Feedback makes hormone output independent of target-tissue needs
Feedback gives each hormone the same action throughout the body
questions.explanation: Endocrine feedback regulates hormone levels; either excess or deficiency can disturb body functions.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly follows urine from its formation to its exit from the body?
choices: Kidneys → ureters → bladder → urethra
Kidneys → urethra → bladder → ureters
Bladder → ureters → kidneys → urethra
Kidneys → bladder → urethra → ureters
questions.explanation: Kidneys form urine; ureters carry it to the bladder, and the urethra carries it outside.

questions.question: Which description best captures the kidneys’ role in maintaining the internal environment?
choices: Filter blood wastes and regulate water, salts, and pH
Store formed urine until release is appropriate
Conduct formed urine from the kidneys into a storage organ
Conduct stored urine from the bladder to the outside
questions.explanation: Kidneys remove wastes while regulating fluid, electrolytes, and pH.

questions.question: Which organ pair is identified in the course as retroperitoneal?
choices: Kidneys and pancreas
Stomach and gallbladder
Spleen and urinary bladder
Appendix and liver
questions.explanation: The kidneys and most of the pancreas lie behind the peritoneum. The pancreatic tail is an exception; the course groups the pancreas with retroperitoneal structures.

questions.question: Which group consists entirely of female genital system structures?
choices: Ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, and cervix
Ovaries, ureters, uterus, and cervix
Ovaries, fallopian tubes, bladder, and cervix
Ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, and urethra
questions.explanation: Ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and vagina belong to the female genital system.

questions.question: Which group consists entirely of male genital system structures?
choices: Testicles, epididymis, vas deferens, and seminal vesicles
Testicles, ureters, vas deferens, and seminal vesicles
Testicles, epididymis, bladder, and seminal vesicles
Testicles, epididymis, vas deferens, and kidneys
questions.explanation: Testicles, epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate, and penis are listed male genital structures.

questions.question: A patient moves air adequately but has severely reduced blood flow to tissues. Why can cellular oxygen delivery still fail?
choices: Oxygen must be carried from the lungs to tissues by adequate blood flow
Normal air movement establishes sufficient oxygen delivery despite the low flow
Reduced tissue flow increases the blood’s capacity enough to preserve delivery
Diffusion across the alveoli directly supplies distant tissues without blood transport
questions.explanation: The life support chain depends on both respiratory exchange and circulatory delivery to cells.

questions.question: Which comparison correctly describes cellular energy production?
choices: Adequate oxygen supports more efficient aerobic ATP production; limited oxygen can lead to anaerobic metabolism and lactic acid buildup
Limited oxygen produces more ATP than adequate oxygen because anaerobic metabolism is more efficient
Aerobic metabolism uses no oxygen, while anaerobic metabolism requires oxygen
Anaerobic metabolism supplies the same energy yield as aerobic metabolism without accumulating wastes
questions.explanation: Aerobic metabolism uses oxygen efficiently to produce more ATP; anaerobic metabolism is less efficient and can lead to lactic acid accumulation.

questions.question: Tissue perfusion remains inadequate. Which sequence best explains the resulting cellular threat?
choices: Reduced oxygen delivery → anaerobic metabolism → lactic acid buildup and cell dysfunction
Reduced oxygen delivery → increased aerobic ATP production → improved cell function
Reduced blood flow → increased oxygen delivery → reduced waste production
Reduced blood flow → complete removal of carbon dioxide → improved pH regulation
questions.explanation: Sustained hypoperfusion limits oxygen delivery, promotes anaerobic metabolism, and can cause lactic acid buildup and organ dysfunction.

questions.question: Oxygen concentration is higher on one side of a gas-exchange membrane than the other. How does passive diffusion move oxygen?
choices: From the higher concentration toward the lower concentration
From the lower concentration toward the higher concentration
Equally in both directions regardless of the concentration difference
Only after both sides reach equal concentrations
questions.explanation: Passive diffusion moves gases down a concentration gradient.

questions.question: Gas exchange worsens, and carbon dioxide begins accumulating. Which linked changes are expected?
choices: CO₂ rises, pH falls, and respiratory drive increases
CO₂ rises, pH rises, and respiratory drive increases
CO₂ rises, pH falls, and respiratory drive decreases
CO₂ rises, pH rises, and respiratory drive decreases
questions.explanation: CO₂ accumulation lowers pH and may stimulate increased breathing, but a compensatory response may not restore effective exchange.

questions.question: Which question is primarily about pathophysiology?
choices: How does an airway obstruction alter gas exchange and cellular function?
How does gas exchange normally occur at an unobstructed alveolus?
Where are the lungs located in the thoracic cavity?
What shape does the sternum have?
questions.explanation: Pathophysiology examines functional changes caused by illness or injury.

questions.question: A muscle pulls on a bone to move a joint. Which structure transmits the muscle’s pull to the bone, and which tissue cushions articulating bone ends?
choices: Tendon; articular cartilage
Ligament; articular cartilage
Tendon; synovial membrane
Articular cartilage; ligament
questions.explanation: Tendons attach muscle to bone; articular cartilage covers and cushions articulating bone ends.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly identifies the socket receiving the femoral head and the junction of the left and right pubic bones?
choices: Acetabulum; pubic symphysis
Pubic symphysis; acetabulum
Greater trochanter; sacrum
Ilium; greater trochanter
questions.explanation: The femoral head articulates at the acetabulum; the pubic symphysis joins the pubic bones.

questions.question: Why does movement of air through the trachea not itself establish that gas exchange is occurring?
choices: It conducts air but lacks the alveolar surface needed for exchange
It exchanges oxygen but has no role in carbon dioxide movement
It exchanges carbon dioxide but has no role in oxygen movement
It exchanges both gases whenever respiratory rate is within normal limits
questions.explanation: Dead space conducts air but has no alveoli and little or no gas exchange.
tags: Dead space and alveolar gas exchange

questions.question: After a normal exhalation, a person forcibly breathes out an additional amount of air. What is this extra volume called?
choices: Expiratory reserve volume
Residual volume
Inspiratory reserve volume
Tidal volume
questions.explanation: Expiratory reserve volume is the additional amount that can be forcibly exhaled after a normal breath.

questions.question: Which vessel returns blood from the abdomen, pelvis, and lower extremities toward the heart?
choices: Inferior vena cava
Superior vena cava
Pulmonary vein
Pulmonary artery
questions.explanation: The inferior vena cava drains the lower-body regions; the superior vena cava drains the head, neck, shoulders, and upper limbs.

questions.question: A patient has fewer platelets but a normal red-cell count. Which function is most directly affected by the platelet change?
choices: Initial blood-clot formation
Oxygen transport through hemoglobin
The principal liquid transport provided by plasma
White-cell defense against infection
questions.explanation: Platelets are essential to initial clot formation; their role differs from red cells, white cells, and plasma.

questions.question: Which brainstem system is most directly associated with regulating consciousness?
choices: Reticular activating system
Occipital visual processing area
Cerebellar coordination system
Peripheral somatic motor nerves
questions.explanation: The reticular activating system regulates consciousness within the brainstem.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly distinguishes cushioning of the central nervous system from delivery of oxygenated blood to the head?
choices: Cerebrospinal fluid; carotid arteries
Cerebrospinal fluid; jugular veins
Plasma; carotid arteries
Plasma; jugular veins
questions.explanation: CSF cushions the brain and spinal cord; carotid arteries supply oxygenated blood to the head.

questions.question: Which layer produces replacement epidermal cells, and which is the surface layer of dead cells?
choices: Germinal layer; stratum corneum
Stratum corneum; germinal layer
Dermis; subcutaneous tissue
Subcutaneous tissue; dermis
questions.explanation: The germinal layer produces new cells; the stratum corneum forms the dead-cell surface.

questions.question: Which pair describes liver functions other than bile production?
choices: Forming clotting factors and filtering harmful substances
Storing bile and producing digestive enzymes in saliva
Producing insulin and glucagon
Absorbing water from intestinal contents and forming stool
questions.explanation: The liver forms factors needed for blood clotting and processes harmful substances. Bile storage, pancreatic hormone production, and stool formation belong to other structures.

questions.question: Which description adds a circulatory role to the lymphatic system’s immune functions?
choices: A network supporting circulation and helping remove excess tissue fluid
A pressure-generating pump that drives systemic arterial blood
A filtration pathway carrying blood wastes into the urinary bladder
A conducting pathway returning oxygenated blood from lungs to the left atrium
questions.explanation: The lymphatic network supports fluid balance and immune defense alongside circulation.

questions.question: What is perfusion?
choices: Blood circulation through tissue in amounts sufficient for current cellular needs
Movement of air into and out of the lungs
The pressure measured in arteries while the heart rests
Loading oxygen onto hemoglobin in the bloodstream
questions.explanation: Perfusion is adequate tissue blood flow for cellular needs. Ventilation, diastolic pressure, and oxygenation are related but distinct concepts.

questions.question: What does pathophysiology study?
choices: Functional changes that accompany disease or a syndrome
The location and structure of normal body parts
The normal functions of body systems alone
The construction and meaning of medical words
questions.explanation: Pathophysiology examines disease-related functional changes; anatomy, physiology, and medical terminology have different focuses.

questions.question: What is tidal volume?
choices: The amount of air moved during a single breath
The total amount of air moved in one minute
Air that does not reach the alveoli for gas exchange
Air remaining after maximal forced exhalation
questions.explanation: Tidal volume is volume per breath; minute volume, dead space, and residual volume describe other respiratory quantities.

questions.question: What is a ligament?
choices: A band of connective tissue joining bone to bone
Connective tissue joining muscle to bone
Tissue cushioning the articulating ends of bones
Muscle tissue producing voluntary joint movement
questions.explanation: Ligaments join bones. Tendons connect muscles to bones, cartilage cushions joint surfaces, and skeletal muscle produces movement.

questions.question: In anatomic position, which pairing locates the two forearm bones correctly?
choices: Radius on the thumb side; ulna on the little-finger side
Ulna on the thumb side; radius on the little-finger side
Radius in the upper arm; ulna on the thumb side
Humerus on the thumb side; radius on the little-finger side
questions.explanation: The radius is lateral, on the thumb side; the ulna is medial, on the little-finger side.

questions.question: Which sequence follows the sternum from its superior part to its inferior tip?
choices: Manubrium → body → xiphoid process
Xiphoid process → body → manubrium
Body → manubrium → xiphoid process
Manubrium → xiphoid process → body
questions.explanation: The sternum consists of the manubrium superiorly, the body, and the xiphoid process inferiorly.

questions.question: A burn destroys a patch of skin. Besides temperature regulation, which pair of functions may be impaired at that site?
choices: Environmental protection and sensory information transmission
Blood-cell production and mineral storage
Hormone secretion and blood glucose regulation
Bile production and nutrient processing
questions.explanation: Skin protects against the environment and transmits sensory information to the brain, in addition to regulating temperature.

questions.question: Which mechanism normally moves swallowed food from the pharynx toward the stomach?
choices: Contraction of muscles in the esophageal wall
Pressure produced by the diaphragm alone
Bile flow through the common digestive passage
Gravity acting on a rigid, nonmuscular tube
questions.explanation: The esophagus is a collapsible muscular tube whose wall propels food to the stomach.

questions.question: Which sequence follows material from the stomach through the three sections of the small intestine?
choices: Duodenum → jejunum → ileum
Jejunum → ileum → duodenum
Ileum → duodenum → jejunum
Duodenum → ileum → jejunum
questions.explanation: The sections are duodenum, jejunum, and ileum in that order.

questions.question: Which structure is a narrow tube that opens into the cecum in the right lower abdomen?
choices: Appendix
Gallbladder
Pancreas
Rectum
questions.explanation: The appendix opens into the cecum in the right lower quadrant.

questions.question: After an ordinary inspiration, a person takes in the additional air available with a deepest possible breath. Which volume is being used?
choices: Inspiratory reserve volume
Expiratory reserve volume
Residual volume
Tidal volume
questions.explanation: Inspiratory reserve is the additional volume that can be inhaled beyond a normal breath.

questions.question: If cardiac output stays constant while systemic vascular resistance falls, what happens to mean arterial pressure in the relationship MAP = CO × SVR?
choices: It falls
It rises
It remains unchanged
It becomes equal to the heart rate
questions.explanation: With CO held constant, a decrease in SVR decreases their product, MAP.

questions.question: Which set correctly classifies patients aged 8, 16, 35, and 52 years, respectively?
choices: School-age, adolescent, early adult, middle adult
Preschooler, adolescent, middle adult, older adult
School-age, early adult, early adult, older adult
Adolescent, adolescent, middle adult, middle adult
questions.explanation: These ages fall within school-age (6–12), adolescent (12–18), early adult (19–40), and middle adult (41–60) ranges.

questions.question: Why can airway obstruction develop more readily in an infant than in an adult?
choices: A relatively large tongue occupies a smaller, narrower airway
A relatively small tongue occupies a longer, rigid airway
A large head is paired with a proportionately wider trachea
A smaller pharynx is offset by a proportionately smaller tongue
questions.explanation: Infants have relatively large tongues and short, narrow airways, increasing obstruction risk.

questions.question: Why can excessive neck flexion or extension compromise a small infant’s airway?
choices: The large occiput and flexible trachea make positioning important
The large occiput makes maximum extension the most reliable position
The trachea is rigid, so changing neck position mainly changes oxygen demand
The infant’s small tongue leaves enough room to tolerate any neck position
questions.explanation: A proportionately large occiput and flexible trachea make excessive flexion or extension capable of occluding the airway.

questions.question: Why is abdominal movement especially noticeable during infant breathing?
choices: A flexible rib cage and horizontal ribs make diaphragmatic movement especially important
A rigid rib cage limits diaphragm movement and makes intercostal contraction dominant
The infant’s more vertical ribs produce the same chest expansion pattern as an adult
The infant’s smaller abdominal organs leave room for predominantly upper-chest expansion
questions.explanation: The infant’s less rigid rib cage and horizontal ribs help explain the prominent abdominal movement.

questions.question: A startled neonate opens both arms, spreads the fingers, and appears to grasp at the air. Which reflex is demonstrated?
choices: Moro
Rooting
Palmar grasp
Sucking
questions.explanation: The Moro reflex is the startle response with arm opening and finger spreading.

questions.question: Which sequence best matches typical infant development at about 2, 6, and 12 months?
choices: Tracks objects → sits upright and babbles → walks with minimal assistance
Walks with assistance → tracks objects → begins babbling
Sits and babbles → walks with assistance → recognizes familiar faces for the first time
Tracks objects → completes toilet training → begins sitting upright
questions.explanation: The listed milestones progress from visual tracking to sitting/babbling to assisted walking.

questions.question: Which comparison correctly describes typical fontanelle closure?
choices: Posterior by about 3 months; anterior between 9 and 18 months
Anterior by about 3 months; posterior between 9 and 18 months
Both normally close by about 3 months
Both normally remain open until after the second birthday
questions.explanation: The posterior fontanelle closes earlier than the anterior fontanelle.

questions.question: A 10-month-old becomes distressed when the caregiver steps away but settles when the caregiver returns. What is the best developmental interpretation?
choices: Separation anxiety
An anxious-avoidant attachment pattern
A Moro response
Preconventional moral reasoning
questions.explanation: Distress linked to caregiver separation is consistent with common separation anxiety in older infants.

questions.question: A calm 5-year-old has a pulse of 110/min, respirations of 23/min, and systolic pressure of 90 mm Hg. How do these values compare with the supplied course’s preschool reference ranges?
choices: All three fall within expected preschool ranges
The pulse is above range because an adult upper limit applies
The respiratory rate is below range because preschoolers normally breathe 30–40/min
The systolic pressure is above range because preschool values should be below 80 mm Hg
questions.explanation: The supplied preschool ranges are pulse 80–140, respirations 20–25, and systolic pressure 80–100; all three fit. These values alone do not establish overall stability.

questions.question: Why does sustained increased breathing effort warrant concern in a preschooler?
choices: Immature respiratory muscles may fatigue during prolonged increased effort
A faster respiratory rate assures an adequate volume with each breath
Adult-like cardiovascular findings establish adult-like respiratory reserve
A lower metabolic demand makes prolonged respiratory effort easier to sustain
questions.explanation: Young children’s underdeveloped respiratory muscles make sustained breathing effort difficult to maintain.

questions.question: A 3-year-old insists on holding the assessment equipment and repeatedly says, “I do it.” Which developmental concept best explains this behavior?
choices: Developing autonomy and ability to express preferences
School-age conventional reasoning driven primarily by peer approval
Adolescent identity development driven primarily by body-image concerns
Older-adult adjustment to loss of independence
questions.explanation: Toddlers and preschoolers develop independence and language for expressing themselves.

questions.question: A school-age child says, “I followed the rule because my friends would think badly of me if I did not.” Which reasoning level is most consistent with this explanation?
choices: Conventional
Preconventional
Postconventional
Autonomy versus shame and doubt
questions.explanation: Conventional reasoning seeks approval from peers or society.

questions.question: A person explains, “I would oppose an unfair rule even if my friends approved of it, because it violates a principle I believe should apply to everyone.” Which level of moral reasoning does this illustrate?
choices: Postconventional
Conventional
Preconventional
Autonomy versus shame and doubt
questions.explanation: The reasoning appeals to a principle beyond approval or punishment. That is the distinction tested by postconventional reasoning; a person’s age alone does not establish the level.

questions.question: An 8-year-old who is normally independent becomes clingy and uses younger-sounding speech during a painful illness. What is the best interpretation of the behavior alone?
choices: Illness can cause temporary regression to an earlier developmental pattern
The behavior proves the child’s usual school-age abilities were never present
The behavior means the child should now be classified as a toddler
School-age independence makes regression incompatible with illness
questions.explanation: School-age children can regress during illness or injury; the behavior should be interpreted in its clinical context.

questions.question: A 16-year-old with abdominal discomfort becomes hesitant when questions turn to pregnancy and sexual activity in front of family. Which approach best supports obtaining a useful history?
choices: Offer an opportunity to answer sensitive questions privately when possible
Continue every question with family present so they can supply missing details
Omit sensitive questions because adolescent self-consciousness makes them inappropriate
Direct the entire interview to the parents because adolescent vital signs resemble adult values
questions.explanation: Privacy and self-consciousness are important in adolescence; private sensitive questioning can improve the history.

questions.question: Which pattern most accurately characterizes adolescence?
choices: Vital signs approach adult ranges while reproductive maturation and rapid growth continue
Adult-like vital signs mean reproductive development is already complete at the start of adolescence
Reproductive maturation continues, but adolescent growth is slower than every adult period
Physical maturation prevents significant identity and privacy concerns
questions.explanation: Adolescence combines approaching physiologic maturity with growth and reproductive changes.

questions.question: A teenager reports feeling pressured by friends to take risks despite personal reservations. Which developmental issue is most relevant?
choices: Peer acceptance competing with developing personal values
Separation anxiety when away from a primary caregiver
Adjustment to retirement and increasing dependence
Responsibility for both children and aging parents
questions.explanation: Adolescence involves peer pressure, identity formation, and development of a personal code of ethics.

questions.question: Which age range does the supplied life-span material describe as a period of optimal physiologic function?
choices: 19–25 years
12–18 years
41–60 years
61–75 years
questions.explanation: The materials identify approximately ages 19–25 as the period of optimal body function, while individual health varies.

questions.question: Which combination most closely matches common early-adult psychosocial priorities?
choices: Establishing work, family, and lasting lifestyle habits
Adapting primarily to declining physiologic reserve and increasing dependence
Centering on peer acceptance while establishing an adolescent identity
Adjusting primarily to retirement and increasing concerns about mortality
questions.explanation: Early adulthood commonly centers on work, family, stress, and solidifying lifelong habits.

questions.question: A 50-year-old reports stress from paying a child’s college expenses while arranging care for an aging parent. Which developmental pattern best fits?
choices: Middle-adult financial and caregiving demands across generations
Early-adult establishment of work and a first independent household
Adolescent identity development centered on peer acceptance
Later-adult adjustment primarily to retirement and personal dependence
questions.explanation: Middle adults may support children and aging parents while managing finances and life goals.

questions.question: Which statement best describes health changes during middle adulthood?
choices: Chronic disease risks become more prominent even while pulse and respiratory ranges remain similar to early adulthood
Normal adult vital-sign ranges rule out emerging diabetes or hypertension
Vision and hearing changes begin only after age 61
Exercise and diet cannot influence the effects of aging during this period
questions.explanation: Middle adulthood brings increased chronic health risks despite broadly similar resting pulse and respiratory ranges.

questions.question: Which chain best explains why an older adult may tire more quickly during increased respiratory demand?
choices: Reduced lung elasticity and a stiffer chest increase breathing effort and reduce reserve
Reduced lung elasticity and a more flexible chest reduce effort and increase reserve
Increased alveolar surface area compensates fully for a stiffer chest
Stronger cough and gag reflexes compensate for reduced lung elasticity
questions.explanation: Reduced elasticity and increasing chest rigidity make breathing more labor intensive and reduce reserve.

questions.question: An older adult has reduced kidney blood flow and filtration. Which consequence is most consistent with these changes?
choices: Less effective waste clearance and reduced ability to conserve fluids
Faster waste clearance and greater ability to conserve fluids
Reduced urine storage capacity as the only effect, with filtration unchanged
Improved clearance because smaller kidneys require less blood flow
questions.explanation: Age-related renal changes reduce both waste clearance and the ability to conserve fluid when needed.

questions.question: An older patient responds slowly to a spoken question but gives a coherent answer after it is repeated clearly. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Hearing or slower processing may affect the response; age alone does not establish loss of knowledge or decision-making ability
The delay proves cognitive impairment even though the eventual answer is coherent
Normal aging necessarily produces deafness, so further communication is unlikely to help
A coherent answer means sensory function must be unchanged
questions.explanation: Older adults can have sensory changes and slower neural responses while retaining knowledge and skills.

questions.question: How can age-related brain shrinkage increase vulnerability to bleeding after a head injury?
choices: Brain volume decreases, increasing space and stretching bridging veins
Brain volume decreases, reducing the space between the brain and dura
Brain volume increases, compressing bridging veins against the skull
The skull expands while brain volume stays constant, stretching bridging veins
questions.explanation: Age-related shrinkage increases the space between brain and dura; stretched bridging veins may tear and allow blood to collect.

questions.question: Which classification correctly matches patients aged 2 weeks, 6 months, 2 years, and 67 years?
choices: Neonate, infant, toddler, older adult
Infant, toddler, preschooler, middle adult
Neonate, preschooler, infant, older adult
Toddler, infant, school-age child, middle adult
questions.explanation: The supplied stages identify the first month as neonatal, later first-year patients as infants, ages 1–3 as toddlers, and 61+ as older adults.
tags: Neonate infant toddler and older-adult categories

questions.question: Touching a neonate’s cheek causes a head turn, while placing an object in the palm causes the fingers to close. Which reflexes occur in that order?
choices: Rooting; palmar grasp
Moro; sucking
Palmar grasp; rooting
Sucking; Moro
questions.explanation: Rooting is the cheek-triggered head turn; palmar grasp is the response to an object in the palm.

questions.question: A child says, “I did it so I would get the prize and avoid being punished.” Which reasoning level best matches that explanation?
choices: Preconventional
Conventional
Postconventional
Autonomy versus shame and doubt
questions.explanation: Preconventional reasoning centers on obtaining desired outcomes and avoiding punishment.

questions.question: How can age-related reduction in cough and gag reflexes affect an older adult?
choices: Greater risk of aspiration and airway obstruction
Improved clearance of secretions from the airway
Increased volume of air exchanged with each breath
Increased efficiency of gas exchange across alveolar membranes
questions.explanation: Reduced protective reflexes can increase aspiration and obstruction risk.

questions.question: An older patient reports stretching prescribed medication because it is unaffordable. What is the most useful interpretation during history taking?
choices: Financial limits may restrict access; explore the actual medication use without assuming deliberate disregard
Age alone shows that the patient cannot understand the prescription
A prescribed medication can be assumed to be taken exactly as written
The financial explanation rules out any health effect from missed doses
questions.explanation: Financial constraints can affect access to care and medications, so the history should establish actual use and circumstances.

questions.question: What is the rooting reflex?
choices: An infant turning toward a cheek touch to seek food
An infant grasping an object placed in the palm
An infant spreading the arms and fingers after a startle
An infant pulling away after a painful stimulus
questions.explanation: The rooting reflex turns the head toward a cheek stimulus; palmar grasp and Moro responses differ.

questions.question: What is separation anxiety?
choices: Distress associated with being apart from a caregiver
A secure emotional bond with a caregiver
A moral judgment based on avoiding punishment
A change from abdominal breathing to chest breathing
questions.explanation: Separation anxiety is distress during separation; bonding, moral reasoning, and breathing development are different concepts.

questions.question: An older adult has lost regular social contact and reports feeling increasingly alone. Which psychosocial challenge should the EMT recognize while assessing current needs?
choices: Isolation and possible depression
A required loss of decision-making capacity with age
The adolescent conflict between peer approval and identity
The toddler conflict between autonomy and shame
questions.explanation: Isolation and depression are potential older-adult psychosocial challenges; assess the individual rather than assuming incapacity.

questions.question: An alert patient with generalized weakness cannot walk down a narrow flight of stairs. The patient has no suspected trauma and can tolerate sitting upright. Beyond the stairs is a clear, level route to the ambulance. Which movement plan best fits both parts of the route?
choices: Use a stair chair on the stairs, then transfer to a wheeled stretcher for the level route
Use a backboard on the stairs, then transfer to a wheeled stretcher for the level route
Use a wheeled stretcher for both the stairs and the level route
Use a stair chair for both the stairs and ambulance transport
questions.explanation: A stair chair suits a conscious patient who can tolerate sitting during movement on stairs. After the stairs, transfer to the wheeled stretcher for rolling movement to the ambulance and transport.
tags: Choosing equipment for stairs and level transport

questions.question: Four providers are ready to lift, but they disagree about when to start and where to stand. What should happen before the lift?
choices: The leader assigns positions, describes the sequence, and uses a coordinated command
Each provider chooses a comfortable position and lifts when ready
The strongest provider begins lifting so the others can follow
The team discusses the sequence after the stretcher is raised
questions.explanation: A coordinated lift requires assigned positions, a shared sequence, and preparatory commands.

questions.question: Which adjustment most directly reduces leverage and strain on an EMT’s back during a lift?
choices: Keeping the load close to the body while lifting
Holding the load farther forward to improve visibility
Reaching across the patient without changing foot position
Turning the upper body while keeping the feet planted
questions.explanation: Keeping the load close reduces leverage on the back; use an upright posture, the legs, and coordinated movement.

questions.question: Which sequence uses the power lift to raise a patient-carrying device?
choices: Balance the feet → bend the legs with back upright → grasp close to the body → extend the legs
Balance the feet → bend the waist with knees straight → grasp → extend the back
Lock the knees → reach forward with extended arms → raise with the shoulders
Bend the legs → grasp → twist the torso while rising
questions.explanation: The power lift uses properly placed flexed legs to raise the load while maintaining upright alignment and keeping it close.

questions.question: An EMT says, “My back stayed straight,” but lifted while bent far forward at the hips. What is the best assessment of the technique?
choices: It can still strain the back because the torso was not upright over the pelvis
It is safe because straightness alone prevents strain regardless of torso angle
It is safer than a leg-powered lift because the hips provide all the lifting force
It is safe if the hands are held farther from the legs
questions.explanation: Keeping the back straight does not make lifting safe when the torso is significantly bent forward at the hips.

questions.question: Which hand position correctly describes a power grip on a stretcher handle?
choices: Palms up, fingers curled firmly, with the handle supported on the curved palms
Palms down, with the handle supported mainly by the fingertips
Palms up, with fingers spread and the handle hanging from the fingertips
Palms facing each other, with the handle resting across the thumbs alone
questions.explanation: A power grip fully supports the handle in the curved palms with a firm finger grip.

questions.question: A stable supine patient has no suspected spinal injury and needs to slide from a bed onto an adjacent stretcher of similar height. A draw sheet is already beneath the patient. Which method uses that sheet as intended?
choices: A coordinated transfer with rescuers gripping the sheet close to the patient
A direct carry with rescuers supporting the shoulders, hips, and legs
An extremity lift with one rescuer at the head and one at the feet
A ground lift with rescuers positioned side by side
questions.explanation: A draw-sheet transfer uses the underlying sheet to support the coordinated move between adjacent surfaces. The other choices are different lifting methods.

questions.question: An EMT cannot complete a bed transfer without reaching far across the mattress. What adjustment best follows safe reaching principles?
choices: Kneel on the bed, pull in controlled increments, and reposition rather than overreach
Keep both feet on the floor and extend the arms farther on each pull
Bend farther at the waist so the hands can reach the opposite edge
Pull continuously without repositioning until the patient reaches the edge
questions.explanation: Kneeling on the bed limits reaching distance; incremental pulling and repositioning maintain safer mechanics.

questions.question: The course’s manual-lifting guidance calls for at least four providers for patients over 250 lb. Two EMTs prepare to manually lift a stable 280-lb patient. The stretcher’s capacity is sufficient. What should they do?
choices: Obtain enough assistance to meet the lifting guidance before starting
Proceed because the stretcher’s capacity exceeds the patient’s weight
Proceed using a power grip, then request help if the lift feels difficult
Move the patient to the ambulance first and request help with loading
questions.explanation: Equipment capacity and personnel capacity are separate. Arrange assistance before the manual lift, not after testing an unsafe load.

questions.question: A conscious, stable patient can safely sit upright and needs to descend a narrow flight of stairs. Which device best fits?
choices: Stair chair
Wheeled ambulance stretcher
Long backboard
Scoop stretcher
questions.explanation: A stair chair is suited to a conscious patient whose condition permits sitting during stair movement.

questions.question: During a stair-chair carry of a stable patient, one provider develops sudden sharp back pain. What is the best response?
choices: Coordinate a safe stop and obtain additional lifting assistance
Change grip and continue because stopping may delay transport
Switch to walking the patient without reassessing whether that is safe
Speed up the carry to shorten the time under load
questions.explanation: A provider who develops sharp pain should stop the move safely and request help rather than continue risking injury.

questions.question: Smoke and flames are advancing toward a patient already accessible to the crew. The crew has a safe route out but cannot remain safely at the current location. What takes priority?
choices: Move the patient to safety promptly while minimizing avoidable spinal movement
Complete the primary assessment and all indicated spinal packaging before moving
Wait for a full nonurgent lift plan despite the advancing hazard
Use the mechanism of injury alone to decide whether the hazard matters
questions.explanation: An immediate threat that cannot be controlled justifies an emergency move before assessment and care at the unsafe location.

questions.question: Immediate danger requires an EMT alone to remove an unresponsive patient from a vehicle. Which sequence best matches the one-person technique?
choices: Clear the legs from the pedals → turn the back toward the open door → support under the shoulders and head → drag to safety
Pull the torso out first → free the legs afterward → support the head once outside
Leave the feet at the pedals → pull both wrists through the door
Turn the chest toward the door → lift by the forearms without supporting the head
questions.explanation: The technique clears the legs first, turns the back toward the opening, and supports the patient through the armpits with the head against the rescuer’s body.

questions.question: At a safe scene, a patient has shock and needs to be moved quickly. There is time for brief measures to limit spinal movement. Which category best fits?
choices: Urgent move
Emergency move solely because the patient has shock
Nonurgent move because there is no scene hazard
Routine transfer without regard to the patient’s condition
questions.explanation: Shock can require an urgent move; urgent movement allows brief consideration of spinal protection while proceeding quickly.

questions.question: Which patient has the strongest reason for rapid extrication from a vehicle?
choices: A patient who needs an immediate intervention that requires a supine position
A stable patient who can be fully assessed and treated in the current seat
A stable patient who prefers a faster departure despite no urgent care need
A patient selected solely because every collision requires rapid extrication
questions.explanation: An immediate intervention that cannot be performed seated provides a specific rapid-extrication indication.

questions.question: A stable patient is supine on the floor, has no suspected spinal injury, and must be carried a short distance to the stretcher. There is room for rescuers to stand side by side. Which method best fits?
choices: Direct ground lift
Extremity lift
Draw sheet transfer
Clothes drag
questions.explanation: A direct ground lift fits a supine patient without suspected spinal injury who needs carrying to the stretcher.

questions.question: An older patient with marked spinal curvature cannot lie comfortably flat on a rigid board. Which consideration best guides packaging?
choices: Consider a device such as a vacuum mattress that can accommodate the patient’s shape
Explain the procedure compassionately but use the rigid flat surface without adapting support
Assume the discomfort is unrelated to packaging because the board is rigid
Use the same flat position regardless of skeletal rigidity or curvature
questions.explanation: Geriatric skeletal changes can make rigid supine packaging harmful; a vacuum mattress is an alternative that molds around the patient.

questions.question: What is bariatrics?
choices: The prevention or management of obesity and related diseases
The care of conditions associated with older age
The restriction of spinal movement after an injury
The assessment of breathing and gas exchange
questions.explanation: Bariatrics concerns obesity and associated diseases; geriatrics, spinal protection, and respiratory assessment concern other needs.

questions.question: A bariatric stretcher’s rated capacity exceeds the patient’s weight. What can the crew conclude from that fact alone?
choices: The rating supports equipment selection, but personnel, route, and lifting assistance still require evaluation
The rating guarantees that the usual two-person crew can manually lift the patient
A higher capacity eliminates the need to plan loading into the ambulance
Additional personnel are required only after the first lifting attempt fails
questions.explanation: Higher equipment capacity does not remove the danger to providers; safe movement still requires resource and route planning.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly matches specialized equipment with its intended use?
choices: Basket stretcher: remote uneven terrain; flexible stretcher: confined spaces
Basket stretcher: routine seated stair carry; flexible stretcher: rigid spinal board
Scoop stretcher: use when only one side of the patient is accessible; stair chair: unresponsive supine transport
Flexible stretcher: rigid support for suspected spinal injury; basket stretcher: routine seated stair carry
questions.explanation: Basket stretchers serve remote or technical rescue settings; flexible stretchers conform around patients for confined-space movement.

questions.question: After transporting a patient, a stretcher has no visible soil. What determines whether it is ready for the next patient?
choices: Completion of the required post-use decontamination process under local procedures
Visual appearance alone because no visible soil means no contamination
Secure storage alone because contamination ends once equipment is put away
Replacement of the mattress alone while leaving the frame and straps unaddressed
questions.explanation: Equipment must be decontaminated after use to protect patients and crews, following local procedures.

questions.question: An unresponsive patient is breathing adequately and has no suspected spinal, hip, or pelvic injury. Which position best matches transport positioning guidance?
choices: Recovery position
Supine position
Fowler position
Prone position
questions.explanation: The recovery position is indicated for an unresponsive patient without the specified suspected injuries.

questions.question: A conscious patient has nontraumatic chest discomfort and difficulty breathing, with no signs of shock. Which position is most appropriate?
choices: A position of comfort, usually Fowler or semi-Fowler
Supine with the legs elevated
Prone with the head turned to one side
Flat supine on a rigid backboard
questions.explanation: For a patient without suspected injury who has chest pain or respiratory distress, a comfortable upright or semi-upright position is typical.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly matches positioning to the patient’s needs?
choices: Suspected spinal injury: maintain required spinal restriction; nausea or vomiting: comfort with attention to airway protection
Suspected spinal injury: maintain required spinal restriction; nausea or vomiting: flat supine in every case for easier monitoring
Suspected spinal injury: freely adjust the torso for comfort; nausea or vomiting: comfort with attention to airway protection
Suspected spinal injury: freely adjust the torso for comfort; nausea or vomiting: flat supine in every case for easier monitoring
questions.explanation: Movement with suspected spinal injury must preserve appropriate restriction; positioning with vomiting must consider comfort and protect the airway.

questions.question: A patient in late pregnancy becomes hypotensive and uncomfortable while lying supine. Which change best fits the positioning guidance?
choices: Left lateral position
Supine with the legs elevated
Right lateral position
Prone position
questions.explanation: Late-pregnancy patients who are hypotensive or uncomfortable supine should be positioned and transported on the left side.

questions.question: Which use fits the backboard’s described patient-moving role?
choices: Supporting a supine patient during removal from an awkward location
Seated transport of a stable patient down a narrow staircase
Providing a comfortable surface for a prolonged routine transport
Keeping a responsive patient upright during respiratory distress
questions.explanation: A rigid board can support supine movement and access from awkward places; selecting it does not remove planning or make it the best device for every case.

questions.question: Which description correctly distinguishes a clothes drag from a blanket drag?
choices: Clothes drag: pull clothing at the neck and shoulder area; blanket drag: pull material placed beneath the patient
Clothes drag: pull the ankles; blanket drag: pull a blanket placed over the chest
Clothes drag: pull the wrists; blanket drag: pull the patient’s shirt
Clothes drag: lift by the belt; blanket drag: carry without using the blanket
questions.explanation: These emergency techniques differ in whether appropriate clothing or an underlying blanket supports the pull.

questions.question: A stable patient has no suspected spinal or extremity injury. The confined space prevents two rescuers from standing side by side. Which method fits, with one rescuer at the head and the other at the feet?
choices: Extremity lift
Direct ground lift
Draw sheet transfer
Clothes drag
questions.explanation: The extremity lift can fit a small space when side-by-side lifting is impractical and the injury exclusions are met.

questions.question: A patient lies on a flat surface, but a fixed obstacle blocks access to one whole side. Which limitation matters when considering a scoop stretcher?
choices: Both sides must be accessible to fit the split components around the patient
Only head access is needed because the halves attach from the top
Access to either one side is always enough for both components
The split design makes patient securing unnecessary after assembly
questions.explanation: The scoop’s parts fit around the patient from both sides, so access to both is needed.

questions.question: What is the principal advantage of a powered wheeled stretcher’s undercarriage?
choices: Raising and lowering the stretcher with less manual lifting
Powering the stretcher along the route to the ambulance
Automatically selecting the required number of lifting providers
Holding the patient in position without separate straps
questions.explanation: Powered adjustment can reduce provider and patient injury risk, but route, capacity, and securing considerations remain.

questions.question: A patient without suspected spinal injury is nauseated and begins vomiting during transport. What consideration should guide a comfortable position?
choices: Maintain airway protection and drainage while choosing a tolerable position
Require flat supine positioning because it is convenient for the monitor
Use comfort alone and defer any airway reassessment until vomiting stops
Treat the original position as fixed even when airway conditions change
questions.explanation: Positioning should consider comfort and airway protection; a changing condition requires reassessment.

questions.question: What does body mechanics describe?
choices: The relationship between anatomic structures and forces during lifting, moving, and carrying
The maximum weight allowed by a stretcher manufacturer
The verbal commands used to coordinate a team lift
The steps used to disinfect patient-moving equipment
questions.explanation: Body mechanics concerns how body structures and physical forces interact; equipment ratings, commands, and decontamination are separate considerations.

questions.question: Which description defines the continuum of care?
choices: Coordinated care by a unified health care team from first patient contact through discharge.
The period when an ambulance crew retains responsibility from patient contact until hospital handoff.
The progression from basic procedures to advanced procedures as a patient becomes more seriously ill.
The division of patient care into separate stages managed independently by each receiving service.
questions.explanation: The continuum of care links providers as a unified team throughout the patient’s care, from first contact through discharge.
questions.category: The Team Approach to Health Care
tags: The Team Approach to Health Care

questions.question: Which arrangement demonstrates continuity between emergency care and care in the community?
choices: An ambulance service changes partners each shift to give providers experience with several teams.
A mobile integrated health care team coordinates follow-up at home after a patient leaves the hospital.
A hospital schedules the same clinicians together so they become familiar with one another’s skills.
A rescue service divides responders into separate triage, treatment, and transport functions.
questions.explanation: A mobile integrated health care team can maintain involvement after discharge, providing coordinated follow-up in the patient’s community.
questions.category: The Team Approach to Health Care
tags: The Team Approach to Health Care

questions.question: Which set contains the five essential elements of a group?
choices: A common goal, group identity, continuity, shared values, and different roles.
A common goal, group identity, continuity, diverse competent skills, and different roles.
A common goal, group identity, coordinated leadership, shared values, and different roles.
A common goal, clear communication, continuity, shared values, and different roles.
questions.explanation: The five elements are a common goal, an image of themselves as a group, a sense of continuity, shared values, and different roles.

questions.question: At a large incident, a transport group coordinates patient movement from several treatment locations. What makes this a group under NIMS?
choices: Its members use the same type of vehicle and equipment.
Its responsibility is limited to one geographic section of the scene.
Its members perform a specific function that may cross geographic boundaries.
Its responsibility includes directing all functions throughout the incident.
questions.explanation: NIMS groups organize an incident by function. A transport group can perform that function across geographic boundaries.
questions.category: The Team Approach to Health Care
tags: The Team Approach to Health Care

questions.question: Which change most clearly turns independently working providers into a coordinated patient-care team?
choices: Each provider completes an individual task and reports only when that task is finished.
Providers choose separate tasks according to personal preference without assigning a leader.
Providers use the same equipment but retain separate plans for the patient’s care.
Providers take defined roles and coordinate their actions under a designated leader.
questions.explanation: A team combines assigned roles, interdependent work, coordination, and a designated leader to pursue a common patient-care goal.
questions.category: The Team Approach to Health Care
tags: The Team Approach to Health Care

questions.question: Two EMTs are individually competent but unfamiliar with one another’s equipment preferences and work habits. What does practicing together add?
choices: It permits either member to direct procedures outside their usual scope of practice.
It helps them anticipate task transitions by learning each other’s tools, techniques, and capabilities.
It makes clear role assignments less necessary when they join an unfamiliar crew.
It allows them to rely on familiar routines instead of adjusting to the patient’s condition.
questions.explanation: Joint practice develops familiarity with each other’s tools, techniques, capabilities, and preferences, allowing smoother coordination between steps.
questions.category: The Team Approach to Health Care
tags: The Team Approach to Health Care

questions.question: A crew shares a goal, has clear roles, communicates effectively, and has supportive coordinated leadership. Which additional element completes the five essentials of effective team performance?
choices: A sense that the crew will remain together over time.
A supervisor who specifies how every task must be performed.
Diverse and competent skill sets among its members.
Matching experience and qualifications for every member.
questions.explanation: The fifth element is diverse and competent skill sets. Together, the five elements support coordinated and capable patient care.
questions.category: The Team Approach to Health Care
tags: The Team Approach to Health Care
Five elements of effective team performance

questions.question: An EMT joins a temporary crew. Two providers begin the same task while another needed task is left undone. Which team element needs the most direct correction?
choices: Clear roles and responsibilities.
A shared goal for patient care.
Diverse and competent skill sets.
A sense of continuity as a group.
questions.explanation: Duplicate work alongside an unassigned task indicates that responsibilities need to be clarified. Each provider should know what to do and what is expected.
questions.category: The Team Approach to Health Care
tags: The Team Approach to Health Care

questions.question: A team member notices a patient change that the leader cannot see. Which response illustrates crew resource management?
choices: Complete the assigned task and leave interpretation to the leader’s own observations.
Tell another member privately so that the leader receives fewer competing reports.
Assume control of the team before discussing the observation with the leader.
Report the change to the leader so the team can update its shared understanding.
questions.explanation: CRM uses active participation and communication between members and the leader to develop and maintain a shared understanding of the emergency.
questions.category: The Team Approach to Health Care
tags: The Team Approach to Health Care

questions.question: Which sequence correctly expands the PACE communication mnemonic?
choices: Probe, Alert, Confirm, Emergency.
Probe, Alert, Challenge, Emergency.
Plan, Assess, Challenge, Evaluate.
Prepare, Alert, Confirm, Execute.
questions.explanation: PACE stands for Probe, Alert, Challenge, Emergency. It supports clarification, raising concerns, challenging unsafe decisions, and signaling the need for immediate action.
questions.category: The Team Approach to Health Care
tags: The Team Approach to Health Care

questions.question: An EMT has raised a concern about a proposed action, but the concern remains unresolved. The EMT says, “I disagree with proceeding because this could harm the patient. We need to reassess the plan.” Which PACE step is this?
choices: Probe.
Alert.
Challenge.
Emergency.
questions.explanation: Challenge explicitly and respectfully questions a decision or action for patient safety. This statement goes beyond asking for clarification or simply pointing out a concern.
questions.category: The Team Approach to Health Care
tags: The Team Approach to Health Care

questions.question: During hand-over, critical care continues, but unrelated conversations repeatedly prevent the receiving clinician from hearing the report. Which transfer element most directly needs improvement?
choices: Minimal interference
Common language or system
Uninterrupted critical care
Common priorities
questions.explanation: Background conversation that obstructs the report is interference. Reduce interruptions so pertinent information can be exchanged while care continues.
questions.category: The Team Approach to Health Care
tags: The Team Approach to Health Care

questions.question: Which set lists the five critical elements of effective transfer of patient care?
choices: Uninterrupted critical care; minimal interference; respectful interaction; common priorities; equipment inventory.
Uninterrupted critical care; minimal interference; joint training; common priorities; common language.
Uninterrupted critical care; minimal interference; respectful interaction; common priorities; common language.
Uninterrupted critical care; assignment of a new leader; respectful interaction; common priorities; common language.
questions.explanation: The five elements preserve essential care and a clear, respectful exchange between providers: uninterrupted critical care, minimal interference, respectful interaction, common priorities, and a common language or system.
questions.category: The Team Approach to Health Care
tags: The Team Approach to Health Care

questions.question: After hearing a hand-over report, which response best verifies that the receiving clinician understands the patient’s current needs?
choices: “Report received; I’ll review the details when I enter the chart.”
“The patient still needs assisted ventilation; I’ll continue it. Is there another immediate concern?”
“Please leave the paperwork here, and we’ll discuss it if anything is unclear later.”
“I know this chief complaint, so I can take over without further discussion.”
questions.explanation: Restating the important need and clarifying remaining concerns checks understanding and helps establish a shared picture of the patient.
questions.category: The Team Approach to Health Care
tags: The Team Approach to Health Care

questions.question: A clinician maintains eye contact, reduces distractions, asks clarifying questions, and summarizes an incoming hand-over. Which of the five receiving steps is not yet represented?
choices: Summarize the immediate care priorities.
Confirm that the report is understood.
Limit environmental distractions.
Gather supplementary patient documentation.
