Use the increased resistance as evidence that tube position remains secure
questions.explanation: Absent ETCO2, falling oxygenation, resistance, and poor ventilation are warning signs requiring immediate reassessment and correction.

questions.question: An ET tube was confirmed and secured before movement. Why must the EMT continue checking ventilation, perfusion, and tube position?
choices: Movement and evolving problems can cause dislodgement or ineffective ventilation after initial confirmation
The securing device makes repeat airway assessment unnecessary
A normal earlier SpO2 guarantees that later ventilation remains adequate
Only the time of placement matters when interpreting later ETCO2
questions.explanation: Confirmation is not a one-time guarantee; the patient and airway must be monitored continuously.

questions.question: Which monitoring method provides both a numeric end-tidal CO2 value and a waveform?
choices: Capnography
Capnometry alone
Conventional pulse oximetry
An oxygen flowmeter
questions.explanation: Capnography displays a waveform as well as a numeric value; capnometry supplies the number.

questions.question: A trauma patient vomits during assisted ventilation while a partner stabilizes the head. What sequence addresses the immediate hazard?
choices: Turn the patient as a unit onto the side, clear the airway, return to the ventilation position, and resume support
Keep the patient supine and continue squeezing the bag through the vomit
Insert a larger adjunct without clearing material
Stop ventilation for the remainder of transport after the first episode
questions.explanation: Vomited material must be cleared while protecting the spine, then effective ventilation resumed.

questions.question: An oxygen regulator lowers cylinder pressure, and a flowmeter controls the output. Which pairing correctly describes these functions?
choices: Regulator: reduces cylinder pressure; flowmeter: controls liters per minute
Regulator: controls liters per minute; flowmeter: reduces cylinder pressure
Regulator: controls inspired oxygen percentage; flowmeter: reduces cylinder pressure
Regulator: reduces cylinder pressure; flowmeter: controls breath volume
questions.explanation: The regulator reduces high cylinder pressure; the flowmeter controls gas flow measured in liters per minute.

questions.question: A pressure-compensated flowmeter with a float ball is lying sideways. Why does this matter?
choices: The float depends on gravity to indicate flow correctly
Turning the unit sideways changes the cylinder’s stored pressure
The float directly measures mask seal pressure when horizontal
Horizontal use makes the regulator deliver a fixed oxygen percentage
questions.explanation: The float-ball pressure-compensated flowmeter must be upright. A Bourdon-gauge flowmeter can be used in any position.

questions.question: An apneic patient is being ventilated, but chest rise is poor and air leaks around the mask. What correction should be tried before simply squeezing harder?
choices: Reposition the airway and improve the mask seal, then reassess chest rise
Increase bag force while leaving the airway position and leak unchanged
Increase rate to compensate for every breath lost around the mask
Switch to oxygen by cannula without providing ventilation
questions.explanation: Airway position and a proper seal are essential to delivering an effective breath. Observe chest rise and avoid excessive rate or force.
tags: Ventilation reassessment: chest rise and seal

questions.question: Which pocket-mask feature allows supplemental oxygen to be added during mouth-to-mask ventilation?
choices: An oxygen inlet
The transparent mask body
The head strap
The soft sealing edge
questions.explanation: A mask with an oxygen inlet allows supplemental oxygen to be supplied during mouth-to-mask ventilation.

questions.question: A patient has progressive upper-airway swelling after an infection, with no eating or small-object history. What care approach fits the suspected cause?
choices: Support the airway and arrange rapid transport
Begin repeated abdominal thrusts
Attempt removal with a finger sweep
Treat as mild foreign-body obstruction and encourage coughing only
questions.explanation: Swelling can obstruct an airway without a removable foreign body. Repeated attempts to remove an object may be harmful; the patient needs specific care and rapid transport.

questions.question: What is ventilation?
choices: The physical movement of air into and out of the lungs
The loading of oxygen onto hemoglobin
The exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide across membranes
The circulation of blood through tissues
questions.explanation: Ventilation is air movement. Oxygenation, respiration, and perfusion describe the other processes.

questions.question: What is oxygenation?
choices: Loading oxygen molecules onto hemoglobin in the bloodstream
Moving air into and out of the lungs
Circulating enough blood to meet tissue needs
Removing an obstruction from the upper airway
questions.explanation: Oxygenation is loading oxygen onto hemoglobin; ventilation and perfusion are separate processes.

questions.question: Before inserting a suction catheter into the mouth, which preparation helps limit excessive insertion?
choices: Measure from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe, as for an OPA
Use the full catheter length as the insertion distance
Measure across the width of the mouth
Advance until the patient gags to establish the required distance
questions.explanation: Measure the catheter before insertion using the oral-airway sizing technique. Avoid contact with the back of the airway that can provoke gagging.

questions.question: Which patient is the strongest candidate for CPAP?
choices: An alert, cooperative patient breathing spontaneously with severe distress and adequate blood pressure
An apneic patient with a pulse and an open airway
A poorly responsive patient who cannot protect the airway
A patient with severe respiratory distress and marked hypotension
questions.explanation: CPAP requires spontaneous breathing, ability to cooperate and protect the airway, and acceptable blood pressure.

questions.question: Which observation describes pharmacodynamics rather than pharmacokinetics?
choices: A medication blocks a receptor, preventing another substance from activating it
A medication is absorbed through nasal mucosa into the bloodstream
A medication is removed from the body through elimination
Reduced tissue blood flow delays a medication’s absorption
questions.explanation: Pharmacodynamics describes medication actions on the body, such as receptor blockade. Absorption and elimination describe the body’s handling of the medication.

questions.question: Naloxone binds opioid receptors and prevents opioids from producing their usual effects. Which term describes this mechanism?
choices: Antagonism
Agonism
Elimination
Absorption
questions.explanation: An antagonist blocks receptor activation by other substances.

questions.question: A medication is given at 14:00. Improvement first appears at 14:03 and is greatest at 14:10. What do these observations identify?
choices: Onset at 3 minutes; peak at 10 minutes
Peak at 3 minutes; onset at 10 minutes
Duration of 3 minutes; elimination at 10 minutes
Onset at 10 minutes; duration of 7 minutes
questions.explanation: Onset is the interval until effects begin; peak is when the maximum clinical effect occurs.

questions.question: Which measurement describes a medication’s duration?
choices: The length of time its clinical effects persist
The interval from administration to the first clinical effect
The time at which its clinical effect is strongest
The amount administered to produce the desired effect
questions.explanation: Duration describes how long clinical effects last.

questions.question: Which comparison correctly distinguishes unintended from untoward medication effects?
choices: Unintended: undesirable with little risk; untoward: potentially harmful
Unintended: desired clinical response; untoward: potentially harmful
Unintended: potentially harmful; untoward: undesirable with little risk
Unintended: undesirable with little risk; untoward: delayed therapeutic onset
questions.explanation: The distinction concerns the risk of undesired effects, not whether a drug is effective.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly identifies an indication followed by a therapeutic effect?
choices: Suspected cardiac chest pain; inhibition of platelet aggregation by aspirin
Inhibition of platelet aggregation; suspected cardiac chest pain
Aspirin allergy; inhibition of platelet aggregation
Aspirin allergy; nausea after aspirin
questions.explanation: An indication is the reason to give a drug; the therapeutic effect is its intended action.

questions.question: A patient in shock responds more slowly than expected to a medication delivered into tissue. Which explanation is consistent with altered pharmacokinetics?
choices: Reduced tissue blood flow can delay absorption and delivery
Shock guarantees more rapid absorption from every tissue
Slow onset establishes that the medication was an antagonist
A delayed response proves that the medication had no indication
questions.explanation: Shock and route can affect absorption and delivery; response timing alone does not establish mechanism or appropriateness.

questions.question: A patient has suspected cardiac chest pain and a documented severe allergy to aspirin. How should the allergy affect aspirin administration?
choices: It is a contraindication even though the complaint otherwise supports aspirin
It is a relative concern that the chest-pain indication automatically outweighs
It is a reason to reduce the dose while keeping the oral route
It matters only if a reaction occurs after administration
questions.explanation: Aspirin allergy is a contraindication to aspirin. A relevant indication does not make the same medication safe in a patient with a severe allergy.

questions.question: What distinguishes a relative contraindication from an absolute one?
choices: Potential benefits may outweigh the risk, requiring appropriate clinical direction
The medication has no risk and requires no further evaluation
The medication must never be given under any circumstance
It is simply another name for a medication’s indication
questions.explanation: A relative contraindication requires risk-benefit consideration rather than an unconditional prohibition.

questions.question: A patient’s complaint matches an indication for a medication. What still needs to be established before administration?
choices: That contraindications are absent and all required safety checks and authorization are satisfied
That the indication is present, then treat the complaint without further medication checks
That the drug produced benefit in another patient with a similar complaint
That the medication’s trade name sounds appropriate for the symptom
questions.explanation: An indication is necessary but does not complete assessment of safety, dose, route, or authorization.

questions.question: Which pair lists a generic medication name followed by its trade name?
choices: naloxone — Narcan
Narcan — naloxone
Viagra — sildenafil
EpiPen — epinephrine
questions.explanation: Naloxone is the generic name; Narcan is a trade name.

questions.question: Two medication containers have different manufacturer brand names. What is the safest conclusion before treating them as different drugs?
choices: Compare their generic names and other medication details; one drug can have multiple trade names
Different brands establish different active medications
An identical route establishes an identical medication regardless of the labels
A prescription label makes the generic name unnecessary
questions.explanation: Brand names alone do not establish that the active medications differ.

questions.question: Which pair contains two enteral routes?
choices: Oral and rectal
Intramuscular and subcutaneous
Intranasal and intravenous
Sublingual and intraosseous
questions.explanation: Oral and rectal administration enter through the digestive system.

questions.question: A tablet is placed under the tongue to dissolve rather than swallowed. How does this change the intended path to the bloodstream?
choices: Absorption occurs through oral mucosa rather than the digestive tract
Both methods require passage through the stomach before any absorption
The tablet becomes a transdermal medication because it dissolves
The drug becomes an inhaled medication if it remains in the mouth
questions.explanation: Sublingual delivery uses the mucosa beneath the tongue for relatively rapid uptake.

questions.question: Which description correctly distinguishes IV from IO administration?
choices: IV enters a vein directly; IO reaches circulation through bone marrow
IV enters fatty tissue; IO enters muscle
IV enters bone marrow; IO enters a vein directly
IV enters muscle; IO passes through the digestive tract
questions.explanation: IV delivers into a vein; IO uses the marrow circulation.

questions.question: Medication is injected into fatty tissue between the skin and muscle. Which route is this?
choices: Subcutaneous
Intramuscular
Intraosseous
Transcutaneous
questions.explanation: SC injection deposits medication beneath the skin in fatty tissue.

questions.question: Which comparison of delivery routes is most accurate?
choices: IV delivery enters the bloodstream directly; swallowed medication must first be absorbed through the digestive system
Swallowed medication enters the bloodstream directly; IV delivery requires gastrointestinal absorption
All routes have the same onset if the medication name is the same
A transdermal patch is normally the fastest route for an immediate effect
questions.explanation: Route influences response timing; IV offers direct bloodstream delivery while oral uptake is slower.

questions.question: A mucosal atomizer turns liquid medication into a spray directed into the nostril. Which route and absorption site does this use?
choices: Intranasal; nasal mucosa
Inhalation; alveoli as the required deposition site
Sublingual; tissues beneath the tongue
Transcutaneous; skin of the face
questions.explanation: The atomized medication is delivered to the nasal lining for quick absorption.

questions.question: Which description defines the transdermal route of medication administration?
choices: Through the skin for absorption into the bloodstream
Onto the skin surface to act at the application site
Under the skin by injection into fatty tissue
Through the digestive tract after being swallowed
questions.explanation: Transdermal medication is absorbed through the skin and can produce systemic effects. This differs from a topical medication used for an effect at the application site.

questions.question: An order specifies medication administration PR. Which route does that abbreviation indicate?
choices: By rectum
By mouth
Under the tongue
Beneath the skin
questions.explanation: PR denotes per rectum.

questions.question: A liquid medication contains particles that settle when it stands. Why is mixing it before administration important?
choices: To redistribute undissolved particles in a suspension
To dissolve a solution that has no suspended particles
To convert a sustained-release preparation into an immediate dose
To change a liquid preparation’s intended absorption route
questions.explanation: Suspended particles do not dissolve and may settle, making redistribution important for dosing.

questions.question: Which medication form consists of a gelatin shell containing powder or liquid?
choices: Capsule
Compressed tablet
Suspension
Gel
questions.explanation: A capsule encloses medication in a gelatin shell.

questions.question: Which comparison correctly distinguishes a local skin treatment from a systemic skin-delivery treatment?
choices: Topical medication acts at the application area; transdermal medication may reach the bloodstream and affect the body more broadly
Both are defined by passage through the digestive system
Transdermal medication acts only on the skin; topical medication always provides a systemic effect
Both require injection beneath the skin
questions.explanation: The chapter distinguishes local topical action from systemic transdermal absorption.

questions.question: Why should an EMT verify the medication’s form as well as its name?
choices: Form helps determine the intended route and release timing
The same medication name makes every form interchangeable by every route
Form determines the patient’s diagnosis without further assessment
Only the trade name determines whether a drug may be injected
questions.explanation: The manufacturer selects a form for the route, timing, and intended effects; matching the name alone is insufficient.

questions.question: Two patients at one scene have similar symptoms. A dose has been prepared for one, but the partner indicates the other patient. Which medication right must resolve this mismatch first?
choices: Right patient
Right medication
Right dose
Right time
questions.explanation: The right-patient check prevents a correct drug and dose from being given to the wrong person.

questions.question: A partner is available while you prepare a medication. Which action best reduces selection and dose errors before administration?
choices: Perform a verbal cross-check of patient, medication, dose, and the relevant safety details
Tell the partner the medication name only after it has been administered
Rely on the familiar package color without reading the label
Use the previous patient’s dose because the complaint is similar
questions.explanation: A preadministration verbal cross-check can identify a mismatch before the medication reaches the patient.

questions.question: A patient with decision-making capacity asks about likely adverse effects before accepting a medication. What should the EMT do?
choices: Explain the intended medication and likely effects, then respect the informed decision
Explain why the medication is indicated but defer discussion of adverse effects until after administration
Ask the partner to administer it before discussion delays transport
Withhold all information about adverse effects to avoid influencing the decision
questions.explanation: The rights include education and the right of a capable patient to refuse.

questions.question: A medication label matches the intended drug and dose, but the expiration date has passed. Which conclusion follows?
choices: Matching drug and dose does not complete the right-time check; do not use the expired medication
The matching dose makes the expiration date irrelevant
A valid indication automatically extends the labeled expiration
A correct route permits use without considering the container’s condition
questions.explanation: The right-time check includes expiration and medication condition.

questions.question: After assisting a patient with a prescribed inhaler, what immediate follow-up best establishes whether treatment helped?
choices: Reassess breathing and other relevant findings, then document the response
First complete a routine call reporting administration while postponing reassessment
Check expiration for the first time and assume the response is satisfactory
Give another treatment immediately without reassessing or checking authorization
questions.explanation: Right response/evaluation requires reassessment for benefit and adverse effects; document what is observed.

questions.question: Which entry best supports continuity of care after medication administration?
choices: Medication, dose, route, time, patient response, and relevant medical-control instructions
Medication trade name and the EMT’s initials only
A statement that treatment was successful without objective reassessment
The planned dose without the actual time or response
questions.explanation: Documentation should capture what was given, how and when, and how the patient responded.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly distinguishes online and off-line medical direction?
choices: Direct physician communication; standing written orders
Standing written orders; direct physician communication
The patient’s prescription; direct physician communication
Direct physician communication; the manufacturer’s directions
questions.explanation: Online direction involves direct orders; standing orders provide off-line authorization within their conditions.

questions.question: An EMT knows a medication is often carried by other agencies. What determines whether this EMT may administer it in the current system?
choices: State and local protocols and medical direction
Whether the medication is sold without a prescription
Whether the EMT has personally taken it before
Whether another agency permits it for all personnel
questions.explanation: Medication authority depends on the EMT’s system and applicable medical direction.

questions.question: An EMT helps an alert patient use the patient’s own prescribed nitroglycerin under authorized conditions. Which category does this illustrate?
choices: Patient-assisted medication
Peer-assisted medication
EMT-administered medication
Online medical direction
questions.explanation: The EMT is assisting with the patient’s own medication.

questions.question: Which example represents peer-assisted rather than patient-assisted medication?
choices: An EMT helps a partner administer a medication after the partner’s toxic-agent exposure
An EMT helps a patient use the patient’s prescribed inhaler
An EMT directly gives aspirin to a patient under protocol
An EMT applies oxygen to a hypoxic patient
questions.explanation: Peer-assisted administration concerns oneself or one’s partner.

questions.question: What is aspirin’s principal benefit during a suspected heart attack?
choices: Inhibiting platelet aggregation
Directly dissolving the existing coronary clot
Dilating veins to reduce cardiac preload
Blocking opioid receptors to improve breathing
questions.explanation: Aspirin inhibits platelet clumping, helping limit further clot development.

questions.question: A patient has suspected cardiac chest pain and reports an aspirin allergy. Which decision follows?
choices: Withhold aspirin and continue other indicated care under medical direction
Give aspirin because the cardiac indication overrides the reported allergy
Give nitroglycerin as a substitute without checking blood pressure or medication history
Give a smaller aspirin dose to bypass the allergy
questions.explanation: Hypersensitivity to aspirin is a contraindication; the cardiac indication does not eliminate it.

questions.question: Which action pairing correctly distinguishes aspirin from nitroglycerin in cardiac care?
choices: Aspirin: platelet inhibition; nitroglycerin: vascular relaxation
Aspirin: vascular relaxation; nitroglycerin: platelet inhibition
Aspirin: clot dissolution; nitroglycerin: vascular relaxation
Aspirin: platelet inhibition; nitroglycerin: increased venous return
questions.explanation: These drugs address different mechanisms: platelet clumping versus vessel tone and cardiac workload.

questions.question: Why must blood pressure be checked before nitroglycerin and monitored afterward?
choices: Venous relaxation can reduce blood return to the heart and lower blood pressure
Nitroglycerin increases venous return and consistently raises pressure
Only the tablet form affects pressure; the spray does not
Pain relief guarantees pressure cannot fall after dosing
questions.explanation: Nitroglycerin relaxes veins, reducing return, workload, and potentially blood pressure.

questions.question: A patient with cardiac chest pain has a normal blood pressure and reports taking sildenafil earlier today. What is the appropriate medication decision?
choices: Withhold nitroglycerin because of the potentially dangerous interaction and notify medical control
Give nitroglycerin because the current blood pressure is normal
Give nitroglycerin first, then ask about medication interactions
Use spray instead of tablets to avoid the interaction
questions.explanation: Recent sildenafil use can make nitroglycerin unsafe despite a normal initial pressure.

questions.question: A medication list includes nitroglycerin and sildenafil, but you do not know when sildenafil was last taken. What information is needed before deciding about nitroglycerin?
choices: Ask about the timing of sildenafil use and apply the interaction restriction
Request nitroglycerin authorization without mentioning sildenafil or its timing
Infer that sildenafil was not taken because it is not the current complaint
Treat the medication list alone as proof that the combination is safe
questions.explanation: The timing of interacting-drug use is important to safe treatment and must be clarified.

questions.question: How is nitroglycerin metered-dose spray administered for its intended mucosal absorption?
choices: Deposit it on or under the tongue without inhaling the spray
Spray it into a spacer and inhale it deeply
Swallow it immediately with water to use gastrointestinal absorption
Spray it onto intact skin for rapid absorption
questions.explanation: The spray is deposited on or under the tongue; it is not an inhaler treatment.

questions.question: A patient still has chest pain after nitroglycerin. Before a protocol-permitted repeat dose, what should guide the decision?
choices: Reassess blood pressure, symptoms, and continuing appropriateness, and confirm the authorized interval
Repeat solely because pain remains, without another pressure check
Repeat as soon as possible because the first dose established safety for all later doses
Treat a mild headache as proof that no reassessment is needed
questions.explanation: Repeat treatment requires current assessment and authorization; persistent pain alone is insufficient.

questions.question: Which storage method preserves the stated requirements for nitroglycerin tablets?
choices: Its original tightly capped glass container
A daily pill organizer with a labeled compartment
A labeled paper medication envelope
A plastic bag holding the required number of tablets
questions.explanation: The supplied material specifies the original tightly closed glass container.

questions.question: A responsive patient with diabetes is weak and confused, has confirmed low blood glucose, and can swallow and protect the airway. Which medication addresses the identified problem?
choices: Oral glucose
Naloxone
Aspirin
Nitroglycerin
questions.explanation: Oral glucose supplies glucose to counter hypoglycemia in a patient who can safely receive it.

questions.question: A patient is being evaluated for an oral medication but cannot swallow or protect the airway. What should govern the decision?
choices: Do not use the oral route; prioritize airway support and an authorized alternative plan
Place the medication farther back in the mouth to ensure delivery
Use a smaller oral dose to eliminate aspiration risk
Treat a patent airway at first contact as proof that swallowing remains safe
questions.explanation: Oral administration requires safe swallowing and airway protection, which must be assessed at the time of treatment.

questions.question: Which combination explains why epinephrine can help a life-threatening allergic reaction with breathing difficulty and poor perfusion?
choices: Bronchodilation, vasoconstriction, and increased heart rate
Bronchodilation, vasodilation, and decreased heart rate
Bronchoconstriction, vasoconstriction, and increased heart rate
Bronchodilation, vasoconstriction, and decreased heart rate
questions.explanation: Epinephrine’s airway and circulatory effects address major threats in anaphylaxis.

questions.question: After an allergen exposure, a patient develops widespread allergic findings, severe breathing difficulty, and low blood pressure. Why is an authorized epinephrine auto-injector more appropriate than relying only on the patient’s bronchodilator?
choices: Epinephrine addresses both airway and circulatory features of life-threatening anaphylaxis
A bronchodilator alone is sufficient because breathing difficulty is present
Epinephrine is chosen only because it is easier to carry
The two medications have identical airway and blood-pressure effects
questions.explanation: Epinephrine’s actions include airway dilation and circulatory support; treating breathing alone does not address the whole reaction.

questions.question: Which finding most strongly supports naloxone in a suspected opioid overdose?
choices: Slow, inadequate respirations
Isolated tachycardia with adequate breathing
Isolated hypertension with adequate breathing
Agitation without respiratory depression
questions.explanation: Naloxone reverses opioid effects; respiratory depression is the key supplied indication.

questions.question: A suspected opioid-overdose patient has a pulse but barely moves air. A partner is preparing naloxone. What should you do during preparation?
choices: Open the airway and support ventilation rather than waiting for the drug to work
Give naloxone before beginning ventilation, then reassess whether breaths are needed
Apply oxygen alone despite the inadequate air movement
Complete the medication history before assisting breaths
questions.explanation: Medication preparation and onset must not leave inadequate ventilation unsupported.

questions.question: Breathing improves after naloxone but becomes slow again during transport. Which explanation and response fit?
choices: The opioid may outlast naloxone; reassess, support breathing, and consider further authorized dosing
The first response proves that later respiratory depression cannot be opioid-related
Naloxone permanently eliminates the opioid, so reassessment is unnecessary
A later decline establishes that the first dose was a medication-selection error
questions.explanation: Naloxone’s effect may end before the opioid’s; recurrence requires reassessment and continued care.

questions.question: A family member gave naloxone before EMS arrival. The patient is now agitated and vomiting. Which approach best accounts for the medication history?
choices: Clarify the prior dose and timing, reassess breathing and airway safety, and consider withdrawal and scene safety
Assume no medication has been given until an EMT personally administers it
Repeat naloxone immediately based only on agitation
Treat the agitation as proof that opioid effects cannot recur
questions.explanation: Prior naloxone affects care; reversal can precipitate withdrawal, and breathing must still be monitored.

questions.question: A cooperative patient has difficulty coordinating the prescribed MDI spray with inspiration. Which comparison of aids is accurate?
choices: A spacer aids MDI delivery; an SVN takes longer and needs an external gas source
A spacer aids MDI delivery; an SVN provides a faster dose without an external gas source
A spacer changes the dose to oral absorption; an SVN requires an external gas source
A spacer replaces the need to inhale; an SVN requires precise spray–breath timing
questions.explanation: The devices address delivery differently while retaining inhalation as the route and requiring evaluation.

questions.question: Why should the EMT verify age and weight-related instructions rather than assume an adult dose is suitable for a child?
choices: Dose can depend on age, weight, and intended action; use the authorized patient-specific instructions
The same complaint requires the same dose at every age
A trade name uniquely fixes the dose for all patients
A child’s dose can always be obtained by halving any adult dose
questions.explanation: Age and weight are stated dose factors; there is no universal child-dose fraction.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes an epinephrine auto-injector?
choices: A preset intramuscular dose
An adjustable intramuscular dose
A preset intravenous dose
An adjustable subcutaneous dose
questions.explanation: The auto-injector automatically delivers a preset IM amount.

questions.question: A patient has an indication for an epinephrine auto-injector. What must still be verified before using it?
choices: The correct patient, medication, preset dose, route, expiration, and required authorization
Only that the injector contains epinephrine, because every preset dose fits every patient
Only that the patient owns the injector, because ownership replaces authorization
Only that the needle mechanism works, because it replaces the medication checks
questions.explanation: An auto-injector simplifies delivery but does not replace the rights or authorization requirements.

questions.question: A patient says there are no medications because they use only vitamins, herbal products, and nonprescription pain relievers. How should you proceed?
choices: Include those substances in the medication history and ask about their use
Record no medications because none require a prescription
List only the pain reliever if it was taken in the last hour
Omit supplements unless the patient has already had an allergic reaction
questions.explanation: Nonprescription drugs and supplements can be active and relevant to presentation or treatment.

questions.question: A patient’s medication bottles are available, but the patient admits taking some doses differently from the labels. What information should accompany transport?
choices: Both the prescribed medications and the actual doses or timing taken, with the containers or an accurate list
Only the label instructions because actual use is unreliable by definition
Only the trade names because timing cannot affect presentation
No medication details unless a specific overdose has been proved
questions.explanation: Actual use may differ from the prescription and affect the emergency; communicate both.

questions.question: Why should a patient’s beta blocker or anticoagulant be considered during assessment even when it was not taken for the current complaint?
choices: Patient medications can alter vital signs or bleeding risk and change interpretation of the presentation
Only medications prescribed for the current complaint can influence assessment
A medication list conclusively establishes the cause of every symptom
Normal vital signs make medication history irrelevant
questions.explanation: Medication effects can modify the clinical picture and inform treatment and handoff.

questions.question: You discover a medication error just as the patient deteriorates. What is the immediate priority?
choices: Provide needed patient care and promptly notify medical control
Finish writing the incident report before addressing deterioration
Discuss blame with the partner before reassessing the patient
Wait until arrival at the hospital to mention the error
questions.explanation: Patient care comes first, with rapid medical-control notification, protocol follow-through, and honest documentation.

questions.question: Lighting is poor and interruptions keep breaking the medication check. Which change most directly reduces the contributing error risks?
choices: Improve lighting, organize the equipment, and reduce distractions while completing the check
Complete the check from memory to shorten time in poor light
Let the interruptions replace a structured partner cross-check
Use package color to avoid reading labels in poor light
questions.explanation: The medication environment should support accurate label reading and an uninterrupted structured check.
tags: Preventing errors in a chaotic scene

questions.question: An order calls for intramuscular administration. Which proposed injection site description indicates a route error?
choices: Medication placed in fatty tissue between skin and muscle
Medication placed within muscle tissue
A needle used to reach the ordered muscle tissue
Medication delivered into muscle rather than a vein
questions.explanation: Fatty tissue between skin and muscle is the subcutaneous route; an IM order requires delivery into muscle.

questions.question: Oxygen is being prepared for a hypoxic patient. Which interpretation of medication administration applies?
choices: Its gas form does not remove the need for correct route, delivery, authorization, and reassessment
Only injected drugs require a right-patient check
An oxygen label replaces all checks of the delivery device
A visible improvement permits omitting documentation
questions.explanation: Oxygen is a medication in gas form. The form influences delivery but does not exempt it from medication checks and evaluation.

questions.question: A medication error has been addressed, the patient is stable, and medical control has been notified. What follow-up supports safety and continuity?
choices: Document the error and response honestly, follow protocol, and review it with the supervisor or medical director
Record only the intended medication because the patient is now stable
Change the recorded dose to match the order if no harm is apparent
Discuss the event informally but omit it from the patient record
questions.explanation: Accurate documentation and supervisor/medical-director review support ongoing care and quality improvement after immediate needs have been met.

questions.question: What does pharmacodynamics describe?
choices: How a medication produces effects on the body
How the body absorbs and eliminates a medication
The time until the first clinical effect appears
The length of time clinical effects persist
questions.explanation: Pharmacodynamics describes medication action on the body. Pharmacokinetics concerns body actions on medication; onset and duration describe timing.

questions.question: What does pharmacokinetics describe?
choices: How the body acts on a medication, including its elimination
How a medication stimulates or blocks receptors
The condition for which a medication is given
A harmful effect caused by the medication
questions.explanation: Pharmacokinetics concerns body actions on the medication; pharmacodynamics, indications, and untoward effects describe the other concepts.

questions.question: What is an agonist?
choices: A medication that stimulates receptors
A medication that blocks receptor activation by another substance
A condition that prevents safe medication administration
An undesired effect that poses little risk
questions.explanation: An agonist stimulates receptors; an antagonist blocks them. Contraindications and unintended effects describe other medication concepts.

questions.question: What is a medication contraindication?
choices: A circumstance in which a medication could harm the patient or provide no benefit
A condition that supports giving the medication
The desired therapeutic action of the medication
The point at which the medication has its maximum effect
questions.explanation: A contraindication argues against giving a medication; an indication, therapeutic effect, and peak have different meanings.

questions.question: What does medication elimination describe?
choices: Removal of a medication or chemical from the body
Movement of medication through tissue into the blood
Binding of a medication to stimulate a receptor
The interval before the first clinical effect appears
questions.explanation: Elimination describes removal of a medication or chemical from the body.

questions.question: What is medication absorption?
choices: Movement of a medication through body tissues into the bloodstream
Removal of a medication from the body
The maximum clinical effect of a medication
Stimulation or blockade of a receptor by a medication
questions.explanation: Absorption is the process of a medication traveling through body tissues into the bloodstream.

questions.question: Which comparison correctly distinguishes swallowed from sublingual medication?
choices: Swallowed medication uses gastrointestinal absorption; sublingual medication uses mucosa beneath the tongue
Both depend on gastrointestinal absorption, but sublingual tablets dissolve sooner
Swallowed medication enters blood directly; sublingual medication must first be swallowed
Both have the same onset whenever they contain the same active drug
questions.explanation: The routes have different absorption paths. Exact onset depends on the drug and patient, so there is no universal one-hour oral limit or fixed timing for every sublingual medication.

questions.question: Which feature distinguishes a solution from a suspension?
choices: The medication is dissolved rather than present as particles that settle
The medication is contained in a compressed solid tablet
The medication must be delivered through the lungs
The medication is enclosed within a gelatin shell
questions.explanation: A solution contains dissolved substances; a suspension contains undissolved particles that can separate while standing.

questions.question: Which description most accurately defines shock?
choices: Inadequate cellular perfusion, which may exist before blood pressure falls
Any low blood-pressure reading, regardless of cellular perfusion
A rapid pulse that always indicates blood loss
Reduced oxygen in the lungs with otherwise adequate tissue delivery
questions.explanation: Shock concerns inadequate perfusion of cells, not one isolated vital sign or a single cause.

questions.question: Which set correctly matches the three parts of the perfusion triangle?
choices: Heart: pump; vessels: container; blood: contents
Heart: container; vessels: contents; blood: pump
Heart: contents; lungs: pump; vessels: container
Lungs: container; heart: pump; glucose: contents
questions.explanation: Adequate circulation depends on a functioning pump, an appropriate vascular container, and sufficient circulating contents.

questions.question: Why can shock injure cells even when waste products are still being produced normally?
choices: Reduced blood flow delays transport of wastes away from tissues
Reduced blood flow raises the rate of waste removal above its production
Adequate ventilation clears tissue wastes even when their blood transport is impaired
Normal waste production means clearance remains adequate despite reduced flow
questions.explanation: Inadequate perfusion compromises clearance as well as delivery, allowing damaging waste accumulation.

questions.question: Which combination lists the three described ways carbon dioxide travels from tissues toward the lungs?
choices: Dissolved in plasma, as bicarbonate, and attached to hemoglobin
Dissolved in plasma, as glucose, and attached to platelets
As bicarbonate, attached to platelets, and stored in red-cell nuclei
Attached to hemoglobin only, without dissolved or bicarbonate transport
questions.explanation: The blood carries CO2 dissolved in plasma, in bicarbonate form, and attached to hemoglobin.

questions.question: Which response helps preserve vital-organ perfusion during early shock?
choices: Increased heart rate and contraction strength with peripheral vasoconstriction
Decreased heart rate and contraction strength with peripheral vasodilation
Increased blood flow to skin and intestines at the expense of the brain
A reduction in cardiac contraction strength while circulating volume is unchanged
questions.explanation: Sympathetic hormones increase cardiac effort and constrict less essential vascular beds.

questions.question: A bleeding patient has a rapid pulse and cool pale skin while blood pressure remains near baseline. What explains the skin findings?
choices: Peripheral vasoconstriction redirects flow toward more critical organs
All circulating blood has stopped reaching every organ
Generalized vasodilation has increased skin flow
The skin findings prove that compensation has already ceased
questions.explanation: Peripheral vasoconstriction can reduce skin perfusion while helping maintain vital-organ flow and blood pressure.

questions.question: A patient’s blood pressure is 102/82 mm Hg. What is the pulse pressure, and how should it be interpreted in the shock assessment?
choices: 20 mm Hg; narrow pulse pressure
82 mm Hg; narrow pulse pressure
102 mm Hg; wide pulse pressure
184 mm Hg; wide pulse pressure
questions.explanation: Pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic: 102 − 82 = 20. A value below 25 may occur in shock but is not a standalone diagnosis.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly distinguishes preload, contractility, and afterload?
choices: Blood available to fill the heart; strength of cardiac contraction; resistance to outflow
Resistance to outflow; blood available to fill the heart; strength of contraction
Strength of contraction; resistance to outflow; blood available to fill the heart
Blood pressure during rest; respiratory depth; heart rate
questions.explanation: Cardiac output depends on filling, contraction strength, and resistance against which the heart pumps.

questions.question: Which set identifies the three basic causes underlying the shock categories?
choices: Pump failure, poor vessel function, and low fluid volume
Hypotension, anxiety, and rapid breathing
Anemia, hypoxia, and fever as the only possible causes
Low systolic pressure, low diastolic pressure, and narrow pulse pressure
questions.explanation: The three causes concern failure of the pump, vascular function, or circulating volume.

questions.question: After several days of vomiting and diarrhea, a patient is confused, tachycardic, and hypotensive without visible bleeding. Which mechanism best explains the shock concern?
choices: Loss of circulating fluid volume without hemorrhage
Mechanical obstruction of cardiac filling caused by the diarrhea
Loss of sympathetic vessel control from a spinal injury
Primary myocardial failure established by the low pressure alone
questions.explanation: Substantial gastrointestinal fluid loss can produce nonhemorrhagic hypovolemic shock.

questions.question: Why can extensive thermal burns cause hypovolemic shock without major external whole-blood bleeding?
choices: Plasma loss and fluid shifts reduce circulating volume
Selective red-cell loss leaves circulating plasma volume unchanged
Vascular constriction creates a container too large for its blood volume
Primary myocardial failure accounts for the fluid deficit
questions.explanation: Severe burns can cause loss of fluid from the vascular space, including plasma.

questions.question: A patient has multiple severe fractures and abdominal trauma but little visible external bleeding. Why should shock remain a concern?
choices: Significant internal blood loss can occur despite minimal visible bleeding
Shock from volume loss requires an open wound with active bleeding
Fractures only cause pump failure and cannot affect circulating volume
Normal-looking external dressings establish adequate perfusion
questions.explanation: Major injuries can conceal internal blood loss; visible bleeding is not required for shock.

questions.question: Blood volume is initially unchanged, but small vessels dilate widely. How can perfusion decrease?
choices: Blood pools in the expanded vascular beds, making the volume insufficient for the enlarged container
The blood volume must immediately double when vessels dilate
Vasodilation necessarily increases pressure and organ delivery
Only destruction of the heart muscle could explain the change
questions.explanation: A poorly regulated enlarged vascular container can cause inadequate distribution even without initial blood loss.

questions.question: Which mechanism defines cardiogenic shock?
choices: The heart cannot maintain sufficient output to meet tissue needs
A temporary emotional reaction dilates vessels despite a normal pump
Fluid is lost through vomiting while the heart remains structurally normal
A pulmonary vessel clot physically blocks blood flow
questions.explanation: Cardiogenic shock is primary pump failure.

questions.question: A patient with severe cardiac dysfunction has poor perfusion and pulmonary edema. How are these findings related?
choices: Reduced forward output with backup into pulmonary vessels
Reduced blood volume with compensatory collapse of pulmonary vessels
Primary airway obstruction with otherwise normal forward cardiac output
Systemic vasodilation with increased forward output and no backup
questions.explanation: Inadequate pumping can both impair systemic delivery and cause pulmonary backup.

questions.question: Which finding most strongly favors cardiogenic pump failure over isolated volume loss in a patient with poor perfusion?
choices: A cardiac history with chest discomfort and evidence of pulmonary fluid backup
Several days of substantial diarrhea without respiratory findings
A rapidly bleeding limb wound
Extensive burns with plasma loss
questions.explanation: Cardiac dysfunction with pulmonary backup fits cardiogenic shock; the other mechanisms primarily reduce volume.

questions.question: Which set contains three causes of obstructive shock?
choices: Cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax, and massive pulmonary embolism
Sepsis, anaphylaxis, and neurogenic shock
Hemorrhage, diarrhea, and extensive burns
Myocardial pump failure, dehydration, and syncope
questions.explanation: Each listed obstructive condition physically impedes filling or forward circulation.

questions.question: Fluid accumulates between the myocardium and pericardial sac and restricts ventricular filling. Which explanation fits the resulting shock?
choices: External restriction of filling produces obstructive shock
Loss of plasma through skin produces hypovolemic shock
Spinal loss of vessel tone produces neurogenic shock
Primary failure of myocardial contraction alone defines this obstruction
questions.explanation: Tamponade impairs filling because fluid around the heart compresses it.

questions.question: After chest trauma, trapped air builds pressure in the chest and compresses the heart and great vessels. Why can shock occur?
choices: Reduced venous return and impaired cardiac filling
Loss of plasma through damaged peripheral capillaries
Loss of sympathetic vascular tone below a spinal injury
Primary failure of cardiac muscle contraction without external restriction
questions.explanation: Tension pressure can impair cardiac filling and circulation as well as collapse a lung.

questions.question: A large clot blocks pulmonary blood flow, creating backup and severe strain in the right ventricle. Which shock category fits the primary mechanism?
choices: Obstructive
Hypovolemic
Neurogenic
Psychogenic
questions.explanation: A massive pulmonary embolism mechanically obstructs forward blood flow.

questions.question: Which mechanism is shared by distributive shock types?
choices: Widespread dilation and blood pooling
Loss of circulating whole blood
External restriction of cardiac filling
Primary loss of myocardial pumping strength
questions.explanation: Distributive shock involves poor vascular distribution, often with an expanded vascular bed.

questions.question: Which combination most accurately explains septic shock?
choices: Vessel damage and leak combined with widespread dilation
Isolated loss of sympathetic impulses after spinal trauma
Uniform vasoconstriction that prevents plasma leakage
Mechanical restriction of the ventricles by pericardial fluid
questions.explanation: Severe infection can impair vessel tone and increase permeability, causing pooling and plasma loss.

questions.question: Why can septic shock involve both poor vessel function and reduced effective circulating volume?
choices: Vessels dilate while plasma leaks through damaged vessel walls
Vessels contract tightly while new plasma enters the circulation
All plasma loss must arise from an external laceration
Poor vessel function prevents any change in circulating volume
questions.explanation: Dilation enlarges the container while leakage reduces the contents available within it.
tags: Sepsis as mixed vessel and volume problem

questions.question: A recently hospitalized patient has fever, altered mental status, tachycardia, and hypotension. There is no evident traumatic blood loss. Which cause deserves particular concern?
choices: Severe infection causing septic shock
Psychogenic syncope solely because the patient is confused
Neurogenic shock without a spinal-injury history
Hemorrhagic shock established solely by the low blood pressure
questions.explanation: The infection context and poor-perfusion findings raise concern for septic shock, while assessment must still consider other causes.

questions.question: How can a high spinal cord injury produce neurogenic shock?
choices: Loss of sympathetic signals allows vessels below the injury to dilate and blood to pool
The injury forces all vessels below it to constrict permanently
The injury must sever a large blood vessel before neurogenic shock can occur
The heart becomes surrounded by fluid because sympathetic signals are lost
questions.explanation: Interrupted sympathetic control removes normal vessel tone and expands vascular capacity.

questions.question: After suspected high spinal injury, a patient is hypotensive with warm dry skin and a relatively slow pulse. Which mechanism best fits this combination?
choices: Neurogenic loss of sympathetic tone
Typical hemorrhagic compensation with peripheral vasoconstriction
Septic shock proved by skin warmth alone
Cardiogenic shock proved by the pulse rate alone
questions.explanation: The spinal context, vasodilated skin, and slow pulse are a characteristic neurogenic pattern.

questions.question: After a known allergen exposure, a patient develops hives, throat swelling, wheezing, and low blood pressure. Which interpretation best fits?
choices: Anaphylaxis with airway and circulatory threats
Isolated lower-airway disease without a systemic problem
Cardiogenic shock established by low pressure alone
Psychogenic fainting without airway involvement
questions.explanation: The exposure and combined skin, airway, and circulatory findings fit a severe systemic allergic reaction.

questions.question: What does sensitization mean in the explanation of anaphylactic shock?
choices: Developing sensitivity after an earlier exposure that may not have produced a reaction
Producing a transient circulatory response to an emotional stimulus
Developing tolerance that prevents a later allergic reaction
Losing circulating plasma after an unrelated thermal injury
questions.explanation: Earlier exposure can establish sensitivity; a later exposure can provoke a severe reaction.

questions.question: A sudden emotional stimulus causes brief generalized vasodilation and fainting. Which mechanism is described?
choices: Psychogenic shock with transient reduction in cerebral perfusion
Neurogenic shock caused by interruption of spinal vessel signals
Cardiogenic shock from persistent myocardial failure
Obstructive shock from blocked pulmonary vessels
questions.explanation: The chapter describes temporary nervous-system-mediated dilation and syncope as psychogenic shock.

questions.question: Which comparison correctly classifies two causes of hypovolemic shock?
choices: Internal bleeding: hemorrhagic; prolonged diarrhea: nonhemorrhagic
Internal bleeding: nonhemorrhagic; prolonged diarrhea: hemorrhagic
Internal bleeding: obstructive; prolonged diarrhea: cardiogenic
Both are necessarily neurogenic if blood pressure falls
questions.explanation: Hypovolemia can result from blood loss or from other fluid loss.

questions.question: A trauma patient has worsening restlessness, tachycardia, and pale clammy skin, but systolic pressure is 118 mm Hg. Which interpretation is appropriate?
choices: Compensated shock remains possible despite the maintained pressure
Shock is excluded until systolic pressure falls below 90 mm Hg
The normal systolic pressure proves adequate cellular perfusion
The skin findings establish irreversible shock
questions.explanation: Compensation may preserve pressure while other findings show impaired perfusion.

questions.question: A patient initially has a rapid pulse with near-baseline blood pressure. Later, systolic pressure falls and responsiveness declines. What does this trend indicate?
choices: Progression toward decompensated shock
Resolution because the initial compensatory response has ended
A harmless variation established by the earlier normal pressure
A specific shock cause that can be identified from pressure alone
questions.explanation: Falling pressure with worsening mental status indicates failing compensation and worsening perfusion.

questions.question: Which finding most strongly adds concern for advanced shock rather than a typical early compensatory pattern?
choices: Loss of peripheral pulses with worsening responsiveness
Restlessness with a rapid pulse and maintained blood pressure
Pale cool skin with a palpable rapid radial pulse
Rapid shallow breathing with maintained responsiveness
questions.explanation: Peripheral pulse loss and neurologic deterioration are concerning late findings.

questions.question: Why is hypotension especially alarming in an injured child with other poor-perfusion findings?
choices: Children may maintain pressure during substantial blood loss, so a pressure fall can mark advanced deterioration
Children reliably become hypotensive before any other shock sign
A normal earlier pressure guarantees that later hypotension is harmless
Hypotension in a child identifies only a breathing problem and excludes volume loss
questions.explanation: Pediatric compensation can preserve pressure until severe compromise; a fall is a late warning.

questions.question: In an infant or child, which capillary-refill finding supports concern for poor peripheral perfusion?
choices: 4 seconds
2 seconds
1 second
Less than 1 second
questions.explanation: Delayed refill greater than 2 seconds is a supplied sign of poor peripheral perfusion and should be interpreted with the rest of the assessment.

questions.question: Why should warm skin not automatically exclude shock?
choices: Some distributive mechanisms produce vasodilation, so skin findings vary by cause
Every shock patient must have cool clammy skin
Warm skin proves a normal blood volume and cardiac output
Only an elevated temperature can change the skin pattern in shock
questions.explanation: Distributive mechanisms, especially the supplied neurogenic example, can produce warm skin despite poor perfusion.

questions.question: A high-risk injured patient reports intense thirst and increasing anxiety while the pulse becomes rapid and weak. How should these findings be interpreted?
choices: They add to the concern for shock when combined with the injury and perfusion assessment
Thirst proves that oral fluids are the only needed treatment
Anxiety excludes a physical cause of the symptoms
A rapid weak pulse establishes a specific shock type without further assessment
questions.explanation: Subjective symptoms can accompany shock and must be integrated with objective perfusion findings.

questions.question: A patient has profound shock. What limitation matters when deciding whether to continue urgent treatment?
choices: There is no clear field assessment that establishes exactly when shock has become irreversible
Absent radial pulses always prove that no treatment can help
One very low pressure reading establishes irreversible cellular damage
Anxiety continuing for several minutes proves irreversible shock
questions.explanation: The supplied material emphasizes that the point of irreversible injury cannot be identified by a simple field finding.

questions.question: An older injured patient takes medications that may mask shock signs. The pulse is not markedly rapid, but the patient is confused and poorly perfused. What conclusion is safest?
choices: The absence of marked tachycardia does not exclude shock; evaluate the combined findings and medication context
A nonrapid pulse establishes that blood loss is insignificant
Medications make mental status and skin assessment unnecessary
The findings can be dismissed as normal aging
questions.explanation: Medication effects can mask or mimic shock; no single expected sign should override the entire presentation.

questions.question: A patient’s pressures change from 120/80 to 108/88 mm Hg while restlessness and pallor increase. How does the pressure trend add to the assessment?
choices: Pulse pressure narrows from 40 to 20 mm Hg and reinforces the concern for shock
Pulse pressure widens from 20 to 40 mm Hg and proves recovery
A diastolic increase always offsets any fall in systolic pressure
The trend by itself distinguishes septic from cardiogenic shock
questions.explanation: Subtracting diastolic from systolic shows narrowing, which adds concern alongside the clinical decline.

questions.question: A patient has massive life-threatening external bleeding and also needs airway assessment. What should the initial sequence prioritize?
choices: Immediately control the catastrophic bleeding, then assess and manage airway and breathing
Complete airway assessment before doing anything about the massive hemorrhage
Obtain a medication history before addressing either problem
Wait for a blood-pressure reading before controlling bleeding
questions.explanation: The supplied shock assessment prioritizes life-threatening external bleeding before the usual ABC sequence.

questions.question: Airway, breathing, and immediate bleeding threats have been addressed in a patient with possible shock. What history most helps distinguish causes while transport is arranged?
choices: Ask about symptoms, fluid loss, infection, allergy exposure, injuries, and relevant medications through a focused SAMPLE history
Complete a lengthy unrelated past-history interview before transport begins
Treat low pressure as sufficient to identify blood loss and omit history
Ask only whether the patient is anxious because all shock is stress-related
questions.explanation: A focused history helps identify medical and traumatic causes after immediate threats are managed.

questions.question: A patient has poor-perfusion findings, and no distal pulse is palpable. What assessment is needed before concluding that no circulation is present?
choices: Check for a central pulse
Treat the missing distal pulse as proof of cardiac arrest
Rely solely on the previous blood-pressure reading
Wait for a complete history before checking circulation again
questions.explanation: The supplied circulation assessment calls for a central pulse check when a distal pulse is absent.

questions.question: A patient with major abdominal trauma initially has near-normal vital signs. Which approach is appropriate?
choices: Recognize the risk of internal bleeding, support the patient, and repeatedly reassess while arranging prompt transport
Wait for hypotension to prove shock before changing transport priority
Use the normal vital signs to rule out internal bleeding
Delay care until a specific injured organ can be identified
questions.explanation: A serious mechanism can justify early concern before shock signs become obvious.

questions.question: A patient has poor perfusion after significant trauma. Immediate threats have been treated and transport is ready. How should further examination be handled?
choices: Perform a rapid appropriate examination and continue assessment en route without delaying needed transport
Complete every detail of the head-to-toe examination on scene before leaving
Stop all examination once the first life threat has been corrected
Use a focused wrist examination alone despite major multisystem trauma
questions.explanation: Further assessment should identify additional threats quickly without delaying definitive care.

questions.question: Which set should be reassessed during care of a shock patient?
choices: ABCs, mental status, vital signs, chief complaint, and response to interventions
Blood pressure alone because it defines all perfusion
The chief complaint alone because treatment fixes circulation
Only the original injury mechanism, which cannot change
questions.explanation: Shock reassessment includes current life threats, perfusion findings, symptoms, and treatment response.

questions.question: During transport, a shock patient’s mental status declines and breathing becomes shallow. What should the EMT reassess and address first?
choices: Airway and ventilation needs while continuing circulation support
Only the SAMPLE history because it may explain the change
Only the recorded initial blood pressure
Transport destination paperwork before revisiting the patient
questions.explanation: New altered responsiveness and shallow breathing can create immediate airway and ventilation threats.

questions.question: Direct pressure has not quickly controlled life-threatening bleeding from an extremity. Which intervention best addresses the continuing blood loss?
choices: Apply a tourniquet
Apply a pressure dressing and continue monitoring before escalating
Elevate the limb while a partner obtains baseline vital signs
Give oxygen and proceed with the secondary examination
questions.explanation: Persistent life-threatening extremity bleeding needs effective hemorrhage control. Do not delay indicated tourniquet use for monitoring or other supportive measures.

questions.question: A trauma patient has suspected internal bleeding and poor perfusion, with no external wound to control. What is the most important overall plan?
choices: Support airway and breathing, conserve heat, and transport rapidly for definitive care
Remain on scene until repeated examinations identify the precise internal bleeding site
Give oral water to restore volume during a prolonged scene assessment
Treat the lack of external bleeding as a reason to defer shock care
questions.explanation: Internal bleeding requires rapid definitive care, with immediate supportive treatment during transport.

questions.question: A shock patient has a pulse and an open airway but inadequate shallow respirations. What support addresses the breathing deficit?
choices: Assist ventilation with oxygen
Give oxygen by mask alone and wait for depth to improve
Keep the patient warm but defer breathing support until arrival
Measure another pressure before assisting breaths
questions.explanation: Oxygen alone cannot correct inadequate air movement; assisted ventilation is needed.

questions.question: Which action directly addresses the risk of heat loss during shock care?
choices: Place blankets under and over the patient
Provide blankets only after hypothermia has been confirmed
Leave the patient exposed for the entire transport after the examination
Give a hot drink to replace warming measures
questions.explanation: The supplied care includes early heat conservation with blankets both beneath and above the patient.

questions.question: A patient with suspected shock is very thirsty and asks to drink. Which response fits the emergency-care plan?
choices: Explain that oral intake should be withheld pending physician evaluation while continuing supportive care
Allow drinking because thirst identifies a safe way to correct shock
Give fluids only if the pulse is rapid
Use drinking as a substitute for transport if pressure improves briefly
questions.explanation: The supplied shock plan withholds food and drink before physician evaluation.

questions.question: An alert patient with cardiogenic shock is severely short of breath and becomes more distressed when laid flat. What should guide positioning?
choices: Choose a supported position that eases breathing and reassess perfusion
Keep the patient flat because that is the usual general shock position
Elevate the legs while keeping the torso flat to maximize venous return
Use the upright position and stop monitoring pressure once breathing feels easier
questions.explanation: The general positioning approach must be adapted to the patient’s breathing needs. Positioning for comfort does not remove the need to monitor perfusion.

questions.question: A patient with suspected cardiogenic shock has chest pain and marked hypotension. Why should nitroglycerin not be given for the pain?
choices: It can further lower blood pressure through vascular relaxation
It increases clot formation in the coronary arteries
It constricts the coronary arteries while relaxing systemic veins
It increases venous return enough to worsen the hypotension
questions.explanation: The supplied cardiogenic-shock care excludes nitroglycerin in the hypotensive patient.

questions.question: Tension pneumothorax is suspected in a deteriorating trauma patient. ALS can meet the ambulance en route. What plan fits the EMT role?
choices: Begin transport with supportive care and arrange the ALS intercept
Provide supportive care on scene until ALS can perform decompression
Complete a detailed chest examination on scene before requesting the intercept
Use improvement in oxygen saturation to decide whether decompression assessment is still needed
questions.explanation: Decompression is the described ALS intervention; EMT support and rapid transport should proceed without avoidable delay.

questions.question: A patient has suspected septic shock with declining perfusion. Which care and communication plan fits?
choices: Begin supportive care and prompt transport with an early sepsis alert
Remain on scene until fever decreases before deciding transport priority
Base transport urgency on skin temperature after oxygen is applied
Complete the full infection history before beginning transport preparations
questions.explanation: Septic shock needs hospital management while EMT care supports vital functions and prepares the receiving team.

questions.question: A patient with suspected high spinal injury has poor perfusion and inadequate breathing. Which combination addresses the immediate needs?
choices: Protect the spine, maintain the airway, assist ventilation, conserve heat, and transport promptly
Elevate the legs before addressing shallow respirations or spinal protection
Treat warm skin as proof that circulation support is unnecessary
Provide spinal protection alone and omit airway assessment
questions.explanation: Neurogenic shock care includes respiratory support, spinal protection, heat conservation, and prompt transport.

questions.question: A patient develops airway swelling and hypotension after a likely allergen exposure. A bystander can explain the trigger. What should take priority?
choices: Begin indicated anaphylaxis treatment and airway support, gathering exposure history without delaying care
Complete the trigger interview before giving epinephrine or providing support
Wait for the reaction to become more severe before treating
Use reassurance alone because an exposure has been identified
questions.explanation: Life-threatening anaphylaxis requires immediate treatment and transport; exposure history helps but must not delay support.

questions.question: An older patient briefly fainted after an upsetting event. They are alert again but now cannot walk because of pain after the fall. What is the best plan?
choices: Assess for injury and other causes of syncope and arrange prompt evaluation
Use the emotional trigger and recovery of consciousness to classify the episode as uncomplicated fainting
Help the patient stand to see whether walking returns before assessing injuries
Focus on injury alone because recovery of consciousness excludes another medical cause
questions.explanation: The emotional trigger may be relevant, but neither it nor recovery excludes injury or a serious cause of syncope. Assess both the fall and the preceding event.

questions.question: During treatment and transport of a shock patient, what reassessment schedule fits the emergency-care plan?
choices: Record vital signs approximately every 5 minutes, and reassess immediately if the condition changes
Record vital signs every 15 minutes even if responsiveness declines
Wait until hospital arrival because movement makes trends unhelpful
Reassess only after a medication is given
questions.explanation: The supplied plan calls for roughly 5-minute vital-sign reassessment during shock care; new deterioration requires immediate assessment.

questions.question: A patient has normal-appearing air movement but severely impaired circulation. Why does the circulation problem still threaten cellular function?
choices: Cells require blood flow for oxygen and nutrient delivery and removal of wastes
Adequate ventilation alone guarantees adequate tissue perfusion
Only the lungs require circulation to remove carbon dioxide
Normal air movement makes glucose delivery independent of blood flow
questions.explanation: Perfusion requires more than ventilation: blood must deliver oxygen and nutrients and carry wastes away from cells.
tags: Shock: oxygen delivery, nutrients, and waste removal

questions.question: A patient with suspected cardiac tamponade has a blood pressure of 78/50 mm Hg, a weak pulse, and worsening responsiveness. The airway is patent and breathing is adequate. Transport can begin now, but ALS has not arrived. Which plan best addresses the immediate problem?
choices: Provide oxygen, begin rapid transport, and continue reassessment while arranging ALS support en route if available.
Provide oxygen, wait on scene for ALS, and reassess before deciding whether transport should begin.
Provide oxygen and use improvement in oxygen saturation to decide whether rapid transport remains necessary.
Provide oxygen, complete the full secondary examination on scene, and then arrange transport.
questions.explanation: Tamponade restricts cardiac filling and can cause obstructive shock. Oxygen and EMT support do not relieve that restriction. With worsening perfusion, begin prompt transport for treatment of the cause and arrange ALS assistance without postponing needed care.

questions.question: What does syncope mean?
choices: A brief loss of consciousness from inadequate blood flow to the brain
Persistent confusion while remaining conscious
A sustained seizure with repeated muscle contractions
A loss of blood volume from external hemorrhage
questions.explanation: Syncope means fainting or temporary loss of consciousness associated with reduced cerebral perfusion. It is not synonymous with confusion, seizure activity, or hemorrhage.

questions.question: What is pulse pressure?
choices: The difference between systolic and diastolic blood pressures
The pressure in arteries between heartbeats
The peak pressure produced during a heartbeat
The number of palpable beats in one minute
questions.explanation: Pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic pressure; diastolic pressure, systolic pressure, and pulse rate describe the other measures.

questions.question: An EMT team is performing CPR and using an AED while a paramedic prepares IV medication. Which distinction explains these roles?
choices: CPR and AED use provide basic support; IV medication is an advanced intervention
AED use is advanced care because it analyzes the rhythm, while IV medication is basic care
Both CPR and IV medication are basic care if neither uses an advanced airway
All three interventions are advanced care because the patient is in cardiac arrest
questions.explanation: BLS supports circulation and ventilation through basic interventions; IV medication is among the described ALS procedures. Provider arrival does not change an intervention’s category.

questions.question: A pulseless adult is on a safe scene. ALS is arriving in several minutes, and the AED is being brought to you. What should you do now?
choices: Begin high-quality CPR while the AED and ALS are brought into the resuscitation
Finish collecting the medication history before starting CPR
Delay compressions until a monitor identifies the exact rhythm
Wait to begin all care when the paramedic can establish an IV
questions.explanation: CPR must begin rapidly after arrest is recognized; it supports vital-organ perfusion while definitive interventions are arranged.

questions.question: An adult is unresponsive but has a definite carotid pulse and adequate normal breathing. Which conclusion is supported?
choices: The patient needs continued assessment and airway protection, but not chest compressions
Unresponsiveness alone establishes cardiac arrest and requires compressions
The pulse can be disregarded because the patient cannot answer questions
Adequate breathing proves that the patient needs no emergency evaluation
questions.explanation: An unresponsive patient may or may not need CPR. A definite pulse with adequate breathing calls for assessment and appropriate airway protection rather than compressions.

questions.question: Why does an adult still require definitive treatment even when CPR is producing effective chest rise and compressions?
choices: CPR temporarily supports circulation and ventilation while the cause of arrest and need for defibrillation are addressed
A complete cycle of effective CPR establishes that a shock is no longer needed
Chest rise during rescue breaths confirms that the heart is pumping again
Restoration of external blood flow corrects the underlying cause of every arrest
questions.explanation: CPR buys time by supporting circulation and ventilation; it does not by itself resolve every cause of arrest or replace definitive care.

questions.question: After cardiac arrest is recognized, which sequence places the initial interventions in the correct order?
choices: Compressions → airway → breaths
Airway → breaths → compressions
Breaths → compressions → airway
Airway → compressions → breaths
questions.explanation: The C-A-B sequence prioritizes circulation through compressions, then airway opening and breathing support.

questions.question: Bystanders activate EMS promptly, but no CPR is performed during the wait for the AED. Why is rapid activation alone insufficient?
choices: The chain also requires immediate circulation support while defibrillation and further care are arranged
Early EMS activation replaces bystander CPR when an AED will arrive soon
The AED supports blood flow during the time before pads are attached
Rapid advanced airway placement makes the interval without compressions unimportant
questions.explanation: The links work together. Immediate high-quality CPR supports perfusion during the interval before defibrillation and advanced care.
tags: Chain of survival as a system

questions.question: A patient regains a pulse and spontaneous breathing after resuscitation. Which plan continues the chain of survival?
choices: Provide ongoing assessment and appropriate oxygenation, monitoring, and advanced post-arrest care
Provide oxygen but defer reassessment until arrival because a pulse has returned
Continue the arrest compression cycle until hospital arrival despite confirmed adequate circulation
Focus only on the initial AED result instead of looking for recurrent deterioration
questions.explanation: Return of circulation begins a new phase of care; the patient still needs support, reassessment, and treatment of the underlying problem.

questions.question: You witness an adult collapse. Cardiac arrest is confirmed, your partner starts CPR, and an AED is beside you. What should you do?
choices: Apply the AED promptly while coordinating with ongoing CPR and its prompts
Complete two full minutes of CPR before beginning AED setup
Wait for ALS to decide whether the AED is needed
Attempt to identify a specific rhythm by palpating the pulse before applying pads
questions.explanation: For witnessed adult cardiac arrest, begin CPR and apply the AED as soon as it is available.
tags: AED integration in witnessed adult arrest

questions.question: An AED is needed for a 4-year-old in cardiac arrest. Pediatric equipment is available. Which setup is preferred?
choices: Pediatric pads with an energy-attenuating system
Pediatric pads attached to a system without energy attenuation
Adult pads with conductive surfaces trimmed to fit
Adult pads overlapping on the front of the chest
