questions.explanation: The pediatric equipment described combines pediatric-size pads with dose attenuation.

questions.question: Only adult-size AED pads are available for a small child in cardiac arrest. They would touch if both were placed on the front of the chest. Which adaptation fits?
choices: Leave the pads intact and use anterior-posterior placement
Trim the conductive portions until both pads fit on the front
Overlap the pads so their combined surface fits the chest
Withhold the available AED solely because pediatric pads are missing
questions.explanation: Adult pads may be used intact with one on the front and one on the back of a small patient.
tags: Adult AED pads on a small child

questions.question: An adult in cardiac arrest has an implanted device beneath the upper chest skin near the planned pad location. What adjustment is appropriate?
choices: Place the electrode at least 1 inch away from the implanted device
Place the electrode directly over the implant because it is not an external medication patch
Use the implant as the reason to continue CPR without any AED assessment
Keep the standard electrode location even when it is less than 1 inch from the implant
questions.explanation: Keep AED electrodes at least 1 inch (2.5 cm) from a pacemaker or implanted defibrillator.

questions.question: A pulseless adult has been removed from a pool. CPR is underway, the chest is wet, and an AED is ready. Which preparation best supports prompt pad application?
choices: Dry the chest at the pad sites and attach the pads promptly
Dry the patient’s entire torso and clothing before attaching pads
Begin the next full CPR cycle before preparing the wet chest
Attach the pads and press firmly against the wet skin
questions.explanation: Dry the skin for pad attachment without delaying for complete drying of the patient and clothing. Coordinate preparation with ongoing CPR.

questions.question: A medication patch occupies the intended AED pad site. What should you do before attaching that pad?
choices: Remove the patch and wipe away the remaining medication residue
Place the pad 1 inch from the patch without clearing residue from the intended site
Move the patch elsewhere on the chest and put the pad on the uncleared original site
Pause AED setup until the medication’s name and dose have been identified
questions.explanation: Remove a transdermal patch at the pad site and wipe the skin before attaching the electrode.
tags: Medication patch beneath an AED pad

questions.question: A cardiac-arrest patient lies in snow with a chest that can be dried. Which conclusion is appropriate?
choices: The AED can be used after drying the chest as much as possible
Any contact with snow makes AED use impossible
AED use must wait until the patient’s clothing is dry
The cold environment removes the need for chest preparation
questions.explanation: The special-situation guidance permits AED use in snow or a small puddle, with the chest dried as much as possible.
tags: AED in snow or a small puddle

questions.question: An adult is pulseless on a soft mattress. Which positioning change most directly improves compression effectiveness?
choices: Move the patient promptly to a firm, flat surface in the supine position
Add a pillow beneath the head and continue on the mattress
Roll the patient onto the side while continuing compressions
Elevate the legs while leaving the torso on the soft mattress
questions.explanation: Effective CPR requires the patient supine on a firm, flat surface; a soft support can absorb compression movement.

questions.question: An adult is found face down and cardiac arrest is recognized. Which positioning plan supports effective two-rescuer CPR?
choices: Turn the patient as a unit into a supine position on a firm, flat surface with room for both rescuers
Roll onto the side, using the recovery position as the compression position
Roll supine but retain a soft cushion under the chest to absorb compression force
Turn only the upper torso to expose the sternum while leaving the hips prone
questions.explanation: The patient should be supine on a firm, flat surface, with sufficient working room; a coordinated turn avoids twisting during positioning.

questions.question: During cardiac arrest, what is the immediate physiologic purpose of rhythmic chest compressions?
choices: To create blood flow to vital organs despite the lack of an effective spontaneous heartbeat
To move fresh oxygen into the lungs in place of rescue breaths
To establish an electrical rhythm that proves the need for a shock
To maintain a pulse that shows spontaneous circulation has already returned
questions.explanation: External compressions act as a pump to support circulation. They are not evidence that spontaneous circulation has returned.

questions.question: A rescuer achieves downward compression but keeps body weight on the chest between compressions. Why should this be corrected?
choices: Leaning impairs recoil and the heart’s refilling between compressions
Leaning improves refill by maintaining pressure over the sternum
Recoil is needed only during pauses for rescue breaths
Full recoil matters only after the patient regains a pulse
questions.explanation: The relaxation phase permits refilling; avoid leaning so the chest can return between compressions.

questions.question: Where should the pressure of adult chest compressions be directed?
choices: The lower half of the sternum
The xiphoid process where the sternum meets the upper abdomen
The lower left ribs to direct pressure toward the heart
The upper half of the sternum near the clavicles
questions.explanation: The lower half of the sternum is the described compression location; proper placement reduces injury and supports effective circulation.

questions.question: An unresponsive adult has evidence of a significant fall and possible spinal injury. Which initial manual airway maneuver fits this concern?
choices: Jaw thrust while avoiding unnecessary neck movement
Head tilt–chin lift with extension before considering spinal injury
Rotation of the head to the side to bring the tongue away from the airway
A head lift supported by padding beneath the occiput as the sole airway maneuver
questions.explanation: Use a jaw thrust when spinal injury is suspected to open the airway while limiting neck movement.
tags: Airway opening with suspected spinal injury

questions.question: Which manual maneuver is appropriate to open the airway of an unresponsive adult when spinal injury is not suspected?
choices: Head tilt–chin lift
Jaw pressure alone without moving the mandible forward or lifting the chin
Head tilt with pressure on the soft tissue beneath the chin
Chin-to-chest flexion followed by opening the mouth
questions.explanation: Head tilt–chin lift is the described basic airway-opening maneuver when spinal injury is not suspected.

questions.question: An unresponsive adult has a definite pulse, breathes adequately, and has no suspected spine, hip, or pelvic injury. Which position supports airway protection?
choices: The recovery position on the side
Supine with a head pillow as a substitute for airway protection
Seated upright with the chin allowed to rest against the chest
Supine with compression cycles because the patient remains unresponsive
questions.explanation: The recovery position is appropriate for an unresponsive patient who breathes adequately and has no relevant injury concern. It permits drainage and helps protect the airway.

questions.question: Which finding prevents routine use of the recovery position for an unresponsive patient who is breathing?
choices: Suspected pelvic injury following a fall
A need to let secretions drain from the mouth
A definite pulse during the primary assessment
Absence of any trauma history or injury signs
questions.explanation: Suspected spine, hip, or pelvic injury is a contraindication to routine recovery positioning.

questions.question: Which description fits effective artificial ventilation during adult CPR?
choices: About 1 second per breath, just enough for visible chest rise
About 1 second per breath, emptying the entire bag
A rapid breath of less than half a second, stopping at chest rise
A sustained breath until abdominal movement is visible
questions.explanation: Use slow, deliberate breaths of about 1 second, assessing chest rise rather than forcing excessive volume or speed.

questions.question: During bag-mask ventilation, the abdomen becomes distended after rapid, forceful breaths. What correction addresses the likely cause?
choices: Reopen the airway as needed and use slower controlled breaths just sufficient for chest rise
Force the next breaths faster to overcome presumed airway resistance
Maintain the same force but increase the rate to compensate for poor air entry
Keep the rapid breath pattern and treat suction readiness as sufficient prevention
questions.explanation: A well-opened airway and controlled breaths reduce gastric inflation; ventilation should produce chest rise, not stomach distention.

questions.question: An apneic adult has a confirmed complete laryngectomy and a permanent neck stoma without a tube. How should a pocket mask or bag-mask device be applied?
choices: Seal the device directly over the stoma
Use a standard face seal and cover the stoma to direct air through the mouth
Use a standard face seal while leaving the stoma open without a seal
Place the mask beside the stoma and rely on high oxygen flow instead of a sealed breath
questions.explanation: For the described stoma airway, place the ventilation device directly over the opening.

questions.question: An apneic adult is receiving artificial ventilation and develops gastric distention. Which equipment should be immediately available for a likely complication?
choices: A suction unit for vomited material
An oxygen cylinder, with airway-clearance equipment deferred until vomiting occurs
A second bag-mask device to deliver stronger breaths if the stomach remains distended
An airway adjunct as a substitute for equipment to remove vomited material
questions.explanation: Gastric distention can lead to vomiting; suction should be ready to clear material from the airway.

questions.question: A lone rescuer is providing adult CPR without an advanced airway. Which compression-to-ventilation cycle should be repeated?
choices: 30 compressions followed by 2 breaths
15 compressions followed by 2 breaths
30 compressions followed by 1 breath
15 compressions followed by 1 breath
questions.explanation: Single-rescuer adult CPR uses a 30:2 compression-to-ventilation ratio.

questions.question: An adult is unresponsive and has no normal breathing. At 10 seconds of simultaneous assessment, you still cannot confidently detect a carotid pulse. What should you do?
choices: Begin CPR rather than prolonging the pulse search
Spend another 30 seconds finding a different pulse before deciding
Treat the uncertain pulse as definite circulation and give breaths alone
Wait for the AED to announce whether a pulse is present
questions.explanation: Limit simultaneous breathing and pulse assessment to 10 seconds; if no normal breathing and no confident pulse are identified, begin CPR.

questions.question: A second EMT joins adult CPR without an advanced airway. Which adjustment is appropriate?
choices: Divide compression and ventilation roles while retaining the adult 30:2 cycle
Change to 15:2 because the compression-to-breath ratio changes whenever any second rescuer joins
Keep one provider performing the entire cycle while the second waits for ALS
Alternate compressors after every set of 30 without coordinating breath delivery
questions.explanation: Two providers can share tasks and reduce fatigue, but the adult compression-to-ventilation cycle remains 30:2.

questions.question: During two-rescuer CPR, the compressor is approaching 2 minutes of work. Which plan best maintains compression quality?
choices: Prepare a coordinated switch with the shortest practical interruption
Keep the same compressor until fatigue visibly reduces depth
Pause now to exchange roles and review the patient’s history
Switch after every set of 30 compressions to prevent any fatigue
questions.explanation: A planned brief switch about every 2 minutes limits fatigue while minimizing lost compression time.

questions.question: In a 10-minute resuscitation interval, compressions were performed for 8.5 minutes. What is the compression fraction, and does it exceed the stated target of 80%?
choices: 85%; yes
80%; it only equals the target
questions.explanation: Compression fraction is compression time divided by the total interval: 8.5 ÷ 10 = 85%, which is greater than 80%.

questions.question: How does active compression-decompression differ from conventional manual compression and release?
choices: It actively pulls the chest upward after compression, which may improve venous return
It maintains continuous downward pressure without allowing upward chest movement
It uses a band to distribute only the downward compression around the chest
It limits air entry during recoil without actively lifting the chest
questions.explanation: The device actively lifts the chest toward its neutral position or beyond after compression, potentially increasing blood return.

questions.question: Which device description is correctly matched?
choices: A mechanical piston device allows compression depth and rate to be configured
An impedance threshold device actively pulls the chest upward after each compression
A load-distributing band limits air entry through the airway during recoil
An active compression-decompression device generates compression through a circumferential band
questions.explanation: A mechanical piston device permits configuration of compression depth and rate. The other devices have different circulation-related mechanisms.

questions.question: A team has access to mechanical CPR equipment. Which conclusion about its role is supported?
choices: It can assist circulation in selected circumstances, while manual chest compressions remain the standard of care
They should replace manual CPR whenever available, regardless of circumstances
Their compression action makes periodic assessment of technique unnecessary
They should be used before any initial manual compressions, even if setup takes several minutes
questions.explanation: Mechanical devices can assist the team, but their availability does not replace the role of manual CPR or the rest of resuscitation.

questions.question: A child has progressive respiratory failure that is not corrected. Which sequence explains how cardiac arrest may follow?
choices: Respiratory failure leads to hypoxia and cardiac ischemia, then arrest
Primary cardiac ischemia must occur first, followed by hypoxia from stopped breathing
Loss of breathing is generally a consequence of pediatric cardiac arrest rather than a precursor
Hypoxia affects the brain but cannot impair the heart before arrest
questions.explanation: Pediatric arrest often follows respiratory failure, with hypoxia and ischemia impairing the heart.

questions.question: A child is rescued after submersion and has inadequate breathing but a definite pulse of 100/min. Why is prompt airway and ventilation support especially important?
choices: Correcting hypoxia may prevent progression from respiratory failure to cardiac arrest
Submersion causes only a primary electrical heart problem, so ventilation has no role
A pulse excludes a serious threat from the child’s respiratory problem
Chest compressions are required solely because the child was underwater
questions.explanation: Submersion is among the supplied causes of pediatric respiratory compromise; correcting breathing can prevent hypoxic cardiac arrest.

questions.question: Which site is used for the initial pulse check in an unresponsive infant?
choices: The brachial artery on the inside of the upper arm
The carotid artery in the neck
The radial artery at the wrist
The dorsalis pedis artery on the foot
questions.explanation: Palpate the brachial artery in an infant while assessing breathing.

questions.question: One EMT is performing CPR on a pulseless child with 30 compressions and 2 breaths. No advanced airway is in place. A second EMT arrives to share CPR. Which cycle should the two rescuers use?
choices: 15 compressions and 2 breaths
Continue 30 compressions and 2 breaths because the adult two-rescuer ratio also stays 30:2
15 compressions and 1 breath
30 compressions and 1 breath
questions.explanation: Pediatric CPR changes from 30:2 with one rescuer to 15:2 with two rescuers.

questions.question: An apneic child has an open airway and a definite pulse of 100/min. Which breathing support is indicated?
choices: One breath every 2–3 seconds
One breath every 6 seconds
Two breaths after every 30 compressions
Two breaths after every 15 compressions
questions.explanation: For pediatric apnea with a pulse, provide rescue breathing every 2 to 3 seconds, using only enough volume to produce chest rise.

questions.question: A small child’s large occiput flexes the head forward when the child lies flat, partly blocking the airway. Where should padding be placed to improve alignment?
choices: Under the upper chest and shoulders
Under the occiput to increase the head’s height
Under the neck alone while the upper chest stays flat
Beneath the pelvis to tilt the whole body toward the head
questions.explanation: Padding beneath the upper chest and shoulders counters the forward flexion caused by the relatively large occiput.

questions.question: During CPR on a child between 1 year and puberty, how should the rescuer choose between one-hand and two-hand chest compressions?
choices: Use the method appropriate to the child’s size and the rescuer’s ability to provide effective compressions
Use one hand until puberty even if it cannot produce effective compressions
Use two fingers whenever the patient is smaller than an adult
Use two stacked hands in every child regardless of body size
questions.explanation: A child may need one or both hands for effective compression depending on body size and rescuer capability.

questions.question: Which pulseless, apneic patient has an additional finding supporting a decision not to begin CPR?
choices: A patient with dependent lividity and rigor mortis
A patient who collapsed moments ago and is unresponsive
A patient with gasping and no detectable pulse after a witnessed collapse
A patient whose skin is pale and cool after a brief arrest
questions.explanation: Irreversible signs such as dependent lividity and rigor mortis support withholding resuscitation; absence of pulse and breathing alone describes potentially treatable arrest.

questions.question: An apneic, pulseless adult has no obvious irreversible signs of death. A relative believes a DNR exists but cannot produce or verify it. What is the appropriate initial approach?
choices: Begin CPR while the team seeks clarification of any valid directive
Continue searching for paperwork before starting resuscitation
Withhold CPR based only on the relative’s uncertain recollection
Assume every older patient has declined resuscitation
questions.explanation: When a valid directive cannot be confirmed, the supplied approach is to begin resuscitation and clarify the situation without delaying care.

questions.question: A person lies motionless beside an active downed power line. The electrical hazard has not been controlled. What governs the immediate decision to approach for CPR?
choices: Do not enter the hazard; arrange scene safety before providing CPR
Make a rapid approach to check the pulse, then decide whether the hazard justifies withdrawal
Begin CPR without moving the patient while waiting for the line to be shut off
Assume lack of visible sparks means the line is no longer dangerous
questions.explanation: An unsafe scene is a reason not to begin CPR there; rescuers must arrange safe access before providing care.

questions.question: A paramedic arrives during CPR but has not yet assumed care or arranged compressor coverage. What does the arrival mean for the EMT’s compressions?
choices: Continue until care is actually transferred with uninterrupted coverage
Stop immediately because arrival alone completes the transfer
Stop while the paramedic reviews the history, even without replacement compressions
Leave the patient because any higher-level provider on scene ends EMT responsibility
questions.explanation: The STOP transfer criterion requires an actual handoff to an equally or more highly trained provider, not mere arrival.

questions.question: A lone rescuer feels tired but can still deliver effective CPR. Another trained rescuer is about to take over. Which decision fits the stopping criteria?
choices: Continue and coordinate the replacement rather than stopping solely because of fatigue
Stop for a brief rest now, before the replacement has assumed compressions
Continue until hospital arrival and decline a qualified replacement
Treat the two-minute rotation point as an automatic end to the entire CPR attempt
questions.explanation: Out of strength means physically unable to continue, not merely tired; coordinate a replacement while maintaining care.

questions.question: During an appropriate reassessment, an adult has a definite pulse and begins breathing adequately. Which change is appropriate?
choices: Stop chest compressions and provide ongoing supportive post-arrest care
Continue compressions until a fixed number of cycles has been completed
Stop all care and assessment because breathing has returned
Resume compressions after every spontaneous breath despite the pulse
questions.explanation: Return of a pulse and adequate breathing meets the supplied criterion for stopping CPR, while continued supportive care is still required.
tags: Confirmed return of pulse and breathing

questions.question: An adult begins coughing during a meal but can still speak and move air with a strong cough. What response fits these findings?
choices: Encourage coughing and observe closely for worsening obstruction
Begin thrusts immediately solely because food was being eaten
Perform a blind finger sweep before the next cough
Treat speaking as proof that no further observation is needed
questions.explanation: An effective cough and air movement indicate mild obstruction; avoid interfering while monitoring for deterioration.

questions.question: Which change most strongly indicates that an initially mild airway obstruction has become severe?
choices: The patient can no longer speak or cough effectively and is making unsuccessful breathing efforts
The patient coughs forcefully while speaking in full sentences
The patient becomes anxious but still moves air with a strong cough
The patient reports throat discomfort while breathing normally
questions.explanation: Loss of effective speech, cough, and air movement indicates severe obstruction and the need for intervention.

questions.question: A responsive infant suddenly cannot cry or cough effectively and has severe airway obstruction. Which maneuver sequence is appropriate?
choices: Five back slaps followed by five chest thrusts, repeated as needed
Five back slaps followed by five abdominal thrusts
Five chest thrusts followed by five abdominal thrusts
Repeated chest compressions at the CPR rate despite continued responsiveness
questions.explanation: For a responsive infant with severe obstruction, alternate five back slaps and five chest thrusts; do not use abdominal thrusts.

questions.question: How should a responsive choking infant be supported for back slaps?
choices: Face down along the forearm, supporting the jaw and head, with the head lower than the chest
Face down on the forearm with the head kept higher than the chest
Face down while supporting the trunk but allowing the head to hang unsupported
Face up with supported head and neck while delivering back slaps
questions.explanation: Support the infant’s jaw and head on the forearm, with the head below the chest, while delivering back slaps.

questions.question: A responsive patient in advanced pregnancy has severe choking. When obstruction-clearing thrusts are needed, which type replaces abdominal thrusts?
choices: Chest thrusts
Lower-force abdominal thrusts
Chest compressions in the supine position
A blind finger sweep
questions.explanation: Advanced pregnancy calls for chest rather than abdominal thrusts. This item tests the thrust modification, not the full choking sequence, which differs between the supplied older material and 2025 guidance.

questions.question: An adult being treated for severe choking suddenly becomes unresponsive. What immediate change in approach is indicated?
choices: Lower the patient to the ground and begin chest compressions
Continue standing abdominal thrusts while supporting the unconscious patient
Delay further care until a finger sweep has located an object
Leave the patient sitting upright and wait for spontaneous coughing
questions.explanation: When a choking patient becomes unresponsive, lower the patient and begin compressions, which can support circulation and help dislodge the object.

questions.question: After compressions for an unresponsive choking patient, you open the airway and inspect the mouth. Which finding permits finger removal?
choices: An object is clearly visible and easily grasped
No object is visible, but the patient had been eating
A suspected object can only be sought by sweeping blindly
The mouth is empty, but the chest failed to rise earlier
questions.explanation: Remove an object only when it is visible and retrievable; do not perform a blind finger sweep.

questions.question: Several relatives are asking questions during a resuscitation, and sufficient personnel are available. Which communication plan best supports both care and the family?
choices: Assign a team member who is not performing hands-on CPR to give clear, consistent updates
Let the provider performing compressions answer relatives between individual compressions
Ask each clinician to give an independent update about their intervention without a designated communicator
Have the airway provider leave ventilation duties to give a detailed explanation while CPR continues
questions.explanation: A designated communicator can provide honest, compassionate updates while the clinical team maintains resuscitation.

questions.question: After unsuccessful resuscitation, which approach best supports the first conversation with the family?
choices: Use a quiet private setting, clear words, and compassionate acknowledgment of the loss
Begin with a detailed technical account so the family can evaluate the care
Use indirect expressions and avoid saying that the patient died
Wait until the family stops crying before explaining the outcome
questions.explanation: The first conversation should be understandable, honest, and compassionate in a suitable setting. Technical details can follow according to the family’s needs.

questions.question: A currently certified EMT has not practiced CPR for a long period. Which training plan best addresses the risk of skill deterioration?
choices: Frequent manikin-based practice, with video or computer refreshers that include hands-on work
No practice until certification expires because certification guarantees lasting technique
Video viewing alone as a complete replacement for motor-skill practice
Memorizing the chain of survival without performing compressions or ventilation
questions.explanation: CPR skills deteriorate; frequent hands-on practice maintains technique. Self-directed modules can help when they include practice.

questions.question: What is the principal role of community compression-only CPR and AED education?
choices: Allow early circulation support and AED use before EMS arrives
Teach the full professional EMT treatment sequence to every bystander
Limit bystander action to recognition and EMS activation
Make public AED use dependent on arrival of a trained EMS crew
questions.explanation: Public education strengthens early links of the chain by preparing bystanders to act before professional help arrives.

questions.question: An adult with suspected opioid overdose is apneic and pulseless. CPR and the AED are ready, and naloxone is available under local authorization. What takes priority?
choices: Start CPR and use the AED as indicated while medication is integrated without delaying resuscitation
Give naloxone first and wait for its effect before starting compressions
Provide naloxone instead of ventilation because it always restores breathing immediately
Withhold the AED because an overdose cannot produce a shockable rhythm
questions.explanation: Confirmed cardiac arrest needs immediate circulation and ventilation support and defibrillation when indicated; naloxone does not replace them.

questions.question: A pregnant adult is in cardiac arrest, with the uterine fundus at the level of the umbilicus. The team can provide CPR and an additional positioning maneuver. Which plan fits?
choices: Continue high-quality CPR and manually displace the uterus to the left
Place the patient fully on her left side while using that position for the entire compression attempt
Use supine CPR without displacement because uterine pressure matters only in non-arrest patients
Pause compressions until left uterine displacement alone restores a pulse
questions.explanation: Continue CPR with manual left uterine displacement when the fundus is at or above the umbilicus, reducing pressure on major vessels and improving return of blood.

questions.question: Which description distinguishes an impedance threshold device from a mechanical chest compressor?
choices: It limits air entry during chest recoil rather than supplying compression force
It actively pulls the chest upward after compressions
It creates compression through a circumferential chest band
It drives a piston whose rate and depth can be configured
questions.explanation: An ITD restricts air entry during recoil; it does not generate the compression force. The outline does not recommend it for conventional CPR.

questions.question: An EMT’s shoulders are behind the hands and elbows bend with each adult chest compression. Which correction most directly improves the compression mechanics?
choices: Position the shoulders directly over the hands and keep the elbows straight
Keep the shoulders behind the hands and push chiefly by repeatedly bending the elbows
Maintain the bent elbows and move the hands from the sternum to the left ribs
Lean continuously on the sternum to compensate for the inefficient downward movement
questions.explanation: Shoulders above the hands and straight elbows direct upper-body force straight down through the correct hand position.

questions.question: After a failed resuscitation, a grieving relative is crying while a young child waits nearby without support. What approach is most appropriate?
choices: Remain available without hovering, acknowledge the child, and ask whether a trusted support person can come
Focus entirely on the adult and assume the child does not understand enough to need support
Stay continuously beside the adult and discourage contact with other support people
Require both the adult and child to discuss their emotions immediately
questions.explanation: Grief reactions vary. Offer space and support, include children appropriately, and help connect the family with trusted people.

questions.question: CPR is ongoing, there is no return of circulation, and an authorized physician directs the team to discontinue under the applicable process. Which STOP criterion applies?
choices: P: physician directs discontinuation
S: the patient starts breathing and has a pulse
T: transfer to a provider of equal or higher training
O: the team is physically unable to continue
questions.explanation: Physician direction is the P criterion. It differs from return of circulation, transfer, and physical inability to continue.

questions.question: What is basic life support (BLS)?
choices: Noninvasive lifesaving care for threats such as airway obstruction and respiratory or cardiac arrest
Care defined by invasive advanced-airway placement and medication administration
Chest compressions alone in every patient needing emergency care
Hospital care provided only after spontaneous circulation returns
questions.explanation: BLS is rapid noninvasive emergency care addressing airway, breathing, and circulation threats; it includes more than compressions alone.

questions.question: What is cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR)?
choices: Chest compressions and artificial ventilation to support a patient without an effective pulse or normal breathing
Assisted ventilation alone for a patient with a definite pulse
Supplemental oxygen alone for a patient breathing adequately
Electrical analysis and shock delivery without circulation or ventilation support
questions.explanation: CPR provides circulation and ventilation support in cardiac arrest. Rescue breathing, oxygen therapy, and AED use alone do not describe the complete intervention.

questions.question: Which pair of chest-compression techniques is recommended for infant CPR under 2025 AHA guidance?
choices: Two fingers or two stacked hands
Two-thumb encircling hands or the heel of one hand
Two fingers or two-thumb encircling hands
Heel of one hand or two stacked hands
questions.explanation: Infant CPR uses the two-thumb encircling-hands technique or the heel of one hand. These options are not restricted to a particular number of rescuers.

questions.question: You are performing CPR on a 7-month-old infant but cannot physically encircle the chest with your hands. Which compression technique should you use under 2025 AHA guidance?
choices: Two fingers over the lower half of the sternum
Two stacked hands over the lower half of the sternum
Two thumbs without encircling or supporting the chest
The heel of one hand over the lower half of the sternum
questions.explanation: When the rescuer cannot physically encircle the infant’s chest, use the heel of one hand. Maintain the recommended infant compression depth and allow full recoil.
tags: Infant compressions when chest cannot be encircled

questions.question: A responsive adult cannot speak or cough effectively after food becomes lodged in the airway. The patient is not pregnant, and you can encircle the abdomen. After a bystander activates EMS, which sequence should you use under 2025 AHA guidance?
choices: Five back blows followed by five abdominal thrusts
Five back blows followed by five chest thrusts
Repeated abdominal thrusts without back blows
Five abdominal thrusts followed by five back blows
questions.explanation: For a responsive adult with severe foreign-body airway obstruction, begin with five back blows, then five abdominal thrusts if the obstruction persists. Repeat while needed until the object is expelled or the patient becomes unresponsive.

questions.question: A responsive 4-year-old cannot speak or cough effectively after choking on food. A partner has activated EMS. Which sequence is recommended under 2025 AHA pediatric BLS guidance?
choices: Five back blows followed by five chest thrusts
Repeated abdominal thrusts without back blows
Five back blows followed by five abdominal thrusts
Five abdominal thrusts followed by five back blows
questions.explanation: For a responsive child with severe foreign-body airway obstruction, give five back blows, then five abdominal thrusts if the obstruction persists. Repeat while needed until the object is expelled or the child becomes unresponsive. The infant sequence uses chest thrusts instead.

The _____ is a step within the patient assessment process that identifies and initiates treatment of immediate and potential life threats.

_____ is the way in which a patient responds to external stimuli, including verbal stimuli (sound), tactile stimuli (touch), and painful stimuli.

_____ are coarse, low-pitched breath sounds heard in patients with chronic mucus in the upper airways.

The _____ is the tough, fibrous, white portion of the eye that protects the more delicate inner structures.

_____ are respirations characterized by little movement of the chest wall (reduced tidal volume) or poor chest excursion.

A _____ is an objective finding that can be seen, heard, felt, smelled or measured.

_____ is breathing that occurs without assistance.

_____ in the context of airway, is the introduction of vomitus or other foreign material into the lungs.

A _____ is a protective item, such as a pocket mask with a valve, that limits exposure to a patient’s body fluids.

A _____ is an opening through the skin and into an organ or other structure; for example, in the neck, it connects the trachea directly to the skin.

_____ are medications that enter the body through the digestive system.

A _____ is a semiliquid substance that is administered orally in capsule form or through plastic tubes.
The _____ is the original chemical name of a medication (in contrast with one of its proprietary or trade names); the name is not capitalized.
The _____ are the therapeutic uses for a specific medication.
An _____ is an injection into the bone; a medication delivery route.
A _____ is a substance that is used to treat or prevent disease or relieve pain.
A _____ is the inappropriate use of a medication that could lead to patient harm.
A _____ is a miniature spray canister through which droplets or particles of medication may be inhaled through the mouth and into the lungs.
A _____ is a device that is used to change a liquid medication into a spray and push it into a nostril.
_____ is a medication that increases cardiac perfusion by causing blood vessels to dilate; EMTs may be allowed to assist the patient to self-administer the medication.
_____ is a simple sugar that is readily absorbed by the bloodstream; it is carried on the EMS unit.
_____ is a gas that all cells need for metabolism; the heart and brain, especially, cannot function without it.

Per os (PO) means _____

_____ is the study of the properties and effects of medications.
_____ is the use of multiple medications on a regular basis.

A _____ is a liquid mixture that cannot be separated by filtering or allowing the mixture to stand.
A _____ is an injection into the fatty tissue between the skin and muscle; a medication delivery route.
A _____ is a mixture of ground particles that are distributed evenly throughout a liquid but do not dissolve.
The _____ is the desired or intended effect a medication is expected to have on the body.
The _____ is the brand name that a manufacturer gives a medication; the name is capitalized.

_____ is the loss of water from the tissues of the body.

_____ is the presence of abnormally large amounts of fluid between cells in body tissues, causing swelling of the affected area.

_____ is the flow of blood through body tissues and vessels.
A _____ is a collection of fluid between the pericardial sac and the myocardium.
_____ is the precontraction pressure in the heart as the volume of blood builds up.
_____ is shock caused by a sudden, temporary reduction in blood supply to the brain that causes fainting (syncope).
The _____ is the difference between the systolic and diastolic pressures.
_____ is the process of developing a sensitivity to a substance that initially caused no allergic reaction.
_____ is shock caused by severe infection, usually a bacterial infection.

A _____ is a device that depresses the sternum via a compressed gas-powered or electric-powered plunger mounted on a backboard.
A _____ is the return of a pulse and effective blood flow to the body in a patient who previously was in cardiac arrest.
_____ is the stiffening of the body muscles; a definitive sign of death.
_____ is blood settling to the lowest point of the body; causing discoloration of the skin; a definitive sign of death.

_____ is an inflammation of the meningeal coverings of the brain and spinal cord; can be highly contagious.

questions.answer: Oversight of the patient-care aspects of an EMS system by the Medical Director. Direction can be either off-line or on-line.

questions.question: Who is the Medical Director?
questions.answer: A physician who assumes ultimate responsibility for the patient-care aspects of the EMS system.

questions.question: Define the 911 system.
questions.answer: A system for telephone access to report emergencies. A dispatcher takes the information and alerts EMS or the fire or police department as needed. Enhanced 911 also identifies the caller’s phone number and location automatically.

questions.question: What is off-line medical direction?
questions.answer: Standing orders issued by the Medical Director that allow EMTs to give certain medications or perform certain procedures without speaking to the Medical Director or another physician.

questions.question: What is on-line medical direction?
questions.answer: Orders from the on-duty physician given directly to an EMT in the field by radio or telephone.

questions.question: Define patient outcomes.
What does peer-reviewed mean?
questions.answer: Submitted to a professional journal and reviewed by several of the researcher’s peers.

questions.question: Define protocols.
questions.answer: Lists of steps, such as assessments and interventions, to be taken in different situations. Protocols are developed by the Medical Director of an EMS system.

questions.question: What is quality improvement?
questions.answer: A process of continual self-review with the purpose of identifying and correcting aspects of the system that require improvement.

questions.question: What are standing orders?
questions.answer: Policies or protocols issued by a Medical Director that authorize EMTs and others to perform particular skills in certain situations.

questions.question: What are the primary components of the Emergency Medical Services system?
questions.answer: 911 or another emergency access system, dispatchers, EMTs, the hospital emergency department, physicians, nurses, physician’s assistants, and other health professionals.

questions.question: What are some of the special designations that hospitals may have?
questions.answer: Specialty centers such as trauma centers, burn centers, pediatric centers, cardiac centers, stroke centers, and more. [Specify regional specialty centers if needed]

questions.question: What are the four national levels of EMS training and certification?
questions.answer: Emergency Medical Responder (EMR), Emergency Medical Technician (EMT), Advanced EMT (AEMT), and Paramedic.

questions.question: What are the roles and responsibilities of the EMT?
questions.answer: Safety, patient assessment and care, lifting, moving, and transporting patients, transfer of care, and patient advocacy.

questions.question: What is the definition of the term quality improvement?
questions.answer: A process of continual self-review with the purpose of identifying and correcting aspects of the system that require improvement.

questions.question: What is the difference between on-line and off-line medical direction?
questions.answer: On-line medical direction involves direct orders from an on-duty physician via radio or telephone, while off-line medical direction involves standing orders and protocols issued by the Medical Director.

questions.question: abandonment
questions.answer: leaving a patient after care has been initiated and before the patient has been transferred to someone with equal or greater medical training.

questions.question: advance directive
questions.answer: a DNR order; instructions written in advance of an event.

questions.question: assault
questions.answer: placing a person in fear of bodily harm.

questions.question: battery
questions.answer: causing bodily harm to or restraining a person.

questions.question: confidentiality
questions.answer: the obligation not to reveal information obtained about a patient except to other health care professionals involved in the patient’s care or under subpoena or in a court of law or when the patient has signed a release of confidentiality.

questions.question: consent
questions.answer: permission from the patient for care or other action by the EMT.

questions.question: crime scene
questions.answer: the location where a crime has been committed or any place that evidence relating to a crime may be found.

questions.question: do not resuscitate (DNR) order
questions.answer: a legal document, usually signed by both patient and physician, which states that the patient has a terminal illness and does not wish to prolong life through resuscitative efforts.

questions.question: duty to act
questions.answer: an obligation to provide care to a patient.

questions.question: ethical
questions.answer: regarding a social system or social or professional expectations for applying principles of right and wrong.

questions.question: expressed consent
questions.answer: consent given by adults who are of legal age and mentally competent to make a rational decision with regard to their medical well-being.

questions.question: Good Samaritan laws
questions.answer: a series of laws, varying by state, designed to provide limited legal protection for citizens and some health care personnel when they are administering emergency care.

questions.question: implied consent
questions.answer: the consent it is presumed a patient or patient’s parent or guardian would give if they could, such as for an unconscious patient or a child whose parents cannot be contacted when care is needed.

questions.question: in loco parentis
questions.answer: literally ‘in place of a parent,’ indicating a person who may give consent for care of a child when the parents are not present or able to give consent.

questions.question: liability
negligence
questions.answer: a finding that there was failure to act properly in a situation in which there was a duty to act, that needed care as would reasonably be expected of the EMT was not provided, and that harm was caused to the patient as a result.

questions.question: organ donor
questions.answer: a person who has completed a legal document that allows for donation of organs and tissues in the event of death.

questions.question: Physician’s Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment (POLST)
questions.answer: physician orders that state not only the patient’s wishes regarding resuscitation attempts but also the patient’s wishes regarding artificial feeding, antibiotics, and other life-sustaining care if the person is unable to state the person’s desires later.

questions.question: res ipsa loquitur
questions.answer: a Latin term meaning ‘the thing speaks for itself.’

questions.question: safe haven law
questions.answer: a law that permits a person to drop off an infant or child at a police, fire, or EMS station or to deliver the infant or child to any available public safety personnel. The intent of the law is to protect children who may otherwise be abandoned or harmed.

questions.question: scope of practice
questions.answer: a set of regulations and ethical considerations that define the scope, or extent and limits, of the EMT’s job.

questions.question: slander
standard of care
questions.answer: for an EMT providing care for a specific patient in a specific situation, the care that would be expected to be provided by an EMT with similar training when caring for a patient in a similar situation.

questions.question: Explain the difference between expressed and implied consent.
questions.answer: Expressed consent is given by adults who are of legal age and mentally competent to make a rational decision with regard to their medical well-being, while implied consent is assumed when a patient is unconscious or when a parent cannot be contacted for a child's care.

questions.question: What are the components required to prove negligence?
questions.answer: 1. Duty to act 2. Breach of duty 3. Causation

questions.question: What is your first priority at a crime scene: evidence preservation or patient care? Why?
questions.answer: Patient care is the first priority because the primary duty of an EMT is to ensure the well-being and survival of the patient.

questions.question: You bring a patient to the hospital and the nurse tells you, “Put the patient in bed 5; I’ll be right there.” The nurse doesn’t come over, and you leave. Is this abandonment? Why or why not?
questions.answer: Yes, this is abandonment because you left the patient without transferring care to someone with equal or higher training.

questions.question: You have a patient who weighs 400 pounds. You want other EMTs at your squad to know this so they can be prepared. Can you leave a copy of your patient care report on the bulletin board at the station to notify the others?
questions.answer: No, this would violate patient confidentiality. You can inform other EMTs verbally about the patient's weight but should not share the patient care report.

questions.question: What roles and responsibilities of an EMT are important in preventing lawsuits?
questions.answer: Following scope of practice, adhering to the standard of care, obtaining proper consent, documenting all actions thoroughly, maintaining patient confidentiality, and providing appropriate and timely care.

questions.question: What can I do when lifting and moving patients to help prevent injury to patients and the lawsuits that may result?
questions.answer: Use proper lifting techniques, ensure the use of appropriate equipment, work with a team to lift heavy patients, and follow protocols to avoid causing harm.

questions.question: contamination
questions.answer: the introduction of dangerous chemicals, disease, or infectious materials.

questions.question: critical incident stress management (CISM)
questions.answer: a comprehensive system that includes education and resources to both prevent stress and deal with stress appropriately when it occurs.

questions.question: decontamination
questions.answer: the removal or cleansing of dangerous chemicals and other dangerous or infectious materials.

questions.question: hazardous material incident
questions.answer: the release of a harmful substance into the environment.

questions.question: multiple-casualty incident (MCI)
pathogens
questions.answer: the organisms that cause infection, such as viruses and bacteria.

questions.question: personal protective equipment (PPE)
questions.answer: equipment that protects the EMS worker from infection and/or exposure to the dangers of rescue operations.

questions.question: resilience
questions.answer: toughness; an ability to recover quickly from difficult situations.

questions.question: Standard Precautions
questions.answer: a strict form of infection control that is based on the assumption that all blood and other body fluids are infectious; also known as body substance isolation (BSI).

questions.question: stress
questions.answer: a state of physical and/or psychological arousal to a stimulus.

questions.question: Differentiate between acute stress, delayed stress, and cumulative stress. Give an example of each.
questions.answer: Acute stress occurs immediately after a traumatic event (e.g., car accident); delayed stress manifests after some time (e.g., PTSD from a past event); cumulative stress builds up over time due to ongoing stressors (e.g., burnout from constant emergency calls).

questions.question: Name some of the causes of stress for an EMT and explain some ways the EMT can alleviate job-related stress.
questions.answer: Causes: long hours, traumatic calls, high responsibility. Alleviation: exercise, peer support, hobbies, professional counseling.

questions.question: What are the stages a person may express when confronted with death and dying?  Why is it important for the EMT to understand these reactions?  How should the EMT deal with these emotions?
questions.answer: Stages: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance. Understanding helps EMTs provide compassionate care.  EMTs should remain supportive, listen, and provide comfort.

questions.question: List the types of personal protective equipment used in Standard Precautions. Identify a condition or patient with which each one should be used.
questions.answer: Gloves: any patient contact Goggles/Face shield: risk of splashes (e.g., vomiting) Gown: significant body fluid exposure (e.g., severe bleeding) Mask: respiratory infections (e.g., TB)

questions.question: Body substance isolation is an important concept to protect you from disease. Linking with the roles and responsibilities of an EMT in Introduction to Emergency Medical Services and the material covered in this chapter, list the types of Standard Precautions you would use in each of the following circumstances: A patient who has severe bleeding from his arm A patient who is vomiting A patient who is spitting up blood
questions.answer: Gloves, gown, face shield Gloves, goggles, gown Gloves, mask, goggles, gown

questions.question: blunt-force trauma
questions.answer: injury caused by a blow that does not penetrate the skin or other body tissues.

questions.question: danger zone
questions.answer: the area around the wreckage of a vehicle collision or other incident within which special safety precautions should be taken.

questions.question: index of suspicion
questions.answer: awareness that there may be injuries.

questions.question: mechanism of injury
questions.answer: a force or forces that may have caused injury.

questions.question: nature of the illness
questions.answer: what is medically wrong with a patient.

questions.question: penetrating trauma
questions.answer: injury caused by an object that passes through the skin or other body tissues.

questions.question: scene size-up
questions.answer: steps taken when approaching the scene of an emergency call: checking scene safety, taking Standard Precautions, noting the mechanism of injury or nature of the patient’s illness, determining the number of patients, and deciding what, if any, additional resources to call for.

questions.question: For each of the following dangers, describe actions that must be taken to remain safe at a collision scene. Leaking gasoline Toxic or hazardous material spill Vehicle on fire Downed power lines
questions.answer: Keep a safe distance, avoid ignition sources, notify the fire department. Establish a safe zone, use PPE, notify HazMat team. Keep a safe distance, use fire extinguisher if trained, wait for the fire department. Keep a safe distance, do not touch, notify the power company.

questions.question: List several indicators of violence or potential violence at an emergency scene. (4)
questions.answer: Weapons present, angry or aggressive behavior, loud voices/arguing, signs of substance abuse.

questions.question: Describe several situations where it is appropriate to wear disposable gloves.  Describe situations where you would also wear protective eyewear and mask.  Describe situations where you would wear an N-95 or HEPA respirator.
questions.answer: Gloves: any patient contact. Gloves, eyewear, mask: risk of splashes (e.g., vomiting). N-95/HEPA: respiratory infections (e.g., TB).

questions.question: Describe common mechanism-of-injury patterns (4)
questions.answer: Falls: fractures, head injuries, spinal injuries. Motor vehicle collisions: whiplash, fractures, internal bleeding. Penetrating injuries: organ damage, internal bleeding, infection risk. Blunt-force trauma: bruises, fractures, internal organ damage, concussions.

questions.question: List sources of information about the nature of a patient’s illness.
questions.answer: Patient history, bystanders, medical alert tags, medications. The scene.

questions.question: List several medical and trauma situations where you may require additional assistance. (4)
questions.answer: Multiple patients, hazardous material exposure, entrapment, severe trauma, environmental hazards (ie. downed power lines)

questions.question: You respond to a head-on collision of two automobiles late at night. There are no apparent fluids leaking, no smoke involved, no wires down, and no abnormal smells.  What PPE should you put on as you exit the ambulance?  What PPE should you have available close by, in case it is needed?
questions.answer: Wear: gloves, reflective vest. Available: goggles, face mask, gown, respirator

questions.question: A patient has stab wounds to the lower anterior ribs and lower posterior ribs.  What organs are most at risk of injury from the different wounds?
questions.answer: Anterior: liver, stomach, intestines. Posterior: kidneys, spleen.

questions.question: You responded to a call with possible domestic violence. Because the scene did not appear to be safe, you did not go into the house, but retreated and called for police assistance. Another EMT says that you committed abandonment when you did that.  What is your response?
questions.answer: Explain that ensuring scene safety is a priority, and entering an unsafe scene could result in harm to the EMTs and delay in effective care.

questions.question: What are your list of priorities on a scene? (4)
questions.answer: 1. You 2. Your crew 3. The patient 4. Bystanders

questions.question: Give 2 examples of airborne pathogens
Give 3 examples of bloodborne pathogens
Give 3 examples of contact pathogens
Give 3 examples of Fecal-Oral pathogens
What are the differences between Level A, B, and C PPE?
questions.answer: Level A: Totally chemically/vaporally resistant Level B: Chemical Resistant; NOT vapor resistant Level C: Not designed for chemical exposures and no SCBA

questions.question: What is the best way to decontaminate yourself?
What miniumum % alcohol is an appropriate hand sanitizer?
What is the difference between cleaning, disinfection, and sanitizing?
questions.answer: Cleaning: Done with soap and water, also called gross decon Disinfection: Done with approved solutions that eliminate pathogens Sanitizing: Done with high temperatures such as an autoclave or ultrasonic cleaner

questions.question: What are the requirements if you are exposed from an airborne/bloodborne pathogen?
questions.answer: Airborne: The receiving facility is required to notify your designated officer (DO) within 48 hours if positive exposure. Bloodborne: You determine if you have a possible exposure, you complete a form and are evaluated at the ED, and the ED is required to notify your DO within 48 hours of possible exposure

questions.question: What are the roles and responsiblities of EMTs?
questions.answer: Personal Safety Safety of others Patient assessment Emergency care Safe lifting and moving Transport and transfer of care Record keeping and data collection Patient advocacy

questions.question: What is a living will?
questions.answer: It is a document that often directs more general health care issues, including the use of long-term life support equipment such as ventilators and feeding tubes.

questions.question: What is a healthcare durable power of attorney?
questions.answer: Designates a person to make health care decisions for the signer of the document if he is incapacitated.  Decisions by health care proxies usually pertain only to in-hospital or long-term care facility situations.

questions.question: What are things you should look out for when a DNR is in question?
questions.answer: Know your states laws/protocols DNR must be present DNR must be valid If there are ANY questions, start resuscitation

questions.question: What are presumptative signs of death? (5)
questions.answer: No pulse, breathing, or breath sounds Complete unresponsiveness No pupil response Absence of a blood pressure No reflexes

abdominal quadrants
questions.answer: Four divisions of the abdomen used to pinpoint the location of a pain or injury: the right upper quadrant (RUQ), the left upper quadrant (LUQ), the right lower quadrant (RLQ), and the left lower quadrant (LLQ).

questions.question: anatomic position
questions.answer: The standard reference position for the body in the study of anatomy. In this position, the body is standing erect, facing the observer, with arms down at the sides and the palms of the hands forward.

questions.question: anatomy
anterior
questions.answer: The front of the body or body part.

questions.question: bilateral
combining form
questions.answer: A word root with an added vowel that can be joined with other words, roots, or suffixes to form a new word; for example, the combining form therm/o added to meter makes the new word thermometer.

questions.question: compound
questions.answer: A word formed from two or more whole words; for example, the compound smallpox formed from small and pox.

questions.question: distal
dorsal
questions.answer: Referring to the back of the body or the back of the hand or foot. A synonym for posterior.

questions.question: Fowler position
questions.answer: A sitting position when the patient is in a stretcher with their head/torso leaning up 45-60 Degrees.

questions.question: inferior
questions.answer: Away from the head, usually compared with another structure that is closer to the head (e.g., the lips are inferior to the nose).

questions.question: lateral
questions.answer: To the side, away from the midline of the body.

questions.question: medial
questions.answer: Toward the midline of the body.

questions.question: midaxillary (mid-AX-uh-lair-e) line
questions.answer: A line drawn vertically from the middle of the armpit to the ankle.

questions.question: midclavicular (mid-clah-VIK-yuh-ler) line
questions.answer: The line through the center of each clavicle.

questions.question: midline
questions.answer: An imaginary line drawn down the center of the body, dividing it into right and left halves.

questions.question: palmar
questions.answer: Referring to the palm of the hand.

questions.question: physiology
plantar
questions.answer: Referring to the sole of the foot.

questions.question: posterior
questions.answer: The back of the body or body part.

questions.question: prefix
questions.answer: Word part added to the beginning of a root or word to modify or qualify its meaning; for example, the prefix bi- added to the word lateral forms the word bilateral.

questions.question: proximal
recovery position
questions.answer: Lying on the side. Also called lateral recumbent position.

questions.question: suffix
questions.answer: Word part added to the end of a root or word to complete its meaning; for example, the suffix -itis added to the root laryng forms the word laryngitis.

questions.question: superior
questions.answer: Toward the head (e.g., the chest is superior to the abdomen).

questions.question: supine
unilateral
ventral
questions.answer: Referring to the front of the body. A synonym for anterior.

questions.question: Define the following pairs of anatomic terms: medial and lateral
questions.answer: Medial: Toward the midline of the body. Lateral: To the side, away from the midline of the body.

questions.question: Define the following pairs of anatomic terms: anterior and posterior
questions.answer: Anterior: The front of the body or body part. Posterior: The back of the body or body part.

questions.question: Define the following pairs of anatomic terms: proximal and distal
questions.answer: Proximal: Closer to the torso. Distal: Farther away from the torso.

questions.question: List two prefixes that mean “below.”
List two suffixes that mean “pertaining to.”
Describe the difference between the prone and supine positions.
questions.answer: Prone: Lying facedown. Supine: Lying on the back.

questions.question: Describe the anatomic location of the midaxillary line.
questions.answer: A line drawn vertically from the middle of the armpit to the ankle.

questions.question: Describe how the abdomen is divided into quadrants.
questions.answer: The abdomen is divided into four quadrants: right upper quadrant (RUQ), left upper quadrant (LUQ), right lower quadrant (RLQ), and left lower quadrant (LLQ).

questions.question: acetabulum (AS-uh-TAB-yuh-lum)
questions.answer: the pelvic socket into which the ball at the proximal end of the femur fits to form the hip joint.

questions.question: acromioclavicular (ah-KRO-me-o-klav-IK-yuh-ler) joint
questions.answer: the joint where the acromion and the clavicle meet.

questions.question: acromion (ah-KRO-me-on) process
questions.answer: the highest portion of the shoulder.

questions.question: alveoli (al-VE-o-li)
questions.answer: the microscopic sacs of the lungs where gas exchange with the bloodstream takes place.

questions.question: aorta (ay-OR-tah)
questions.answer: the largest artery in the body. It transports blood from the left ventricle to begin systemic circulation.

questions.question: appendix
questions.answer: a small tube located near the junction of the small and large intestines in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen, the function of which is not well understood. Its inflammation, called appendicitis, is a common cause of abdominal pain.

questions.question: arteriole (ar-TE-re-ol)
artery
questions.answer: any blood vessel carrying blood away from the heart.

questions.question: atria (AY-tree-ah)
questions.answer: the two upper chambers of the heart. There is a right atrium (which receives unoxygenated blood returning from the body) and a left atrium (which receives oxygenated blood returning from the lungs). Singular atrium.

questions.question: automaticity (AW-to-muh-TISS-it-e)
questions.answer: the ability of the heart to generate and conduct electrical impulses on its own.

questions.question: autonomic (AW-to-NOM-ik) nervous system
questions.answer: the division of the peripheral nervous system that controls involuntary motor functions.

questions.question: bladder
questions.answer: the round, saclike organ of the renal system used as a reservoir for urine.

questions.question: blood pressure
questions.answer: the pressure caused by blood exerting force against the walls of blood vessels. Usually arterial blood pressure (the pressure in an artery) is measured. See also diastolic blood pressure; systolic blood pressure.

questions.question: brachial artery
questions.answer: artery of the upper arm; the site of the pulse checked during infant CPR.

questions.question: bronchi (BRONG-ki)
questions.answer: the two large sets of branches that come off the trachea and enter the lungs. There are right and left bronchi. Singular bronchus.

questions.question: buffer system
questions.answer: a system that helps manage the pH of the body to maintain it at a normal level.

questions.question: calcaneus (kal-KAY-ne-us)
capillary (KAP-i-lair-e)
questions.answer: a thin-walled, microscopic blood vessel where the oxygen/carbon dioxide and nutrient/waste exchange with the body’s cells takes place.

questions.question: cardiac conduction system
questions.answer: a system of specialized muscle tissues that conducts electrical impulses that stimulate the heart to beat.

questions.question: cardiac muscle
questions.answer: specialized involuntary muscle found only in the heart.

questions.question: cardiovascular (KAR-de-o-VAS-kyu-ler) system
questions.answer: the system made up of the heart (cardio) and the blood vessels (vascular). Sometimes called the circulatory system.

questions.question: carotid (kah-ROT-id) arteries
questions.answer: the large neck arteries, one on each side of the neck, that carry blood from the heart to the head.

questions.question: carpals (KAR-pulz)
central nervous system (CNS)
central pulses
questions.answer: the carotid and femoral pulses, which can be felt in the central part of the body.

questions.question: clavicle (KLAV-i-kul)
coronary (KOR-o-nar-e) arteries
questions.answer: blood vessels that supply the muscle of the heart (myocardium).

questions.question: cranium
questions.answer: the top, back, and sides of the skull.

questions.question: cricoid (KRIK-oid) cartilage
questions.answer: the ring-shaped structure that forms the lower portion of the larynx.

questions.question: dermis (DER-mis)
questions.answer: the inner (second) layer of skin, rich in blood vessels and nerves, found beneath the epidermis.

questions.question: diaphragm (DI-uh-fram)
questions.answer: the muscular structure that divides the chest cavity from the abdominal cavity; a major muscle of respiration.

questions.question: diastolic (di-as-TOL-ik) blood pressure
questions.answer: the pressure in the arteries when the left ventricle is refilling.

questions.question: digestive system
questions.answer: system by which food travels through the body and is digested, or broken down, into absorbable forms.

questions.question: dorsalis pedis (dor-SAL-is PEED-is) artery
questions.answer: artery supplying the foot, lateral to the large tendon of the big toe.

questions.question: endocrine (EN-do-krin) system
questions.answer: system of glands that produce chemicals called hormones that help to regulate many body activities and functions.

questions.question: epidermis (ep-i-DER-mis)
epiglottis (EP-i-GLOT-is)
questions.answer: a leaf-shaped structure that prevents food and foreign matter from entering the trachea.

questions.question: epinephrine (EP-uh-NEF-rin)
questions.answer: a hormone produced by the body. As a medication, it dilates respiratory passages and is used to relieve severe allergic reactions.

questions.question: exhalation (EX-huh-LAY-shun)
questions.answer: a passive process in which the intercostal (rib) muscles and the diaphragm relax, causing the chest cavity to decrease in size and air to flow out of the lungs.

questions.question: femoral (FEM-o-ral) artery
questions.answer: the major artery supplying the leg.

questions.question: femur (FEE-mer)
questions.answer: the large bone of the thigh.

questions.question: fibula (FIB-yuh-luh)
questions.answer: the lateral and smaller bone of the lower leg.

questions.question: gallbladder
questions.answer: a sac on the underside of the liver that stores bile produced by the liver.

questions.question: humerus (HYU-mer-us)
questions.answer: the bone of the upper arm, between the shoulder and the elbow.

questions.question: hypoperfusion
questions.answer: inability of the body to adequately circulate blood to the body’s cells to supply them with oxygen and nutrients; a life-threatening condition. Also called shock. See also perfusion.

questions.question: ilium (IL-e-um)
questions.answer: the superior and widest portion of the pelvis.

questions.question: inhalation (in-huh-LAY-shun)
questions.answer: an active process in which the intercostal (rib) muscles and the diaphragm contract, expanding the size of the chest cavity and causing air to flow into the lungs.

questions.question: involuntary muscle
questions.answer: muscle that responds automatically to brain signals but cannot be consciously controlled.

questions.question: ischium (IS-ke-um)
questions.answer: the lower, posterior portions of the pelvis.

questions.question: kidneys
questions.answer: organs of the renal system used to filter blood and regulate fluid levels in the body.

questions.question: large intestine
questions.answer: the muscular tube that removes water from waste products received from the small intestine and moves anything not absorbed by the body toward excretion from the body.

questions.question: larynx (LAR-inks)
ligament
questions.answer: tissue that connects bone to bone.

questions.question: malleolus (muh-LEE-oh-lus)
questions.answer: protrusion on the side of the ankle. The lateral malleolus, at the lower end of the fibula, is seen on the outer ankle; the medial malleolus, at the lower end of the tibia, is seen on the inner ankle.

questions.question: mandible
manubrium (mah-NOO-bree-um)
questions.answer: the superior portion of the sternum.

questions.question: maxillae (mak-SIL-e)
questions.answer: the two fused bones forming the upper jaw.

questions.question: metacarpals (met-uh-KAR-pulz)
metatarsals (met-uh-TAR-sulz)
musculoskeletal (MUS-kyu-lo-SKEL-e-tal) system
questions.answer: the system of bones and skeletal muscles that support and protect the body and permit movement.

questions.question: nasal bones
nasopharynx (na-so-FAIR-inks)
questions.answer: the area directly posterior to the nose.

questions.question: nervous system
questions.answer: the system of brain, spinal cord, and nerves that govern sensation, movement, and thought.

questions.question: orbits
questions.answer: the bony structures around the eyes; the eye sockets.

questions.question: oropharynx (o-ro-FAIR-inks)
questions.answer: the area directly posterior to the mouth.

questions.question: ovaries
questions.answer: egg-producing organs within the female reproductive system.

questions.question: pancreas (PAN-kree-as)
questions.answer: a gland located behind the stomach that produces insulin and juices that assist in digestion of food in the duodenum of the small intestine.

questions.question: patella (puh-TEL-uh)
pelvis
questions.answer: the basin-shaped bony structure that supports the spine and is the point of proximal attachment for the lower extremities.

questions.question: perfusion (per-FYU-zhun)
questions.answer: the supply of oxygen to and removal of wastes from the cells and tissues of the body as a result of the flow of blood through the capillaries.

questions.question: peripheral nervous system (PNS)
questions.answer: the nerves that enter and leave the spinal cord and travel between the brain and organs without passing through the spinal cord.

questions.question: pharynx (FAIR-inks)
questions.answer: the area posterior to the nose and mouth. It is made up of the oropharynx and the nasopharynx.

questions.question: plasma
questions.answer: the fluid portion of the blood.

questions.question: platelets
questions.answer: components of the blood; membrane-enclosed fragments of specialized cells.

questions.question: pulmonary (PUL-mo-nair-e) arteries
questions.answer: the vessels that carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle of the heart to the lungs.

questions.question: pulmonary veins
questions.answer: the vessels that carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium of the heart.

questions.question: radial artery
questions.answer: artery of the lower arm; the artery felt when taking the pulse at the thumb side of the wrist.

questions.question: radius
questions.answer: the lateral bone of the forearm.

questions.question: red blood cells
questions.answer: components of the blood. They carry oxygen to and carbon dioxide away from the cells.

questions.question: renal system
questions.answer: the body system that regulates fluid balance and the filtration of blood. Also called the urinary system.

questions.question: reproductive system
questions.answer: the body system that is responsible for human reproduction.

questions.question: respiration
questions.answer: the process of moving oxygen and carbon dioxide between circulating blood and the cells.

questions.question: respiratory system
questions.answer: the system of nose, mouth, throat, lungs, and muscles that brings oxygen into the body and expels carbon dioxide.

questions.question: scapula
scrotum
skeletal muscle
questions.answer: muscle that can be consciously controlled.

questions.question: small intestine
questions.answer: the muscular tube between the stomach and the large intestine, divided into the duodenum, the jejunum, and the ileum, which receives partially digested food from the stomach and continues digestion. Nutrients are absorbed by the body through its walls.

questions.question: spleen
questions.answer: an organ located in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen that acts as a blood filtration system and a reservoir for reserves of blood.

questions.question: sternum
stomach
questions.answer: muscular sac between the esophagus and the small intestine where digestion of food begins.

questions.question: subcutaneous (sub-ku-TAY-ne-us) layers
questions.answer: the layers of fat and soft tissues found below the dermis.

questions.question: tarsals
tendons
questions.answer: tissue that connects muscle to bone.

questions.question: testes
questions.answer: the male organs of reproduction used for the production of sperm.

questions.question: thorax
tibia (TIB-e-uh)
questions.answer: the medial and larger bone of the lower leg.

questions.question: ulna (UL-nuh)
questions.answer: the medial bone of the forearm.

questions.question: ureters (yu-RE-ters)
questions.answer: the tubes connecting the kidneys to the bladder.

questions.question: urethra (yu-RE-thra)
questions.answer: tube connecting the bladder to the vagina or penis for excretion of urine.

questions.question: uterus (YU-ter-us)
questions.answer: female organ of reproduction used to house the developing fetus.

questions.question: vagina
questions.answer: the female organ of reproduction used for both sexual intercourse and as an exit from the uterus for the fetus.

questions.question: ventilation
questions.answer: the process of moving gases (oxygen and carbon dioxide) between inhaled air and the pulmonary circulation of blood.

questions.question: ventricles (VEN-tri-kulz)
questions.answer: the two lower chambers of the heart. There is a right ventricle (which sends oxygen-poor blood to the lungs) and a left ventricle (which sends oxygen-rich blood to the body).

questions.question: venule (VEN-yul)
vertebrae
questions.answer: the thirty-three bones of the spinal column.

questions.question: white blood cells
questions.answer: components of the blood. They produce substances that help the body fight infection.
