aerobic (air-O-bik) metabolism
questions.answer: the cellular process in which oxygen is used to metabolize glucose. Energy is produced in an efficient manner, with minimal waste products.

questions.question: anaerobic (AN-air-o-bik) metabolism
questions.answer: the cellular process in which glucose is metabolized into energy without oxygen. Energy is produced in an inefficient manner, with many waste products.

questions.question: cardiac output
questions.answer: the amount of blood ejected from the heart in one minute (heart rate ∙ stroke volume).

questions.question: chemoreceptors (ke-mo-re-cept-erz)
questions.answer: chemical sensors in the brain and blood vessels that identify changing levels of oxygen and carbon dioxide.

questions.question: dead air space
questions.answer: air that occupies the space between the mouth and alveoli but that does not actually reach the area of gas exchange.

questions.question: dehydration (de-hi-DRAY-shun)
questions.answer: an abnormally low amount of water in the body.

questions.question: diaphoresis (DI-uh-for-EE-sis)
questions.answer: sweating; condition of cool, pale, and moist/sweaty skin.

questions.question: edema (eh-DEE-muh)
questions.answer: swelling associated with the movement of water into the interstitial space.

questions.question: electrolyte (e-LEK-tro-lite)
questions.answer: a substance that, when dissolved in water, separates into charged particles.

questions.question: hydrostatic (HI-dro-STAT-ik) pressure
questions.answer: the pressure within a blood vessel that tends to push water out of the vessel.

questions.question: hypersensitivity
questions.answer: an exaggerated response by the immune system to a particular substance.

questions.question: hypoperfusion (HI-po-per-FEW-zhun)
questions.answer: inability of the body to adequately circulate blood to the body’s cells to supply them with oxygen and nutrients. A life-threatening condition. Also called shock. See also perfusion.

questions.question: metabolism (meh-TAB-o-lizm)
questions.answer: the cellular function of converting nutrients into energy.

questions.question: minute volume
questions.answer: the amount of air breathed in during each respiration multiplied by the number of breaths per minute.

questions.question: patent (PAY-tent) airway
questions.answer: an airway that is open and clear/free from obstruction.

questions.question: pathophysiology (path-o-fiz-e-OL-o-je)
questions.answer: the study of how disease processes affect the function of the body.

questions.question: perfusion (per-FEW-zhun)
questions.answer: the supply of oxygen to and removal of wastes from the cells and tissues of the body as a result of the flow of blood through the capillaries.

questions.question: plasma oncotic (PLAZ-ma on-KOT-ik) pressure
questions.answer: the pull exerted by large proteins in the plasma portion of blood that tends to pull water from the body into the bloodstream.

questions.question: stretch receptors
questions.answer: sensors in blood vessels that identify internal pressure.

questions.question: stroke volume
questions.answer: the amount of blood ejected from the heart in one contraction. (usually 70 ml)

questions.question: systemic vascular resistance (SVR)
questions.answer: the pressure in the peripheral blood vessels that the heart must overcome to pump blood into the system.

questions.question: tidal volume
questions.answer: the volume of air moved in one cycle of breathing (~500 ml)

questions.question: V/Q match
questions.answer: ventilation/perfusion match. This implies that the alveoli are supplied with enough air and that the air in the alveoli is matched with sufficient blood in the pulmonary capillaries to permit optimum exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Summarize the coordinated processes required of the cardiopulmonary system to maintain perfusion.
questions.answer: Heart pumps blood, vessels transport it, lungs oxygenate blood, and tissues receive oxygen/nutrients.

questions.question: Contrast the processes of aerobic and anaerobic metabolism in cells.
questions.answer: Aerobic: uses oxygen, efficient, minimal waste. Anaerobic: no oxygen, inefficient, produces lactic acid.

questions.question: Relate the composition of air with the demands of the cardiopulmonary system.
questions.answer: Air: ~21% oxygen; necessary for aerobic metabolism and efficient energy production in cells.

questions.question: Distinguish between the processes of ventilation, respiration, and perfusion.
questions.answer: Ventilation: air in/out of lungs. Respiration: gas exchange in alveoli. Perfusion: blood flow to tissues.

questions.question: Identify the structures of the airway.
questions.answer: Nose, mouth, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, lungs.

questions.question: Explain the impact on the body of changes in the tidal volume, minute volume, and dead air space.
questions.answer: Decreased tidal/minute volume reduces gas exchange; increased dead air space reduces efficiency.

questions.question: Explain circumstances that lead to respiratory dysfunction.
questions.answer: Obstructions, infections, asthma, COPD impede airflow and gas exchange.

questions.question: Describe the mechanism by which the body attempts to compensate for disruptions of respiration.
questions.answer: Increased breathing rate/depth, use of accessory muscles to enhance air intake.

questions.question: Describe the functions of the various components of blood.
questions.answer: RBCs transport oxygen, WBCs fight infection, platelets clot, plasma transports nutrients/waste.

questions.question: Describe the consequences of reduction of blood volume, red blood cells, and water-retaining proteins.
questions.answer: Reduced blood volume/RBCs: less oxygen transport, potential shock. Reduced proteins: risk of edema.

questions.question: Distinguish the functions of arteries, veins, and capillaries.
questions.answer: Arteries: carry oxygenated blood from heart. Veins: return deoxygenated blood to heart. Capillaries: exchange gases/nutrients with tissues

questions.question: Explain how the nervous system can correct low and high blood pressure.
questions.answer: Baroreceptors detect changes; autonomic nervous system adjusts heart rate and vessel dilation.

questions.question: Predict the impact on heart function with a change in the balance of sympathetic and parasympathetic components.
questions.answer: Sympathetic: increases heart rate/contractility. Parasympathetic: decreases heart rate/contractility.

questions.question: Analyze how loss of blood vessel tone, increased permeability, and increased systemic vascular resistance affect blood pressure.
questions.answer: Loss of tone: lowers BP. Increased permeability: fluid leakage/edema. Increased resistance: raises BP.

questions.question: Illustrate the interaction of stroke volume, cardiac preload, cardiac contractility, and cardiac output.
questions.answer: Stroke volume depends on preload and contractility; cardiac output = stroke volume x heart rate.

questions.question: Predict the consequences of mechanical and electrical dysfunctions of the heart.
questions.answer: Mechanical: impaired pumping, heart failure. Electrical: arrhythmias, inefficient contractions.

questions.question: Explain the concept of V/Q (ventilation–perfusion) match.
questions.answer: Optimal gas exchange needs matched air in alveoli (ventilation) and blood in capillaries (perfusion).

questions.question: Summarize the pathophysiology of shock.
questions.answer: Inadequate perfusion leads to insufficient oxygen/nutrient delivery, causing cellular/tissue dysfunction.

questions.question: Describe the mechanism which underlies all forms of shock.
questions.answer: Inadequate perfusion leading to insufficient oxygen and nutrient delivery to tissues.

questions.question: Contrast hypovolemic, distributive, cardiogenic, and obstructive shock.
questions.answer: Hypovolemic: blood loss. Distributive: blood vessel tone is lost. Cardiogenic: heart pump failure. Obstructive: blood flow blockage.

questions.question: Categorize patient presentations as compensated or decompensated shock.
questions.answer: Compensated: body maintains perfusion.  Decompensated: compensation fails, perfusion inadequate.

questions.question: Summarize the concept of fluid balance in the body and recall the distribution across the body
questions.answer: Regulated distribution of water across intracellular, intravascular, and interstitial spaces. - Intracellular: 65% - Intravascular: 10% - Interstitial: 25%

questions.question: Identify the structures that regulate fluid distribution throughout the spaces of the body.
List disruptions of fluid balance.
questions.answer: Dehydration, overhydration, edema, and fluid shifts.

questions.question: Explain how trauma can result in nervous system dysfunction.
questions.answer: Direct damage to brain/spinal cord causing loss of function and coordination.

questions.question: Explain how medical problems can result in nervous system dysfunction.
questions.answer: Infections can cause inflammation of the brain (Meningitis/encephalitis), metabolic disorders (hypoglycemia), vascular issues impairing nervous system function (stroke)

questions.question: List of symptoms that suggest a nervous system dysfunction (9)
questions.answer: Altered mental status,  Seizures, Inability to speak or difficulty speaking, Visual or hearing distubance, Inability to walk or difficulty walking Paralysis Weakness Loss of Sensation Pupil changes

questions.question: Signs of compensated shock (6)
questions.answer: Slight mental status changes, including anxiety and feeling of impending doom Increased heart rate Increased respiratory rate Delayed capillary refill time Pale skin that is cool and moist to touch Sweating

questions.question: What are the symptoms of decompensated shock? (2)
questions.answer: Decreased blood pressure Altered mental status

questions.question: Recall the structures primarily at the root of endocrine dysfunction (4)
questions.answer: Pituitary gland, thyroid gland, adrenal glands, pancreas.

questions.question: Recall potential causes of nausea and vomiting (4)
questions.answer: Infections, toxins, GI obstructions, CNS issues.

questions.question: Describe the consequences of ongoing loss of blood or fluid through the gastrointestinal tract. (3)
questions.answer: Leads to hypovolemia, dehydration, and shock.

questions.question: Summarize the mechanism by which a response by the immune system can lead to shock.
questions.answer: Severe allergic reactions release histamine, causing vasodilation, fluid leakage, and shock.

questions.question: adolescence
questions.answer: stage of life from 13 to 18 years.

questions.question: bonding
questions.answer: the sense that needs will be met.

questions.question: early adulthood
questions.answer: stage of life from 19 to 40 years.

questions.question: infancy
questions.answer: stage of life from birth to 1 year of age.

questions.question: late adulthood
questions.answer: stage of life from 61 years and older.

questions.question: middle adulthood
questions.answer: stage of life from 41 to 60 years.

questions.question: Moro reflex
questions.answer: a response to being startled in which the infant throws out both arms, spreads the fingers, then grabs with fingers and arms.

questions.question: palmar reflex
questions.answer: a grasping reflex in which an infant grabs onto a finger placed in the infant’s palm.

questions.question: preschool age
questions.answer: stage of life from 3 to 5 years.

questions.question: rooting reflex
questions.answer: a reflex response in which a hungry infant automatically turns toward the stimulus when the cheek or one side of the mouth is touched.

questions.question: scaffolding
questions.answer: building on what one already knows.

questions.question: school age
questions.answer: stage of life from 6 to 12 years.

questions.question: sucking reflex
questions.answer: a reflex in which stroking a hungry infant’s lips causes the infant to start sucking.

questions.question: temperament
questions.answer: the infant’s reaction to the infant’s environment.

questions.question: toddler phase
questions.answer: stage of life from 12 to 36 months.

questions.question: trust versus mistrust
questions.answer: concept developed from an orderly, predictable environment versus a disorderly, irregular environment.

questions.question: Recall the physiologic characteristics of infants.
questions.answer: Infants have a rapid growth rate, high metabolic rate, and immature immune systems.

questions.question: Infant Vital Sign Range (Newborn and 1 Year)
questions.answer: Newborn: HR 120-200 bpm, RR 30-60/minute, BP 50-70 mmHg Up to 1 year: HR 90-160 bpm, RR 24-30/minute, BP 90 mmHg systolic

questions.question: Match infant age ranges with cognitive (mental) developmental milestones.
questions.answer: 0-2 months: track objects with eyes; 2-4 months: smile, coo; 4-6 months: reach for objects; 6-8 months: sit without support.

questions.question: Categorize toddlers’ vital signs as normal or abnormal.
questions.answer: Normal: HR 80-140 bpm, RR 24-40 breaths/min, BP 90 + (age/2) mmHg systolic.

questions.question: Categorize a preschooler’s vital signs as normal or abnormal.
questions.answer: Normal: HR 70-120 bpm, RR 22-34 breaths/min, BP 90 + (age/2) mmHg systolic.

questions.question: Categorize a school-age child’s vital signs as normal or abnormal.
questions.answer: Normal: HR 65-120 bpm, RR 18-30 breaths/min, BP 90+ (age/2) mmHg systolic.

questions.question: Differentiate between normal and abnormal adolescent vital signs.
questions.answer: Normal: HR 60-100 bpm, RR 12-20 breaths/min, BP 107-117 mmHg systolic.

questions.question: Differentiate between normal and abnormal adult vitals
questions.answer: HR: 60-100 BPM, RR: 12-20/minute, BP: <120 mmHg Systolic

questions.question: airway
questions.answer: The passageway by which air enters and leaves the body. The structures are the nose, mouth, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs.

questions.question: bronchoconstriction (BRON-ko-kun-STRIK-shun)
questions.answer: The contraction of smooth muscle that lines the bronchial passages, resulting in a decreased internal diameter and increased resistance to airflow.

questions.question: gag reflex
questions.answer: Vomiting or retching that occurs when something is placed in the back of the pharynx; tied to the swallow reflex.

questions.question: glottic opening
questions.answer: The level of the vocal cords that defines the boundary between the upper and lower airways.

questions.question: head-tilt, chin-lift maneuver
questions.answer: A method of correcting blockage of the airway by the tongue by tilting the head back and lifting the chin. Used when no trauma is suspected.

questions.question: jaw-thrust maneuver
questions.answer: A method of correcting blockage of the airway by moving the jaw forward without tilting the head or neck. Used when trauma is suspected.

questions.question: nasopharyngeal (NAY-zo-fah-RIN-jeul) airway
questions.answer: A flexible breathing tube inserted through the nostril into the pharynx to help maintain an open airway.

questions.question: oropharyngeal (OR-o-fah-RIN-jeul) airway
questions.answer: A curved device inserted through the mouth into the pharynx to help maintain an open airway.

questions.question: patent airway
questions.answer: An airway that is open and clear, allowing for the passage of air into and out of the body.

questions.question: stridor (STRI-dor)
questions.answer: A high-pitched sound generated from partially obstructed airflow in the upper airway.

questions.question: suctioning (SUK-shun-ing)
questions.answer: The use of a vacuum device to remove blood, vomitus, and other secretions or foreign materials from the airway.

questions.question: Name the main structures of the airway.
questions.answer: Nose, mouth, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs.

questions.question: Explain why care for the airway is a vital part of emergency care.
questions.answer: An open airway is necessary for oxygenation and ventilation, critical for patient survival.

questions.question: Describe the signs of an inadequate airway.
questions.answer: Signs include stridor, gurgling, snoring, and absence of breath sounds.

questions.question: Explain when the head-tilt, chin-lift maneuver should be used and when the jaw-thrust maneuver should be used to open the airway, and why each method should be used.
questions.answer: Head-tilt, chin-lift: No trauma suspected. Jaw-thrust: Trauma suspected to prevent spinal injury.

questions.question: Explain how airway adjuncts and suctioning help in airway management.
questions.answer: Airway adjuncts maintain airway patency; suctioning clears obstructions like vomitus or secretions.

questions.question: You are treating a patient with a spine injury who is immobilized on a backboard. He begins to vomit. In addition to suctioning, what do you do?
questions.answer: Log-roll the patient to clear vomit while maintaining spinal precautions.

questions.question: Describe the signs of a partially obstructed airway.
questions.answer: Stridor, choking, gagging, cyanosis, and increased effort to breathe. (Trouble talking, nasal flaring, "sniffing position" too)

questions.question: Describe how an altered mental status might impact the airway of your patient.
questions.answer: Decreased consciousness can lead to loss of muscle tone, causing airway obstruction by the tongue or aspiration.

questions.question: Describe why trauma to the neck might be both an immediate and an ongoing threat to the airway.
questions.answer: Immediate threat: airway obstruction from swelling or bleeding. Ongoing threat: potential for progressive airway compromise due to swelling or hematoma.

questions.question: List causes of obstruction of the upper and lower airway.
questions.answer: Upper: Tongue, foreign bodies, swelling. Lower: Bronchoconstriction, mucus, inflammation.

questions.question: List the steps to airway assessment in the primary assessment. (5)
questions.answer: 1. Check responsiveness. 2. Look for chest rise and fall. 3. Listen for breath sounds. 4. Feel for air movement. 5. Assess for signs of obstruction.

questions.question: List signs of inadequate airway that are more likely in children than in adults.
questions.answer: Nasal flaring, retractions, grunting, and stridor.

questions.question: Identify general rules for using airway adjuncts.
questions.answer: Use oropharyngeal airway in unconscious patients without gag reflex. Use nasopharyngeal airway when gag reflex is present.

questions.question: List the sequence of steps used in the insertion of an oropharyngeal airway. (5)
questions.answer: 1. Select proper size. 2. Open the mouth. 3. Insert upside down. 4. Rotate 180 degrees. 5. Advance until flange rests on lips.

questions.question: Identify instances when a nasopharyngeal airway offers benefits over an oropharyngeal airway.
questions.answer: In conscious or semi-conscious patients with an intact gag reflex.

questions.question: List the sequence of steps used in the insertion of a nasopharyngeal airway. (5)
questions.answer: 1. Select proper size. 2. Lubricate airway. 3. Insert into nostril with bevel towards septum. 4. Advance gently. 5. Confirm placement.

questions.question: Match the components and attachments of suction devices with their designed purposes.
questions.answer: Wide-bore tubing: Prevents clogging. Rigid tips: Clears thick secretions. Flexible catheters: Suctions smaller or delicate areas.

questions.question: Recall the general rules that apply to all suctioning techniques. (6)
questions.answer: Use sterile technique (PPE), limit suctioning to 10 seconds, position patient as necessary, vacuum immediately in the case of vomiting, be careful not to suction soft tissues, keep suction tip in sight.

questions.question: Alveolar ventilation
questions.answer: The amount of air that reaches the alveoli.

questions.question: Artificial ventilation
questions.answer: Forcing air or oxygen into the lungs when a patient has stopped breathing or has inadequate breathing. Also called positive pressure ventilation.

questions.question: Automatic transport ventilator (ATV)
questions.answer: A device that provides positive pressure ventilations. It includes settings designed to adjust ventilation rate and volume, is portable, and is easily carried on an ambulance.

questions.question: Bag–valve mask (BVM)
questions.answer: A handheld device with a face mask and self-refilling bag that can be squeezed to provide artificial ventilations to a patient. It can deliver air from the atmosphere or oxygen from a supplemental oxygen-supply system.

questions.question: Cellular respiration
questions.answer: The exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between cells and circulating blood.

questions.question: Cyanosis (SY-uh-NO-sis)
questions.answer: A blue or gray color resulting from lack of oxygen in the body.

questions.question: Diffusion
questions.answer: A process by which molecules move from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration.

questions.question: Flowmeter
questions.answer: A valve that indicates the flow of oxygen in liters per minute.

questions.question: Humidifier
questions.answer: A device connected to the flowmeter to add moisture to the dry oxygen coming from an oxygen cylinder.

questions.question: Hypoxia (hi-POK-se-uh)
questions.answer: An insufficiency of oxygen in the body’s tissues.

questions.question: Nasal cannula (NAY-zul KAN-yuh-luh)
questions.answer: A device that delivers low concentrations of oxygen through two prongs that rest in the patient’s nostrils.

questions.question: Nonrebreather (NRB) mask
questions.answer: A face mask–and–reservoir bag device that delivers high concentrations of oxygen. The patient’s exhaled air escapes through a valve and is not rebreathed.

questions.question: Oxygen cylinder
questions.answer: A cylinder filled with oxygen under pressure.

questions.question: Partial rebreather mask
questions.answer: A face mask and reservoir oxygen bag with no one-way valve to the reservoir bag, so some exhaled air mixes with the oxygen; used in some patients to help preserve carbon dioxide levels in the blood to stimulate breathing.

questions.question: Pocket face mask
questions.answer: A device, usually with a one-way valve, to aid in artificial ventilation. A rescuer breathes through the valve when the mask is placed over the patient’s face. It also acts as a barrier to prevent contact with a patient’s breath or body fluids. It can be used with supplemental oxygen when fitted with an oxygen inlet.

questions.question: Positive pressure ventilation
Pressure regulator
questions.answer: A device connected to an oxygen cylinder to reduce cylinder pressure so it is safe for delivery of oxygen to a patient.

questions.question: Pulmonary respiration
questions.answer: The exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between the alveoli and circulating blood in the pulmonary capillaries.

questions.question: Respiration (RES-pir-AY-shun)
questions.answer: The diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide between the alveoli and the blood (pulmonary respiration) and between the blood and the cells (cellular respiration). Also used to mean, simply, breathing.

questions.question: Respiratory arrest
Respiratory distress
questions.answer: Increased work of breathing; a sensation of shortness of breath.

questions.question: Respiratory failure
questions.answer: The reduction of breathing to the point where oxygen intake is not sufficient to support life.

questions.question: Tracheostomy mask
questions.answer: A device designed to be placed over a stoma or tracheostomy tube to provide supplemental oxygen.

questions.question: Venturi mask
questions.answer: A face mask–and–reservoir bag device that delivers specific concentrations of oxygen by mixing oxygen with inhaled air.

questions.question: Describe the signs of respiratory distress (7)
questions.answer: - Increased work of breathing - Shortness of breath - Use of accessory muscles - Nasal flaring - Retractions (intercostal, supraclavicular) - Agitation or anxiety - Cyanosis (late sign)

questions.question: Describe the signs of respiratory failure (6)
questions.answer: - Marked increase in respiratory effort - Cyanosis - Decreased level of consciousness - Inadequate respiratory rate and depth - Poor air movement - Diminished or absent breath sounds

questions.question: Name and briefly describe the techniques of artificial ventilation (mouth-to-mask or BVM).
questions.answer: - Mouth-to-mask: A rescuer breathes into a mask placed over the patient's face. - Bag-valve mask (BVM): A self-inflating bag is squeezed to deliver air to the patient's lungs.

questions.question: For BVM ventilation, describe recommended variations in technique for one or two rescuers and for a patient with trauma suspected or trauma not suspected.
questions.answer: - One rescuer: Use the "E-C" clamp technique to hold the mask and squeeze the bag. - Two rescuers: One rescuer holds the mask with both hands to ensure a better seal while the other squeezes the bag. - Trauma suspected: Maintain cervical spine stabilization and use a jaw-thrust maneuver. - Trauma not suspected: Head-tilt, chin-lift maneuver can be used.

questions.question: Describe how positive pressure ventilation moves air differently from how the body normally moves air.
questions.answer: Positive pressure ventilation forces air into the lungs, whereas normal breathing relies on negative pressure created by the diaphragm contracting to draw air in.

questions.question: Name patient problems that would benefit from administration of oxygen, and explain how to decide what oxygen-delivery device (nonrebreather mask, nasal cannula, or other) should be used for a particular patient.
questions.answer: - Problems: Hypoxia, respiratory distress, shock, trauma, cardiac arrest. - Device selection:    - Nonrebreather mask for high-concentration oxygen needs.   - Nasal cannula for low-concentration oxygen needs.   - Venturi mask for specific oxygen concentration requirements.   - BVM for patients needing assisted ventilation.

questions.question: Describe how the process of moving air in and out of the chest might be interfered with by: Penetrating trauma to the chest.
questions.answer: - Can cause a pneumothorax or hemothorax, leading to collapsed lung and impaired ventilation. - Chest wall damage may inhibit proper expansion and contraction during breathing.

questions.question: Describe how the process of moving air in and out of the chest might be interfered with by: A spinal injury that paralyzes the diaphragm.
questions.answer: - Diaphragm paralysis leads to loss of primary muscle for breathing, resulting in respiratory failure. - Requires mechanical ventilation support.

questions.question: Describe how the process of moving air in and out of the chest might be interfered with by: Swelling around the vocal cords.
questions.answer: - Causes airway obstruction and difficulty moving air past the vocal cords. - Can lead to respiratory distress or failure if severe.

questions.question: Describe how the process of moving air in and out of the chest might be interfered with by: Severe asthma attack.
questions.answer: - Bronchoconstriction narrows airways, causing difficulty in air movement. - Increases work of breathing and can lead to hypoxia.

questions.question: Describe when to use the following techniques of artificial ventilation: Mouth-to-mask, Two-rescuer bag-valve mask, One-rescuer bag-valve mask, Flow-restricted, oxygen-powered ventilation device.
questions.answer: - Mouth-to-mask: When only one rescuer is available, for better tidal volume. - Two-rescuer BVM: Preferred method for effective ventilation and better seal. - One-rescuer BVM: Used when only one rescuer is available and no mask is present. - Flow-restricted, oxygen-powered ventilation device: When high-flow oxygen is needed and other methods are not available.

questions.question: Describe the differences between respiratory distress, respiratory failure, and respiratory arrest.
questions.answer: - Respiratory distress: Increased effort and difficulty in breathing. - Respiratory failure: Inadequate breathing to sustain life. - Respiratory arrest: Complete cessation of breathing.

questions.question: Describe how to determine adequate artificial ventilation. (4)
questions.answer: - Equal chest rise and fall with each breath. - Appropriate rate (adults: 10-12/min, children: 12-20/min). - Heart rate returns to normal range. - Improved color and oxygen saturation levels.

questions.question: Auscultation (os-kul-TAY-shun)
questions.answer: Listening. A stethoscope is used to auscultate for characteristic sounds.

questions.question: Blood pressure monitor
questions.answer: A machine that automatically inflates a blood pressure cuff and measures blood pressure.

questions.question: Brachial (BRAY-key-al) artery
questions.answer: The major artery of the arm.

questions.question: Brachial (BRAY-key-al) pulse
questions.answer: The pulse felt in the upper arm.

questions.question: Bradycardia (BRAY-duh-KAR-de-uh)
questions.answer: A slow pulse; any pulse rate below 60 beats per minute.

questions.question: Carotid (kah-ROT-id) pulse
questions.answer: The pulse felt along the large carotid artery on either side of the neck.

questions.question: Constrict (kon-STRIKT)
Dilate (DI-late)
Oxygen saturation (SpO2)
questions.answer: The ratio of the amount of oxygen present in the blood to the amount that could be carried, expressed as a percentage.

questions.question: Palpation
questions.answer: Touching or feeling. A pulse or blood pressure may be palpated with the fingertips.

questions.question: Pulse oximeter
questions.answer: An electronic device for determining the amount of oxygen carried in the blood, known as the oxygen saturation or SpO2.

questions.question: Pulse quality
questions.answer: The rhythm (regular or irregular) and force (strong or weak) of the pulse.

questions.question: Pulse rate
questions.answer: The number of pulse beats per minute.

questions.question: Radial (RAY-de-ul) pulse
questions.answer: The pulse felt at the wrist.

questions.question: Reactivity (re-ak-TIV-uh-te)
questions.answer: In the pupils of the eyes, reacting to light by changing size.

questions.question: Respiration (res-puh-RAY-shun)
questions.answer: The act of breathing in and breathing out.

questions.question: Respiratory (RES-puh-ruh-tor-e) quality
questions.answer: The normal or abnormal (shallow, labored, or noisy) character of breathing.

questions.question: Respiratory (RES-puh-ruh-tor-e) rate
questions.answer: The number of breaths taken in one minute.

questions.question: Respiratory (RES-puh-ruh-tor-e) rhythm
questions.answer: The regular or irregular spacing of breaths.

questions.question: Sphygmomanometer (SFIG-mo-mah-NOM-uh-ter)
questions.answer: The cuff and gauge used to measure blood pressure.

questions.question: Systolic (sis-TOL-ik) blood pressure
questions.answer: The pressure created when the heart contracts and forces blood out into the arteries.

questions.question: Tachycardia (TAK-uh-KAR-de-uh)
questions.answer: A rapid pulse; any pulse rate above 100 beats per minute, for an adult.

questions.question: Vital signs
questions.answer: Outward signs of what is going on inside the body, including respiration; pulse; skin color, temperature, and condition (plus capillary refill in infants and children); pupils; and blood pressure.

questions.question: Name the vital signs (5)
questions.answer: - Respiration - Pulse - Skin color, temperature, and condition - Pupils - Blood pressure

questions.question: Explain why vital signs should be taken more than once (3)
questions.answer: - To detect changes in a patient's condition over time. - To assess the effectiveness of treatments. - To identify trends that may indicate improvement or deterioration.

questions.question: What intervention should you take to improve a patient's oxygen saturation when SpO2 is 92%?
questions.answer: Administer supplemental oxygen, possibly using a nasal cannula or a nonrebreather mask depending on the patient's condition and comfort.

questions.question: What can you do to improve oxygen saturation in a trauma patient with SpO2 of 90%? (4)
questions.answer: - Ensure a good seal on the bag-valve-mask (BVM) unit. - Increase the flow rate of oxygen. - Check for obstructions in the airway and ensure proper technique. - Consider advanced airway management if necessary.

questions.question: How much time should the EMT spend looking for a pulse when the radial pulse is absent or extremely weak?
questions.answer: No more than 10 seconds. If the pulse is not found, quickly reassess using a different method or location (e.g., carotid pulse).

questions.question: How should you react when the blood pressure monitor gives a reading that is extremely different from previous readings you got? (5)
questions.answer: - Reassess manually with a sphygmomanometer. - Check the positioning of the cuff. - Ensure the patient is calm and in a proper position. - Verify the monitor’s calibration and functionality. - Try on a different arm

questions.question: How can you get an accurate pulse oximeter reading on a patient with thick artificial nails? (3)
questions.answer: - Place the sensor on a different site, such as the earlobe or a toe. - Ensure the sensor is clean and properly positioned. - Warm the site to improve blood flow if needed.

questions.question: Why is the pulse so weak in a patient with an electrical heart problem and a heart rate of more than 200 beats per minute?
questions.answer: - The heart is beating too fast to fill properly between contractions, reducing the volume of blood pumped with each beat. (inadequate cardiac preload leads to smaller contractility and thus smaller stroke volume) (This results in a weak, thready pulse.)

questions.question: What effect does epinephrine have on blood vessels, leading to pale, sweaty skin?
questions.answer: - Epinephrine causes vasoconstriction, which reduces blood flow to the skin. - This results in pale, cool, and clammy skin.

questions.question: Why is chronically high diastolic pressure strongly associated with heart disease?
questions.answer: - Chronically high diastolic pressure indicates constant high pressure in the arteries. - This increases the workload on the heart and can lead to damage to the heart muscle and blood vessels. - It can result in conditions such as hypertrophy of the heart, atherosclerosis, and increased risk of heart attack and stroke.

questions.question: Describe the physiologic processes indicated by each vital sign.
questions.answer: - **Respiration**: Indicates the effectiveness of oxygen exchange. - **Pulse**: Reflects heart rate and rhythm. - **Skin color, temperature, and condition**: Show circulatory status and perfusion. - **Pupils**: Indicate neurologic function and autonomic nervous system status. - **Blood pressure**: Reflects cardiac output and vascular resistance.

questions.question: Explain causes of abnormal vital signs.
questions.answer: - **High blood pressure**: Stress, pain, cardiovascular diseases. - **Low blood pressure**: Shock, blood loss, dehydration. - **Rapid pulse**: Fever, anxiety, hypovolemia, cardiac conditions. - **Slow pulse**: Medication effects, hypothermia, cardiac conditions. - **Abnormal respirations**: Respiratory conditions, metabolic imbalances, neurological issues.

questions.question: Describe modifications of assessing circulation in children (3)
questions.answer: - Use of capillary refill time (<2 seconds normal). - Palpate brachial or femoral pulses instead of radial pulse in infants. - Consider age-specific norms for pulse and respiratory rates.

questions.question: Compare vital signs of infants and children with those of adults. (4)
questions.answer: - **Pulse**: Higher in infants and children. - **Respiratory rate**: Higher in infants and children. - **Blood pressure**: Lower in infants and children. - **Capillary refill**: More commonly assessed in infants and children.

questions.question: Recognize characteristics that can lead to difficulty or false readings when obtaining vital signs (generally speaking) (4)
questions.answer: - **Movement**: Causes inaccurate readings. - **Poor circulation**: Affects pulse and capillary refill assessment. - **External temperature**: Influences skin condition and capillary refill. - **Ill-fitting equipment**: Results in inaccurate blood pressure readings.

questions.question: Compare auscultation, palpation, and automatic blood pressure monitor approaches to obtaining a blood pressure.
questions.answer: - **Auscultation**: Accurate, but requires skill. - **Palpation**: Simple, but provides only systolic pressure. - **Automatic monitors**: Convenient, but can be inaccurate with movement or irregular rhythms.

questions.question: Identify patients for whom the use of a monitoring device will provide useful information.
questions.answer: - Respiratory distress (use pulse oximeter). - Diabetic patients (check blood glucose levels). - Patients with altered mental status (both devices). - Suspected hypoxia (use pulse oximeter).

questions.question: Outline the steps of using various monitoring devices.
questions.answer: - **Pulse oximeter**: Place sensor on finger/toe/ear, ensure good perfusion, read SpO2. - **Glucometer**: Clean finger, use lancet, apply blood to test strip, read glucose level.

questions.question: Interpret findings of pulse oximetry.
questions.answer: - Normal SpO2: 95-100% - Mild hypoxia: 91-94% - Moderate hypoxia: 86-90% - Severe hypoxia: <85%

questions.question: What is aspirin used for in medical treatment?
questions.answer: A medication used to reduce the clotting ability of blood to prevent and treat clots associated with myocardial infarction.

questions.question: What is an atomizer?
questions.answer: A device attached to the end of a syringe that atomizes medication (turns it into very fine droplets).

questions.question: What are contraindications?
questions.answer: Specific signs or circumstances under which it is not appropriate and may be harmful to administer a drug to a patient.

questions.question: What does enteral refer to in medication administration?
questions.answer: Referring to a route of medication administration that uses the gastrointestinal tract, such as swallowing a pill.

questions.question: What is epinephrine used for?
questions.answer: A drug that helps to constrict the blood vessels and relax passages of the airway. It may be used to counter a severe allergic reaction.

questions.question: What are indications?
questions.answer: Specific signs or circumstances under which it is appropriate to administer a drug to a patient.

questions.question: What is an inhaler?
questions.answer: A spray device with a mouthpiece that contains an aerosol form of a medication that a patient can spray into the airway.

questions.question: What is naloxone used for?
What is nitroglycerin used for?
questions.answer: A drug that helps to dilate the coronary vessels that supply the heart muscle with blood.

questions.question: What is oral glucose used for?
questions.answer: A form of glucose (a kind of sugar) given by mouth to treat an awake patient (who is able to swallow) with an altered mental status and a history of diabetes.

questions.question: What is oxygen used for in medical treatment?
questions.answer: A gas commonly found in the atmosphere. Pure oxygen is used as a drug to treat any patient whose medical or traumatic condition may cause hypoxia, or low oxygen.

questions.question: What does parenteral refer to in medication administration?
questions.answer: Referring to a route of medication administration that does not use the gastrointestinal tract, such as an intravenous medication.

questions.question: What is pharmacodynamics?
questions.answer: The study of the effects of medications on the body.

questions.question: What is pharmacology?
questions.answer: The study of drugs, their sources, their characteristics, and their effects.

questions.question: What is a side effect?
questions.answer: Any action of a drug other than the desired action.

questions.question: What is an untoward effect?
questions.answer: An effect of a medication in addition to its desired effect that may be potentially harmful to the patient.

questions.question: Name the drugs that are commonly carried on the ambulance and may be administered by the EMT under certain circumstances.
questions.answer: Aspirin, oral glucose, oxygen, naloxone, epinephrine.

questions.question: Name the drugs that the EMT may assist the patient in taking if they have been prescribed and if administration has been approved by medical direction.
Medications may take the form of tablets. Name several other forms in which medications may appear.
questions.answer: Liquids, gels, suspensions, fine powder for inhalation, gases for inhalation, sublingual sprays.

questions.question: Describe the difference between on-line medical direction and off-line medical direction. Provide examples of each.
questions.answer: On-line medical direction involves direct communication with a physician, such as via radio or phone. Off-line medical direction involves following protocols or standing orders written by a physician.

questions.question: Name several routes by which medications may be administered. (9)
questions.answer: Oral, sublingual, inhalation, intranasal, intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous, intraosseous, endotracheal.

questions.question: List the “five rights” of medication administration.
questions.answer: Right patient, right medication, right dose, right route, right time, (right documentation). (Memory Aid: Please Mom, Don't Ruin The Dinner)

questions.question: What elements would you reassess after the administration of medication? What findings might be significant?
questions.answer: Reassess vital signs, level of consciousness, airway, breathing, and circulation. Significant findings include changes in heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, and overall improvement or deterioration in the patient's condition.

questions.question: A patient is complaining of chest pain. “Here’s some nitroglycerin,” says a family member. “Give him that.” What do you do?
questions.answer: Verify the five rights: patient, medication, dose, route, and time. Confirm the medication is prescribed to the patient, check for contraindications (e.g., low blood pressure), and obtain on-line medical direction if needed before administering.

questions.question: Which medications may be carried by the EMT?
questions.answer: Aspirin, oral glucose, oxygen, naloxone. (Others depending on the jurisdiction)

questions.question: Which medications may the EMT assist patients in taking?
questions.answer: Bronchodilators (e.g., albuterol inhaler), nitroglycerin, epinephrine auto-injectors.

questions.question: What should be considered when administering any medication?
questions.answer: Five Rights (right patient, right medication, right dose, right route, right time), indications, contraindications, potential side effects, desired effects, and untoward effects.

questions.question: What is the role of medical direction in medication administration?
questions.answer: Provides protocols and standing orders (off-line medical direction) and direct authorization via radio or phone (on-line medical direction).

questions.question: How may the EMT assist with IV therapy?
questions.answer: Identifying parts of IV equipment, preparing IV fluid and tubing, assisting with setup, and troubleshooting issues like flow problems.

questions.question: Describe the actions of aspirin.
questions.answer: Reduces the clotting ability of blood to prevent and treat clots associated with myocardial infarction.

questions.question: Describe the actions of oral glucose.
questions.answer: Increases blood sugar levels in conscious patients with low blood glucose.

questions.question: Describe the actions of oxygen.
questions.answer: Treats hypoxia by increasing oxygen levels in the blood.

questions.question: Describe the actions of naloxone.
questions.answer: Reverses the effects of narcotic overdoses by blocking opioid receptors.

questions.question: Identify the routes by which medications carried on the ambulance are administered.
Describe the actions of bronchodilators.
questions.answer: Relax the muscles around the airways, improving airflow in conditions like asthma and COPD.

questions.question: Describe the actions of nitroglycerin.
questions.answer: Dilates coronary vessels, improving blood flow to the heart muscle.

questions.question: Describe the actions of epinephrine auto-injectors.
questions.answer: Constricts blood vessels and relaxes airway passages to counter severe allergic reactions.

questions.question: Describe the role of medical direction in assisting with administration of patients' prescribed medications.
questions.answer: Ensures appropriate use through protocols and on-line approval, enhancing patient safety and care quality.

questions.question: Relate the actions of albuterol and epinephrine to the correction of the pathophysiology of anaphylaxis and asthma.
questions.answer: Albuterol relaxes airway muscles for asthma; epinephrine constricts blood vessels and opens airways for anaphylaxis.

questions.question: What is the difference between chemical, generic, and trade names of drugs.
questions.answer: Chemical: exact chemical composition; Generic: common name; Trade: brand name.

questions.question: How do you assess indications and contraindications for a medication before giving it?
questions.answer: Evaluate patient history, symptoms, and specific medical conditions to determine appropriate use.

questions.question: What should you anticipate before giving a medication?
questions.answer: Desired effects (therapeutic outcomes), known side effects (common but non-harmful reactions), untoward effects (potentially harmful reactions).

questions.question: Identify the steps of reassessment and documentation required after administering a medication.
questions.answer: Monitor vital signs, symptoms, and patient condition; document drug, dose, time, route, effects, and any adverse reactions.

questions.question: Identify the parts of the equipment and supplies required for IV therapy.
questions.answer: IV catheter, IV tubing, IV fluid bag, antiseptic wipes, tourniquet, tape, and dressings.

questions.question: Outline the steps of preparing the IV fluid and intravenous tubing.
questions.answer: Select IV fluid, spike the IV bag, fill drip chamber, flush air from tubing, and connect to IV catheter.

questions.question: Recognize other tasks EMTs can assist with, if asked, when assisting with IV therapy.
questions.answer: Securing the IV line, monitoring fluid administration, adjusting flow rates, and observing for complications.

questions.question: Describe how to troubleshoot an IV that is not running, running too slowly, or running too quickly.
questions.answer: Check for kinks, reposition the extremity, adjust the roller clamp, and check the IV site for infiltration or complications.

questions.question: allergen
questions.answer: something that causes an allergic reaction.

questions.question: allergic reaction
anaphylaxis (an-ah-fi-LAK-sis)
questions.answer: a severe or life-threatening allergic reaction in which the blood vessels dilate, causing a drop in blood pressure, and the tissues lining the respiratory system swell, interfering with the airway. Also called anaphylactic shock.

questions.question: auto-injector
questions.answer: a syringe preloaded with medication that has a spring-loaded device that pushes the needle through the skin when the tip of the device is pressed firmly against the body.

questions.question: Indications for administration of an epinephrine auto-injector (2)
questions.answer: Signs and symptoms of respiratory distress or signs and symptoms of shock that are associated with an allergic reaction.

questions.question: Common causes of allergic reactions
questions.answer: - Food (e.g., shellfish, peanuts) - Insect stings (e.g., bees, wasps) - Medications (e.g., penicillin) - Latex

questions.question: Signs of anaphylactic reaction: Skin (4)
questions.answer: Hives, itching, flushed or pale skin

questions.question: Signs of anaphylactic reaction: Respiratory system
questions.answer: Wheezing, difficulty breathing, tightness in the chest, swelling of the tongue or throat

questions.question: Signs of anaphylactic reaction: Cardiovascular system (4)
questions.answer: Rapid or weak pulse, low blood pressure, dizziness or fainting

questions.question: Differences between a mild allergic reaction and anaphylaxis
questions.answer: Mild allergic reactions: localized symptoms such as itching, hives, and mild swelling. Anaphylaxis: severe, life-threatening reaction with symptoms including difficulty breathing, throat swelling, rapid or weak pulse, and low blood pressure.

questions.question: Treating a patient experiencing an allergic reaction
questions.answer: For anaphylaxis, administer epinephrine immediately and provide oxygen if needed. Monitor the patient's airway and breathing.

questions.question: Signs and symptoms of allergic reactions and their underlying pathophysiologic processes
questions.answer: Histamine release leads to symptoms such as hives (skin), wheezing (respiratory), and low blood pressure (cardiovascular) due to vasodilation and increased permeability.

questions.question: Recognizing assessment findings that point toward an allergic reaction
questions.answer: Look for signs such as hives, itching, swelling, difficulty breathing, wheezing, and a history of exposure to a known allergen.

questions.question: Distinguishing the severity of patient allergic reactions
questions.answer: Mild: localized itching, hives, widespread hives, mild respiratory distress. Severe (anaphylaxis): coughing, difficulty breathing, mouth/throat swelling (struggle to swallow and speak/ tightness of throat), low blood pressure.

questions.question: Pharmacology of epinephrine
questions.answer: Epinephrine constricts blood vessels, increases heart rate, and relaxes the muscles in the airways, helping to alleviate severe allergic reactions.

questions.question: Priority of the administration of epinephrine with other patient interventions
questions.answer: Administer epinephrine as soon as anaphylaxis is identified, then provide oxygen, monitor vitals, and prepare for additional interventions as needed.

questions.question: When would one call for paramedic assistance for a patient that is suffering from an allergic reaction?
questions.answer: Consider if the patient's condition is severe, if multiple doses of epinephrine are required, or if advanced airway management may be necessary.

questions.question: abrasion
amputation
questions.answer: the surgical removal or traumatic severing of a body part, usually an extremity.

questions.question: avulsion
questions.answer: the tearing away or tearing off of a piece or flap of skin or other soft tissue. This term also may be used for an eye pulled from its socket or a tooth dislodged from its socket.

questions.question: bandage
questions.answer: any material used to hold a dressing in place.

questions.question: closed wound
questions.answer: an internal injury with no open pathway from the outside.

questions.question: contusion
crush injury
questions.answer: an injury caused when force is transmitted from the body’s exterior to its internal structures. Bones can be broken; muscles, nerves, and tissues damaged causing internal bleeding. In extreme cases where the torso is compressed, internal organs such as the stomach or urinary bladder can be ruptured, causing internal bleeding and allowing digested food or urine to spread into the abdominal cavities.

questions.question: dermis
questions.answer: the inner (second) layer of the skin found beneath the epidermis. It is rich in blood vessels and nerves.

questions.question: dressing
questions.answer: any material (preferably sterile) used to cover a wound that will help control bleeding and prevent additional contamination.

questions.question: epidermis
questions.answer: the outer layer of the skin.

questions.question: full thickness burn
questions.answer: a burn in which all the layers of the skin are damaged. There are usually areas that are charred black or areas that are dry and white. Also called a third-degree burn.

questions.question: hematoma
questions.answer: a swelling caused by the collection of blood under the skin or in damaged tissues as a result of an injured or broken blood vessel.

questions.question: laceration
occlusive dressing
questions.answer: any dressing that forms an airtight seal.

questions.question: open wound
questions.answer: an injury in which the skin is interrupted, exposing the tissue beneath.

questions.question: partial thickness burn
questions.answer: a burn in which the epidermis (first layer of skin) is burned through and the dermis (second layer) is damaged. Burns of this type cause reddening, blistering, and a mottled appearance. Also called a second-degree burn.

questions.question: pressure dressing
questions.answer: a dressing applied tightly to control bleeding.

questions.question: puncture wound
questions.answer: an open wound that tears through the skin and destroys underlying tissues. A penetrating puncture wound can be shallow or deep. A perforating puncture wound has both an entrance and an exit wound.

questions.question: rule of nines
questions.answer: a method for estimating the extent of a burn. For an adult, each of the following areas represents 9 percent of the body surface: the head and neck, each upper extremity, the chest, the abdomen, the upper back, the lower back and buttocks, the front of each lower extremity, and the back of each lower extremity. The remaining 1 percent is assigned to the genital region. For an infant or child, the percentages are modified so 18 percent is assigned to the head, 14 percent to each lower extremity.

questions.question: rule of palm
questions.answer: a method for estimating the extent of a burn. The palm and fingers of the patient’s own hand, which equal about 1 percent of the body’s surface area, are compared with the patient’s burn to estimate its size.

questions.question: subcutaneous layers
questions.answer: the layers of fat and soft tissues found below the dermis.

questions.question: superficial burn
questions.answer: a burn that involves only the epidermis, the outer layer of the skin. It is characterized by reddening of the skin and perhaps some swelling. A common example is a sunburn. Also called a first-degree burn.

questions.question: universal dressing
Three types of closed soft-tissue injuries
Four types of open soft-tissue injuries
When to remove an object impaled in the cheek
questions.answer: Remove if the object interferes with breathing or cannot be stabilized. Otherwise, stabilize the object in place.

questions.question: Three classifications of burns
questions.answer: - Superficial (first-degree): affects only the epidermis. - Partial thickness (second-degree): affects the epidermis and dermis. - Full thickness (third-degree): affects all layers of the skin.

questions.question: Difference between a dressing and a bandage
questions.answer: A dressing is applied directly to a wound to control bleeding and prevent contamination. A bandage is used to secure a dressing in place.

questions.question: Qualities and purpose of an effective bandage
questions.answer: - Secure the dressing - Control bleeding - Provide support Effective bandages should be snug but not too tight to cut off circulation.

questions.question: Standard Precautions for an agitated person with a lip laceration and missing teeth
questions.answer: - Gloves - Eye protection - Mask - Gown if there is a risk of splashing blood

questions.question: Standard Precautions for a small cut to the left hand, oozing blood
questions.answer: - Gloves - Eye protection if there's a risk of splashing blood

questions.question: Standard Precautions for a laceration to the right forearm with bright red, spurting blood
Assessing a wound covered with numerous dressings
questions.answer: Carefully remove the topmost dressings to inspect the wound without disturbing the clot. Apply fresh dressings if needed and control bleeding.

questions.question: Why look for a source of bleeding in a burn patient who is tachycardic, pale, and hypotensive?
questions.answer: Burn patients can lose large amounts of fluid through damaged vascular membranes, but other sources of bleeding may also contribute to shock and should be identified and controlled.

questions.question: List the soft tissues in the body. (6)
questions.answer: - Skin - Muscles - Nerves - Blood vessels - Fat - Connective tissues

questions.question: Describe the anatomy and physiology of the skin.
questions.answer: - Epidermis: Outer layer providing protection. - Dermis: Middle layer containing blood vessels, nerves, sweat glands, and hair follicles. - Subcutaneous layer: Deepest layer containing fat and connective tissue.

questions.question: Relate the potential for complications to the mechanisms that cause soft-tissue injuries.
questions.answer: - Direct impact: Can cause contusions or hematomas. - Sharp objects: Can lead to lacerations or puncture wounds. - Crushing forces: Can result in crush injuries and compartment syndrome. - Burns: Can damage all layers of the skin and underlying tissues.

questions.question: Recognize the characteristics of specific types of soft-tissue wounds.
questions.answer: - Abrasions: Superficial scrapes. - Lacerations: Cuts with varying depth and length. - Avulsions: Tearing away of skin or tissue. - Puncture wounds: Deep, narrow wounds. - Contusions: Bruises with bleeding under the skin. - Hematomas: Swelling from pooled blood under the skin.

questions.question: Steps to take care of a bleeding patient (6)
questions.answer: - Assess the type and extent of injury. - Control bleeding. - Clean and dress wounds. - Immobilize affected areas if necessary. - Monitor for signs of shock. - Transport to appropriate medical facility.

questions.question: Compare the general approach to closed soft-tissue wounds with the approach to open soft-tissue wounds.
questions.answer: - Closed wounds: Apply cold packs, elevate, and monitor for internal bleeding. - Open wounds: Control bleeding, clean the wound, apply dressings and bandages, monitor for infection.

questions.question: Outline the specific considerations in managing a patient with penetrating trauma.
questions.answer: - Assess for entry and exit wounds. - Do not remove impaled objects unless obstructing airway or CPR. - Stabilize object with bulky dressings. - Control bleeding, prevent infection. - Monitor for shock.

questions.question: Outline the specific considerations for treating an injury with an impaled object.
questions.answer: - Do not remove the object. - Stabilize the object to prevent movement. - Control bleeding around the object. - Use bulky dressings to secure the object. - Monitor the patient for signs of shock.

questions.question: Compare the approaches to managing partial and complete avulsions.
questions.answer: - Partial avulsions: Clean the wound, fold the skin back into place, dress and bandage. - Complete avulsions: Retrieve the avulsed part, wrap in sterile dressing, place in a plastic bag, keep cool, transport with patient.

questions.question: Describe the care of amputations. (4)
questions.answer: - Control bleeding with pressure and tourniquets if necessary. - Retrieve and preserve the amputated part by wrapping in a sterile dressing, placing it in a plastic bag, and keeping it cool. - Transport the amputated part with the patient. - Treat for shock and monitor vital signs.

questions.question: Describe the approach to managing a patient with injuries to the genitalia. (5)
questions.answer: - Control bleeding with direct pressure. - Preserve any avulsed parts. - Use sterile dressings. - Provide emotional support. - Monitor for signs of shock.

questions.question: Outline the prioritization for care for a variety of portrayals of burn patients (8)
questions.answer: - Ensure scene safety. - Stop the burning process. - Assess airway, breathing, and circulation. - Estimate burn severity (depth, extent, location). - Prevent hypothermia. - Provide pain relief. - Monitor for signs of shock. - Transport to appropriate facility.

questions.question: Classify the severity of a variety of portrayals of burn injuries.
questions.answer: - Minor: Superficial burns or small partial thickness burns. - Moderate: Larger partial thickness burns. - Critical: Full thickness burns, burns involving the face, hands, feet, genitalia, or major joints, and any burn associated with inhalation injury.

questions.question: Differentiate the steps in the approaches to treating specific types of burns.
questions.answer: - Thermal burns: Cool with water, cover with sterile dressing. - Chemical burns: Flush with copious amounts of water. - Electrical burns: Ensure the source is off, monitor for cardiac arrhythmias. - Radiation burns: Remove from exposure, treat as thermal burns.

questions.question: Explain complications commonly sustained with different types of burns.
questions.answer: - Infection - Hypothermia - Hypovolemia - Electrolyte imbalance - Respiratory issues (inhalation burns) - Scarring and contractures

questions.question: Match specific burn characteristics to the most appropriate dressing and bandaging techniques.
questions.answer: - Superficial burns: Cool compresses, aloe vera or hydrating gel. - Partial thickness burns: Sterile, non-stick dressings, avoid breaking blisters. - Full thickness burns: Dry, sterile dressings, avoid wet dressings. - Chemical burns: Continuous irrigation, sterile dressings after flushing.

questions.question: evisceration (e-vis-er-AY-shun)
questions.answer: An intestine or other internal organ protruding through a wound in the abdomen.

questions.question: flail chest
questions.answer: Fracture of two or more adjacent ribs in two or more places that allows for free movement of the fractured segment.

questions.question: paradoxical motion
questions.answer: Movement of ribs in a flail segment that is opposite to the direction of movement of the rest of the chest cavity.

questions.question: pneumothorax
sucking chest wound
questions.answer: An open chest wound in which air is “sucked” into the chest cavity.

questions.question: tension pneumothorax
questions.answer: A type of pneumothorax in which air that enters the chest cavity is prevented from escaping.

questions.question: What signs and symptoms would alert you that your patient has a flail chest?
questions.answer: - Paradoxical motion of the chest wall segment. - Severe pain at the injury site. - Difficulty breathing. - Bruising or discoloration. - Crepitus (a grating sound or feeling) over the rib fractures. - Signs of respiratory distress or inadequate oxygenation.

questions.question: What are the differences between a pneumothorax and a tension pneumothorax?
questions.answer: - **Pneumothorax**: Presence of air in the chest cavity causing lung collapse, with symptoms like shortness of breath and chest pain. - **Tension pneumothorax**: Air enters the chest cavity and is trapped, increasing pressure on the heart and lungs, leading to severe respiratory distress, hypotension, tracheal deviation, and potential cardiac arrest.

questions.question: Describe the care for a penetrating wound to the chest.
questions.answer: - Ensure scene safety and use Standard Precautions. - Apply an occlusive dressing to seal the wound. - Tape the dressing on three sides to create a flutter valve. - Monitor the patient's respiratory status. - Provide high-flow oxygen if necessary. - Transport to a trauma center promptly. - Be prepared to assist with ventilation if the patient’s condition worsens.

questions.question: Describe the care for an open abdominal wound.
questions.answer: - Ensure scene safety and use Standard Precautions. - Cover the wound with a sterile, moist dressing. - Place an occlusive dressing over the moist dressing. - Do not attempt to replace eviscerated organs. - Monitor for signs of shock and provide appropriate treatment. - Position the patient to reduce pain and support the wound. - Transport the patient to a trauma center.

questions.question: angulated fracture
questions.answer: fracture in which the broken bone segments are at an angle to each other.

questions.question: cartilage
questions.answer: tough tissue that covers the joint ends of bones and helps to form certain body parts, such as the ear.

questions.question: closed extremity injury
questions.answer: an injury to an extremity with no associated opening in the skin.

questions.question: comminuted fracture
questions.answer: a fracture in which the bone is broken in several places.

questions.question: compartment syndrome
questions.answer: injury caused when tissues such as blood vessels and nerves are constricted within a space, as from swelling or from a tight dressing or cast.

questions.question: crepitus (KREP-i-tus)
questions.answer: a grating sensation or sound made when fractured bone ends rub together.

questions.question: dislocation
questions.answer: the disruption or “coming apart” of a joint.

questions.question: extremities (ex-TREM-i-teez)
questions.answer: the portions of the skeleton that include the clavicles, scapulae, arms, wrists, and hands (upper extremities) and the pelvis, thighs, legs, ankles, and feet (lower extremities).

questions.question: fracture (FRAK-cher)
greenstick fracture
joints
questions.answer: places where bones articulate, or meet.

questions.question: ligaments
questions.answer: tissues that connect bone to bone.

questions.question: manual traction
questions.answer: the process of applying tension to straighten and realign a fractured limb before splinting. Also called tension.

questions.question: muscles
questions.answer: tissues or fibers that cause movement of body parts and organs.

questions.question: open extremity injury
questions.answer: an extremity injury in which the skin has been broken or torn through from the inside by an injured bone, or from the outside by something that has caused a penetrating wound with associated injury to the bone.

questions.question: sprain
questions.answer: the stretching and tearing of ligaments.

questions.question: strain
questions.answer: muscle injury resulting from overstretching or overexertion of the muscle.

questions.question: traction splint
questions.answer: a splint that applies constant pull along the length of a lower extremity to help stabilize the fractured bone and to reduce muscle spasm in the limb. Traction splints are used primarily on femoral shaft fractures.

questions.question: Functions of the musculoskeletal system (4)
questions.answer: - Support and protection of vital organs - Movement and locomotion - Production of blood cells (hematopoiesis) - Storage of minerals (e.g., calcium and phosphorus)

questions.question: Function of joints (3)
questions.answer: - Facilitate movement and flexibility - Provide stability and support - Absorb shock

questions.question: What is CSM?
questions.answer: - Regular assessment of distal pulses, sensation (e.g., touch, temperature), and motor function (e.g., movement, strength) to monitor for neurovascular compromise - Important for detecting compartment syndrome or arterial occlusion

questions.question: Signs of compartment syndrome (6)
questions.answer: - Severe pain out of proportion to injury - Pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia - Paralysis, poikilothermia (cool extremities)

questions.question: Role of splinting in managing musculoskeletal injuries(3)
questions.answer: - Immobilize injured limb to prevent further damage and reduce pain - Maintain alignment of bone fragments - Minimize soft tissue injury and risk of neurovascular compromise

questions.question: Principles of splinting musculoskeletal injuries (3)
questions.answer: - Immobilization: stabilize the fracture site - Padding: protect bony prominences and ensure comfort - Circulation check: assess neurovascular status before and after splint application

questions.question: Types of splints for musculoskeletal injuries (3)
questions.answer: - Long bone splints (e.g., traction splints, SAM splints) - Joint splints (e.g., knee immobilizers, finger splints) - Soft splints (e.g., pillow splints, air splints)

questions.question: air embolism (EM-boh-lizm)
questions.answer: a bubble of air in the bloodstream.

questions.question: ataxic (AY-taks-ic) respirations
questions.answer: a pattern of irregular and unpredictable breathing commonly caused by brain injury.

questions.question: autonomic nervous system
central nervous system
questions.answer: the brain and the spinal cord.

questions.question: central neurogenic hyperventilation
questions.answer: a pattern of rapid and deep breathing caused by injury to the brain.

questions.question: cerebrospinal (suh-RE-bro-SPI-nal) fluid (CSF)
questions.answer: the fluid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord.

questions.question: Cheyne (CHAY-ne) -Stokes breathing
questions.answer: a distinct pattern of breathing characterized by quickening and deepening respirations followed by a period of apnea.

questions.question: concussion
questions.answer: mild closed head injury without detectable damage to the brain. Complete recovery is usually expected but effects may linger for weeks, months, or even years.

questions.question: brain contusion
questions.answer: in brain injuries, a bruised brain caused when the force of a blow to the head is great enough to rupture blood vessels.

questions.question: cranium (KRAY-ne-um)
questions.answer: the bony structure making up the forehead, top, back, and upper sides of the skull.

questions.question: dermatome (DERM-uh-tohm)
questions.answer: an area of the skin that is innervated by a single spinal nerve.

questions.question: foramen magnum (FOR-uh-men MAG-num)
questions.answer: the opening at the base of the skull through which the spinal cord passes from the brain.

questions.question: hematoma (HE-mah-TO-mah)
questions.answer: in a head injury, a collection of blood within the skull or brain.

questions.question: herniation (her-ne-AY-shun)
questions.answer: pushing of a portion of the brain downward toward the foramen magnum as a result of increased intracranial pressure.

questions.question: intracranial (IN-truh-KRAY-ne-ul) pressure (ICP)
laceration (las-uh-RAY-shun)
questions.answer: in brain injuries, a cut to the brain.

questions.question: malar (MAY-lar)
questions.answer: the cheekbone. Also called the zygomatic bone.

questions.question: mandible (MAN-di-bl)
nasal (NAY-zul) bones
questions.answer: the bones that form the upper third, or bridge, of the nose.

questions.question: neurogenic shock
questions.answer: a state of shock (hypoperfusion) caused by nerve paralysis that sometimes develops from spinal cord injuries.

questions.question: peripheral nervous system
questions.answer: the nerves that enter and exit the spinal cord between the vertebrae, the 12 pairs of cranial nerves that travel between the brain and organs without passing through the spinal cord, and all of the body’s other motor and sensory nerves.

questions.question: pulmonary air embolism (EM-boh-lizm)
questions.answer: a blockage in the blood circulation of the lung caused by a blood clot or air bubble.

questions.question: spinal (SPI-nal) motion restriction
questions.answer: limiting the movement of the spine to prevent additional injury.

questions.question: spinous (SPI-nus) process
questions.answer: the bony bump on a vertebra.

questions.question: temporal (TEM-po-ral) bones
questions.answer: bones that form part of the side of the skull and floor of the cranial cavity. There are right and left temporal bones.

questions.question: temporomandibular (TEM-po-ro-mand-DIB-yuh-lar) joint
questions.answer: the movable joint formed between the mandible and the temporal bone; also called the TMJ.

questions.question: vertebrae (VERT-uh-bray)
questions.answer: the bones of the spinal column (singular vertebra).

questions.question: Name the two components of the central nervous system, and discuss their functions.
questions.answer: The brain and the spinal cord. The brain controls thought, memory, emotion, touch, motor skills, vision, breathing, temperature, and other processes. The spinal cord conducts sensory information from the peripheral nervous system to the brain and motor information from the brain to various effectors.

questions.question: List five signs of a brain injury, and explain why MOI is important in determining possible brain injury.
questions.answer: Five signs: headache, nausea/vomiting, altered mental status, amnesia, and focal neurological deficits (e.g., weakness, numbness). Mechanism of Injury (MOI) helps in assessing the likelihood of a brain injury by indicating the force and direction of impact, which can correlate with potential damage.

questions.question: Describe the appropriate emergency treatment of a patient with a possible head or brain injury. (5)
questions.answer: Ensure airway, breathing, and circulation (ABCs). Stabilize the head and neck to prevent further injury. Administer high-flow oxygen. Monitor vital signs and neurological status. Control bleeding and manage shock if present.

questions.question: List five high-risk mechanisms of injury associated with high rates of spine injury.
questions.answer: 1. High-speed motor vehicle collisions 2. Falls from significant height 3. Penetrating trauma to the neck or back 4. Diving accidents 5. Blunt force trauma to the head or spine

questions.question: Describe the appropriate emergency care for a patient with a possible spine injury. (7)
questions.answer: Ensure ABCs, immobilize the spine using a cervical collar and backboard, avoid any movement that could worsen the injury, administer oxygen, monitor vitals, and transport promptly to an appropriate facility. Continually reassess CSM.

questions.question: How would you provide spinal motion restriction and transport for a patient seated on the driver’s side of a car that was in a collision, complaining of neck pain?
questions.answer: Manually stabilize the head and neck. Apply a cervical collar. Extricate the patient from the vehicle while minimizing movement. Transfer to a long backboard, secure with straps, and transport.

questions.question: How would you provide spinal motion restriction and transport for a patient who was thrown from one of the cars in the collision and is lying on his side in a ditch?
questions.answer: Stabilize the head and neck manually. Apply a cervical collar. Log-roll the patient onto a long backboard while maintaining spinal alignment. Secure with straps and transport.

questions.question: How would you provide spinal motion restriction and transport for a patient from one of the cars in the collision who is found on his feet and is wandering around the scene?
questions.answer: Approach the patient calmly and instruct them to sit down without moving their head or neck. Manually stabilize the head and neck. Apply a cervical collar. Assist them onto a long backboard or stretcher while maintaining spinal alignment. Secure with straps and transport.

questions.question: Your 24-year-old patient has been involved in a serious motor-vehicle collision. He complains of back pain and presents with significant hypotension, but his pulse is normal and his skin is pink, warm, and dry. What condition involving the spine could account for this?
questions.answer: Neurogenic shock caused by spinal cord injury. The normal pulse and warm, pink skin are indicative of loss of sympathetic tone due to spinal cord damage, leading to vasodilation and hypotension.

questions.question: You are treating a patient with a brain injury. He has a decreased mental status, inadequate breathing, and a significant MOI to the head. During treatment, you identify your partner ventilating the patient too fast. What should you instruct your partner to do, and why?
questions.answer: Instruct your partner to slow down the ventilation rate to about 10-12 breaths per minute. Over-ventilating can cause a drop in CO2 levels, leading to vasoconstriction of cerebral blood vessels, which can reduce blood flow to the brain and worsen the injury.

Define active rewarming.
questions.answer: Application of an external heat source to rewarm the body of a hypothermic patient.

questions.question: Define air embolism.
questions.answer: A gas bubble in the bloodstream. The more accurate term is arterial gas embolism (AGE).

questions.question: Define central rewarming.
questions.answer: Application of heat to the lateral chest, neck, armpits, and groin of a hypothermic patient.

questions.question: Define conduction.
questions.answer: The transfer of heat from one material to another through direct contact.

questions.question: Define convection.
questions.answer: Carrying away of heat by currents of air, water, or other gases or liquids.

questions.question: Define decompression sickness.
questions.answer: A condition resulting from nitrogen trapped in the body’s tissues, caused by coming up too quickly from a deep, prolonged dive. A symptom of decompression sickness is “the bends,” or deep pain in the muscles and joints.

questions.question: Define drowning.
questions.answer: The process of experiencing respiratory impairment from submersion/immersion in liquid, which may result in death, morbidity (illness or other adverse effects), or no morbidity.

questions.question: Define evaporation.
questions.answer: The change from liquid to gas. When the body perspires or gets wet, evaporation of the perspiration or other liquid into the air has a cooling effect on the body.

questions.question: Define hyperthermia.
questions.answer: An increase in body temperature above normal, which is a life-threatening condition in its extreme.

questions.question: Define hypothermia.
questions.answer: Generalized cooling that reduces body temperature below normal, which is a life-threatening condition in its extreme.

questions.question: Define local cooling.
questions.answer: Cooling or freezing of particular (local) parts of the body.

questions.question: Define passive rewarming.
questions.answer: Covering a hypothermic patient and taking other steps to prevent further heat loss and help the body rewarm itself.

questions.question: Define radiation.
questions.answer: Sending out energy, such as heat, in waves into space.

questions.question: Define respiration.
questions.answer: Breathing. During respiration, body heat is lost as warm air is exhaled from the body.

questions.question: Define toxins.
questions.answer: Substances produced by animals or plants that are poisonous to humans.

questions.question: Define venom.
questions.answer: A toxin (poison) produced by certain animals, such as snakes, spiders, and some marine life forms.

questions.question: Define water chill.
questions.answer: Chilling caused by conduction of heat from the body when the body or clothing is wet.

questions.question: Define wind chill.
questions.answer: Chilling caused by convection of heat from the body in the presence of air currents.
